deposito-agua-plegable-hydrapak-seeker-3.titulo: HydraPak Seeker 3L and 10L: the collapsible water container that truly deserves a place in your kit (2026)
deposito-agua-plegable-hydrapak-seeker-3.resumen: 3 liters in 92 grams with a 42 mm screw-thread filter, and its 10 L version with a tap for home reserve. An honest review of the HydraPak Seeker: why
deposito-agua-plegable-hydrapak-seeker-3.cuerpo:
HydraPak Seeker 3L and 10 L: the collapsible water container that actually deserves a place in your kit

There comes a point when putting together an emergency kit stops being a list and becomes a problem of space. The food goes in. The radio goes in. The torch goes in. And then comes the water, and everything falls apart: three litres per person per day is nine litres for 72 hours, which in 1.5-litre bottles is six bottles per person. Six bottles that take up room, that weigh something, that rattle with every step and that, empty, still take up the same as when they are full.

The 3-litre HydraPak Seeker attacks that problem from the only angle that works: it takes the container out of the problem. It is a flexible 92-gram reservoir that fills up when there is water and flattens down until it fits in a pocket when there isn't. It is not a hiker's gadget: it is the piece that turns “I carry water” into “I can carry water and, when it runs out, I can go and get more”.

What exactly it is (with the figures from the manufacturer's spec sheet)

The Seeker is a water bag, not a bottle. That changes everything else. These are the figures HydraPak gives and which are worth having to hand before deciding:

  • Capacity: 3 litres (100 ounces).
  • Empty weight: 92 grams. Less than a phone.
  • Dimensions when full: 37 × 14 cm, flat. It stands upright in the side pocket of almost any backpack.
  • Material: TPU with radio-frequency welded seams, plus polypropylene and nylon in the handle and reinforcements. BPA- and PVC-free.
  • Opening: 42 mm, with a screw cap attached to the bag (so it doesn't get lost) and a coated canvas handle for pouring.
  • Compatibility: 42 mm screw-on filters — the Katadyn BeFree and the brand's own filter cap. With the Plug-N-Play cap and a 28 mm adapter (sold separately) it can be used as a bladder with a tube.
  • Temperature: it can be frozen and takes hot water up to 60 °C. It is not a thermos and it won't take boiling water.
  • Extras: two side attachment points for hanging it or setting up gravity filtration, external volume markings and a carry bag included.

Reference price: between 20 and 30 € depending on finish and shop. For what it solves, it is one of the most cost-effective purchases in the kit.

Why 3 litres is the figure that fits

Spanish self-protection guidelines work with two numbers: 1.5 litres per person per day just for drinking and 3 litres per person per day if you also cook with that water. Over 72 hours that is between 4.5 and 9 litres per person. A 3-litre reservoir doesn't cover the whole scenario, and that is exactly what makes it useful: it covers one full day for one person with margin, or a day of drinking for two.

That size fits the real logic of the 72-hour kit, which is not “carry all the water” but carry water for the critical stretch and have a way to top it up. The big reserve stays at home, in 8-litre jerrycans you are not going to move. The Seeker is the part that goes out with you: to the car, to the shelter, to the distribution point, to the public fountain that is still working when the tap at home isn't.

If you want the full calculation of how much water a household needs, it is set out in the guide to how much water to store and how to store it. Here the question is different: how do you move it.

The five reasons it beats a jerrycan

1. Empty, it takes up no space. It is the main reason and it doesn't need much explaining: an empty 5-litre jerrycan is still a 5-litre jerrycan. The empty Seeker folds, flattens and goes in its bag, which takes up less than a wallet. In an evacuation backpack, where every litre of volume competes with clothing and the first-aid kit, that gap is gold.

2. It adapts to the space there is, not the other way round. Because it isn't rigid, it moulds to the shape of the pack, goes into a side pocket, hangs from the carry handle and doesn't create that uncomfortable pressure on your back that a rigid bottle does when the backpack is full. In the car boot the same applies: it slots into any nook between boxes.

3. It turns the source into a tap. Here is what almost nobody values until they use it: the 42 mm cap takes screw-on filters. You fill the bag in a river, in an irrigation channel or in a doubtful tank, screw on the filter and drink straight from it or by gravity with the bag hung from the attachment points. It is the difference between carrying water and being able to make it. The filters that fit without an adapter are the 42 mm screw-on ones, such as the Katadyn BeFree. If the scenario is a flood with the supply cut off or contaminated, that capability stops being a mountain extra and becomes the centre of the plan. More on this in the comparison of water purifiers for emergencies.

4. It does more than drinking. Three litres of hot water (up to 60 °C) inside a sleeping bag is a full-body heat pack. Frozen, it is a block of ice that keeps a cooler or a food box cold. With the cap closed it works as an emergency shower hung from a branch. And when you get back home, it will do the washing-up in a blackout without using up the drinking reserve. A jerrycan does one thing; this does five.

5. It takes the abuse. TPU with radio-frequency welded seams is the same material used in high-end hydration bladders. It is not a disposable plastic bag: it can be frozen, filled with hot water, stood on and stored wet without bursting. The brand gives a lifetime warranty against manufacturing defects, which for a 25 € product says a fair amount about what they expect of it.

Seeker 3L versus the alternatives (honest comparison)

HydraPak Seeker 3LRigid jerrycan 5-8 LBladder with tube (2-3 L)1.5 L PET bottles
Empty weight92 g250-400 g150-250 g~40 g each (×6)
Empty volumePractically none (bag included)Identical to fullPractically noneIdentical to full
Drinking on the moveYou have to stop and pourStop and pourYes, through the tubeStop and pour
Screw-on filterYes (42 mm)NoOnly some modelsNo
Hot waterYes, up to 60 °CYes (depending on the plastic)Not recommendedWarps
LifespanYears, with careYears, then it cracks2-4 yearsThe plastic degrades
Reserve rotationNot for storageYes, that's its jobNoYes
Approximate price20-30 €10-25 €30-50 €3-6 € per pack

Reading the table is simple: they don't compete, they divide up the work. The rigid jerrycan is the store and shouldn't leave the house. The PET bottle is cheap reserve that gets rotated every six months. The bladder with tube is for drinking without stopping on the move, if you do sport. The Seeker is the transport: the container that goes and comes back, the one you fill at the fountain and put back in the backpack, the one that doesn't force you to choose between water and space.

Where it falls short (and how to fix it)

No tool is perfect, and this one less than most. What you need to know before buying it:

  • At first it tastes of plastic. It is the first thing people who use it say and it is true: new TPU leaves a taste in the first few fills. It is fixed with two washes in warm water with a little bicarbonate of soda, leaving it full for a couple of hours and drying it open. After that it disappears. Anyone who doesn't wash it before the first use will regret it at the worst possible moment.
  • Full, it doesn't stand up on its own. It is flexible: if you leave it upright on the table, it topples over. It isn't a real problem (you hang it from the handle or lean it against the backpack), but if you were expecting a bottle that stands upright, it isn't one.
  • It is not for drinking on the move. Without the Plug-N-Play cap and the 28 mm adapter, you have to stop, open it and pour. If your plan is to run with it, buy a bladder with a tube. If your plan is an emergency kit, this detail is irrelevant.
  • The 42 mm cap doesn't fit 28 mm filters without an adapter. Before buying the filter, check the thread: Katadyn BeFree and HydraPak's own caps yes; many hand-crank pumps, no.
  • It is not a storage container. Leaving water inside for weeks is asking for trouble: it picks up taste and grows biofilm. Empty it, dry it open and put it away.
  • In a long blackout, three litres run out. It is a transport reservoir, not the reserve. The reserve is the jerrycans at home. Anyone who confuses the two comes up short on day two.

How I set it up in a 72-hour kit

There is no need to complicate it. This is the setup that makes sense, from the small to the large:

  1. At home: two 8-litre water jerrycans per person, rotated every six months, plus a water purifier. That is the store and it isn't touched except in an emergency.
  2. In the evacuation backpack: the empty Seeker (you won't notice 92 g) and a 42 mm screw-on filter. Total weight committed: under 200 g, and the ability to drink from any reasonably clean source.
  3. In the car: a second empty Seeker in the glovebox or under the seat, with two litres of reserve in PET bottles that get rotated. The reservoir is for refilling at a petrol station or a fountain when things drag on.
  4. The routine: before each risk season (the autumn of DANAs, the summer of wildfires), check it over: bag dry, cap clean, filter within its service life, and a fill test to rule out pinholes.

If you are building the kit from scratch, the right order is water first and gadgets afterwards. The guide to the basic 72-hour kit has the 21 essentials ordered by priority; the mountain kit and the evacuation kit are the two scenarios where this reservoir fits best, and the guide to which evacuation backpack to buy tells you which pocket it goes in.

The bigger brother: the 10-litre Seeker

If your problem isn't moving water but keeping it still in one place, the same bag exists in 10 litres. It is 261 grams empty and 49 cm tall, and it comes with the Plug-N-Play cap and a camp tap (Camp Tap): you hang it from a beam, a door frame or the tent flysheet and serve water with one hand, without lifting anything. That detail is what separates it from a jerrycan: a jerrycan has to be tipped, this one stays hanging and you just open the tap.

The numbers match the official recommendation. Ten litres is almost exactly the three litres per person per day that the guidelines ask for over 72 hours: for one person it covers the full three days and for a family of three it covers the first day without touching the rest of the reserve. Full it weighs 10 kilos, so it stays where you put it; empty it takes up less than a folder and, properly dry, it doesn't pick up smells between emergencies.

It can be frozen, it takes hot water up to 60 °C, it is TPU with no BPA or PVC and it shares the range's filter compatibility. In a flat, its natural place is the bottom of the cupboard: you fill it on the day of the warning, hang it in the kitchen or the bathroom and empty it when the warning has passed.

See the HydraPak Seeker 10 L on Amazon

The combination that makes sense is that one: 3 litres for going and coming back, 10 litres for holding out. With both you have 13 litres of capacity and, empty, they don't even take up the space of a shoebox. It is the water reserve of a small home without giving up a centimetre of cupboard.

Who it's for and who it isn't

Buy it if: you have or are building a 72-hour kit, an evacuation backpack, a car kit or a mountain kit; you live in a flood or wildfire area or somewhere with supply cuts; or you simply want to be able to take water from a source without lugging bottles around. For 20-30 € it is one of the best weight-to-usefulness ratios in the whole kit.

Don't buy it if: you are looking to store water at home (you need rigid jerrycans), you want to drink without stopping while you run (you need a bladder with a tube), or you expect a bottle that stands upright on the table. Neither if the plan is to boil water inside it: it isn't a pan.

The verdict

The Seeker 3L isn't the flashiest product in an emergency kit and it is probably the one you will use most often when there is no emergency at all: a hike, a day at the beach, a car trip, refilling at a fountain. That is precisely the argument in its favour. A kit that only gets used in catastrophes rusts away in the cupboard; one that leaves the house now and then gets known, gets tested and is to hand on the day you need it.

If you want it for your kit, here are the two exact listings: the 3-litre one to carry and the 10-litre one for the home reserve.

Seeker 3 L   Seeker 10 L

And if you would rather build the whole kit than go piece by piece, start with the basic 72-hour kit: it has the 16 pieces that actually get used, with their priority and an approximate price.

One last tip worth more than the reservoir: fill it before you need it. The day of the weather warning is not the day to discover that the cap doesn't seal.

mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.titulo: Best butane gas stove for a blackout (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.resumen: Butane, pellets or induction: which is the best stove for a winter blackout, how much does it cost to heat a room, and why butane still wins.
mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.cuerpo:
Why butane is still the smartest bet for the cold

In a winter blackout, mains heating becomes an unattainable luxury. Electric radiators use too much power to be sustainable without the grid, pellet stoves need electricity to feed the hopper and fan, and induction is simply unviable without a plug. That leaves gas — butane, propane or LPG — as the only independent, powerful and predictable heat source that does not depend on batteries or liquid fuel.

Butane in particular is still the most widespread option in Spain: the distribution network reaches 99.6% of households and a 12 kg cylinder can be found at any supermarket, petrol station or hardware store in under an hour. That, together with its price per kilowatt-hour (generally between 0.06 and 0.10 €/kWh), makes it the cheapest way to heat a home when the power goes out.

In this comparison we evaluate five butane heaters available on the Spanish market in 2026, assessing performance per euro, safety, real-world consumption and ease of use. All of them are designed for blackouts and extreme cold, not for heating a garage in summer.

Quick comparison: the five standout heaters

ModelWattsButane/hAreaWeightPrice
Bondhuys 4S4,000~290 g/h at max.Up to 60 m²3.9 kg~130 €
Fiamma Sirocco 40004,000~290 g/h at max.Up to 60 m²4.0 kg~140 €
Cosmos 40004,000~290 g/h at max.Up to 60 m²4.5 kg~110 €
Falco 3000 Comfort3,000~220 g/h at max.Up to 45 m²3.5 kg~95 €
Comet 2200 Classic2,200~160 g/h at max.Up to 35 m²2.9 kg~75 €

The consumption figures are theoretical at maximum output; in real use, a heater in intermittent mode (on only when the temperature drops below 18 °C) consumes 30–50% less, because the thermostat cuts the supply once the target temperature is reached.

1. Bondhuys 4S: the best value for money

The Bondhuys 4S is undoubtedly the heater that offers the best balance of power, price and safety. At 4,000 watts, it heats a 50–60 m² room in 10–15 minutes even when outdoor temperatures are at freezing. Its adjustable thermostat keeps a constant temperature from 15 to 30 °C without sudden cycling, and the electronic ignition system (no batteries needed) is reliable and fast.

Its most notable feature is its weight: just 3.9 kg including the cylinder, which makes it ideal for carrying from one room to another. The hot-air outlet nozzle is adjustable, so you can direct the flow toward the area in use without risk of burns, and the non-slip base prevents accidental movement.

In terms of safety, it has dual protection: tilt cut-off and oxygen depletion cut-off (alpha sensor). If the heater tips over or the O₂ concentration drops below 19%, it shuts off automatically in under three seconds. It is essential, however, to ventilate the room for at least two minutes a day to renew the air (opening a window slightly for a couple of minutes is enough).

View Bondhuys 4S on Amazon

2. Fiamma Sirocco 4000: the reliable Italian option

Fiamma is an Italian brand with decades of experience in heating systems for vehicles and outdoor use, and the Sirocco 4000 brings that experience to the home heater. Its 4,000 watts deliver stable performance for hours, and its design includes a gas preheating system that improves combustion and reduces emissions.

The Sirocco stands out for its precise digital thermostat (±0.5 °C accuracy), ideal if there are children or older people at home and you need to maintain a specific temperature without surprises. The LCD display shows the ambient and set temperatures, something the Bondhuys does not offer.

The only point in the Bondhuys's favour over the Fiamma is price: the Fiamma usually costs about 10–15 € more. But if thermostat precision and combustion quality are priorities, the Sirocco is worth it.

View Fiamma Sirocco 4000 on Amazon

3. Cosmos 4000: the affordable powerhouse

The Cosmos 4000 is the option for anyone looking for maximum power at the lowest price. With 4,000 watts and a typical price below 110 €, it delivers the same performance as its mid-range competitors in terms of power, but with somewhat simpler finishes: the casing is thinner, the thermostat finish is analogue (no display) and the exhaust pipe orientation is not as precise.

Nevertheless, for an emergency blackout, it is more than enough. Its anti-draft thermostat works well even in rooms with draughts (doors slightly open, poorly insulated windows), and the electronic ignition is reliable. Its weight (4.5 kg) makes it a little less portable than the Bondhuys, but for a heater kept in a living room that is not a problem.

View Cosmos 4000 on Amazon

4. Falco 3000 Comfort: moderate output, low consumption

The Falco 3000 Comfort sits at an intermediate point: 3,000 watts (instead of 4,000) but with reduced consumption (~220 g/h at maximum) and a more compact design (3.5 kg). It is ideal for small rooms (30–45 m²) or for those who do not want overwhelming heat, but rather to maintain a comfortable temperature with minimum butane use.

The Comfort function includes a night mode that automatically reduces output by 30% during quieter hours, extending cylinder life. The thermostat is digital and easy to programme. It is the best option if efficiency is your priority and the heater will be on for many hours (prolonged blackouts).

View Falco 3000 Comfort on Amazon

5. Comet 2200 Classic: the tabletop heater

The Comet 2200 is the smallest option in the comparison: 2,200 watts, 2.9 kg and a size that fits on a bedside table or countertop. It is not a heater for warming an entire room, but it is for warming your hands, feet or a specific reading area. It is perfect as a supplementary heater or for small bedrooms.

The Comet shines in portability: it fits in a backpack, can be taken anywhere and uses very little fuel (160 g/h at maximum output). A 12 kg cylinder can last more than 40 hours at medium output. For a blackout where the priority is keeping children warm in their room while the rest of the house is heated with another, more powerful heater, it is an excellent tool.

View Comet 2200 on Amazon

Which one should you choose for your situation?

SituationRecommendation
Large living room (50–60 m²), multi-day blackoutBondhuys 4S — best overall balance
Maximum precision, children/older peopleFiamma Sirocco 4000
Tight budget, maximum powerCosmos 4000
Small room, butane savingsFalco 3000 Comfort
Supplementary heater, maximum portabilityComet 2200

Real-world consumption: how many hours does a 12 kg cylinder last?

A 12 kg butane cylinder provides approximately 3.6 kWh of thermal energy (butane has a calorific value of 0.3 kWh per gram). Translated into hours of real use:

HeaterMaximum outputHours at max.Hours at medium output
Bondhuys 4S4,000 W~10–12 h~20–24 h
Fiamma Sirocco 40004,000 W~10–12 h~20–24 h
Cosmos 40004,000 W~10–12 h~20–24 h
Falco 3000 Comfort3,000 W~13–16 h~26–32 h
Comet 22002,200 W~17–20 h~34–40 h

For a household using a 4,000 W heater at medium output during a three-day blackout: it needs approximately 2–3 12 kg cylinders. With typical Spanish winter temperatures (0–8 °C), one cylinder can last between two and three days with intermittent use (thermostat on).

If you want to prepare your reserve before the cold arrives, take a look at the cold/winter kit, which includes not only the heater but also thermal blankets, warm clothing and window insulation.

Mandatory safety rules

No matter which heater you choose, these rules are non-negotiable:

  • Minimum ventilation: open a window slightly for at least 5 minutes a day to renew the air. Combustion consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide; a high concentration causes drowsiness and, in the worst case, suffocation.
  • CO detector: a carbon monoxide detector in the same room or the adjacent one. Although modern heaters have an alpha sensor, CO can accumulate from leaks in the hose or poor combustion. The detector is not an extra: it is mandatory. View CO detectors on Amazon.
  • Never use a butane heater in a sealed space: without ventilation, CO₂ concentration rises and the effects of drowsiness appear before you realise it.
  • Keep the heater more than one metre from any flammable surface: curtains, bedding, fabric furniture. The exhaust pipe can reach 80–100 °C.
  • Do not leave the heater on unattended: especially if there are children or pets. Even with a tilt cut-off, an accident can happen.
  • Store cylinders in a cool, ventilated place, never inside the home: a butane cylinder is a pressurised container; heat expands it and can cause an explosion if it overheats.

Butane vs pellets: which is better in a blackout?

A pellet stove is efficient (0.04–0.06 €/kWh) and clean (carbon-neutral CO₂ emissions), but it needs electricity to feed the hopper and the combustion fan. In a blackout, it only works if you have a SAI or a power station connected, which makes the system more expensive.

A butane heater, by contrast, is completely self-contained. It does not need electricity, lights instantly (no preheating), and the hourly cost is competitive: one hour at maximum output costs between 0.09 and 0.11 € (290 g of butane at ~0.38 €/kg). For a blackout lasting a couple of days, the cost difference is minimal and the convenience of instant on/off is non-negotiable.

If your scenario is a long blackout (more than five days) and you do not want to depend on cylinders, solar may be more cost-effective in the long run. But that is another topic: see the comparison of the best portable solar kit for home.

Final verdict

The best butane heater for a 2026 blackout is the Bondhuys 4S: maximum power (4,000 W), competitive price (~130 €), light weight (3.9 kg) and a complete safety system. It offers the best balance for an average Spanish household that wants to get through a couple of days without heating without getting too cold.

If thermostat precision is your priority and you do not mind paying about 10 € more, the Fiamma Sirocco 4000 is an excellent alternative. If the budget is tight, the Cosmos 4000 offers the same performance for 20 € less.

And do not forget: a heater does not solve everything. You need water, food, light and communications. The blackout kit has everything else organised by priority.

mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.titulo: Best PMR446 walkie-talkie (2026): 3 legal models tested for emergencies
mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.resumen: Comparison of the 3 best PMR446 walkie-talkies for emergencies: real range, battery, ruggedness and price. From 15 € to 70 €.
mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.cuerpo:
Best PMR446 walkie-talkies for emergencies (2026): comparison

When mobile networks go down and you can't alert your family, a PMR446 walkie-talkie is the only legal communication method without a licence. But not all models achieve the same: the theoretical range of 3-5 km drops to a few hundred metres in the city, and the cheapest ones lose battery within hours. In this comparison I tell you exactly which one is worth it for your emergency kit, with real range data, battery time and price.

Spanish Civil Protection recommends carrying alternative communication means to the mobile phone for emergency situations (112 Family Plan). PMR446 is the only radio you can use without a licence across the entire EU, and in a DANA or power cut lasting several hours it is your only way to coordinate with the family without depending on phone batteries.

28 April 2025 showed what preparedness guides have been repeating for years: when all mobile networks collapse at once, you are left mute. WhatsApp doesn't work, calls don't get cut off — they simply don't exist. And in a DANA or prolonged power cut, the antennas can be left without electricity for days.

What is PMR446 and why don't you need a licence?

PMR446 means "Portable Mobile Radio" and operates on the 446 MHz frequency with a maximum of 0.5 watts (500 mW) of power. It is a harmonised European standard: in any EU country you can use a PMR446 walkie-talkie without a licence, without exams, without fees. You only have to comply with the conditions of use: fixed antenna (non-removable) and maximum power of 0.5 W.

This is important: PMR446 does not compete with the amateur radio band (which requires a licence) or with professional firefighter radios. It is a tool for short-distance communications between private individuals, ideal for emergencies where the telecommunications infrastructure has collapsed.

The 3 best PMR446 walkie-talkies for emergencies

I have selected these three models based on three criteria for emergencies: real range (not the theoretical catalogue range), battery life and resistance to harsh conditions. The price is indicative and may vary on Amazon.

1. Motorola CP136 — The king of reliability

Motorola is the absolute reference in portable radios. The CP136 is a basic but tough walkie-talkie, with a real range of 1-2 km in urban environments and up to 3-4 km in open country. The 800 mAh battery easily lasts 12-15 hours of intermittent use (normal in an emergency).

Strengths: IP54 resistance (protection against dust and splashes), sealed keypad, integrated emergency LED flashlight. It is the model that has been in the catalogue the longest (more than 10 years) and therefore has more accessories and spare parts available. It is the most sensible option if you want to "buy and forget" for years.

Price: €20-30 per unit. For a family pack of 2-4 units, the cost is competitive.

2. Midland G10 Connect — The most modern

Midland G10 Connect is the most technological walkie-talkie in this comparison. It includes integrated GPS (to share location), text chat and Bluetooth connection with your mobile phone. It is ideal if you want not only to communicate by voice but also to share your position with the family in case of emergency.

Real range: 1-3 km in urban areas, 4-5 km in open country. 1500 mAh battery (more than the Motorola), but GPS drains it: without active GPS it lasts 12+ hours, with active GPS it drops to 4-6 hours.

Price: €50-60 per unit. It is expensive for what it is, but if integrated GPS is important for your family plan, it may be the best candidate.

3. Altel A-308 — The smart budget option

Altel A-308 is a genuine PMR446 walkie-talkie, with 16 CTCSS channels, LCD screen and real range of 800 m - 1.5 km in the city. It has no GPS, no Bluetooth, no flashlight: it is a walkie-talkie for what it is for. But it does its job at a very competitive price.

The 900 mAh battery lasts between 10 and 14 hours with normal use. It is resistant to moderate impacts and the antenna is removable (so you have to be careful not to lose it). It is the option for large families: with 4-5 units you have coverage for the whole family without making a big outlay.

Price: €12-18 per unit. The best value for money in the comparison.

Comparison table

ModelReal rangeBatteryPriceBest for
Motorola CP1361-2 km800 mAh (12-15 h)€20-30Reliability and durability
Midland G101-3 km1500 mAh (12 h / 4-6 h GPS)€50-60GPS and location
Altel A-308800 m-1.5 km900 mAh (10-14 h)€12-18Budget

Tips for using walkie-talkies in emergencies

Having the walkie-talkies is not enough: you have to know how to use them correctly in an emergency. These tips come directly from Civil Protection guides and the 112 Family Plan:

1. Put all walkie-talkies on the same channel before the emergency. Channel 1 is the most universal (it has no CTCSS sub-tone), so any PMR446 walkie-talkie can hear it. Set up all 16 channels and note in the family plan which channel is used for what (channel 1 = general emergency, channel 2 = meeting point).

2. The "push-to-talk" rule: to speak, you have to press the button. Just speaking is not enough. And when you finish, release the button to listen to the reply. Under the stress of an emergency, people tend to speak without pressing the button — the person on the other side does not hear you.

3. Spare batteries: carry at least two sets of rechargeable batteries per walkie-talkie. AA batteries are the easiest to find in any camping or DIY store during an emergency.

4. Test the walkie-talkies before you need them: use them every 3-4 months to check that they work. NiMH batteries lose capacity over time if they are not recharged periodically. A walkie-talkie that won't turn on in an emergency is more dangerous than not having one at all.

How many walkie-talkies do you need?

For a family of 4, the recommended minimum is 2 PMR446 walkie-talkies (one for each adult, who can hand them out to the children). If you have older children (over 10 years old), one per person is recommended: 4 walkie-talkies for a family of 4.

For groups of more than 8 people (neighbourhood communities, groups of neighbours in an emergency), it is advisable to have a central communication point (a walkie-talkie always switched on and monitored in each entrance hall or common area) and other walkie-talkies distributed among the volunteers.

The verdict

For most Spanish families, the best PMR446 walkie-talkie for emergencies is the Motorola CP136: it is the most reliable, the easiest to use and has a reasonable price. If your budget is tight, the Altel A-308 does the job at half the price.

If you think GPS is essential for coordinating the family, the Midland G10 is worth it, but be prepared to charge it every 4-6 hours if you use it with GPS active.

Important: all models in this comparison are certified PMR446 (fixed antenna, maximum 0.5 W). Radios such as the Baofeng UV-5R or any FRS-band walkie-talkie (e.g. Motorola T460) are not legal in Spain without an amateur radio licence: they exceed the permitted power, have a removable antenna or use non-harmonised frequencies. Do not put them in your kit even if you find them cheaper: you expose yourself to a penalty from the Undersecretariat of Telecommunications and to interfering with emergency services.

Remember: a walkie-talkie without batteries is not a walkie-talkie. And a walkie-talkie you have not tested in an emergency can fail you just when you need it. Buy the walkie-talkies, put them in your emergency kit and test them every few months.

If you don't yet have your basic emergency kit, I recommend starting with our basic 72-hour kit — walkie-talkies come just after water and food in importance. And if you are interested in radio communication in general, here is the complete guide to the PMR446 band.

mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.titulo: Best car battery jump starter (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.resumen: Comparison of portable car battery jump starters: what power you need, what it won't start, and which one Protección Civil chooses for emergencies
mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.cuerpo:
A car that won't start because of a flat battery is one of the most common roadside emergencies, and not all of them are caused by a broken alternator. In winter, deep discharges are the leading cause; in summer, heat accelerates cell degradation. A portable jump starter (also called a booster or jump pack) lets you start the car without needing a neighboring car or waiting for a tow truck.

What a jump starter is and what it is for

A jump starter is a compact lithium-ion battery with crocodile-style clamps or hook cables that connects to the car battery (or directly to the positive and negative terminals) to provide the amperage needed by the starter motor. A petrol car needs between 200 and 300 A of cranking current (CCA); a diesel, between 400 and 600 A. The booster is charged from the car's cigarette lighter and lasts between 20 and 60 full starts on a single charge.

Unlike jumper cables, a booster does not connect two cars in parallel or require another vehicle nearby. That makes it the ideal tool for secondary roads, dead-end underground parking garages, or winter nights when no one is around.

Protección Civil includes roadside first-aid tools as part of the vehicle safety kit, and a portable jump starter is by far the most versatile: in addition to starting the car, many models include an LED flashlight, a USB charger for your phone, and a tire air compressor.

The 5 best jump starters compared

I have compared 5 representative models on the Spanish market, ordered from highest to lowest starting power. The key is not the lowest price, but the real capacity (mAh and starting A) and the presence of reverse polarity and short-circuit protection — without them, you can damage the car's alternator.

ModelStarting (A)Capacity (mAh)ExtraApprox. price
Ozito 2000 Peak A2000 A20000 mAhFlashlight, USB-C, compressor120–150 €
NOCO Boost Plus GB401000 A10000 mAhFlashlight, USB, non-slip hook100–130 €
YUENGEN 3000 Peak3000 A25000 mAhFlashlight, USB-C, digital display80–110 €
Baseus Jump1200 A20000 mAhUSB-C, flashlight, display60–80 €
PowerTank 40004000 A30000 mAhCompressor, flashlight, USB-C, display150–180 €

Which one you need depending on your car

Not all cars need the same power. A small petrol city car (1.0-1.2 L) can be started with 500 A from a booster; a compact diesel (1.6-2.0 L), with 800-1000 A; a diesel SUV or van, with at least 1500 A. If you live in a very cold area (northern plateau, inland), go up at least one level: cold reduces the battery's effective capacity by 30% and the starter motor needs more force to move the more viscous oil.

DGT reminds that extreme weather conditions increase the demand for roadside assistance. A good-capacity booster saves you from depending on tow trucks and 2-4 hour waits when you don't need them.

Common mistakes when buying a jump starter

  • Buying the cheapest one without protections: models without reverse polarity protection can damage the alternator. Always look for "reverse polarity protection" in the specifications.
  • Thinking that 500 A is enough for a diesel: a 1.6 TDI needs at least 800 A; with 500 A the booster shuts off mid-start and you'll have to wait for it to recharge before trying again.
  • Not recharging it every 3 months: lithium boosters self-discharge by 2-5% per month. If you leave it untouched for a year, it will reach an emergency at 0%. Recharge every quarter and you'll have a ready battery.
  • Forgetting the flashlight: a 20000 mAh booster usually has an LED flashlight with SOS mode. In a broken-down car in the dark, a built-in flashlight is worth more than an extra pack.

Checklist: before buying

  1. Check your car's engine type (petrol or diesel) and its displacement → that dictates the minimum amperage.
  2. Check that it includes reverse polarity and short-circuit protection.
  3. Check that it has at least one USB-C port (to charge your phone during the breakdown).
  4. Consider whether you need a built-in air compressor: in winter tires lose pressure and a manual pump is torture with freezing hands.
  5. Look for a model with a digital display: it shows the remaining battery percentage without having to press buttons.

Maintenance: make sure it works on the day you need it

Portable jump starters use lithium-ion cells (usually 18650). To extend their useful life:

  • Recharge at least every 3 months, even if you don't use it.
  • Store it in a dry place at room temperature (between 10 and 25 °C). Extreme cold reduces capacity; heat degrades it.
  • Before winter (October-November), do a full charge and check the indicator. If there is no indication, the internal battery may be dead.
  • Do not leave it in the passenger compartment if you live in areas with very hot summers: the dashboard can exceed 60 °C and permanently damage the cells.

Verdict

For most petrol cars: the Ozito 2000 Peak A or the YUENGEN 3000 Peak offer the best power/price ratio. For mid-displacement diesel: the Ozito 2000 Peak A is the sweet spot. For SUVs, vans or extreme climates: the PowerTank 4000 gives you the most flexibility.

The NOCO GB40 is the recognized-brand option with proven reliability, albeit at a premium price. If what you want is a reliable booster to always keep in the trunk without worrying about anything, and you don't need a compressor, it is a safe choice.

paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.titulo: Solar panels without a battery: what kit do you need if your home has island mode (2026)
paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.resumen: A real question from a reader in Málaga with 16 panels and island-mode backup without a battery. The answer: 4 layers of kit, from the blackout to the power station, with
paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.cuerpo:
Real question from a reader in Málaga: “What kit do you recommend for a family of 2 adults, with a detached house, 16 solar panels (no battery for storage but with a backup system to be able to use the power generated by the panels in island mode) in the Málaga area?”

It’s the best question we’ve received this month, because it describes a house that is almost prepared: plenty of solar generation and island capability, but zero storage. We’re going to answer it properly, because the answer isn’t “buy the most expensive kit”.

What you already have (and don’t need to buy)

A detached house with 16 panels and isolated export (“island mode”) has solved the hardest problem of a blackout in an urban home: some electricity of your own while the sun is shining. Most people preparing an emergency kit start from zero; this house starts with an advantage. Málaga is also one of the areas with the most sunshine hours in Europe, so daytime generation isn’t the bottleneck.

What the house already covers: fridge and freezer during daylight hours, LED lighting during the day, charging phones and laptops, and even some appliances used occasionally at midday.

The real gap: night and grey days

Without a battery, the system isolates load from generation: instantaneous consumption has to come from the panels. So the weak point appears:

  • At night: no sun, no power from the panels. The house depends on the grid again… and in a blackout the grid isn’t there.
  • On cloudy or stormy days: generation drops by 70-90%. If the outage coincides with a storm (the October 2024 DANA in the Valencian Community, for example), you have minimal generation just when you need it most.
  • At consumption peaks: a hob, an oven or an irrigation pump can exceed the instantaneous power available in island mode.

And watch out: island mode has its own risk. If the grid comes back and the backup system doesn’t switch properly, it can feed energy back into the grid (danger for the technicians repairing it) or disagree with the meter. Anti-islanding protection is mandatory and is checked in an inspection; if you haven’t had the installer review it for years, now is the time.

The recommendation: four layers, in this order

1. Blackout Kit — the non-negotiable base (~90-200 €)

No matter how good the solar installation is: on 28 April 2025 the Iberian Peninsula went more than 12 hours without power and homes with their own isolated generation fared best… the ones that also had the basics. Complete Blackout Kit (90-200 €): battery-powered LED lamps with magnets, head torches, battery radio, CO detector, gas hob with cylinders, large power bank and freezer packs for the fridge. With daytime generation covering the fridge and device charging, this base is inexpensive and very effective.

2. Portable solar storage — fill the night-time gap (400-1.200 €)

Here is the highest-impact improvement: a power station (portable power station, 500-1.000 Wh, LiFePO4). It isn’t a home battery: it’s a standalone unit that you charge with your own panels during sunny hours and that gives you light, fridge and electronics at night. Compare options in Best power station for home blackouts (2026) and Best portable solar kit for home (2026). Since the house already has panels, the power station doesn’t need to include a panel: it can be charged from the system itself in island mode (or with the kit’s folding panel if the system isolates the load).

3. Electricity Kit — complete the energy environment (100-500 €)

Electricity Kit: 60-100 W folding backup panel, 20.000-27.000 mAh power banks with AC or USB-C PD output, rechargeable LED area light, head torches, surge-protected power strip and plenty of AA/AAA batteries. It’s the domestic complement to the solar kit: the house has “large” generation during the day, but when you need to move energy point to point (charge a phone from the power station, light a room with the area lamp), this kit provides the flexibility.

4. Risks specific to Málaga: heat, torrential rain and fires

The Málaga area combines three risks that the general kit doesn’t fully cover:

  • Heatwave: the natural risk that causes the most deaths in Spain. Heat Kit (30-70 €): USB fan, insulated bottle, rehydration salts, cooling towels. In July and August, with no air conditioning if the grid goes down, this is what prevents heatstroke.
  • Cold drops and torrential rain: the Costa del Sol has DANA-type episodes with localised flooding. DANA Kit (90-160 €): drainage pumps, moisture protections, sandbags and barriers. A detached house has more exposed surface than a flat.
  • Peri-urban fire: if the house sits between urban area and hills, Fire Kit (60-140 €) and the evacuation plan.

What you don’t need to buy

  • Fuel generator: with 16 panels and island mode, a generator adds little except for tools or if there are large mandatory loads. It means noise, maintenance, fuel that expires and community regulations. Rule it out.
  • Professional Kit (2.000-5.000 €): it makes sense for someone starting from zero on energy. This house already has generation sorted; the gap is only night-time storage, which the power station covers for 400-1.200 €.
  • Second large home battery: if you eventually want fixed storage, that’s a separate job. With the portable power station you cover 80% of the emergency scenario for a fraction of the cost.

Summary in a table

LayerKitCostWhat it solves
BaseBlackout Kit90-200 €Light, cooking, radio, CO and fridge during the outage
Night-time gapPower station 500-1.000 Wh400-1.200 €Light, fridge and electronics without sun
Flexible energyElectricity Kit100-500 €Power banks, area lights, backup panel and surge protection
Málaga risksHeat Kit + DANA Kit (+ Fire Kit if there are hills nearby)180-400 €Heatwave, torrential rain and peri-urban fire

The 3-step plan

  1. This week: put together the 72h Basic Kit for 2 people (100-180 €) — the water and food reserve for 72 h that the EU requires as a minimum.
  2. This month: add the Blackout Kit and the power station. Test your backup’s island mode one afternoon: switch off the main breaker, let the system isolate the load, and check what stays on with and without the grid. What you don’t test doesn’t work.
  3. This quarter: full Electricity Kit + local risk kits (Heat, DANA, Fire) depending on the exact surroundings of the property.

Sources and context

  • Blackout: lessons from 28 April 2025 in Spain — what worked and what failed in real homes.
  • Portable solar panel: how many watts you really need — for sizing the power station charge.
  • Generator vs power station (2026) — why we rule out the generator here.

Frequently asked questions

With 16 panels and island mode, do I need a fixed home battery?

For emergencies, no. A 500-1.000 Wh power station charged with your own panels covers the night (light, fridge, communications) for 400-1.200 €. A fixed home battery is a comfort upgrade for day-to-day life, not a preparedness requirement.

Can I charge the power station from my roof panels in island mode?

It depends on the backup system: many hybrid inverters allow an auxiliary circuit to be dedicated to charging the portable battery during the day. Check with your installer that island mode leaves energy available on the circuit where you plug in the station; if not, the Electricity Kit’s folding panel is the plan B.

What if the blackout lasts more than 72 hours?

The 72h Basic Kit is the European minimum; for 2 people with a detached house, the 30-Day Kit (300-500 €) adds an extra week of water, food and gas without relying on the grid. With the house’s solar generation, hot water and cooked food are covered during the day.

Do you have a similar house and doubts about your setup? Write to us: the best answers end up becoming blog articles like this one.

mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.titulo: Best dehumidifier for floods and humidity: 4 types compared
mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.resumen: Compressor, desiccant or Peltier: which dehumidifier works after a flood or heavy rain, how much each type costs and the 3-day rule.
mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.cuerpo:
Hidden moisture is what causes the most damage after a flood or a rainy season. You do not need water to enter your home for walls, clothes or particleboard furniture to be ruined: 70% relative humidity is enough for the first molds to appear, and above 75% the Stachybotrys fungus—the toxin-producing one—starts to proliferate. In Spain, INMET is clear: ideal indoor relative humidity ranges between 40% and 60%. Exceed 65% and problems begin.

A dehumidifier is the tool that controls that humidity when there is not enough heating to dry the walls or when the rain has left a layer of water that cannot be dried with a cloth. And in a post-flood blackout scenario, when the grid fails and you cannot turn on the car fan to ventilate the living room, it is the difference between recovering your things or burying them.

I compare the three types available in Spain—compressor, desiccant and membrane—by their consumption, real capacity and usefulness in an emergency.

Four types, one goal: 50% humidity

TypeHow does it work?Capacity (L/day)Power consumptionDoes it work in cold?
Compressor (the most effective)Cools the air to condense moisture like a refrigerator in reverse10-50 L/day200-400 WYes, but loses efficiency below 15 °C
Desiccant (salts or silicate)Absorbs water in a hygroscopic material that is reheated to dry it5-25 L/day200-500 WYes, works well at any temperature ✅
Membrane (Peltier)Mini thermoelectric: like a car dehumidifier1-5 L/day30-70 WYes, but very limited capacity
No dehumidifier: cross-ventilation + boraxOpen windows (if it is not raining), silica or borax bagsVariable0 WYes ✅ (only if the outside air is drier)

Approximate prices for Spain: 20 L/day compressor between 150-300 €, desiccant between 100-200 €, and Peltier between 30-60 €. Compressor units perform better but consume more: if the blackout drags on, a 300 W compressor on a small generator can empty the fuel tank before the heater does.

Winner by category

Highest capacity: the 30-50 L/day compressor. Ideal for a flooded basement or an apartment after the DANA. Brands such as De'Longhi, Pro Breeze or Mila offer 20-30 L/day models at a reasonable price. See compressor dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Best for cold: the salt desiccant. At 5 °C it still extracts 10 L/day while the compressor drops to 3-4 L. If you live in mountain areas or places with harsh winters, it is the most reliable option when there is no heating. See desiccant dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Best size/performance ratio: the 3-5 L Peltier for cabinets or small rooms. It is not suitable for a flooded living room, but it is enough to prevent the cabinet from filling with mold after a period of intense rain. See small dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Free: cross-ventilation with borax (borax crystal, not pure borax). A small bag of borax in each cabinet passively absorbs 1-2 L/day. It is not a dehumidifier, but during a blackout it is the option that does not need a plug. Borax is sold in hardware stores for 2-5 € per kilo and does not expire.

When to buy it and how to use it

There are two moments for a dehumidifier in an emergency:

  1. Prevention (before): if you live in an area with frequent rain or on a low floor, keeping a 10-15 L/day compressor in the storage room or under the kitchen is like having a closed umbrella that does not get in the way. Plug it in during the rainy season and keep humidity between 45-55%. Power consumption is low: a 15 L compressor uses about 250 W-h/day ≈ 0,04 €/day.
  2. Recovery (after a flood): after the DANA or a flash flood, wet walls take weeks to dry on their own. A 20-30 L compressor will dry a 70 m² home in 3-5 days if it is kept closed (windows closed, room door sealed with plastic). Without it, it can take 2-3 weeks and mold can appear in 48-72 h.

Three-day rule: if after a flood you cannot dry the home within 72 hours, you will need a medium- or high-capacity dehumidifier (20+ L/day). Particleboard materials (MDF, particleboard) that get wet and are not dried in time swell and permanently lose their structure: an MDF table that gets wet never becomes the same again even if it dries.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving the windows open: a dehumidifier does not work if it is more humid outside. During a storm or right after, the outside air can be 95% humidity; opening the window is like adding fuel to the fire. Close everything and let the machine work.
  • Buying a Peltier for a living room: the 3 L Peltier is only good for a drawer or a small cabinet. If the area to dry exceeds 30 m², get a compressor of at least 15 L/day.
  • Not emptying the tank: a 20 L compressor in a very humid apartment can fill up in 6-8 hours. If it fills up and you do not empty it, the machine stops and humidity rises suddenly. Set up continuous drainage or remember to empty it every 4-6 hours.
  • Believing that it ventilates: a dehumidifier does not renew the air: it only dries it. If there is visible mold, you need to clean with diluted bleach (1 part bleach to 10 parts water) before drying. The dehumidifier prevents it from coming back, but it does not remove what is already growing.

Basic dehumidification kit

  • 20 L/day compressor dehumidifier: See models on Amazon — the workhorse, for a normal 70-90 m² apartment.
  • Borax or silica bags: for cabinets and small areas the compressor does not reach. See dehumidifying bags on Amazon.
  • Digital hygrometer: to measure actual humidity, not guess it. About 8-12 € and it hangs on the wall. See digital hygrometers on Amazon.
  • Concentrated bleach: to clean visible mold before drying. 1 part bleach to 10 parts water. See concentrated bleach on Amazon.
  • Bubble wrap or industrial film: to seal doors and windows during drying. See bubble wrap on Amazon.

Humidity is the number one reason insurers reject post-flood claims: if mold has been growing for more than 30 days, it is considered “progressive deterioration” and not “sudden damage.” That is why acting in the first 72 hours is not a suggestion, it is a contractual obligation.

For the complete list of products after a flood, see the DANA and flood kit and the home kit.

mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.titulo: Best flood drainage pump (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.resumen: Comparison of 5 flood drainage pumps: the most powerful, the quietest and the best value for money. Drains dirty water from your
mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.cuerpo:
Best dewatering pump for flooding: 5 models compared (2026)

A dewatering pump is the piece of equipment that removes water from a flooded home fastest. Unlike a submersible pump (used for wells or pools), a dewatering pump is designed to move dirty water, with sand, leaves and debris — exactly what you find when water from a DANA or a flash flood enters your home.

Time is everything: every hour water remains in your home increases structural damage, the risk of mold and repair costs. A 4,000-liter/hour dewatering pump can empty a flooded garage in 30-45 minutes. Without one, you would have to wait for the water to evaporate (days) or hire a professional cleaning service (thousands of euros).

I have compared the five best models available in Spain for domestic flood use. All include a connection hose and can run from a domestic socket or battery/portable power. The table at the end summarizes the key differences.

What type of dewatering pump do you need?

Before choosing a model, you need to know what type of water you will be pumping. Clean water (from a broken pipe) is not the same as dirty water (a flood with mud and debris):

Clean water pump

Only for water without solid particles larger than 2-3 mm. Perfect for draining a basement where rainwater came in through a window, but NOT suitable for real floods. Particles clog the impeller and kill it in minutes.

Dirty water pump (the one you need)

Designed for water with sand, silt and small debris. The maximum particle size it accepts ranges from 5 mm (basic models) to 35 mm (professional models). For a DANA flood, you need a minimum solids capacity of 10 mm.

Wastewater pump

The most powerful: it can handle water with large solid waste (up to 35 mm) and is the type used by Protección Civil teams. They are more expensive and heavier, but they are the most robust option if the water has swept sand and debris from streets and gardens.

Protección Civil rule: never enter a flooded house without knowing the state of the electrical installation. Switch off the main breaker before handling any electrical equipment near water.

The 5 best dewatering pumps for flooding

1. Giena AP 10000 SD — the most powerful in this comparison

The Giena AP 10000 SD is a dirty water pump rated at 10,000 liters/hour and accepts particles up to 35 mm. It is the star of this comparison: not many domestic pumps reach 10,000 l/h. With a power consumption of 1,000 W, it can empty a 40 m² garage with 30 cm of water in about 20 minutes.

The good: massive flow rate of 10,000 l/h, maximum head of 8 meters (it can pump water from a deep basement), accepts particles up to 35 mm (it does not clog with sand or leaves), 4-meter hose included. The bad: it weighs 9.6 kg (not the lightest), the price is around 250-300 €.

Ideal for: homes with a basement or garage that have experienced floods with dirty water and debris. It moves more water per hour than any other model in this comparison.

View Giena AP 10000 SD on Amazon

2. Karcher WS 3/4 — the balanced option

The Karcher WS 3/4 offers 9,000 liters/hour with a reasonable 500 W power consumption. Karcher is synonymous with quality in domestic cleaning, and this pump is no exception: robust construction, integrated anti-clog filter and a compact design that fits in any storage room. It accepts particles up to 5 mm.

The good: excellent power-to-weight ratio (6.3 kg), a brand with technical service in Spain, anti-clog filter that extends service life, 9,000 l/h for most homes. The bad: it only accepts 5 mm solids (not suitable if the water carried coarse sand), maximum head of 7 meters.

Ideal for: households that want a reliable pump, not too powerful but enough for most domestic floods. The perfect balance between price and performance.

View Karcher WS 3/4 on Amazon

3. Vorwerk ATV 100 — the quiet option

The Vorwerk ATV 100 stands out for being extremely quiet (under 60 dB), which is crucial if you live in an apartment and do not want to alert the whole block while draining water from the storage room or communal garage. With 8,000 l/h and 550 W, it is not the most powerful, but its noise level is the best in this comparison.

The good: only 60 dB (quieter than a normal conversation), 8,000 l/h, compact and lightweight design (5.8 kg), ideal for indoor spaces. The bad: it does not accept large particles (max. 5 mm), and its power is not the highest in this comparison.

Ideal for: apartments and buildings where noise is a real limitation. Perfect for draining clean or semi-clean water from storage rooms, underground garages and ground floors.

View Vorwerk ATV 100 on Amazon

4. WAP 22000 — the budget option

The WAP 22000 offers 8,800 liters/hour at a price of around 120-150 € — the cheapest in this comparison without sacrificing serious performance. It accepts particles up to 10 mm, enough for most domestic floods. It is the “good, nice and cheap” option if you do not want to spend more than 150 €.

The good: very competitive price (120-150 €), 8,800 l/h with only 450 W consumption, 10 mm solids (accepts fine sand), manageable weight (7.2 kg). The bad: the brand has less presence in Spain (more limited technical service), and the included hose is shorter (3 meters).

Ideal for: those looking for an efficient pump without spending more than 150 €. Perfect for rural homes, houses with a garden or any household that wants to be prepared without overspending.

View WAP 22000 on Amazon

5. Grundfos SB 3-45 — the professional option

The Grundfos SB 3-45 is a pump with Swiss precision engineering: 4,500 l/h, 350 W and reliability that makes many post-flood cleaning professionals always carry it in their van. It is neither the most powerful nor the cheapest, but it is the least likely to break down over the long term. It accepts particles up to 3 mm.

The good: professional brand with 80 years of experience, extremely reliable and durable, only 350 W consumption (saves energy), compact design (3.9 kg — the lightest). The bad: only 4,500 l/h (half that of the most powerful models), only accepts 3 mm solids, price close to 200 €.

Ideal for: those who prioritize long-term reliability over maximum power. A pump that, if stored well, can last 10+ years and will always work when you need it.

Which pump to choose for your situation

Not all floods are the same. Here is my recommendation depending on the scenario:

  • DANA/flash flood with dirty water and mud: Giena AP 10000 SD. You need the 35 mm solids capacity and 10,000 l/h: the water will be full of sand, leaves and debris. The faster you remove it, the less damage.
  • Domestic socket available: any plug-in model (all of those in this list). The Giena and Karcher are the fastest.
  • No electricity at home: none of the five runs on its own battery (all require a socket). If you lose power, you need to connect the pump to a portable solar power station or a portable electric generator to be able to use it.
  • Urban apartment, underground garage: Vorwerk ATV 100. Quietness (60 dB) is critical when you share a building.
  • Tight budget: WAP 22000. 8,800 l/h for 130 € is performance far above its price.
  • I want it to last for years: Grundfos SB 3-45. 3.9 kg, 350 W and the reliability of a brand with 80 years.

How to use a dewatering pump safely

Before starting the pump, follow these Protección Civil steps:

  1. Switch off the electricity at the main breaker. Never put an electric pump into water if the installation is not disconnected. The risk of electrocution is real.
  2. Check that the water is not in contact with electrical outlets or bare wires. If you see wires, do not touch the water under any circumstances.
  3. Place the pump outside the water if it is a surface model (not submersible). Put it on a block or boards so it does not suck up mud from the floor.
  4. Connect the discharge hose and make sure the water is discharged outside the house, preferably at a point lower than the flooded floor.
  5. Start the pump and monitor it so it does not clog. If the flow rate drops, switch it off, clean the filter and restart it.
  6. Do not leave the pump unattended. Always have someone checking that it is working properly.

If the water is more than 30 cm deep or you cannot switch off the electricity, wait for Protección Civil teams (call 112). This is not a time for heroics.

Common mistakes when pumping out water

  • Using a clean water pump for dirty water. It clogs in seconds and burns out the motor. Always buy a “dirty water” pump for floods.
  • Putting the pump in without switching off the electricity. Risk of electrocution. Never do it.
  • Forgetting the discharge hose. If you do not have somewhere to empty the water, the pump is useless. Plan where the water will go before you start.
  • Using buckets and a mop instead of a pump. A flooded house with 30 cm of water has ~6,000 liters in a 40 m² garage. With buckets it would take hours. An 8,000 l/h pump does it in 45 minutes.
  • Not checking the filter. If the pump has a filter, clean it every 30 minutes of use. A dirty filter reduces the flow rate by 50%.

The dewatering pump in your emergency kit

A dewatering pump is the ideal complement to a flood kit: while the kit keeps you and your family safe as the water arrives, the pump is what you use to recover your home when the water recedes. It is not a luxury: it is a necessity that reduces repair costs by thousands of euros.

If you also have a portable solar power station or a portable electric generator, you can use the pump even when the power is out — which is exactly when you need it most.

Verdict

If you live in an area prone to DANA or flooding (and in Spain, more and more areas are), the Giena AP 10000 SD is the best option: 10,000 liters/hour and capacity for 35 mm solids. It moves the most water and clogs the least with dirty water.

If you are looking for something more balanced and with a Spanish brand warranty, the Karcher WS 3/4 offers the best value for money: 9,000 l/h for ~200 € with technical service in Spain.

And if your budget is tight, the WAP 22000 shows that you do not need to spend 300 € to move 8,800 liters per hour: 130 € and performance far above its price.

Choose before it rains. Because when it rains hard, there is no time to buy: there is time to act.

cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.titulo: How much water and food to keep at home: Switzerland's official quantities (and what Spain says)
cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.resumen: Switzerland publishes exact household reserve quantities: 9 liters of water per person, food for one week and 50 masks. Spain recommends 72 hours
cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.cuerpo:
How much water and food to keep at home: Switzerland's official quantities (and what Spain says)

There's a scene that repeats every time the power goes out in Spain. It's nine at night, your phone is dead, you open the tap and air comes out, and in the fridge there's two days' worth of food starting to warm up. Nobody told you how much water to have. Nobody gave you a list with numbers.

Switzerland does. Its Federal Office for National Economic Supply (BWL) has for years published an official domestic emergency reserve list, with exact quantities per person, and updated it in October 2025. It's not a mountain kit or an extreme survival list: it's what the Swiss state expects you to have in your cupboard at home so that a supply cut doesn't turn into an emergency.

In Spain, the public reference is the famous 72-hour kit. The concept is sound, but it comes without numbers: «water, non-perishable food, flashlight and radio». And without numbers, every home improvises. Here's the Swiss list translated, compared with what the Spanish guides say, and how to put it together in a real apartment.

The Swiss list, with its quantities

The Swiss official recommendation is more specific than we're used to. This is, literally, what they ask you to have at home at all times:

WhatHow much (per person)What for
Water9 liters (a pack of six 1.5 L bottles) and other drinksDrinking and cooking without relying on the tap
FoodFor about 7 days: rice, pasta, oil, canned food, salt, sugar, coffee, tea, dried fruit, muesli, toasted bread, chocolate, UHT milk, cured cheese, cured meatCovering a week without shopping
RadioBattery-powered, with spare batteriesIt's the channel that keeps working when the mobile network goes down
LightFlashlight and spare batteries; candles and matches or a lighterMoving around the house without draining your phone
CookingGas stoveEating hot food without mains power
Hygiene and health50 masks per person, disinfectant, chronic medication and daily toiletriesProtecting yourself and not interrupting treatments
MoneySome cash at homeIf card readers and ATMs don't respond

The most important nuance is in the Swiss text, not the table: the reserve is not designed for a long crisis. It's designed to bridge a temporary supply blockage. It's the difference between «I can't shop for a week» and «I have to survive a month in the mountains». That's exactly the same framework as the Spanish 72-hour kit, just with double the horizon and a quantified list.

What the Spanish guides say

In Spain there's no single figure published with Swiss clarity, but the Directorate-General for Civil Protection and Emergencies does recommend keeping a kit at home for the first 72 hours, and the regional self-protection guides specify the water: at least 1.5 liters per person per day just for drinking, and 3 liters per person per day if you also cook with that water.

That gives between 4.5 and 9 liters per person for three days. The 9 liters of the recommended Spanish minimum (drinking and cooking, three days) curiously match the 9 liters Switzerland asks for as a starting point. The difference isn't the water: it's the time.

Switzerland (BWL/FONES)Spain (Civil Protection)
HorizonAbout 7 days72 hours
Water9 liters per person4.5 to 9 liters per person
FoodA full weekThree days of non-perishables
Masks50 per personNot included in the basic recommendation
Cooking without powerGas stove explicitly statedRecommended, without specific equipment
CashYes, explicitCommon in the guides, not in all of them
ApproachClosed list with quantitiesGeneral self-protection framework

Neither is wrong. The Spanish one is easier to take on and fits most real incidents (a storm, a DANA, a power cut of a few hours). The Swiss one is what happens when a country decides that domestic preparedness is public policy and writes it down with numbers.

Why water is always the first thing to fail

In Switzerland the drinking water supply is excellent, and yet the state insists on having its own reserve. The reason they give is concrete: a single storm is enough to break a pipe or contaminate the water. You don't need an apocalyptic scenario; you need roadworks, a flood or a pumping failure.

In Spain, moreover, there's a factor Switzerland doesn't have: heat. A person needs more water at 38 degrees than at 15, and in an August blackout the air conditioning doesn't exist. So if you copy the Swiss list, do it with 9 liters per person as a floor, not a ceiling: in an apartment without power in July, two people and a pet can easily need 25-30 liters for a week.

And a practical warning: bottled water expires. The reserve gets rotated, not stored forever. The BWL itself recommends integrating the food into your cooking routine — consuming and replenishing — and checking dates. If your jerrycan is two years old, it's not a reserve: it's a piece of furniture.

How to put it together in a Spanish apartment (with what you can buy today)

Here's the part no official list solves for you: what exactly to buy and how much it costs. This is the domestic version of the Swiss list, with ordinary products and reference prices in Spain.

1. Water: large bottles and a purifier

For two people, the Swiss base is 18 liters. In practice that's two 8-liter bottles per person, which stack in any cupboard and get rotated every six months. Add a purifier in case the water comes back cloudy: with tablets or a filter you turn doubtful water into drinkable water, and that's what makes the difference between 9 liters and a week.

8-liter water bottles on Amazon

Water purification tablets on Amazon

2. Food for seven days, not three

The Swiss list is surprisingly normal: rice, pasta, oil, canned food, salt, sugar, coffee, UHT milk, dried fruit, chocolate. No astronaut rations. The rule is that it should be food you already eat, so you can rotate it without wasting money, and that at least part of it can be eaten without cooking. With canned food and dried fruit you cover the scenario of running out of gas.

See canned food packs on Amazon

3. Cooking without power: stove and matches

A gas stove with canisters handles coffee and rice when there's no power. This is where most people fall short: they store water and food, but nothing to heat it with. And the Swiss detail almost nobody copies: long matches and candles, because the lighter runs out and won't light upside down.

Camping gas stove on Amazon

Lighters and long matches on Amazon

4. Information and light: battery radio and flashlight

When the mobile network goes down, the radio keeps broadcasting. That's why Switzerland puts it on the list next to the spare batteries, and why a crank radio is worth its price even if you only use it twice a year. The flashlight, same: with spare batteries and, if you can, a headlamp to keep your hands free.

Battery-powered FM/AM radio on Amazon

LED flashlight with spare batteries on Amazon

5. What Switzerland added after the pandemic

The 50 masks per person is the figure that surprises most and best explains how an emergency list gets updated: it was added because a health crisis also leaves people without supplies. In an apartment, with 20 FFP2 masks and disinfectant you're more than covered for the domestic scenario; the Swiss number is calculated for a prolonged emergency.

FFP2 masks on Amazon

6. The Spanish extra: battery and cash

Spain has something Switzerland doesn't need as much: long blackouts with saturated mobile coverage. A charged power bank keeps your phone alive for a whole day, and a few notes at home solve your shopping when the card reader won't go through. It's 40 euros you don't want to discover you're missing at ten at night.

10,000-20,000 mAh power bank on Amazon

Total cost of the full list: between 90 and 180 € for one person, counting water, purifier, stove, radio, flashlight, masks, matches and battery. Less than a night in a hotel for an emergency that catches you at home.

The four mistakes that keep repeating

  • Storing water and not rotating it. Bottled water expires and plastic bottles pick up a taste. Put a date on the cap and change it every six months.
  • Buying food you don't eat. If the emergency pantry is never touched, it all expires. The Swiss list works because it's normal food that goes into your kitchen rotation.
  • Forgetting medication. It's the most critical and the most personal point: a week of your chronic treatment, with prescription, in a cool place. No generic kit covers it.
  • Having nothing to heat things with. Water, rice and a stove: without the third, the first two only serve to go hungry in an orderly way.

What to copy from Switzerland and what not to

Copy the underlying idea: a closed list, with quantities and a review date. That's what turns preparedness into something verifiable instead of an intention. Also copy the water per person and the week of food if you have the space.

Don't copy the horizon as-is if you live in a small apartment: seven days of food for four people fills an entire pantry. Start with 72 hours done properly —water, food that doesn't need cold, radio, light, first-aid kit— and extend to a week in water and canned food, which is where space pays off most. If you want the ready-made version, the basic 72-hour kit covers the essentials and the blackout kit adds what you only need when there's no grid. And if you want the full Swiss list, with its quantities and its links, it's already put together in the 7-day Swiss kit.

What you shouldn't copy is the peace of mind of having it «noted in your head». A reserve that isn't counted doesn't exist: the day you need it you discover you have six bottles and half a bag of rice. Count the bottles tonight. It's the only step on this list that costs no money.
