mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.titulo: Best power station for home power outages: 5 models compared (2026)
mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.resumen: Which power station will keep your home running in a blackout? 5 power stations compared by watts, capacity and portability, with winners by use case (2026).
mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.cuerpo:
The power goes out at eight o'clock on a Friday night in November. The router turns off, the Wi-Fi dies, and suddenly you have a home without communications, without power, and without a fridge. The first thought is your phone: 15% battery. The second is the fridge: “How long does it hold with the door closed?” The answer to both questions depends on the energy you have inside your home — and if you have none, here is the comparison of the five power stations that give the best price-to-hours ratio in a home blackout in Spain.

Context: Red Eléctrica de España (REE) reported 12 interruptions in 2025, with an average of 0.25 minutes per outage. The grid is reliable on average, but the average does not cover the scenario that matters to you: a blackout lasting more than one night, whether due to a storm, a local distribution failure, or an overload of the street transformer. The International Energy Agency estimates that European households lose an average of 20 to 40 hours of electricity per year when planned outages and extreme events are combined. That is more than a small power station can provide.

1. What a power station is and what is NOT a SAI

A power station (or portable power station) is a large battery with a built-in inverter: it provides 230 V outlets, USB-C, USB-A and, on some models, a solar input. It is the midpoint between a SAI (seconds of protection for the router) and a gasoline generator (kilowatts, but with smoke, noise and a municipal permit): more powerful than a SAI, cleaner than a generator.

  • It can run: router, small fridge, power tools, space heater, microwave, washing machine (short cycles), lights, computer.
  • It does not replace: a gas boiler (it needs gas from the grid), a continuous induction cooktop, or a residential air conditioner (it demands kW that no portable unit can deliver).
  • It is NOT a SAI: a SAI switches to battery in milliseconds without interruption; a power station is turned on manually. If you want the router not to blink even for a second, use a SAI — the power station is for when the grid does not come back.

2. The five power stations, compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain (October 2026): each link opens the product category, so you can see today's price and not the price when this was written.

ModelCapacityContinuous powerPriceBest for
Mini portable (≤100 Wh) ↗80-100 Wh100-200 W80-150 €Router + phone + light only
Entry level (200-400 Wh) ↗200-400 Wh300-600 W200-400 €Communication + light + TV
Mid-range (400-600 Wh) ↗400-600 Wh600-1000 W400-700 €Small fridge + everything else
High capacity (600-1000 Wh) ↗600-1000 Wh1000-1500 W700-1200 €Average home with a standard fridge
High + solar (1000+ Wh) ↗1000-2000+ Wh1500-3000 W1200-2500 €Multi-day autonomy with panels

The progression is not linear: the price difference between the entry range and the high range is 5–8×, but fridge hours multiply by 6. The key decision is which appliance is “essential” for you and for how long you want to power it.

3. The hours calculation: what each power station can run

To calculate runtime, divide the battery capacity (Wh) by the appliance's consumption (W). That simple. One detail that matters: the inverter has an efficiency of 80–90%, so a 500 Wh power station delivers in practice about 400–450 Wh of real energy.

ApplianceConsumptionHours with 500 WhHours with 1000 Wh
Router + ONT15 W~25 h~50 h
LED flashlights (3 units)9 W~44 h~88 h
TV 40" LED40 W~9 h~18 h
Small fridge (50 L)40-80 W~6-12 h~12-24 h
Family fridge (200 L)100-150 W~3-5 h~6-10 h
Portable charger20 W~20 h~40 h
Microwave800 W~0.5 h~1 h

The conclusion is clear: without at least 500 Wh, you cannot run a fridge. Without 1000 Wh, you cannot run a family fridge. With solar panels connected (the models in the third category and above allow this), a small fridge can run indefinitely on a sunny day — because the 500 Wh in the battery are recharged by the sun while the fridge consumes them.

4. Winners by use case

  • Communications only (router + phone + light): a mini portable unit of ≤100 Wh. It is the cheapest option and you do not need anything else if the goal is your phone and the router. See mini power stations ↗
  • Lights, TV and router without a fridge: entry level 200–400 Wh. It provides half a morning of TV or 40 h of router. Ideal for those who only need the home not to go completely dark. See entry range ↗
  • Home with a small fridge: mid-range 400–600 Wh. This is the zone where the price-to-hours ratio is best: ~600 € gives you a full day of fridge, router, TV and light. The option for most people. See mid-range ↗
  • Home with a large fridge: high capacity 600–1000 Wh. If your fridge is a family model and you do not want to open it every hour, you need double the battery. The 1000 Wh models provide a full day of refrigeration. See high-capacity models ↗
  • Multi-day autonomy with panels: high + solar 1000+ Wh. Solar panels recharge the battery during the day, so energy is practically unlimited. It is the ideal complement to the solar generator and the professional kit. See solar portable units ↗

If what you are looking for is complete blackouts: a home without power or internet, the combined solution is a SAI for the router (seconds without interruption) + a power station for the home (hours) + radios for alternative communication. Everything is in the blackout kit.

5. The five most common mistakes when choosing

  • Choosing by capacity without looking at power. 500 Wh will not run a fridge if the inverter only delivers 300 W. The continuous power of the inverter is the limit: nothing that exceeds that number.
  • Buying a 100 Wh unit and expecting it to run the fridge. 100 Wh is for router hours, not refrigeration hours. It is like buying a bucket to put out a fire with a garden hose.
  • Ignoring solar recharging. A 3-day blackout with 500 Wh and no recharging runs out after 12 hours of fridge use. A model with solar input and a 100 W panel recharges by itself on a sunny day.
  • Confusing Wh with mAh. mAh is a unit for the internal cell, not for the complete system. A seller can put “20000 mAh” and mean only the Li-ion battery (3.7 V), which is ~74 Wh. Always look at Wh: it is the real unit of energy.
  • Not checking the weight before buying. A 1000 Wh power station weighs about 9 kg. If you need to carry it upstairs to a second floor or transport it, consider the weight. 300 Wh units weigh ~3 kg and fit in a backpack.

6. Safety, regulations and how it fits your kit

To buy wisely, make sure the power station complies with the European standard UNE-EN IEC 62133-2:2017 (safety of lithium-ion batteries) and that it includes protection against overcharge, overheating and short circuit. Models that comply with this standard carry the CE marking and are sold in the EU with a warranty.

Maintenance in three lines: recharge it at least every three months (lithium-ion batteries degrade if left discharged), store it between 20–30 °C (a hot garage in summer shortens its life) and test it every six months: plug something in and let it run down to 20% to confirm it works.

CNMC forecasts for 2026 point to greater grid stability thanks to the modernization of the European electricity system, but the reality is that extreme weather events — heat waves, DANA, snowstorms — are becoming more frequent. Blackout protection is not forecasting, it is precaution. The complete list of what you need is in the blackout kit; if you are starting from scratch, start with how to build your 72-hour kit.

Our choice, with the verified link

After comparing the five ranges, the piece we include when the goal is to withstand a blackout of hours without installation work: a portable solar generator with the panel included, so you do not have to buy half of it somewhere else.

  • OUKITEL P800 — 800 W power station with a 100 W solar panel. Why this one: the panel is included, the 800 W output runs a small fridge, router and lights, and the capacity falls in the range that covers an 8–12 hour outage. It is the one we use in the electricity kit, where you can see today's price.

mejor-kit-solar-portatil-para-casa.cuerpo:
Best portable solar kit for home: 5 models compared (2026)

A portable solar kit for home is a power station —a stationary battery with inverter and AC/USB ports— to which one or more flexible solar panels can be connected. The result is a system that charges your battery with the sun and delivers clean electricity, with no noise and no fumes. Unlike a petrol generator, you don't need to store fuel and you can leave it plugged in for days without supervision.

What is it useful for at home? Keeping the fridge, fibre router, mobile phone and lights on during a power outage lasting hours or a couple of days. It won't power an entire home (heating, kitchen appliances or the pool pump), but it will power what you really need when the power goes out.

I have tested and compared the five best-selling models in Spain in the 500-1000 Wh category (the one that fits in a suitcase, not a truck). The table at the end sums it all up at a glance.

How to choose your solar power station: what really matters

Before looking at brands, there are three numbers that make the difference between a kit that gets you through the blackout and one that doesn't even last until midday.

Real capacity (Wh): how many charges it gives you

Wh (watt-hours) measure how much “fuel” the battery has. A 500 Wh power station can charge a 60 Wh laptop about 6-7 times (conversion losses included), or keep a 15 W router on for 25-30 hours. With 1000 Wh, you double that.

The practical formula: kit Wh ÷ appliance consumption in W = hours of runtime. For a household that wants to keep the fridge (100-200 W) + router (15 W) + lights (30 W), the combined load is around 150-250 W. A 500 Wh power station would give about 2-3 hours of fridge time (the fridge opens and closes from time to time, so in practice a little more), while a 1000 Wh one would give 4-6 hours.

For 72 hours of off-grid runtime, you need something more: either a 1500-2000 Wh power station with panels that charge during the day, or a petrol generator as backup for nights without sun.

Output power (W): what you can plug in at the same time

Output watts indicate how many devices you can have on at once. A 300-500 W model is enough for a phone, tablet, router and lights; an 800-1000 W one is also enough for a small fridge, a tool charger or a small TV. If you want to keep a large combi fridge running (300-400 W startup), you need at least 1000 W continuous and 2000 W peak.

Included panels: how many W and how they fold

The panel is what recharges the battery during the day. A 100 W panel produces about 60-80 Wh in real terms (losses due to temperature, angle and cloud cover) in Spain on a spring-summer day; in winter, half that. The ideal is a kit that includes at least one 60-100 W panel and allows you to add another one in series.

The 5 best portable solar kits for home in 2026

1. EcoFlow Delta 2 — the one that handles everything

The EcoFlow Delta 2 (1024 Wh, 1800 W output) is by far the most powerful in this comparison. It charges from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes from the mains and in about 4-5 hours with a 160 W panel. It has an expansion port to reach 2048 Wh if you need it.

The good: the output power (1800 W) allows a combi fridge, a small microwave and tools; ultra-fast mains charging; the mobile app to monitor charge and consumption. The bad: it weighs 12 kg and its price (around €1000) is the highest in the comparison.

Ideal for: households that want a complete solution for 1-3 days off-grid, with the possibility of expanding to 2000 Wh.

View EcoFlow Delta 2 on Amazon

2. BLUETTI AC200MAX — the robust one

The BLUETTI AC200MAX offers 2048 Wh (expandable to 4096 Wh) and 2200 W output. It is the largest in the comparison: 26.3 kg, but it fits in a garage. It charges from 0 to 80% in 90 minutes from the mains and with solar panels up to 500 W.

The good: huge capacity for 72 h, expandable with modules, USB-C PD 140 W ports. The bad: the weight (26 kg) limits its real portability and the price exceeds €1500 without panels.

Ideal for: households with space in a garage or storage room that want maximum runtime without a petrol generator.

View BLUETTI AC200MAX on Amazon

3. Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro — the perfect balance

The Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro (1002 Wh, 2000 W) is in the sweet spot: more than enough power for almost any domestic use, 12 kg (not too light but manageable), and a competitive price with included panels (1-2× 100 W). Full charge in 2 h from the mains or about 6-7 h with panels.

The good: balance between power, weight and price; the monitoring app is simple and reliable; the included panels make it easy to start without complications. The bad: no capacity expansion like the Delta 2.

Ideal for: the average user who wants something powerful but doesn't want a 25 kg station in the garage.

View Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro on Amazon

4. Anker Solix F3800 — the new one with LFP lithium

The Anker Solix F3800 is a newer model with a lithium iron phosphate battery (LFP, which lasts 3000+ cycles instead of the 500-1000 of older lithium) and 3840 Wh capacity. With 3600 W output, it is the beast of the comparison. It charges with panels up to 3000 W solar input.

The good: LFP technology (much greater durability), enormous capacity, 3600 W output. The bad: price (€2000+), weight (40+ kg) and it only makes sense if you have the space and budget for a semi-permanent installation.

Ideal for: households that want a long-term solution, without petrol, that can replace the generator permanently.

View Anker Solix F3800 on Amazon

5. VTOMAN Flash 1500 — the value-for-money option

The VTOMAN Flash 1500 offers 1548 Wh and 2000 W at a price around €700-900 (without panel). LFP battery, touchscreen and USB-C PD ports. It has the best capacity-price ratio in the comparison.

The good: the best Wh per euro ratio (≈€0.98/Wh), LFP technology, 2000 W power. The bad: the brand has less presence in Spain than EcoFlow or Jackery, with more limited technical service.

Ideal for: anyone who wants the maximum capacity for their money and doesn't mind seeking technical support on their own.

View VTOMAN Flash 1500 on Amazon

Solar panels: how much they produce in Spain

A 100 W panel in Spain produces, on annual average, between 150 and 200 Wh per day (1.5-2 kWh), depending on orientation and time of year. In winter (December-January), irradiance drops by 40-50%: the same panel delivers 80-120 Wh. In summer, it can exceed 250 Wh.

This means that with a 100 W panel you won't recharge a 1000 Wh power station on a cloudy winter day. The key is to have panels that add up to at least twice what you consume per day, and to orient them south without shade.

Yes, you can also use the panels with the blackout kit as a complement, but for main use you need more than a panel hanging in the balcony window.

Portable solar or petrol generator?

They are not mutually exclusive, and in fact the combination is what most people use. Portable solar charges when there is sun (zero noise, no fumes); the petrol generator comes in when night approaches and solar charging is over. The generator vs power station comparison details when each one makes more sense.

If your priority is silence, not having to store petrol and not carrying it up stairs, portable solar is the right route. If you need to power a large fridge for three days without sun, combine solar + generator.

Checklist before buying

  • Capacity ≥ 500 Wh for minimum use (phone, router, lights). ≥ 1000 Wh with fridge included.
  • Output power ≥ 800 W if you want to connect a small fridge. ≥ 1500 W if you also want a microwave or tools.
  • LFP battery (lithium iron phosphate) if you're going to use it long term: 3000+ cycles vs 500-1000 of older lithium.
  • Included panels or at least compatible ones (MC4 or XT60 connectors).
  • Minimum 2-year warranty with technical service in Spain.
  • Weight and dimensions: make sure you can carry it up the stairs if you live on a high floor.
  • Monitoring app: knowing how much battery is left and how many W you're consuming at any moment is essential.

Common mistakes

  • Buying only the power station without panels. The battery drains in a couple of days off-grid and, if you don't have panels, it won't recharge until the power comes back. Always buy the kit with at least one panel.
  • Pointing the panel north or into the shade. A panel in partial shade loses up to 80% of its output. Always point it south, with no obstacles.
  • Underestimating fridge consumption. A fridge consumes 100-200 W on average but when it starts it draws 300-900 W peak. If the output power isn't enough, the fridge won't start and will cut out.
  • Forgetting the connection cables. Panels have MC4 connectors that sometimes don't fit directly into the power station. Check beforehand or carry adapters.
  • Thinking it will power everything. A portable power station is not a construction generator. Turn off heating, air conditioning and induction hobs; keep the essentials on and the sun will keep it running.

Verdict

For most Spanish households, the Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro is the ideal point: 1000 Wh to keep the fridge and router running, 2000 W output for whatever you plug in, included panels to start without complications and 12 kg that anyone can move. If your budget is tighter, the VTOMAN Flash 1500 gives you more Wh per euro.

If your priority is absolute runtime (72 h+ without sun), the BLUETTI AC200MAX is the most capable, although it weighs 26 kg. And if you want the most advanced model with the highest power, the Anker Solix F3800 is the ultimate beast: 3840 Wh, 3600 W and an LFP battery for years of use.

And remember: a portable solar kit is the energy piece of a blackout kit. Without water, without a first-aid kit and without a radio there is no plan. Start with the basics and add clean energy.

If energy and total autonomy are your thing, the professional energy and autonomy kit includes everything you need (SAI, 800 W of panels, LFP batteries, Starlink) to keep your home running off-grid.

mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.titulo: Best portable inverter generator (2026): power, noise and the real risks
mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.resumen: How to choose an inverter generator without getting the power wrong: starting surges, real consumption per tank, carbon monoxide and noise with neighbours.
mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.cuerpo:
What is an inverter generator and why it is not the same as a cheap one

An inverter generator starts a petrol engine, produces alternating current, converts it to direct current, stabilises it electronically and converts it back into clean alternating current. The result is a sine wave with distortion below 5%, stable even as the load rises and falls. A conventional generator with AVR delivers a dirtier wave and with the frequency fluctuating depending on what you plug into it.

What does that change in your home? That an inverter can power the router, laptop, television, boiler or the SAI of a blackout kit without any nasty surprises, whereas a cheap conventional one makes electronics restart, buzz or simply fail to start. During a blackout, almost everything you want to keep running is electronics: that is where the purchase decision is made.

The price of that difference is real: an inverter costs more per kilowatt than a conventional generator of the same power. For home use it is worth it; for construction sites and power tools, not always.

How much power you really need (and why peak power changes everything)

Every generator advertises two figures that are not the same: continuous power (what it can handle indefinitely) and starting or peak power (what it can handle for a few seconds). The motor of a fridge, a freezer or a pump does not draw its rated power when it starts: it draws 2 to 5 times more during the first second. If the peak is not enough, the generator stalls or the appliance does not start.

ApplianceContinuous consumptionStarting peak
Combi fridge, class A100-200 W400-900 W
Freezer100-250 W500-1,000 W
Router + fibre ONT10-20 W—
Laptop60-90 W—
55" LED TV80-120 W—
Six LED bulbs50-70 W—
Boiler circulation pump60-100 W200-300 W
Microwave800-1,200 W—
Drill or power tool500-1,000 W1,500-2,500 W

The correct calculation: add up the continuous consumption of what you want to have running at the same time and add the peak of the most demanding appliance, not the sum of all the peaks. For an apartment with a fridge, router, laptop and lights, an inverter with 2,000 W continuous and 2,200-2,400 W peak is more than enough. If you also want to cover a boiler, microwave or power tools, the reasonable jump is to 3,000-3,500 W.

How long it lasts on a tank (the calculation almost nobody does)

A small inverter uses between 0.6 and 1 litre per kilowatt-hour generated, depending on how heavily loaded it is. Translated into tanks: a 4-litre tank lasts 3-4 hours at half load; a 10-litre tank, 8-10 hours; a 15-20-litre tank, a day and a half with intermittent use.

For a 72-hour blackout, that is between 25 and 40 litres of petrol. And that is where the part nobody plans for comes in: storing fuel. Ethanol-free, in approved fuel cans, outside the home, and rotating it every three months (with stabiliser it lasts considerably longer). If your scenario is a week or more without the grid, the generator is not the complete answer: first compare a generator and a power station with solar panels, because you do not have to go and buy solar kWh.

What really kills: carbon monoxide

A generator emits carbon monoxide, which is odourless, colourless and kills without warning. Never inside the house. Never in the garage, not even with the door open: the gas builds up indoors and rises. Never on an enclosed balcony or in an indoor drying area. The unit goes outdoors, on a firm surface, with the exhaust pointing away from doors and windows and more than 6 metres from them (20 feet, CDC reference).

And at home, a carbon monoxide detector on the floor where you sleep. It is not an extra: it is the difference between a scare and a tragedy. We cover it in more detail in the comparison of CO detectors.

Noise and neighbours: what the rules say

A 2 kW inverter stays at around 58-65 dB at seven metres; a conventional one goes above 70. There is no specific national law for domestic generators: the municipal noise ordinance applies (typical limits of 55-65 dB by day and 45-55 dB at night in residential areas) and, if you live in a shared building, the community rules. A generator at full load on a terrace at eleven at night is an almost guaranteed complaint, and in many buildings it is directly prohibited. We cover this in generators and community rules.

Petrol inverter generator or power station with solar panels?

 Inverter generatorPower station + solar panels
Sustained powerHigh (2-3.5 kW and more)Medium (0.5-2 kWh battery)
RuntimeAs long as there is fuelUntil the battery and the sun run out
Noise58-65 dBNone
Fumes and COYes: outdoors onlyNo
MaintenanceOil, spark plug, fuelAlmost none
Cost per kWhLow3-5 times higher
When it winsLong blackouts, fridge, boilerApartment, zero noise, daily use

The combination that works in a genuinely prepared home is a mixed one: a power station and solar panels for the small and permanent loads, a generator for what demands a sudden burst of power. If you do not want any kind of combustion, the complete route is the professional energy and self-sufficiency kit, with solar panels and lithium batteries.

Checklist before buying

  • Real continuous power (not the brochure figure) and starting peak.
  • Pure sine wave with declared distortion (below 5%).
  • Tank: from 8-10 litres to last a night without refuelling.
  • Electric start and, if possible, remote control: at three in the morning you do not want to be pulling a cord.
  • Weight and wheels: a 40 kg unit does not get itself up to a third floor.
  • Protection against overload, low oil and automatic shut-off when out of fuel.
  • Technical service with a presence in Spain and a warranty of at least two years.
  • Noise declared at 7 metres, not at one metre.

2 kW inverter options with electric start: see models and prices on Amazon. To also cover a boiler or power tools, the 3 kW ones.

Maintenance: so it starts on the day you need it

  • Oil change at the first 5 hours and afterwards as per the manual (every 50 hours or once a year).
  • Fresh petrol: no fuel that is six months old. Stabiliser if it is going to sit unused.
  • Start it for 15 minutes once a month, with some load plugged in.
  • Spark plug and air filter checked once a year.
  • Never store it with a full tank for months without stabiliser.

Mistakes that cost you dearly

  • Male-to-male cable to the home consumer unit. It is the fastest way to electrocute a worker who is repairing the grid on your street. You connect to the consumer unit with a transfer switch; if you do not have one, use extension leads to the appliances.
  • Buying 5 kW just in case. It uses more, sounds louder and always runs below its optimal load: it gets dirty and wears out sooner.
  • Not calculating the peak. The generator stalls just as the fridge starts.
  • Using old petrol. The engine will not start and you blame the equipment.
  • Skipping the first oil change. The first five hours are what decide the life of the engine.
  • Putting it in the garage. See above: it is the number one cause of CO deaths during blackouts.

Verdict

For a household that wants to get through a one- to three-day blackout without losing the fridge, the router or communications, the target is an inverter with 2,000 W continuous, electric start and an 8-10 litre tank. If you also want a boiler, microwave or power tools, 3,000-3,500 W. Below 1,500 W you will come up short as soon as a fridge kicks in; above 5 kW you will be paying for noise and fuel you do not use.

And remember what a generator does not solve: without water, without a first-aid kit, without a portable light and without a radio, there is no plan. The complete list, with the buying order and what you already have at home, is in the blackout kit and in the basic 72-hour kit.

mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.titulo: Best snow chains 2026: 5 options and when the DGT requires them
mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.resumen: Metal chains, snow socks or winter tyres: 5 options compared by price and use, with what the DGT requires and the most common mistakes.
mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.cuerpo:
The same thing happens every winter: the snow warning comes, the mountains fill up, and drivers who are only going down to the petrol station discover that they don't have chains, don't know how to fit them, or that the ones they bought three years ago no longer fit their current car. Choosing well keeps you from being stranded on a mountain pass with poor visibility—and also from arriving late where you were going—and it isn't expensive: the difference between one set of chains and another is twenty or thirty euros.

The Spanish rule is simple and worth repeating: there are no fixed dates. The obligation to carry chains (or winter tyres that replace them) is set by the signage on each stretch and by the road conditions reported by the DGT, not by a calendar. Before setting off, the official procedure is to check traffic conditions on dgt.es or mapamovilidad.dgt.es, call 011 or listen to radio bulletins; and if there is an AEMET warning for the area, it is better to postpone the plan. Everything else—what to buy, how to fit them and how to store them—is in this comparison.

1. What the DGT requires, in four points

  • The sign rules, not the calendar. Where the mandatory chains sign is posted, you cannot continue without them (or without another authorized device). The official sign catalogue was updated by Royal Decree 465/2025, so some maps and manuals show different codes for the same sign: look at the sign for the stretch, not the letter of the regulation.
  • Winter tyres only replace chains if they are marked. The DGT allows driving without chains—when the sign requires them—with tyres marked with the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol (3PMSF); the M+S marking alone is not enough to replace them. They are designed for temperatures below about 7 °C.
  • Speeds and fitting position: maximum 30 km/h with metal chains and 50 km/h with textile ones; always on the driven axle (both wheels on that axle) and, if the car is four-wheel drive, at the front.
  • Driving with chains is not the same as driving normally: no sudden acceleration or hard braking, and on road without snow braking takes longer—remove them as soon as the stretch ends.

2. The five types compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain. Each link opens the search for that type, so you see the price of the day, not the price when this was written. And before paying, check your tyre size (something like 205/55 R16, on the tyre sidewall or on the driver's door): a chain that is not your size is not a chain, it is a weight in the boot.

TypeWhen it pays offLimitIndicative price

All-season tyres ↗No seasonal change; in repeated snow they perform less well than a proper winter tyreDepending on tyre70-140 € per wheel

3. Winners by use case

  • Most drivers (an occasional trip to the mountains): metal chains in your size, basic ones properly adjusted. They are accepted on all roads and are the cheapest thing that really works.
  • You live in a snowy area or make several weekend trips in a row: 3PMSF winter tyres. With them you comply where the sign requires chains, and you don't spend the rest of the year with a set of chains taking up space in the boot.
  • Cold hands, in a hurry, or never fitted them before: textile socks on stretches that allow fabric (they are the fastest to fit)—and if you don't know whether your route allows them, metal chains.
  • Off-road and unpaved tracks: metal chains with a tensioner, always; gloves and a headlamp in the same bag as them.
  • Tight budget: better a basic chain in your size than a “cheap” one in another size. The following year you add the gloves and the torch.

4. How to fit them, according to the DGT itself

  • Stop in a safe place, off the carriageway and not on a slope: better to pull the car into a wide car park than to stop on a hard shoulder with poor visibility.
  • Driven axle: front if the car is four-wheel drive; rear if it is rear-wheel drive. Both wheels on that axle, never “one on each side”.
  • Fitting: rigid hoop behind the wheel, centred, outer ring, tensioner and any excess hooked up so it doesn't hit the wheel arch.
  • Drive gently, with no sudden acceleration or braking, and remove them at the end of the snowy stretch: on clean asphalt they get in the way and wear down.
  • When storing them: wash and dry them. Road salt corrodes them from the inside, and a rusty chain breaks exactly when you need it most.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Not testing them beforehand. The first fitting in a car park with warm hands takes two minutes; on a snowy mountain pass without gloves, twenty. Do it once at home.
  • Buying by price without checking the size. The cheapest chain that won't fasten on your wheels is not a bargain: it's a trip to the petrol station so you don't even leave the car park.
  • Taking socks to a stretch that only allows metal chains. If the sign specifies it or your usual route requires it, metal chains: they are the ones that work in all cases.
  • Storing them wet or with broken elastic straps. A two-minute check at the end of the season: clean, dry and in a bag without holes.
  • Relying only on the GPS. Road conditions are checked on dgt.es and mapamovilidad.dgt.es, by calling 011 and in radio bulletins; if there is a restriction or an AEMET warning, postpone the trip, don't force it.

6. The boot kit, in six items

In addition to chains in your size: work gloves (winter ones get soaked), a torch with spare batteries, an old towel for your hands and mud, water and something to eat in case you are stranded for a couple of hours, and the blanket or extra coat for passengers. All of that lives in the car kit alongside the V-16 beacon, the high-visibility vest and the first-aid kit; the full breakdown is in what to carry in your car for an emergency. And if the warning comes with the house unprepared, you have the basics for getting through a snowstorm without power in snowstorm at home: what you need; dressing in layers, step by step, in dressing in layers.

mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.titulo: Best emergency backpack 2026: 6 evacuation backpacks compared
mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.resumen: Which backpack would you grab if you had to leave home in ten minutes? 6 types compared by litres, weight and price, winners by scenario and what goes inside (2026).
mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.cuerpo:
At 23:40 the order comes: water is coming in from the street below or smoke is visible from the neighboring town. You have minutes, not hours. That is the only reason for the evacuation backpack: prepared in advance, in the same place for weeks, ready to grab in one go while the rest of the household gets up.

The official framework is European: the Preparedness Union Strategy calls for guidelines so that the population can be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours while help arrives, and Cruz Roja Española brings it down to practical terms: an easy-to-carry backpack, of reasonable weight and accessible, whose contents are checked regularly. What to fill it with is covered in the evacuation kit; here is the question most often left half-answered —which backpack to buy— with six types compared by liters, price and real-world use.

1. Four decisions before looking at prices

  • Capacity by hours, not by wishful thinking. 18–25 liters for 24 hours or for the office; 30–40 liters for two or three days with a coat, water and food; 45–60 liters only if you have to leave with several people's gear. The 72-hour benchmark points an adult who will be walking toward 35–45 liters.
  • Loaded weight: between 10% and 15% of your body weight. It is the same rule applied to school backpacks: 70 kg → 7–10 kg on your back. More than that, after twenty minutes you are slower than someone carrying less, and in an evacuation time is exactly what you don't have to spare.
  • A carry system that distributes the load. Wide, padded shoulder straps, a breathable back panel and, above all, a hip belt: a backpack without a hip belt loaded with more than 10 kg turns your lower back into the weak point. Heavy items close to your back and at shoulder height; soft, bulky items at the bottom; what you need on the way (water, flashlight, documents), within reach.
  • Water and light on the outside, not inside. An outer pocket or mesh for the bottle and an attachment point for the flashlight: stopping to open your backpack in the middle of a crowded corridor is not the same as drinking while you walk.

2. The six types compared

3. Winners by scenario

  • Evacuation on foot (DANA, fire, order to leave): 40–50 L trekking backpack with a hip belt. It's the one that handles the weight without punishing you: 45 L trekking backpacks ↗.
  • Kit ready to grab and go: 35–45 L tactical backpack with external attachment points, if you organize by pockets: MOLLE tactical backpacks ↗. Especially useful if you keep it already assembled in the entryway closet.
  • Household with older people or back problems: the wheeled one, no question. Better to push than to drag a person with a 12 kg backpack.
  • Family with children: one large adult backpack plus a small one for each child. Babies and children in an emergency sets out what each age group carries.
  • Office, car and one-day trip: the 18–25 L one, the only one you'll actually use for the rest of the year: waterproof daypacks ↗.
  • If you have pets: the family backpack plus a separate bag with water, leash, veterinary documents and pet food: emergency plan with dogs and cats.

4. What goes inside: the layout in five compartments

The backpack is the wrapper; the contents are half the kit list. What cannot be missing from any of the six types:

CompartmentWhat it holdsReference
DocumentsCopies in a waterproof bag: ID card, health card, policies, contacts on paperemergency folder
Water and food1.5–3 L per person and energy bars, nuts or canned food that doesn't need cookinghow much water you need
Light and batteryHeadlamp, spare batteries and a charged power bankbest flashlight · best power bank
Health and warmthFirst-aid kit, 5–7 days of chronic medication and layered clothingdressing in layers
What makes the differenceCharged phone, battery-powered radio and the family plan in writing (meeting point and who to call)family emergency plan

If you don't have the basics set up yet, the order is always the same: first build your 72-hour kit, then choose the backpack to carry it. Doing it the other way round costs more.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Overloading it “just in case.” Going over 15% of your body weight turns an evacuation on foot into a trip to the emergency room: the backpack you can't carry with you is not your backpack.
  • Buying the cheapest one without trying it on. Without a hip belt and with thin straps, the difference shows at minute five, not in the product photo.
  • Making the backpack one person's business. If only one person stores and checks it, when that person isn't home the backpack no longer exists: everyone needs to know where it is and what's in it.
  • Never checking it. Dead batteries, expired documents, summer clothes in the middle of winter. Cruz Roja Española insists on regular checks: every six months, ten minutes, on the calendar.
  • Forgetting what doesn't fit in the backpack. The car, the exit route, the water at home and the original documents are prepared separately; the backpack only carries the essentials for moving.

6. The ten-minute test

The only test that counts: set a timer, grab the backpack and walk out the door closing it behind you. Ten minutes with the household asleep is a good target. If you were missing something, write it down and buy it; if you had five minutes to spare, remove weight. Then leave it in the same place —visible, labeled and within everyone's reach— and practice with the family: who grabs it, who collects the documents, who alerts the grandparents. What you practice beforehand is done later with a clear head, and that's where emergencies are won.

Our choice, with the verified link

Of the six types compared, the one that solves the most common case (leaving home with the essentials and your hands free for the children or the dog): a 40-liter waterproof backpack.

  • A AM SeaBlue 40 L — large-capacity waterproof hiking backpack. Why this one: 40 L fits the five-block layout without falling short, the back and hip belt take the load off —which matters from 8 kg upward— and the waterproof fabric protects what can't get wet. It's in the evacuation kit and in the fire kit, with today's price.

mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.titulo: Best SAI (UPS) for home and router: 6 types by VA and watts (2026)
mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.resumen: How long can your router and PC hold out in a blackout? 6 SAI compared by VA and watts, winners by use case, and the 5 most common mistakes (2026).
mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.cuerpo:
It's 12:33 on a Tuesday and the router loses power. Eight seconds, the power comes back and that's it — until by the third week the laptop restarts on its own or the modem drops every time an RCD trips. That's the job of the SAI (uninterruptible power supply): ride out the seconds when the grid can't supply power and protect the home when the power returns.

The data point that structures this article comes from Red Eléctrica: in 2025 the mainland system recorded 12 supply interruptions, 29% fewer than in 2024, with an Average Interruption Time of 0.25 minutes, far from the 15 minutes in Article 26.2 of Royal Decree 1955/2000. The Spanish grid is excellent on average, but averages are no comfort when the outage is yours: here's which SAI you need and how many VA.

1. What a SAI does (and the three things it doesn't)

A SAI is a battery with an inverter and a transfer switch: when the grid voltage drops, disappears or spikes, it switches to battery in milliseconds and keeps supplying power — the router doesn't even notice. It also filters the spikes that arrive just as the power returns.

  • It does power: router, ONT, laptop, TV, chargers, LED lights, carbon monoxide detector: 15 to 300 W.
  • It does not power: fridge, oven, hob, washing machine or heating: over 1,000 W with an even higher startup draw, which a 1,000 VA SAI won't run for even a second. For that there is a generator or power station.
  • It is not a voltage stabilizer: it corrects voltage but doesn't provide a second of battery backup. If the power goes out, it shuts off with it.
  • It is not a generator: it doesn't create energy, it stores it. Its runtime is measured in minutes.

2. The six types, compared

Approximate prices on Amazon Spain: each link opens a search for that type, so you see the current price, not the one from when this was written.

TypeWhen it's worth itApproximate price
DC mini-UPS for router and ONT ↗Communication only: the cheapest and the one that gives the most hours30-60 €
400-650 VA offline SAI ↗First desktop PC or TV + router45-80 €
1,000-1,500 VA line-interactive with AVR ↗Work computer with monitor and peripherals70-140 €
Double-conversion online ↗Equipment that can't afford even a micro-interruption200-500 €
SAI with expandable external batteries ↗You want hours, not minutes: runtime expandable by hand150-400 €
2,000-3,000 VA SAI ↗Several devices at once and a small electrical panel180-350 €

The difference between the first and the last is not the brand: it's how much battery you have inside. One detail that decides the purchase: the output waveform — for a router and TV any model will do, but for power supplies (laptops, audio) the ideal is pure sine wave, because some cheap SAIs have a flattened sine wave that chargers reject with a beep.

3. The VA calculation: how much you really need

SAIs are sold in VA (volt-amperes), not watts, and that's the confusion in almost every purchase. Since the relationship between the two is the power factor — between 0.6 and 0.7 in a domestic SAI — assume that W ≈ VA × 0.6: a 1,000 VA SAI runs around 600 W. The model's datasheet is what counts.

What you want to powerApproximate consumptionRecommended SAIApproximate runtime
Router + ONT15-30 WDC mini-UPS or 400-650 VA SAI2-4 h
Router, TV and chargers80-150 W650-1,000 VA SAI45-90 min
Laptop + monitor60-120 W1,000-1,500 VA SAI1-2 h
Desktop PC with monitor300-500 W1,500-2,000 VA SAI (pure sine wave)8-15 min
Fridge, oven or heating1,000-3,000 WNone: power station or generator—

Runtime figures are ranges calculated on the stock battery (12 V and 7 Ah is around 84 Wh) and the inverter's real efficiency: they serve to compare models, not as a guarantee, and they drop sharply if you leave it discharged or in the heat. In plain terms: what a SAI buys you is not hours of a powered home, it's that your communications don't go down while you decide what to do — and that decision is in the blackout kit.

4. Winners by use case

  • Router and ONT, first of all: DC mini-UPS, the one that gives the most hours for the price. If you prefer a conventional SAI, the 600-900 VA for router and ONT ↗ is the sweet spot: it lasts as long as needed and also protects against the return surge.
  • Remote work with a laptop: 1,000-1,500 VA line-interactive with AVR: see line-interactive SAIs ↗. The AVR maintains voltage without draining the battery during afternoon dips.
  • Desktop PC that can't restart: double-conversion online, which always runs from batteries: the one in the electricity kit.
  • A home where the lights have already gone out several times: SAI with expandable external batteries: see expandable models ↗. The only way to go from minutes to hours.
  • If the goal is the whole home: it's not a SAI, it's a portable power station ↗ with a solar panel: compare first in generator vs. power station.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Buying by VA without checking the actual watts. Work out what you'll plug in using the table above, and only then look at the price.
  • Plugging the fridge into it. Not only will it not run it: it will leave the battery dead just when you need it for the router.
  • Forgetting the battery. Lead-acid ones last 3-5 years; an expired one is a SAI that shuts off with the power. Set a calendar reminder every two years.
  • Buying it and not testing it. Disconnect the grid for a second: if the device restarts, either it's badly connected or the model isn't suitable for that load.
  • Confusing it with a voltage stabilizer or a generator. If you need hours of fridge or heating, you're in the wrong article: look at power banks and power stations.

6. Standard, maintenance and how it fits into your kit

To buy sensibly, just check that the model complies with the harmonized European standard UNE-EN IEC 62040-1:2019 (safety requirements for SAIs, in force in Spain with amendments from 2021, 2023 and 2025): it guarantees that the device is safe to touch, not that it will last for hours.

Maintenance in three lines: load test every six months (disconnect the grid for a minute), ventilation (let the SAI breathe, never in a closed cabinet) and battery replacement before the equipment complains. Golden rule: test it on a normal day, not during the blackout.

In March 2026, the CNMC published its recommendations report on the 28 April 2025 incident: it mitigates abrupt voltage changes and strengthens inspection of protection systems. The grid will improve, but protecting your home is still up to you. The list is in the blackout kit and in the lessons from 28 April; if you don't yet have the basics set up, start with how to build your 72-hour kit.

mejor-extintor-domestico.titulo: Best home fire extinguisher 2026: 6 types and where to place it
mejor-extintor-domestico.resumen: Which fire extinguisher for home: powder, CO₂, foam or Class F. Six types compared by price, where to place it, and the one-minute monthly check.
mejor-extintor-domestico.cuerpo:
A frying pan catches fire, a power strip trips or a candle falls onto the curtain: there is very little margin between a small cooking fire and having to run out, and in Spain that margin is lost every day. In 2024, 234 people died in fires and explosions in Spain, 172 of them inside homes, and among the likely causes, electrical faults top the list, at 41.9%. These are the figures from the Fire Victim Study by Fundación MAPFRE and APTB (Professional Association of Fire Technicians), which has collected data from fire services and forensic medicine institutes since 2010.

The fire extinguisher is the cheap answer: between €25 and €60 for a fire that starts while you are at home. Regulations require them to be installed and maintained in buildings and commercial premises —RIPCI, Royal Decree 513/2017, is the reference regulation— but inside a private home there is no legal obligation. Here you decide which type puts out what, with six compared and where to hang it.

1. First decide this: what class of fire you have

A letter appears on the label of any fire extinguisher: it is the only thing that matters when buying. The UNE-EN 3-7 standard sets out the classes and the “typical household fires” that the device must put out:

ClassWhat burnsWhere you find it at home
ASolids: wood, paper, fabric, cardboardSofa, curtain, wardrobe, wastebasket
BLiquids: gasoline, solvents, oilWorkshop, garage, gas cylinders
CCombustible gasesButane, kitchen gas
DMetals (industrial use)Almost never in a home
FHot cooking fats and oilsFrying pan and deep fryer: the most common at home

The practical translation: ABC powder covers A, B and C, almost everything that burns in an apartment. What it does not cover well is a frying pan (Class F): the oil is extinguished on the surface and reignites as soon as you move it. For cooking, use a Class F extinguisher (foam or water with additive) or, better and faster, cover the pan with its lid or a fire blanket. Pouring water is the classic way to get burned: it vaporizes and carries burning oil all over the kitchen.

2. The six types, compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain for CE-marked fire extinguishers; each link opens a search for the type, so you see the current price, not the price when this was written.

TypeWhen it is worth itIndicative price
ABC powder, 1-2 kg ↗First purchase: backpack, entryway, pantry20-35 €
ABC powder, 6 kg ↗Whole house, garage or communal areas40-70 €
CO₂, 2 kg ↗Electrical panel or workshop: leaves no residue40-65 €
Class F foam (6 L) ↗Kitchen: the only one for hot oil35-60 €
Water with additive / water-based ↗Kitchen and living room: effective and not very messy30-55 €
Fire blanket or aerosol ↗Over the hob and in the car: stops fire early10-25 €

3. Best choice by situation

  • A single device for an apartment: 6 kg ABC powder, the same as the one hanging in stairwells; if the budget is tight, the 2 kg one already covers an incipient fire: see ABC powder extinguishers ↗.
  • Frequent cooking: Class F foam next to the door, never above the hob, plus a fire blanket in the drawer below: see Class F extinguishers ↗.
  • Electrical panel or storage room: 2 kg CO₂, which leaves the device and cables usable afterwards: see CO₂ extinguishers ↗.
  • Garage or workshop with fuel: 6 kg ABC powder on its wall bracket and visible from the entrance: see 6 kg extinguishers ↗.
  • Car trunk and caravan: fire blanket or small extinguisher, because in a van the first things to burn are the fridge and clothing — the rest goes in the car kit: see fire blankets ↗.

Honest warning: a 2 kg extinguisher empties in about 10-15 seconds of discharge. It is for a fire that has just started, not for a room in flames. If two passes have not put it out, it is time to get out.

4. Where to put it (and the one-minute monthly check)

  • Near the exit, never on the other side of the fire. Fire service rule: you do not cross the room that is burning to get it. Visible, with no furniture in front and with signage above.
  • Height and mounting. On its bracket, at hand height and away from heat, moisture and bumps. On the floor or behind a door that opens towards it: the classic mistake.
  • Monthly check (60 seconds): pressure gauge needle in the green zone, tamper seal and pin intact, hose free of cracks, body free of rust. And turn it upside down a couple of times a year so the powder does not compact.
  • Formal inspection: if it hangs in an installation subject to RIPCI, maintenance is carried out by an authorized company: annual inspection and pressure test every five years. In a private home it is not mandatory, but the same applies: service life is around 20 years from manufacture (Tecnifuego) and it must be replaced sooner if the needle does not return to green.
  • During a power outage, double-check. Candles and generators raise the risk exactly when no one is watching: check the gauge and the candle before nightfall. The details are in the power outage kit.

5. Five mistakes that make the extinguisher useless

  • Water on an electrical fire. First switch off the power if you can, then use CO₂ or powder with a dielectric test.
  • Buying by color. Red says nothing: look at the label with the A/B/C/F letters and the rating. An aerosol is not a 6 kg extinguisher.
  • Covering it with the washing machine or boxes. The one that has been in the storage room for years does not exist.
  • Overconfidence. The extinguisher is for a pan fire. If the flame reaches the ceiling or there is dense smoke, close the door and get out.
  • Forgetting the rest of the system. The extinguisher does not warn you: that is what the smoke detector is for, and the flashlight helps you avoid lighting unnecessary fires. All of that is in the fire kit and in passive fire safety and electrical fires.

6. If it breaks out: four steps, in this order

  1. Raise the alarm: call 112 before touching the extinguisher, with the address and what is burning. Wrong information is worse than late information.
  2. Protect the exit: extinguisher in hand, upright, hose aimed at the base of the fire and one step from the door.
  3. One attempt only: two short passes. If it does not go down, drop the extinguisher, close the door behind you and get out without grabbing anything else.
  4. Never go back until the fire service authorizes it, even if “only ashes remain”: smoke is what kills.

That completes the fire equipment. The rest of the home —light, water, warm clothing and documents— can be put together the same afternoon with the first-aid kit guide and with how to build your 72-hour kit; if you only prepare one corner, make it the home or shelter-in-place kit.

mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.titulo: Best carbon monoxide detector: 6 types compared (2026)
mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.resumen: How to choose a CO detector: the thresholds in the UNE-EN 50291 standard, 6 types compared with price, where to place it and what to do if the alarm sounds.
mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.cuerpo:
The cold drops, you light the stove, close the room so the heat doesn't escape, and fall asleep. That scenario—homely, everyday, from any winter in Spain—is the one that most often ends up in the emergency department: carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless and tasteless, it doesn't warn you and neither does your body. The CO detector is the cheapest device in the whole house that decides whether you wake up in time. It costs less than dinner and needs no installation, electricity or app.

The numbers are in official reports: according to the Toxicovigilance Program of the Ministry of Health, carbon monoxide is the most common toxic substance in Spanish emergency departments, with between 5,000 and 10,000 poisonings a year and an average of 125 deaths annually. And the National Plan for Preventive Actions against Low Temperatures 2025-2026 reminds us every winter that cold brings heating systems, braziers and generators: risk rises precisely when you shut yourself in the most.

1. What the standard requires: the table that decides whether it warns you in time

In Spain, everything is sold, from detectors at 15 € to devices at 80 €, and the difference is not the brand: it is whether they comply with the European standard UNE-EN 50291-1:2018 (ratified by AENOR in February 2021), which sets the test methods and performance requirements for domestic CO detectors. A compliant device must alarm within these times:

CO concentrationWhen the alarm must sound
30 ppmNot before 120 minutes (and must sound within that period)
50 ppmBetween 60 and 90 minutes
100 ppmBetween 10 and 40 minutes
300 ppmIn less than 3 minutes

Two readings. First: the standard does not monitor low background levels; rather, it warns before the damage is serious — that is why it does not go off with the chimney open one afternoon, but it does if the generator has been in the garage for half an hour. Second: once it goes off, the alarm does not quiet down until the level falls below 50 ppm: that it “switches itself off” does not mean the air is clean. For placement, EN 50292 applies (selection and installation): every room with a possible combustion source and every bedroom. The electrical side of the same risk is covered in passive fire safety and electrical fires.

2. The six types, compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain for detectors with an electrochemical sensor compliant with EN 50291. Each link opens the search for that type: you see the price of the day, not the one from when this was written.

TypeWhen it is worth itIndicative price
Basic battery-powered with audible alarm ↗First purchase, rented home, bedroom20-30 €
With concentration display (ppm) ↗Home with stove, wood, fireplace or butane30-45 €
Sealed 10-year battery ↗Bedroom and hallway: set it and forget it30-50 €
Combined smoke + CO ↗One device for both outage risks40-70 €
With phone alert or interconnected ↗Large house, several floors, absences50-90 €
For motorhome, caravan or sailboat ↗Use while moving, batteries and wide temperature range30-60 €

3. Winners by category

  • Best value for money: the basic battery-powered model with an electrochemical sensor. If you only buy one, make it this one: see battery-powered CO detectors ↗.
  • Best for the bedroom: sealed 10-year battery, no battery changes and an end-of-life indicator: see long-life battery models ↗.
  • Best with a stove or wood: with a ppm display, to see whether the concentration is rising before it sounds: see detectors with a display ↗.
  • Best for a home expecting a power outage: combined smoke + CO: during a power outage, candles, stoves and generators coexist, and smoke and CO arrive together: see combined detectors ↗. Beware the usual confusion: a smoke detector does not detect carbon monoxide, and vice versa.
  • Best for a motorhome or van: vehicle-specific model, battery-powered: see caravan detectors ↗.

If the budget is very tight, the priority is not the detector: it is ventilating and not heating with combustion inside the home. With that and a well-chosen flashlight you are already covered — the selection is in best stove without power and in maintaining temperature without electricity.

4. Where to put it (and where never to)

  • Yes: in every bedroom, in the hallway serving them and in the room where you burn anything (open kitchen, fireplace, workshop). Follow the manufacturer: most specify 1-3 meters from the source, on the ceiling or a high wall and away from drafts.
  • No: inside a cupboard, behind a curtain, above the extractor hood or next to a window: there the air arrives late or is renewed too quickly and it measures badly.
  • Garage: a domestic detector is not suitable for a running car: that requires higher-range models and, even better, not leaving the engine running in an enclosed space.
  • Maintenance: test monthly with the button, dust it every six months (recommended by the Comunidad de Madrid) and replace it at the end of its service life, 5 to 10 years depending on the model: the device itself will warn you.

5. Five mistakes that cancel out the detector

  • Trusting your sense of smell. CO has no smell at all: by the time you notice it, you have already been breathing it for a while.
  • Heating with the gas oven. The Ministry of Health says it literally: never use the stove or oven to heat a home.
  • Generator, chainsaw or boiler inside the home or garage. Combustion engines in an enclosed space are the classic source of mass poisoning.
  • Stove left on at night with the room closed. Ventilating is the cheapest measure: better to lose some heat than to have no air.
  • One detector for the whole house. Air does not travel between floors or through closed doors: at least one per floor and one in every bedroom.

6. If the alarm sounds: four steps

  1. Get everyone out of the room — without “checking what it is”, without turning anything off and without going back in to look for anyone.
  2. Ventilate from outside and do not go back until the emergency services authorize it.
  3. Call 112 from outside: people affected, symptoms and which combustion source was running.
  4. Have the source checked by a professional before turning it back on: a badly sealed boiler or chimney will repeat the episode.

And the warning most often ignored: headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion that ease when you leave the house are the typical picture. If you wake in the early hours with your head pounding and the heating on, get out.

The detector is the first euro of the winter kit: alongside it go radio, light and warm clothing in the home or confinement kit, electrical safety in the electricity kit and cold in the cold and snow kit. If you haven't put anything together yet, start with how to assemble your 72-hour kit: it takes half an afternoon.

mejor-starlink-espana-precio.titulo: Best Starlink in Spain: price, plans and which one to choose (2026)
mejor-starlink-espana-precio.resumen: Starlink in Spain 2026: the three residential plans with official pricing, kit rental at 10 €/month, Roam, and which one suits you.
mejor-starlink-espana-precio.cuerpo:
Almost every question about Starlink that reaches this blog starts the same way: how much does it really cost, and which plan do I need? In 2026 it changed twice: in March Starlink went from two plans to three, and in June it added 10 €/mes for kit rental for new sign-ups. Here are today's official prices, the comparison, and the verdict for each case.

It is not a niche product: based on network traffic, Starlink would already be the sixth operator in Spain, with more than half a million users, and during the 28 April 2025 blackout, the satellite service was one of the few that kept working. That is the argument of this site: that the connection doesn't disappear just when you need it. The lessons from that day are in the 28 April blackout; the equipment, in the Starlink kit.

1. The five Starlink plans in Spain, compared

Starlink sells two families in Spain: Residential (fixed home) and Mobile (motorhomes, sailboats, use while moving). All include unlimited data and a 30-day trial with a full refund. Prices are those on Starlink's official website for Spain:

PlanPrice/monthDownloadPriorityWho it's for
Residential 10035 €up to 100 Mb/s (capped)NoSmall apartment, second home, basic use
Residential 20045 €up to 200 Mb/sNoFamily with remote work and several devices
Residential Max65 €over 400 Mb/sYes, the highestLarge house, mesh network, many screens
Mobile 100 GB45 €100 GB at high speed then at low speedNoMotorhome or sailboat with occasional use
Mobile unlimited95 €unlimited while movingNoNomadic life, work from anywhere

Winners by category: the Residential 200 (45 €) is the sweet spot: it doubles the basic speed without paying for Max priority. For a small apartment or second home, the Residential 100 (35 €) is more than enough. The Max (65 €) only pays off with several devices connected at once or real priority at peak times. For a van, the Mobile 100 GB (45 €) with Standby Mode.

A warning: Starlink adjusts prices often (twice in 2026). Check the price at checkout on the official plans website, not the price in an article from six months ago.

2. The equipment: since June 2026 it is rented, not bought

What most people miss: since June 2026, new sign-ups also pay 10 €/mes for the kit (antenna and router):

  • Residential 100: 45 €/mes actual (35 plan fee + 10 kit).
  • Residential 200: 55 €/mes actual (45 + 10).
  • Residential Max: 75 €/mes actual (65 + 10).
  • The 10 € comes to 120 € a year, and the equipment is not yours: if you cancel, it is returned.

Two nuances: a «rental adjustment» often appears that brings those 10 € down to 0, so count the checkout price, not the one in the table; and professional installation is optional, from about 172 €, only for tricky roofs (the app tells you where to point it; anyone can assemble the basic setup).

If you choose only one thing, the Starlink Mini: it fits in a backpack, has an integrated router, runs directly on DC power, and exceeds 200 Mb/s. It is the one that makes sense in an emergency kit; here you can see accessories and mounts for Starlink Mini ↗.

3. Is it worth it in your case? Yes if…, no if…

It is worth it when: fiber doesn't reach you or actually arrives at 20 Mb/s; fixed 5G drops at night; you live in a village or an isolated mountain house; or it is a second home used for weeks at a time (with Standby Mode at about 10 €/mes instead of paying the full rate all year).

It is not worth it when: you have stable, cheap fiber; when you need internet anywhere in the country rather than at one address (that is what mobile data is for); or if you don't want a monthly fee, because the big part of the cost is the monthly one.

And the point almost nobody calculates beforehand: power. A terminal consumes 60-75 W active and 20-40 W idle, so without mains power you have to power it: with a portable power station ↗, with a folding solar panel that recharges during the day or, if it is a fixed installation, with the SAI for the router. A 20,000 mAh power bank is not enough for the antenna. How many watts you really need: portable solar panel for 72 hours and generator vs power station.

You also need a clear sky: a tree or a badly oriented roof ruins the connection like a blackout. If the antenna cannot see the sky, Starlink is not your solution: first look at the best 4G emergency router.

4. Cheaper alternatives before paying 45 € a month

OptionWhen it winsTypical cost
4G/5G router with data SIM ↗There is mobile coverage on your street and you don't need more than 100 GBEquipment 0-100 € + 15-40 €/mes
eSIM / second data SIMFor leaving town or for the family's second device0-20 € + data allowance
Starlink Residential 100There is no reliable mobile coverage and you need real bandwidth35 €/mes (+ kit)
Satellite messaging and GPSOnly alerts and location without coverage and with clear sky: little traffic, long battery lifeEquipment + annual fee
PMR446 walkie-talkies ↗Internal group communication when no network is available40-80 € per pair

The full comparison: emergency connectivity, best data SIM and communicating without a mobile network. The rule: layers — mobile for everyday use, router or Starlink for the home, satellite or radio when everything else goes down.

5. The five most common mistakes when signing up

  • Signing up for Max out of habit. Priority is only noticeable at peak times; for a normal home, Residential 200 performs just as well for 30 €/mes less.
  • Reading only the rate. The real price is rate + rental: 45, 55 or 75 € a month. Always look at the total on your first bill.
  • Installing it without checking the sky. The app has an obstruction map: use it BEFORE paying and drilling into the roof.
  • Leaving the trial for the blackout. You have 30 days for a refund: test it on a normal day, in rain and with the TV on.
  • Forgetting where the power will come from. Without a plug, Starlink is a metal dish: first the power source and the battery that keeps it running.

6. Where to start today

If the decision is «yes, I want it», go to the official sign-up website, check your address on the coverage map and choose between Residential 100 and Residential 200. Step-by-step installation is in Starlink during a blackout.

For the complete plan, the Starlink kit gathers the selection, the blackout checklist covers the rest of the house and the method, in how to build your 72-hour kit. Test it one afternoon: the day you need it, it will matter that you had already tested it.

generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.titulo: Generator and noise in the community: how many dB will they tolerate (2026)
generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.resumen: dB limits under Law 37/2003, Royal Decree 1367/2007 and your municipal ordinance: how to use the generator without a fine and without angry neighbours.
generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.cuerpo:
A two-day blackout, the generator you bought 'just in case' and, at 11:40 p.m., a knock at the door: the neighbour can't sleep. The answer to 'and is this legal?' isn't in any forum: it's in the Law 37/2003 on Noise, your council's ordinance and the Horizontal Property Act.

1. National law: where domestic activity begins and where it stops being domestic

The Law 37/2003 of 17 November on Noise is the main rule, and Article 2.2.a) provides the key: excluded from its scope are 'domestic activities or the behaviour of neighbours, when the noise pollution produced by them remains within tolerable limits in accordance with municipal ordinances and local customs'.

Translation: switching on your generator is a domestic activity… until it stops being one. As soon as you exceed what your council considers tolerable, you enter the penalty regime: Article 28.5 allows local ordinances to classify as an infringement 'noise produced by domestic activities or by neighbours'.

SeverityFineWhen it applies (summary)
MinorUp to €600Breaching the law without falling under serious cases
Serious€601 – €12,000Exceeding applicable limit values without serious harm
Very serious€12,001 – €300,000Exceeding them with serious harm or risk to health

2. The figures in Royal Decree 1367/2007: how many dB are tolerated at night

The Royal Decree 1367/2007 sets quality objectives in Annex II. For a residential land sector in existing built-up areas (Table A): 65 dB by day, 65 in the evening and 55 at night. Inside the home (Table B), which is what is measured in the neighbour's bedroom: 45/45/35 in living rooms and 40/40/30 in bedrooms.

Each city sets the periods; the Community of Madrid Ordinance divides the day into daytime (7:00–19:00), evening (19:00–23:00) and night-time (23:00–7:00). Between 65 by day and 55 at night there are 10 decibels, which the ear perceives as twice the noise: what at eleven is a nuisance, at one is grounds for a complaint.

3. Your generator already has the dB on the label

Generators are no exception: Directive 2000/14/EC, transposed in Spain by Royal Decree 212/2002 (BOE-A-2002-4099), requires the guaranteed sound power level of generators under 400 kW to be declared. That figure appears on the label and in the technical data sheet. Typical values, measured at 7 metres — the standard distance in data sheets:

Equipment typeNoise at 7 mWhat it is useful for at home
Soundproof inverter (suitcase type)48 – 60 dB(A)The quiet option: lights, fridge, router
Portable open-frame (cheap)70 – 80 dB(A)The noisiest: it sounds like a vacuum cleaner
Installed generator (standby)60 – 75 dB(A)Detached house with a deadline from the neighbour
Power station (battery)~30 dB(A)Fan only: zero noise and zero fumes

Two rules of physics explain almost all conflicts: every +10 dB is perceived as twice the noise and sound drops by about 6 dB every time you double the distance. A 72 dB open-frame at 7 metres sounds like 66 at 14 and 60 at 28: moving the equipment away from the neighbour's patio is worth more than any barrier.

4. The municipal ordinance: the text that actually fines you

National law provides the framework, but your council draws up the fine. Search for 'noise pollution ordinance' plus your municipality: there you'll find the decibels per zone, the hours and the penalties. As an example, the Seville Ordinance: 'Generators and transformers must be installed in such a way that they are suitably insulated against noise and vibrations'.

Note the word insulated: it doesn't say 'silent', it says insulated against noise and vibrations. Vibrations travel through the building structure and wake the neighbour even when the air is quiet.

5. The homeowners' association: the fast route is not the fine

If the noise comes from a neighbour — or you cause it — the shortest route is the Horizontal Property Act. Article 7 prohibits carrying out in the home activities that contravene the general provisions on nuisance, unhealthy, harmful, dangerous or illegal activities:

  • Request from the chairperson, on their own initiative or that of any owner, with a warning of legal action.
  • Action for cessation if it persists and the general meeting authorises it: the judge may order immediate cessation as an interim measure, 'under warning of committing the offence of disobedience'.
  • Judgment which, in addition to cessation and compensation, may deprive you of the use of the home for a period not exceeding three years.

A badly placed generator can cost you the fine, compensation and, in the worst case, the use of your own home.

6. How to use it without sleeping with the penalty hanging over you

  • Never indoors, nor in the garage, nor in the building's storage room. Carbon monoxide kills before the fine does; a battery-powered CO detector per floor is the cheapest measure in the kit.
  • Move it away and direct it. The 6 dB per doubled distance work in your favour; point the exhaust outwards and never against a wall that reflects sound.
  • Anti-vibration base. A rubber mat cuts the path of vibration into the structure — Seville's ordinance requires it —: anti-vibration mats.
  • Timing. From 23:00 to 7:00 the target drops from 65 to 55 dB: that's when the same nuisance becomes a case file.
  • Eco mode and actual load. Data sheets declare noise at quarter load; with the equipment at maximum watts it rises. For lights and chargers, a silent inverter generator performs the same with half the noise.
  • If you live in a flat, don't buy an engine. A power station provides power without noise, without fumes and without arguments with the homeowners' association.

7. The most costly mistakes

  • Believing that domestic activity is always allowed: the law excludes you only 'within tolerable limits' according to your ordinance.
  • Looking only at the watts in the shop: if the data sheet doesn't give dB(A) at 7 m, it's equipment you don't want in a building.
  • Installing it right against the party wall: noise and vibration for the same neighbour, and the ordinance expressly mentions it.
  • Forgetting CO and fuel: safety is covered in the blackout kit guide and the first decisions in what a blackout taught us.

8. Where to start today

If you don't have a generator, first decide whether you really need one: for a flat, the comparison between generator and power station is conclusive. If you already have one, take out the data sheet, note the dB at 7 m, count the metres to the neighbour's patio and look up your municipal ordinance. To calculate watts before buying: portable solar panel and emergency solar generator.

Noise isn't solved with good intentions: it's solved with decibels, metres and schedules. And what your home must withstand without power is in the electricity and backup kit.
