nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.titulo: Snowed in at home: 8 key tips to get through days without power (2026)
nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.resumen: What you need when a snow warning is issued: safe heating, water, food, light, a car with chains and the mistakes Filomena taught us, with official sources.
nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.cuerpo:
When AEMET's warnings map turns orange, the problem is not picture-postcard snow: it is the days that follow. Roads cut off, power that does not come back, heating down and the supermarket with empty shelves. Storm Filomena (January 2021) is still the benchmark in Spain: AEMET itself describes it as an exceptional event, with snow accumulation of up to 50 cm in Madrid city centre and minimum temperatures of -26.5 °C. In many homes what failed was not that it snowed: it was that no one had prepared for three days without shopping.

This is the list of what I need at home when a snow warning is issued, in order and with the reason why. If you only do one thing, do the first.

1. Check the official warning, not the WhatsApp group

It all starts with the AEMET warnings map: yellow (be careful), orange (significant risk) and red (extreme risk, with implications for your safety). Supplement it with Protección Civil recommendations and with 112 if there is a real emergency.

And before moving the car, DGT repeats it in every winter warning: check the weather forecast and road conditions before setting out, and have chains or winter tyres to hand. Traffic authorities may restrict traffic for vehicles without that equipment and may even close roads preventively. The practical rule: if the journey is not essential, don't make it.

2. Heating: what warms you and what kills

When the power goes out, what kills in winter is not the cold but carbon monoxide: odourless, invisible and produced by any poorly ventilated combustion. It is the first rule on the list:

  • Never run a generator inside the home, not in the garage, not in the entrance hall, not right next to a window. Why, in the generator vs power station comparison: in a flat, a power station is the only option.
  • Gas or combustion heater: only with the room ventilated and never while you sleep. A butane gas heater handles a living room, not a house closed up all night.
  • Battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on every floor and near the bedrooms. It costs less than a dinner out and it is the only thing that warns you before it is too late: battery-powered CO detector.
  • Keep the house warm, not just the people: cover the window at night with a curtain or blanket, close off rooms you are not using and wear layers at home. The detail is in maintaining body temperature without electricity and in dressing in layers.

The cold-specific items are in the cold and snow kit.

3. Water and food: three days without being able to shop

A snowstorm cuts roads and delays deliveries, so plan for at least 3 litres of water per person per day (drinking, hygiene and cooking): the figure and how to store it are in how much water to store per person. Buy food you can eat without gas and without cooking: canned goods, tinned pulses, nuts, sliced bread, coffee and a can opener (if you forget the manual one, a knife and a pot are not enough).

And as soon as the power goes out, the order is: use fresh food first (meat, fish, dairy), then frozen food. The fridge lasts hours, not days; the full timetable is in storing food without a fridge, and if you live alone or want extra margin, in portable cooler for emergencies.

4. Light, information and batteries

The scares during a snowstorm happen in the early hours, in a dark hallway. The kit that solves them, with indicative prices:

ItemWhat it is really forIndicative price
Battery-powered headlampHands-free light for going up to the attic, down to the storage room or helping a neighbour8-15 €
Assorted AA/AAA batteriesTorches, radios and detectors; with the expiry date noted10-20 €
Battery or hand-crank radioOfficial information without mains power or batteries: the radio is the first source when the power fails15-35 €
20,000 mAh power bankThree or four phone charges: to call for help and receive alerts25-50 €
Foldable solar panelExtends battery life for several days; under overcast skies it produces little, so do not count on it as your main power source40-80 €
Candles with a stable holderOccasional backup, always on a sturdy surface and away from curtains5-12 €

The full comparisons are in best emergency torch, best power bank and best hand-crank and solar radio; how many watts you really need, in portable solar panel.

5. The car: chains, tyres and common sense

DGT repeats it every winter: carry chains or winter or all-season tyres if you are going to drive in areas with a snow warning, check road conditions before setting out and keep the left lane clear for snowploughs. If the snow catches you on the road: do not abandon the vehicle, slow down and call 112.

The gear goes in the boot before the storm is announced: snow chains, a pair of waterproof gloves (fitting chains with frozen hands is impossible) and a thermal blanket. The full vehicle list is in the car kit.

6. Neighbours, older people and those who live alone

In a building, logistics are worked out among everyone: who shops if someone cannot go out and who has the key to the older person's flat. A call at the same time every day to someone who lives alone is not courtesy, it is a welfare check: the script is in living alone and being prepared, the equipment in the older person's kit and the phone numbers you cannot do without in official emergency resources. If there is daily medication, check the week's dose and keep the prescription up to date: chronic medication without a pharmacy.

7. The five mistakes repeated in every snowstorm

  • Going out "to have a look" while snow is falling. The road that "is fine" at ten may be closed at twelve.
  • Running the generator or heater in an enclosed space. It is the mistake that causes the most hospitalisations in winter.
  • Buying only food that has to be cooked and discovering at 21:00 that there is no gas, water or can opener.
  • Keeping phone numbers and documents only on the mobile. With no power and the battery at 8%, the contact list does not exist: print it. The full folder is in emergency folder and documents.
  • Waiting for the neighbour to warn you. When the supermarket is overwhelmed, it is already too late to buy what matters: batteries, spare batteries, first-aid kit and medication.

8. Where to start today

If you are starting from scratch, the basic 72-hour kit gives you the common base, and the cold and car gear goes on top. The method for not forgetting anything is in how to build your 72-hour kit, and the first-moment decisions in what a blackout taught us.

A snowstorm gives days of warning: use them, and when it arrives all you will have to do is look out of the window.

generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.titulo: Generator vs power station: 2026 comparison for a blackout
generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.resumen: Generator or power station? We compare power, runtime, noise, cost per hour and regulations to ride out a blackout in Spain.
generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.cuerpo:
On 28 April 2025, at 12:33:30, the mainland electricity system dropped to zero. The Committee for the Analysis of the Circumstances Surrounding the Electricity Crisis of 28 April —created by the National Security Council and whose report the Council of Ministers approved on 17 June 2025— concluded that the origin was multifactorial, ruled out a cyberattack and placed the full restoration of supply on 29 April at 14:36. In many homes the power came back much earlier; the problem was everything that remained unpowered in the meantime: the fridge, the boiler, the entryphone, the water pump.

That is why the buying question is no longer 'what am I missing from the kit', but how much power you need and, above all, where you are going to put it. That is where two very different answers intersect: a fuel generator or a power station (a battery unit with an inverter and, optionally, a solar panel). We compare them using Spanish data —power, runtime, cost per hour, noise and regulations— so you can decide before the next outage, not during it.

What you need to power (do this before looking at prices)

Power is measured in watts and gets used up very quickly. A rough practical rule for the first 72 hours:

  • 100-200 W: router and ONT, phone chargers, three or four LED lights, carbon monoxide detector. Anything in this article can power that.
  • 300-700 W: laptop, TV, kettle, microwave occasionally, vacuum cleaner.
  • 1,000-2,000 W: domestic fridge at startup, oil-fired boiler (circulation pump only), well pump.
  • Above 2,500 W: ceramic hob, oven, washing machine, air conditioning. There, a small generator falls short and a 500 Wh power station cannot even complete one oven cycle.

With that list in front of you, the comparison becomes clear on its own.

Generator vs power station: the table

CriterionPetrol generator (inverter)Power station + solar panel
Continuous power1,000-3,000 W, with peaks of up to double that at startup600-2,000 W output and 500-2,000 Wh capacity
Runtime4-8 h per 4-5 L tank, and as long as there is petrol left500 Wh ≈ 6-10 h for a small fridge or about 10 h for router, lights and chargers
Cost per hour1-1,80 €/h of petrol (indicative)0 € in use; 150-400 € one-off cost for the panel
Noise58-75 dB(A) at 7 m depending on modelSilent: only the fan
Use in an apartmentImpossible ❌ (carbon monoxide, noise and regulations)Yes ✅ inside the home
RechargingPetrol, with stock that expiresSun, grid or car engine: free and no management
Weight15-30 kg8-25 kg
Indicative price350-900 € + 50-100 € for a fuel can400-1.200 € + 100-300 € for the panel

Indicative figures for Spain, intended for comparison, not for placing an order: they assume petrol at around 1,5 €/L and typical retail price ranges. A conventional generator without an inverter is cheaper, but it delivers a waveform that damages sensitive electronics: if you are going to plug in the computer or router, insist on pure sine wave output.

Winner by category

  • City flat or apartment → power station. It does not burn fuel, make noise or emit carbon monoxide. A 1,000-1,500 Wh station and a folding panel cover a small fridge, lights and phones: see portable power stations and 20-40 W folding solar panel, the minimum so you don't run down phone and torch batteries.
  • House with a storage room, ventilated garage or garden → inverter generator. It is the only way to boil, heat or run a large fridge for days: see inverter generators.
  • Router and computer (the first thing to save) → SAI/UPS. Cheap, silent and instant: 600-900 VA UPS. It does not replace the previous two: it buys you the first few minutes while you decide.
  • Long scenario (several days) → both: station for everyday use and generator for high-demand appliances, with the panel as a safety net.

Noise: why a generator does not belong in a communal entrance

Here the comparison is won on points, and this is the figure almost nobody checks before buying. A 'silenced' inverter generator is around 58-65 dB(A) at seven metres according to its datasheet; a conventional one exceeds 70. A building entryphone is around 50-55 dB. On a quiet street at three in the morning, a generator on the balcony can be heard from the flat next door.

And the legal framework leaves no room: Article 7.2 of the Ley de Propiedad Horizontal prohibits carrying out activities in the home that 'contravene the general provisions on nuisance, unhealthy, harmful, dangerous or illegal activities', while the noise limit values for residential areas are set by the Ley 37/2003 del Ruido and its implementing royal decrees (Código del Ruido, BOE) together with each municipality's local ordinance. In practice: plugging in a generator on the balcony or in the garage of a residential building is both a neighbour dispute and an infringement. If you want the regulatory detail, it is in the Código de la Comunidad de Propietarios del BOE.

Carbon monoxide: the argument that settles the debate

The rule is short and admits no exceptions: a generator is never used inside the home, or in the garage, or in the communal entrance, or right next to a window. The engine emits odourless carbon monoxide, and serious poisonings during blackouts usually happen exactly like this, with someone trying to get through a warmer night or charge their phone in the storage room. Protección Civil and the European Commission preparedness plan agree on the same thing: distance, ventilation and a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on the wall, one metre from the bed and away from the ceiling.

If the home is a flat, that option is not even on the table: the generator is out of the equation and the power station wins by default.

Shopping in 10 minutes

  • Small items first: basic 72-hour kit and 20,000 mAh power bank. They cost less than an hour of generator use and solve 80% of nights.
  • If you live in a flat: a 1,000 Wh power station plus a folding panel. The wattage calculation is in portable solar panel: how many watts you really need.
  • If you have a storage room or garden: a 2,000 W inverter generator with pure sine wave output, and the solar generator alternative so you don't depend on petrol.
  • What you don't buy twice: before plugging in heating, check the comparison of heaters for power cuts; the fridge and the rest of the list are in blackout kit and electricity kit.

With 28-A on the table —the official conclusions are in the non-confidential report from the Committee of Analysis— the question is no longer whether there will be another outage, but whether that afternoon you will have a working fridge or you will be knocking on your neighbour's door. Choosing between a generator and a power station is not choosing technology: it is choosing whether your home has somewhere to store twenty kilos of noisy iron… or not.

baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.titulo: V16 beacon mandatory in 2026: rules, 80 € fine and how to choose it
baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.resumen: From 1 January 2026, the connected V16 beacon is the only legal means of signalling a stopped car: what the DGT requires and how to choose an approved one.
baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.cuerpo:
1 January 2026 has already passed, and with it a twenty-six-year-old habit: warning triangles are no longer a valid way to signal a stopped car on the road. From that date, the only legal device is the connected V-16 light beacon, and anyone who still relies on the triangles in the trunk is outside the rules — it is a minor offence and carries an €80 fine.

This is not a technological whim: the DGT estimates that around 25 people die each year after being struck on the road having got out of their vehicle, many while they were placing the triangles. With the V-16 you do not get out of the car: it is switched on from inside and, as well as the light, it sends the vehicle's position to other drivers. Here you can see what the rules require, how it works, where to place it, the fine, the myths and what to check before buying.

What the rules require from 1 January 2026

The obligation is set out in Annex XII of the General Vehicle Regulations and came into force on 1 January 2026: from that date, the connected V-16 is “the only legal means of signalling immobilised vehicles”, according to the DGT.

  • Compulsory for passenger cars, vans, buses, mixed-use vehicles, trucks and non-special vehicle combinations. It is not compulsory for motorcycles, but the DGT considers its use “highly advisable”.
  • Warning triangles may remain in the vehicle's equipment, but they can no longer be used to signal a breakdown on the road.
  • Abroad, it is valid in the countries that signed the Vienna Convention (Portugal, France, Germany, Italy…), which accept the device from the country of registration.
  • And a current note: from 1 October 2026, motorcycles must also carry a high-visibility reflective vest as part of their compulsory equipment (RD 518/2026). The beacon does not replace the vest.

Why it changed: the calculation nobody wanted to make

Signalling with a triangle forces you to walk at least 100 metres along the roadway with traffic passing beside you; the United Kingdom even banned them on high-speed roads for that reason. The V-16 tackles both fronts: it is activated without leaving the cabin and adds virtual visibility to the physical light — the location of the stopped vehicle appears in navigation systems, mobility apps and variable message signs, so that drivers brake before they see you.

How it works: no mobile phone, no app and no subscription

  • Self-contained: built-in, non-removable GPS chip and SIM card. No phone, no apps, no pairing: switch it on and that's it.
  • Connectivity included in the price, with a minimum of 12 years guaranteed by the rules and no surcharge from the operators.
  • When activated, it sends the exact location to the DGT 3.0 platform, which distributes it to navigation systems, apps and signs. Without a data network, the light still works.
  • It does not call 112 or your insurer: it only signals and sends a position. You make the call.
  • Then Article 130.3 of the General Traffic Regulations applies: if the vehicle cannot resume its journey and there is a safe place outside, you get out on the side facing away from traffic; if it is not safe, you stay in the cabin with your seat belt fastened.
Connected V-16 beaconWarning triangle
Status from 1/1/2026Only legal meansNot valid for signalling
PlacementFrom inside, on the highest partOn foot, 100 m along the roadway
Warning to othersLight + position on DGT 3.0Reflected light only
Risk for the person signallingGet out of the car only if safeExposed to traffic
Approximate price8-25 €—

Where to keep it and how to place it

Three DGT rules that are always forgotten: keep it charged in the glove compartment or another accessible place in the vehicle — not in a closed trunk or at home; switch it on and place it from inside, on the highest part of the vehicle; and in buses or trucks, where the roof is out of reach, on the driver's door. Activate it once at home to check that it works and to know where it goes on the day you need it.

Before buying: certification is non-negotiable

There are more than two hundred models on the market, and the DGT is blunt: only the one that appears on its official list of certified devices is valid, all certified by IDIADA or LCOE, with the laboratory and certificate number engraved on the lens.

  • Check the DGT list before paying, not the photos in the listing: it is the only check that saves you from a surprise.
  • Be wary of subscriptions: if they ask for a monthly fee for it to “connect”, it is not the model required by the rules.
  • No registration with your details: no app and no sign-up in your name; when you buy it, the beacon is not linked to any person or number plate.
  • Where to buy it: certified connected V-16 beacon (the one in the car emergency kit), compare certified V-16 beacon models or, if you do not have one yet, reflective vest.

The fine: a minor offence and €80

Not carrying the V-16 beacon is a minor offence punishable with an €80 fine, the same amount that used to apply to anyone driving without warning triangles. That is the easy part: the real cost of going without it is standing on a road shoulder at night waiting for someone to see you. That is why the car emergency kit marks it as essential: it costs about as much as two dinners and is bought once.

Three myths circulating on social media

  1. “It tracks your movements.” It only transmits when activated, and what it sends is the location plus a technical identifier of the device itself: the AEPD confirms that there is no record linking the beacon to the identity of the person using it or to the number plate, and the rules prohibit additional functions.
  2. “You have to register it with your ID or install an app.” False: it does not need an application, a phone or personal details when you buy it.
  3. “It calls 112 on its own.” Also false. If there are injuries or the situation is serious, you call 112 and, if appropriate, your insurer's assistance service.

Ten-minute checklist for this week

  1. Check that your beacon appears on the official DGT list and that the certificate number is engraved on the lens.
  2. Charge it and leave it in the glove compartment; test it once and put it back charged.
  3. Keep the vest within reach — not under the luggage in the trunk — and your phone charged.
  4. Agree at home who gets out and on which side, or whether you simply stay inside with your seat belts fastened.
  5. Check the rest of the car kit: first-aid kit, flashlight, water and power bank, whatever keeps that call to 112 alive.

The beacon solves the signalling, not the rest of the scenario. The context is in the lessons from the 28 April blackout and the full list of what is compulsory and what is advisable in the car emergency kit for 2026. The basis — water, light and food for 72 hours — remains in the 72-hour basic emergency kit.

mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.titulo: Best long-lasting canned foods for emergencies (2026)
mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.resumen: Best long-lasting canned foods for emergencies: 9 products compared, which date to check on the packaging and the 5 common pantry mistakes.
mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.cuerpo:
The power goes out at 21:40 and the first thing you do is open the fridge to see how much is left. After twelve hours the freezer is already warm and, after thirty-six, the question is no longer what you fancy but what can still be eaten. At that point, a well-chosen preserved food is worth more than any gadget: food that lasts months or years without refrigeration, without power and without you doing anything.

That is the official criterion: the European Union Preparedness Strategy calls for 72 hours of self-sufficiency per household and Civil Protection recommends non-perishable food and water for three days. Spain does not lack food, it lacks a plan: the Food Waste Report in Spain 2024 (MAPA) puts what we throw away each year at 1.125 billion kilos or litres, with 97.5% in households and about 24 kilos per person. We buy food that ends up in the bin while the emergency reserve does not exist.

I compare nine long-life preserved foods available in any supermarket or on Amazon Spain: how long they last unopened, what each one is really good for and its weak point.

Best-before is not use-by: the date that decides whether you throw it away or not

AESAN devotes an entire campaign to separating the two concepts, and Regulation (EU) 1169/2011 governs them. Confusing them is the main reason for throwing away a reserve that is still good:

  • Best-before date — canned and jarred foods, pulses, rice, pasta, flour, oil, honey. It indicates how long the food keeps its quality. After that date it is still safe: it may lose texture or flavour, but it is not thrown away because of the date alone.
  • Use-by date — fresh meat and fish, certain dairy products, ready meals. That one cannot be stretched: do not consume it after the date.
  • In a blackout, the fridge is the first thing you lose. Fresh food and items with a use-by date go within 24–48 hours; preserved food is the last thing to leave the plan.

Tip: write the date on each jar or tin when you store it, keep the can opener in the same drawer and apply the FIFO rule —what comes in goes at the front; what is already there gets eaten first—. That way the reserve is renewed with your normal shopping instead of expiring in a cupboard.

Approximate shelf lives for unopened packs in a dry, cool, dark place: the date printed on the packaging is what sets the real shelf life.

Winner by category

  • For the 20-year drawer: the MRE-9 ration. The only one on the list with a stated shelf life of two decades: you buy it once and do not touch it until you need it.
  • For the pantry you use every day: tuna and sardines. They perform in an emergency and they perform in March: the best reserve is the one that gets eaten before it expires.
  • To eat without heat or water: sardines with nuts. If the plan depends on lighting something, it is not a plan.
  • For space and weight: the freeze-dried ration. 140 g per meal: it fits in the evacuation backpack and does not weigh down the cupboard.
  • For the kitchen without a fridge: the jar of pulses. Already cooked, no gas or soaking needed, cold or at room temperature.

Six storage rules decided before the blackout

  1. Dry, cool and dark. Never on the garage floor or next to the boiler: moisture dents cans and heat makes the fat in fish and nuts go rancid.
  2. Out of the sun. A can left in the light all summer tastes like cardboard.
  3. Damaged packaging, out. Dented, bulging, rusty or with the lid popped, it gets thrown away without debate, even if the date is good.
  4. Once open, fridge and use up. In warm conditions, hours; never leave an open jar “for tomorrow” on the counter.
  5. Manual can opener in the same drawer. No power means no socket, and no can opener means no dinner: it is the cheapest item in the kit.
  6. Trial run. A night without power using what you already have stored teaches you more than any list: you will discover that the can opener is missing, not the tuna.

Five mistakes that leave the pantry exactly as it was on day one

  1. Buying special “emergency food”. What you do not eat in normal life you will not eat in an emergency either, and it expires sooner: build the reserve with what you already eat.
  2. Storing it in the storage room or garage. A Spanish summer in a storage room is the worst enemy of preserved food.
  3. Not checking dates when shopping. Two identical cans, two different dates: take the one that lasts longest and note it on the drawer.
  4. Cooking only if there is power. If the whole plan needs the induction hob, there is no plan in a blackout: mix ready-to-eat products with products that only need hot water.
  5. Not knowing how much you have. An inventory on the fridge door, with dates, stops you from emptying the whole cupboard “just in case”.

With this you cover the flank that no torch can fix. The full setup is in how to store water and food at home and in rotating food by date; menus without power are in eating without power: 3-day menus; and what to do with food that spoils when refrigeration is cut off is in storing food without a fridge. The whole set fits into the basic 72-hour kit and the home or lockdown kit.

kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.titulo: Emergency kit for a baby: what to keep at home, by blocks (2026)
kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.resumen: What to keep at home for a baby when the power goes out or you have to evacuate: safe water, formula, hygiene without water, documents and cold. Checklist by blocks.
kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.cuerpo:
The power goes out at three in the morning, and what weighs most isn't the flashlight: it's the baby waking up. In a home with small children, the 72 hours of self-sufficiency recommended by the European Union Preparedness Strategy aren't measured in cans or batteries, but in bottles, diapers and safe water: things that, without power and running water, suddenly stop being automatic. This is the list for putting together a baby's emergency kit without duplicating anything and without overspending, because a good part of it is already at home.

The good news is that a baby doesn't need a giant separate kit: they need the family kit to have a drawer (or a bag) with their name on it. The Baby Kit page brings together 32 essentials at an estimated cost of around 90-170 €, and several of those products are already part of your daily routine — what you need to do is rotate them, not buy twice.

1. Eating and drinking without power

This is priority number one and has three parts:

  • Water for preparing formula. A baby counts as one more person: to the 3 liters per person per day you add the water you need for hygiene. Store water in closed bottles and have a purification method — purification tablets approved for use with infants, dosed exactly according to the instructions. With safe water, formula is prepared just as always.
  • Backup milk. If the baby takes formula, keep an unopened container of the same type they take now, with the best-before date clearly visible, and check expiry every three months. If breastfeeding, the item is a manual breast pump (it doesn't depend on power) and storage bags. Any guidelines for storing expressed milk are set by your midwife or pediatrician: write them in the kit folder, don't rely on memory.
  • Heating without electricity. A chemical bottle warmer works without gas or a plug in just a few minutes. A more homemade alternative: fill a wide-mouth thermos with hot water before the power goes out.

A public health detail worth remembering in any scenario: AESAN advises against raw milk without first boiling it because of the risk of pathogenic microorganisms. If an emergency puts you in front of a neighbor with cows and no power, that doesn't change.

2. Hygiene without running water

When tap water doesn't come through, the diaper-changing routine gets complicated — but not so much if the supplies are together:

  • Backup diapers (a pack of 20-25 in the current size) and cleaning wipes as a plan B for washing.
  • Watertight bags for dirty clothes and used diapers: without water, smell is the first problem and the bags contain it.
  • Washing bottles and nipples: if there's no mains water, wash with purified or boiled water and mild soap, and sterilize with cold-water tablets. You don't need electricity, you need a plan.
  • Barrier cream and mild soap in bar form — the bar lasts for months and doesn't melt like gel.

3. Health, temperature and documents

This is where an emergency gets expensive if you're not prepared:

  • Digital thermometer, oral rehydration solution with dosing syringe (for vomiting or diarrhea, the dosage is set by the instructions or your pediatrician) and nasal aspirator with saline solution: a cold that is a nuisance at home weighs more in a blackout without heating.
  • The watertight pouch with the health record, vaccination card and the baby's ID or passport, inside the kit — not in a drawer in another room. Include a child ID card with name, date of birth, allergies, medication and two contact phone numbers that don't depend on your mobile phone.
  • Favorite small toys and backup pacifiers in a watertight bag. It isn't a luxury: it's what separates an acceptable night from an impossible one.

4. Warm clothing and evacuation

Cold and leaving are the other two fronts:

  • Spare warm clothing: a sleep sack or one-piece pajamas in the current size plus one in the next size up, a hat, mittens and a children's emergency thermal blanket (or a small fleece blanket if you prefer). Babies lose heat faster than adults.
  • Ergonomic baby carrier: if you have to leave in a hurry, the baby carrier leaves your hands free for the backpack and for the other child. It's worth trying it out in daylight, not for the first time at three in the morning.
  • The rest of the scenario is covered by the household plan: meeting point and who picks up each child, and the evacuation bag ready by the entrance.

Checklist in a table

SectionEssentialYou already have it at home
Eating and drinkingUnopened container of formula, stored water, purification tablets, chemical warmerThermos, clean bottles, spoon
HygienePack of diapers, wipes, watertight bags, cold-water sterilizing tabletsMild soap, changing bag
HealthThermometer, oral rehydration solution, nasal aspirator, watertight pouch with documentsCream, gels, regular medication
Warm clothing and leavingSpare sleep sack, thermal blanket, tested baby carrierHat, mittens, fleece blanket

The four common mistakes

  1. Buying formula “just in case” of a different type from the one the baby takes now: they may reject it exactly when there is no alternative. Store exactly the same one.
  2. Spreading it around the house: if you have to leave in two minutes, something gets left behind. One drawer or one bag, all together and labeled.
  3. Not writing anything down: allergies, feeding schedule, pediatrician's phone number, where the backup supplies are. In a panic, nobody remembers anything.
  4. Relying only on the mobile phone: your only flashlight and source of information. A separate flashlight and a battery-powered radio solve what the phone can't.

The baby kit isn't put together in a single Sunday shopping trip: it's reviewed every three months to change diapers for size and check expiry dates, just as you go over the age-based checklist for babies and children and the basic 72-hour kit that supports the rest of the household. If you only do one thing today, make it this: put three days' worth of diapers, an unopened can of formula and the pouch with the documents into a bag. The rest will follow.

mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.titulo: Best water purifier for emergencies (2026): 7 filters compared
mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.resumen: Best water purifier for emergencies: 7 filters compared by price and use, what each method removes and the 5 mistakes that leave the water just as it was.
mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.cuerpo:
After the DANA, several municipalities were left without drinking water for days while bottles ran out in shops. And in a winter blackout the problem is not just electricity: within three days a household reaches the 72 hours of self-sufficiency recommended by the European Union Preparedness Strategy, and you decide whether to drink from the tap, the river or a bottle. That is where the emergency water purifier comes in: it is not for surviving in the jungle, it is so that any cloudy water can be drunk without ending up in the emergency room.

I compare seven real options from Amazon Spain —personal filters, gravity filters for home, a bottle with a filter and tablets— with their price, their ideal use and, above all, with what each one does not do. In emergency water, the mistake is not noticed today: it is noticed at 36 hours.

What Spanish regulations require and what a filter does not solve

In Spain, tap water is regulated by Real Decreto 3/2023, which sets the technical and health criteria and quality control: if it comes out of the tap, it is fit for drinking. The problem appears when supply is cut or when turbidity rises after a storm. That is where Protección Civil takes over: water for three days and, if there are doubts about quality, boiling or disinfecting. Its Family Emergency Plan guide expressly includes “water purification tablets” and “water (for 3 days)”.

And here is the part almost no one explains when buying:

  • Membrane filters (0.1–0.2 microns, depending on the manufacturer) remove bacteria, parasites and most microplastics. They do not remove viruses, which are much smaller, nor solvents, pesticides or hydrocarbons.
  • Chlorine or chlorine dioxide tablets do cover viruses, but they leave a taste and need contact time (minutes) before drinking, and they do not remove turbidity or chemicals either.
  • Boiling is the safest and crudest method: it kills everything living, but it does not remove dirt or heavy metals and it uses gas or batteries just when you do not have them.
  • No method fixes water with chemicals (a leak, a spill, diesel in the estuary). That water cannot be made potable: discard it.

The conclusion: a filter alone is never enough. The real combo is filter + tablets + the ability to boil. And do not forget the reserve —three liters per person per day—, set out step by step in how much water you need and how to store it.

Comparison: the seven emergency water purifiers

Winner by category (depending on the scenario you face)

  • Best for the evacuation backpack: the LifeStraw. It fits in a pocket, needs no replacement parts and works without learning anything: it is the one you buy if you only buy one.
  • Best for home: the gravity filter with bag. You fill it, hang it and it drips into a container: it gives several people drinking water without bending down to a puddle. The most comfortable with children and elderly people.
  • Best budget: the Membrane Solutions for 18,99 €. It does the job without spending more than a box of canned food.
  • Best value for money: the Waterflow 3-stage. With activated carbon it improves smell and taste: river or cistern water, without carbon, tastes bad and ends up being thrown away.
  • Best mandatory add-on: water purification tablets. Cheap, light and long-dated: the only thing on this list that covers viruses. Without them, the filter alone leaves a false “safe water”.

Three real uses in a Spanish household

  • After a DANA or a flood. It comes out cloudy or with a boil-water notice: filter for drinking and chlorine for surfaces. The cleaning order is in returning home after a flood.
  • Multi-day blackout. The cistern and water heater are still full, but the pump does not work. Filling jugs from the bathtub and filtering them is faster than carrying bottles upstairs. The full script is in the blackout kit.
  • Field or trail water. River, spring or camper van tank: the same filter works for the weekend. Which is exactly what most kits lack: equipment that never gets used.

The five mistakes that leave water just as it was

  1. Filtering very cloudy water directly. Dirt clogs the membrane and leaves it with no flow in minutes. First let it settle or prefilter it with a clean cloth, then filter it.
  2. Using the filter for water with chemicals (diesel, solvent, cistern treated with garden products). Nothing on this list removes it: discard the water.
  3. Buying tablets and not checking the expiry date. Tablets lose strength; keep them dry, in their closed jar, and write the date on the jar with a marker. As with pantry food: expired is not a reserve.
  4. Filtering and drinking without allowing contact time if you also use tablets: with cold water it takes several minutes. Write it on the jug label, so the thirstiest person does not decide it.
  5. Not testing it beforehand. Equipment that has never been used gets used wrong. Filter a glass of water at home and see how long it takes: in a blackout you will already know what it does.

What to buy today (and what to leave ready)

Minimum, cheap list: a three-stage filter for the home, a personal filter for each person who leaves the house, a strip of water purification tablets and a pot with a lid for boiling. That covers bacteria, viruses and the emergency route without electricity. The set fits in the basic 72-hour kit and, if you live in a flood-prone area, in the DANA and flood kit.

And an idea that saves money: the water reserve is still the first thing. A purifier does not replace the jugs, it extends them. The three-liter-per-person-per-day rule, containers and rotation in how to store water and food at home.

mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.titulo: Best heater for a power cut: 5 types to get through a blackout (2026)
mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.resumen: Butane, pellets or electric: which heater works when the power goes out, what each one costs per hour and why electric heating is useless in a blackout.
mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.cuerpo:
In April the blackout lasted a few hours at eighteen degrees. In January, the same outage at three in the morning is another matter: without heating a home loses degrees in a few hours, and the National Plan for preventive actions for low temperatures of the Ministry of Health says it bluntly: cold not only causes hypothermia, it also “favours traffic accidents and falls due to ice, or fires and carbon monoxide poisoning from gas stoves, braziers, etc.” That sentence sums up this article: choosing the best stove for when the power goes out is a matter of not turning the living room into a medical problem.

I compare the five types bought in Spain —butane, pellets, electric, catalytic and the no-stove option— with their cost per hour and what they need to work when the grid is down.

How much heat you need (and why heating the whole house is a trap)

A 4,000 W stove does not heat a flat: it heats its room. The strategy during a blackout is to reduce the volume —small room, closed door, people together—. Guide rule for a closed room of 15-20 m²:

  • Well insulated (thick walls, double glazing): 700-1,000 W is enough.
  • Poorly insulated or with high ceilings: it asks for 1,500-2,000 W.
  • Above 2,500-3,000 W in 15 m² is money burned and more risk.

And an idea that weighs more than watts: heating does not replace clothing. What works: clothing in layers + hot food + low stove; the breakdown is in dressing in layers in an emergency and the night plan in how to maintain body temperature without electricity.

Comparison: the five types of stove without power

Pellet stove6-8 kW · 1.2-1.6 kg pellets/h0,70-0,95 €Yes, but needs a plug for auger and fan
Electric heater (convector or split)2,000 W · 0,15-0,18 €/kWh0,30-0,36 €No ❌ (only with power or generator)
Butane catalytic stove (flameless)2,400-3,000 W · smaller cylinder0,30-0,45 €Yes ✅

Approximate prices for Spain: 12.5 kg cylinder at 15-18 €, pallet pellets at 0,45-0,60 €/kg and electricity at 0,15-0,18 €/kWh. They are for comparison, not for signing a contract.

Winner by category

  • Best for a real blackout: the butane stove with oxygen cut-off. It does not depend on anyone, heats in minutes and one cylinder lasts several nights: 4,200 W with automatic oxygen depletion cut-off (about 84 €). The cut-off prevents the stove from going out and continuing to burn in a closed room.
  • Best for a whole house: pellets, if you already have the stove and the pallet. It heats a whole floor and is cheap per hour, but almost all need a plug for the auger, fan and ignition: without power, they do not start.
  • Best combo cooking + heat: the portable butane stove (20-45 €). It is not a stove, but it heats water and food without turning on the home kitchen: in three days of outage it pays for itself with the first pot.
  • Best budget: the no-stove option. A survival thermal blanket (3-8 €), a reusable electric body warmer when the power returns and a warm sleeping bag get you through the night: less than a cylinder, and it cannot fail.

And the catalytic stove? It is the cleanest version of butane: it burns without a visible flame and gives softer heat, more pleasant in a small room. It is worth it if the person spending the day there is an older adult or a child; for a budget kit, the money is better spent on butane and a CO detector.

The serious mistake: buying an electric heater for the blackout

It is the most common mistake: a 2,000 W convector is cheap, silent and does not generate carbon monoxide, which is why it sells so well. The problem is that in a blackout there is no voltage and the electric heater becomes furniture. To make it work you would need a 1,500-2,000 W generator; what batteries can actually handle is in best power bank for a blackout and in emergency solar generator.

Data from the Spanish context: according to the CNMC Household Panel, 43.2% of households have contracted a power capacity of between 4 and 6 kW and spent an average of 47,8 € per month on electricity. With two 2,000 W convectors plugged in you are already at the limit of that capacity; in an outage that is not a bill problem: it is that there is no current to consume.

Carbon monoxide: the four rules that save the night

CO does not smell, does not sting and does not warn: initial symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea) are confused with a cold, and cases are concentrated from October to March, just when stoves are turned on. Official recommendations are identical across all administrations:

  • Ventilate twice a day, 15 minutes each time, even if it is cold. It is the literal indication of the Ministry of Health's cold plan.
  • Turn off electric and gas stoves during the night. Also from the cold plan: sleeping with the stove on is the decision most regretted.
  • Do not use camping stoves, barbecues, braziers or the kitchen oven inside the home, and do not cover ventilation grilles. It is the recommendation of the 112 services and Civil Protection.
  • Battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on the wall, one metre from the bed and away from the ceiling. It costs between 15 and 35 €: see CO detectors. No stove in this article is complete without it.

Checklist before the first cold snap

  • Butane stove with oxygen cut-off and two spare cylinders: the second always runs out the first night.
  • CO detector with new batteries and replacement date noted.
  • Tape and plastic to seal windows: a poorly sealed room requires double the power.
  • Blankets, warm sleeping bag and thermal clothing; lighters and long matches out of children's reach.
  • Food and water that do not need fire: three-day menus without cooking.

If the outage drags on, the stove is only one piece: the complete list is in the cold and winter kit and in the blackout kit.

mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.titulo: Best power bank for emergency kit 2026: 4 models and real mAh
mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.resumen: How much capacity you really need in a blackout: 4 charges per 20,000 real mAh, 4 models compared and the mistakes that drain the kit's battery.
mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.cuerpo:
The blackout of 28 April 2025 left half the country without power and phones at 2%. Most people solved it with the power bank they had charged in a drawer. But if the power goes out for several days, that drawer runs out: in 24-48 hours your phone becomes a glass weight, and with it streaming radio, maps, family WhatsApp and the phone flashlight. This is the guide to choosing the emergency power bank that actually keeps you going for 72 hours — with the real capacity you need, the honest figure brands hide (mAh) and four models compared.

How much capacity you really need for 72 hours

A modern smartphone has a 4,000-5,000 mAh battery. On a normal day, one full charge lasts; in an emergency you will use the phone much more (calls, WhatsApp, flashlight, maps), so the realistic estimate is 2 charges per day. On that basis:

  • 72 hours, 1 phone: 10,000-20,000 mAh.
  • 72 hours, 2 phones (couple or family): 20,000-30,000 mAh.
  • 7 days or more: 30,000 mAh + portable solar panel to recharge during the day.

There is a nuance no product listing tells you and that changes the purchase: the advertised mAh are not what reaches your phone. A 20,000 mAh battery at 3.7 V stores about 74 Wh; when converting to USB output (5-9 V) and with electronics losses, what actually arrives is between 13,000 and 14,500 mAh — that is, 65% to 72% efficiency, the range independent labs measure with known-brand units. In plain terms: a 20,000 mAh power bank gives 4 full phone charges, not the 8-10 the brochure suggests. With 10,000 real mAh (about 2 charges) you just get through 72 hours; with 4 charges, comfortably. That is why 20,000 mAh is the recommended minimum and not a whim.

Comparison: the 4 emergency power banks I recommend

Ordered by use case, not by price. All are listings verified on Amazon.es with the same criteria: published real capacity, USB-C input and output, and a price consistent with what they offer.

ModelCapacityOutputsApprox. priceBest for
High-capacity power bank ≥20,000 mAh with cables included20,000 mAh (74 Wh)USB-C + USB-A, dual output25-50 €The 72h kit standard: 4 phone charges and two devices at once.
External battery 10,000-20,000 mAh, two outputs10,000-20,000 mAhDual USB output20-40 €Second battery for your partner or child: redundancy for less than 30 €.
Compact power bank 10,000-20,000 mAh10,000-20,000 mAhUSB-C + USB-A15-35 €The one that stays in your bag daily: if it always goes with you, you never forget it.
Lightweight power bank + USB cable10,000 mAhUSB-C25-50 €Mountain and evacuation kit: lightweight and keeps your phone going for the weekend.

The winner for most people: the first one, 20,000 mAh with cables. It is the one used in the basic 72-hour kit, the blackout kit, the earthquake kit and the connectivity kit: four different scenarios have ended up choosing the same one, and that consensus says more than any brochure.

What to require from an emergency power bank (the checklist)

  1. Capacity: 20,000 mAh minimum — 4 full phone charges, the number that gets you through 72 hours without anxiety.
  2. Dual output — charge two people’s phones at once, or phone + radio, without taking turns.
  3. USB-C input and output — recharging the power bank itself takes 3-4 hours and it is the connector you already have at home. If it also supports Power Delivery (PD), it can charge tablets and some light laptops too.
  4. Real percentage indicator — the usual four LEDs lie halfway through the charge; a numeric display (or percentage) tells you how much is really left when you decide whether to turn on the light or not.
  5. Built-in LED flashlight — it costs no extra and in the kit it serves as a backup if your main flashlight runs out.
  6. Shock-resistant — it falls off the table at 3 a.m. in the dark; it has to keep working.

Typical mistakes with the kit’s power bank

  • Buying it discharged. The power bank is checked like the rest of the kit: 100% charged and rotated every 3-6 months. A battery that has been in the drawer at 10% for a year will not save you the night you need it.
  • Trusting the mAh on the label. 20,000 real mAh are 4 phone charges; if the price is suspiciously low, distrust the real capacity (with unknown brands it is common to deliver half).
  • Using it as a permanent tap. Full discharge and recharge extend cell life; keeping it plugged into the wall at 100% all year does it no favors.
  • Forgetting the cable. A power bank without a cable is an elegant brick. Store it with the battery, not in another drawer, and keep a spare if you depend on USB-C.
  • Overlooking flights. If you are going to evacuate by car it does not apply, but if you have to fly: IATA (and European EASA) allows up to 100 Wh without authorization (≈27,000 mAh), always in carry-on baggage and never in the hold; between 100 and 160 Wh you need airline permission, and above 160 Wh you cannot fly. A 20,000 mAh (74 Wh) travels without problems.

And if the blackout lasts more than three days

The power bank is the reserve, not the power plant: it runs out, full stop. To go beyond 72 hours, the combination that works is power bank + 30-50 W portable solar panel. In summer sun, a 30-50 W panel recharges a 20,000 mAh every 2-3 days (in winter, multiply by two or three); that way the phone and radio do not depend on the power coming back. You have the real watt calculations in portable solar panel for emergencies and the full combo in 72-hour solar generator. And do not forget the radio: official information comes via hand-crank radio, which does not use up your battery reserve.

The verdict

A 20,000 mAh power bank with USB-C and dual output is the 72h kit standard: 4 phone charges, 74 Wh (flies without paperwork) and 25-50 € well spent. If you have a partner or children, add a second 10,000-20,000 mAh one — the cheap redundancy that turns a scare into a minor detail. And remember the only rule that matters: it comes out of the drawer 100% charged and is rotated every 3-6 months. The full kit list, with the energy already sorted, is in the basic 72-hour kit.

mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.titulo: The best emergency radio with hand crank and solar panel (2026)
mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.resumen: Emergency radios with hand crank and solar panel compared: battery-free runtime, range, phone charging and which to choose for 72 hours.
mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.cuerpo:
When the power grid goes down, mobile phones lose signal and WiFi goes out. Radio is the ONLY device that can keep receiving official information for your area during a prolonged blackout. Don't underestimate it: it's your link to the outside world when everything else fails.

Why a hand-crank radio?

A mobile phone with a power bank lasts for hours (maybe a day). A hand-crank radio has INFINITE runtime: crank it for 3 minutes and you get 15-30 minutes of broadcast. The solar panel is the perfect complement: leave it in the sun and it charges itself.

Non-negotiable features

  • FM + AM + SW: Official stations use different bands. You can't choose. An emergency radio must receive ALL of them.
  • Portable and lightweight (<400g): If you have to carry it with you during an evacuation, it can't weigh like a brick.
  • USB charging: In addition to hand crank and solar, it must be able to charge via USB cable. It is the main charging method.
  • LED flashlight: A radio without a built-in flashlight is an incomplete radio.
  • USB to charge your phone: It works as a power bank. Your phone is your main communication tool; the radio keeps it going.

The best options for a 72h kit

The emergency radios with hand crank and solar panel that meet ALL the above requirements are:

2-IN-1 HAND-CRANK RADIO WITH SOLAR PANEL

Receives FM, AM, SW and NOAA (if you have it handy). Includes LED flashlight, SOS emergency light and power bank for your phone. Water-resistant IPX4 (withstands light rain). Weight: ~380g. Runtime: 30 min with full hand crank, 4h in low mode on battery.

HAND-CRANK EMERGENCY RADIO

Simpler but lighter (~300g). Works with hand crank, solar or AA batteries. Perfect if you only need the basics without complications. Includes flashlight and SOS mode.

The verdict

The emergency radio is the most underrated item in a 72h kit. Invest ~25-35€ in one that receives FM+AM and has a hand crank+solar panel. When the blackout comes, you'll appreciate every euro.

mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.titulo: The 7 best flashlights for a 72-hour emergency kit (2026)
mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.resumen: 7 emergency flashlights compared by real runtime (lumens and hours), price and durability: which one deserves a place in your 72-hour kit.
mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
A 72-hour kit without light is like a backpack with no bottom: nice-looking but useless. A flashlight is one of the first five items that appear in ALL civil preparedness guides in Spain, Europe, and the U.S. It is non-negotiable.

Why a flashlight (and not candles)?

Candles pose a fire risk you don't need during an emergency. A quality LED flashlight offers:

  • Instant power-on (no waiting for it to light)
  • Zero fire risk
  • Up to 100,000 hours of LED life
  • Adjustable brightness (full light to search for something, dim light to avoid blinding)

What you should demand from an emergency flashlight

  1. Water resistance (IPX7 or higher): A DANA won't warn you. If it rains inside the backpack, the flashlight must keep working.
  2. Minimum runtime of 8 hours: In low mode. If it only lasts 30 minutes in high mode, check the low mode.
  3. Rechargeable batteries or USB: Batteries run out and get forgotten. A USB one recharges with a power bank.
  4. SOS mode: A button that flashes in Morse. It can be the difference between being found and not.
  5. Hook or magnet: To leave it on the ceiling and keep your hands free.

The 7 flashlights we recommend for your kit

I have tested or researched them in depth. These are the ones that best balance quality and response for a 72-hour kit:

1. Waterproof LED flashlight with built-in power bank

The most practical option: it is the flashlight AND the external battery. You charge it with one cable and already have two kit items. Runtime: ~8h in low mode, ~1.5h in high. Water resistance: IPX7. Weight: ~200g.

2. Hand-crank flashlight with solar radio

If you're looking for an all-in-one solution: you turn the crank for 2 minutes and get 15 minutes of light. The radio lets you listen to official broadcasts if the network goes down. Ideal as a secondary flashlight.

3. USB-rechargeable LED headlamp

If you need to keep your hands free (changing a light bulb, searching in a backpack, helping someone), a headlamp is best. It goes on your head and doesn't fall off.

4. Magnetic emergency flashlight with dusk sensor

It sticks to any metal surface and turns on by itself when the house lights go out. Perfect for the storage room, fuse box, or fridge.

5. "Fireball"-type flashlight (EMERGENCY GLOBE)

No, it's not a weird Chinese invention. Spherical flashlights with a solar panel and pull switch have been in civil protection guides in Canada and Finland for years. 360° light (non-directional). Ideal for lighting an entire room.

6. Headlamp with basic night vision

For the more adventurous: it lets you see in total darkness with infrared light invisible to the human eye. It's a gadget you probably don't need... but if you ever need to move around your house at 3 a.m. without turning anything on, it's pure gold.

7. Kit of 3 small flashlights (redundancy strategy)

Three flashlights at ~5€ each, stored in different places in the backpack. If one gets lost, another works, and the third is for when a neighbor asks for one. Redundancy is the basis of preparedness.

The verdict

For a basic 72-hour kit: a rechargeable USB LED flashlight + a pack of 2 small flashlights as backup. Total investment: ~25€. It keeps you safe during the first 72 dark hours.

botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.titulo: Complete emergency first-aid kit: 15 must-have items (2026)
botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.resumen: What an emergency first-aid kit should contain and what you don't need: a block-by-block list for every household, expiry date checks and 8 mistakes that make it useless.
botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.cuerpo:
Health is the second block of the 72h kit (after water) and the one with the most variations depending on your family. Here is the universal base list and the adaptations for special cases.

The base first aid kit: 15 non-negotiable items

  1. Sterile gauze (pack of 4): To cover wounds without fibers getting in.
  2. Elastic bandages (3 units, 8 cm): To immobilize or hold gauze in place.
  3. Adhesive bandages (assorted sizes, 20 units): For small wounds and scratches.
  4. Antiseptic in single-dose units (10 units): Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine. Alcohol-free.
  5. Blunt-tipped scissors: To cut bandages or clothing if necessary.
  6. Tweezers: To remove splinters or debris from a wound.
  7. Paracetamol (500 mg and 1 g): Pain and fever. Always follow the package leaflet and do not combine it with other medicines without checking their summary of product characteristics.
  8. Anti-inflammatory (ibuprofen 400 mg): Inflammation and pain. Not suitable for everyone: allergies, stomach, kidney, or heart problems are contraindications. Check its summary of product characteristics (AEMPS) and confirm with a healthcare professional.
  9. Antihistamine (loratadine or cetirizine): Allergic reactions. Important if you live in an area with many plants or bees.
  10. Antidiarrheal (oralit + loperamide): Diarrhea in an emergency is much more dangerous than at home (dehydration).
  11. Antipyretics (children's paracetamol): If there are children at home.
  12. Nitrile gloves (pair): To protect yourself when treating someone.
  13. Emergency thermal blanket: Prevents hypothermia. Weighs 20 g and can save your life.
  14. Burn cream: Aloe vera gel or a specific cream. Burns are common in emergencies with improvised cooking.
  15. Family medical list: Names of regular medicines, allergies, blood type, emergency phone numbers.

Important: this list is for guidance only, not medical advice. Before taking any medicine, read the package leaflet and its summary of product characteristics (available on the AEMPS website) and, if you have doubts—pregnancy, children, chronic illnesses, or other medicines—consult a healthcare professional or pharmacist.

Adaptations by situation

With babies: add pediatric oral rehydration solution, a digital thermometer, extra pacifiers (if they are used to them), spare diapers.

With older adults: Chronic medication for 5 extra days (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid, heart). Include a manual blood pressure monitor.

With pets: External antiparasitic, veterinary collar (so they do not lick wounds), medications if chronic.

The verdict

A basic emergency first aid kit costs between 30-50€ if you buy everything new. But the most valuable part is not the kit itself: it is your family's chronic medication. If someone at home takes daily medication, those 5-7 days of reserve ARE the emergency kit.

alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.titulo: Emergency food: what to eat, how much to store, and how to rotate it without throwing anything away
alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.resumen: Which foods last for years and which expire soon: date-based rotation, order of consumption, and how to build a pantry you won't have to throw out.
alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.cuerpo:
Why food expires before the emergency

Water shortage is the priority, and you should not wait until you are intensely thirsty to look for it. Food is the second thing people forget when preparing a kit, and also the thing that spoils most often: people buy cans or special "emergency" tins that end up in the trash because they expire. The solution is simpler: the best emergency food is the food you already eat.

Many European and Spanish guides recommend a reserve of at least 72 hours; it is not a legal obligation. The key is not to buy "emergency food" but to rotate what you already eat: that way the reserve is used, replenished, and does not become a museum of cans.

The golden rule: buy to eat, not to store

The most effective method is FIFO (First In, First Out — first in, first out). It works like this:

  1. Buy an extra of what you already consume regularly: one more pack of pasta, two more cans of tuna, an extra packet of crackers.
  2. When you use the extra in your normal life, put it straight back into the reserve.
  3. Your emergency stock rotates by itself, without you having to think about dates or expiry dates.

This turns an "emergency reserve" into something that requires no management: it is simply your usual pantry with an extra 20-30%. If you already do your shopping every week, you do not need a special purchase: add one unit of what you already eat and let rotation do the rest.

Non-perishable foods: the list that actually works

Not all foods last the same amount of time. The dates in the table are approximate and refer to quality in a dry, cool pantry; the manufacturer's label takes precedence. They are not a safety guarantee if the packaging is damaged or has been stored badly.

FoodApproximate shelf lifeHow to store itSafety note
White rice (sealed)2 yearsAirtight container, dry, cool placeCooked rice: refrigerate and keep no more than 3-4 days
Honey2 years or more if well sealedClosed jar, not refrigeratedDo not give honey to children under 12 months due to risk of botulism
SaltPractically no expiry dateClosed container, away from moistureIt does not replace drinking water or medical care
Dry pasta2 yearsSealed package, away from lightOnce cooked, refrigerate and keep for 3-4 days
Low-acid canned foods (tuna, legumes, meat)2-5 yearsUnopened, cool, dry placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep for 3-4 days
High-acid canned foods (tomato, fruit)12-18 monthsUnopened, cool, dry placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep for 3-4 days
Saltine crackers or crackers6-9 monthsWell-sealed packageIf they become damp or smell bad, discard them
Nuts6-12 monthsAirtight container, cool placeRancid ones are noticeable by smell and taste; do not use them
Dark chocolate6-12 monthsAway from heatHeat bloom is not dangerous, but it loses quality
Powdered milk3-5 years unopened, depending on packagingDry place; once opened, follow the labelDo not use expired milk for a baby
Energy bars6-12 monthsIndividually wrapped, unopenedCheck allergens before storing them
Brick-pack brothThe date on the package; usually around 1 yearUnopened, cool placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep for 3-4 days

What people forget: salt keeps practically indefinitely and honey lasts a long time if well sealed, but neither replaces a varied diet or hydration. Salt does not "prevent fainting": if someone feels dizzy or is dehydrated, assess the situation and seek help; do not give spoonfuls of salt.

How much food for 72 hours: a practical reference

There is no single figure: it depends on whether you have a kitchen available or not. If the blackout leaves the fridge not working but you can heat canned food over a fire, you need fewer ready meals. If you have no safe way to cook, you need everything ready to eat.

Scenario1 person (72 h)2 people (72 h)Family of 4 (72 h)
With a safe cooking setup3-4 main servings + 2-3 snacks + 100 g nuts6-8 servings + 4-6 snacks + 200 g nuts12-16 servings + 8-12 snacks + 400 g nuts
Without cooking (ready to eat)5-6 ready servings + 4 snacks + 150 g nuts10-12 servings + 8 snacks + 300 g nuts20-24 servings + 16 snacks + 600 g nuts

A family of 4 needs approximately 20-24 ready servings, snacks, and nuts for 72 hours without cooking. This is a reference, not a prescription: adjust according to ages, appetite, medication, and special needs. The cost depends on the supermarket and brands; you do not need to buy "survival" products to cover it.

The "double packet" rule in practice

The simplest method that works does not require inventories or dates. Every time you go to the supermarket, apply these rules:

  • Canned foods: if you buy a pack of 4 cans of tuna, add 2 more. The extra ones are your reserve; do not separate them from the pantry.
  • Pasta or rice: if you use a 500 g package a week, keep another one closed. One is consumed, the other restocks.
  • Crackers or biscuits: an extra package. They are the first-day snack, when you still do not want to open a can.
  • Nuts: an extra bag. They expire before canned foods, so they go first in the rotation.

With normal shopping and a little foresight, a family can have the complete reserve without a huge outlay. You do not need to fill a cupboard all at once: rotation does the work.

When to check the reserve: a practical schedule

You do not need a calendar or alarms. Do the check every time the clocks change (March and October), just as you would with remote-control batteries:

  • Check dates: 2 minutes. Look at the dates on nuts, crackers, powdered milk, and canned foods.
  • Complete what is missing: if something has expired, replace it with a new one and put it at the front.
  • Replenish what has been used: if the reserve has gone down (because of a trip or outing), complete it with your next shop.
  • Verify special needs: if there are babies, allergens, or restricted diets, check that the stock is still valid and sufficient.

Preparedness is a habit, not a one-off act. Checking twice a year takes less than 10 minutes and prevents throwing food away or discovering a problem when there is no supermarket left.

Common mistakes with emergency food

1. Buying special "emergency food." Freeze-dried meals can last for years, but they also cost more and do not always match what you eat. With canned foods and dry foods you already consume, you have a reserve that rotates and is not wasted.

2. Having nothing ready to eat. If the power goes out and you do not have a safe cooking setup, unopened cans will not solve dinner. Keep bars, crackers, and nuts for the first day.

3. Storing food in a hot or humid place. Heat and humidity degrade packaging and food. Choose a cool, dry, dark place; if the pantry gets very hot in summer, find another spot.

4. Forgetting salt and hydration. Salt is useful for cooking, but it is not a medicine and does not by itself prevent fainting. In an emergency, water and medical care come first.

5. Not thinking about dependents. Babies (formula or infant milk), older people (soft or special diets), pets, and people with allergies have their own needs. Each one needs their own reserve and check.

How much does the setup cost?

The cost depends on the store, the brands, and what you already have at home. There is no fixed figure: 12-24 main servings, snacks, nuts, pasta, crackers, and broth can cost from a normal shop to quite a lot more if you choose prepared products. Start with what you consume and add one extra unit; you do not need to set up a restaurant pantry.

Buying canned foods: Search for assorted canned foods on Amazon →

Buying energy bars: Search for energy bars on Amazon →

Buying nuts in bulk: Search for mixed nuts on Amazon →

Food inside the 72h kit

Food is only one piece of the puzzle. If you want a complete pack with water, light, power, and food, the Basic 72-Hour Kit has everything verified. For specific scenarios, the blackout kit includes emergency cooking, and the DANA kit adds supply protection.

And if you only want the food without the rest, apply the double packet rule on your next supermarket shop. In two weeks you will have the 72 h reserve, without spending on "emergency food" and without throwing anything away.

Do canned foods really expire?

For canned foods, the date usually indicates quality rather than safety: an intact can with no dents at the seams, no rust, no bulging, and no leaks may keep its quality beyond the "best before" date, but that does not authorize adding years to the date. If in doubt, discard it. But do not use that as a general rule: if the can is dented, bulging, smells bad, or releases gas when opened, discard it. When in doubt, do not risk it.

Can you cook without electricity or gas?

Yes, but you need a safe heat source and ventilation. A camping stove should only be used outdoors or in a well-ventilated space; never inside a home, a tent, or a car, because of the risk of carbon monoxide. Without a safe cooking setup, eat ready-to-eat foods and do not improvise with fuels.

What should you do if there are babies or allergens?

For babies, always follow the label on formula or infant milk and the preparation instructions; do not use expired products and discard any leftover after a feeding. If there are allergies, keep foods labeled as free from the allergen and check the labels every time: formulations change. For medical diets, consult a professional before setting up the reserve.

If you found this article useful, share it with someone who lives alone. A person without a reserve is the one who suffers most in the first 24 hours of any emergency.
