starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.titulo: Starlink during a power outage: setting it up, powering it, and whether it's worth it (2026)
starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.resumen: Practical guide to Starlink in emergencies: actual power consumption, how to power it without the grid, cost, installation, and which alternatives to stack before buying.
starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.cuerpo:
When the power goes out across an entire area, the first thing that fails is not the fridge: it is information. The router goes down, the phone loses data, and local networks become saturated. At that moment many people think of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite constellation that promises internet from any point with a clear view of the sky. This article is the practical guide: what Starlink solves in a 72-hour emergency, what it does not solve, how much it consumes and how to power it when there is no power grid, so you can decide sensibly whether it deserves a place in your preparedness plan — or whether something simpler and cheaper is enough.

The official recommendation is the usual one: the European Union Preparedness Strategy calls for households to have supplies for 72 hours, and the Directorate-General for Civil Protection and Emergencies insists on keeping a reliable source of information during any incident. Starlink can be that source, but only if you are clear about how to keep it running without a plug. Let's take it step by step.

What Starlink is (and why it comes up in every emergency)

Starlink is a constellation of low-orbit satellites that provide broadband internet without relying on terrestrial infrastructure: there is no need to lay fibre and no mobile phone towers are involved. You only need three things: a terminal with a clear view of the sky, an active data connection through its network and electrical power to run it. That last condition is the one to remember, because it is often missing exactly when you need it most.

In an emergency scenario, that architecture has a specific advantage: even if the power plants, substations or mobile towers in your area are out of service, the satellites are still up there. If the local power grid is down but the satellite operator's infrastructure is working, you can restore connectivity in minutes. It is exactly the opposite of what happens with the mobile network, which depends on towers with limited battery backup and generators.

What Starlink is NOT: three mistaken expectations

Before you spend money, it is worth dismantling three common ideas:

  • It is not a cheap emergency backup plan. The terminal is a serious purchase and the monthly fee is recurring. If you are not going to use it day to day, it makes no sense to buy it 'just in case': you will have spent money on a piece of equipment that loses value in a drawer while your 72-hour plan is still missing the basics (water, power, first-aid kit, radio).
  • It does not work blindly or indoors. It needs line of sight to the sky: narrow balconies, inner courtyards with high walls or dense forest noticeably degrade the signal.
  • It does not replace official radio or 112. For official alerts and Civil Protection warnings, the route is still the emergency radio and national emergency channels; for real emergencies, 112. Starlink gives you additional paths (messaging, checking sources, calls over data), not a replacement.

That said, there are scenarios where it completely changes the situation: evacuations to rural areas without coverage, work in the mountains, houses on industrial estates or villages with poor mobile coverage, and of course long blackouts where the mobile network becomes saturated with people trying to call.

The important part: how much it consumes and how to power it without the grid

Here is the question that really matters. A typical residential Starlink terminal consumes around 60-75 W in active use and a little more than 20-40 W in standby, depending on the model and whether it is in sleep mode. Translated into a three-day blackout, with reasonable use of about 10-12 hours a day, you are talking about between 0.7 and 1.2 kWh per day… and that is where most plans break, because that comfortably exceeds the capacity of almost any handheld power bank.

The realistic routes, in order of practicality:

  • Power station. This is the serious option: a 1,000-2,000 Wh battery with 220 V output gives you one or two days of Starlink plus the router, lights and phone charging. Turn it on only when you need it and put the terminal in standby to stretch the margin. The Electricity Kit covers the selection, and the article on portable solar panels explains how many watts you really need to recharge it with solar.
  • Portable solar panel. With a well-oriented 100-200 W panel, a decent sunny morning returns a good part of a full day's consumption. It is the combination that lasts the most days, but it depends on the sky: on a stormy day or with heavy cloud cover, generation drops, and that is where the battery buffer comes in.
  • Large power bank as short reserve. A 20,000 mAh or larger power bank with 65 W output (the 20,000 mAh model in the kit is an example) powers the terminal for a few hours: it is enough for a quick look at maps and warnings, not for working or leaving it on all night.
  • Car alternative (with care). Some terminals work with 12 V vehicle adapters. Use it with the engine running or with a monitored auxiliary battery: leaving the vehicle draining the starter battery is a reliable way to end up without a car and without internet at the same time.

Golden rule of thumb: Starlink is the last link in the power chain, not the first. First you secure water, power and heating or cooling; then communications; Starlink comes into that third layer, along with the phone and the radio.

What it really costs, without surprises

We are talking about two separate items, and it is worth not mixing them:

  • Equipment (one-off). The terminal is around 500-700 € for the standard residential model and goes above that figure for mobile or higher-performance versions. Add accessories depending on the installation: roof or mast mount, a long extension cable if the good window is far away, and a container or carrying case if you are going to move it.
  • Subscription (monthly). In Spain the residential plan is around 45-60 € per month, with portable plans somewhat more expensive because of use while moving. Cancelling and reactivating is possible, but with a repositioning cost in some cases: read that before, not after.

The total figure for the Starlink Kit (terminal + accessories + one year of service) is easily the budget of a family trip or more. The useful question is not 'can I afford it?', but 'what other gap in my preparedness plan does this money leave uncovered?'. If your first-aid kit is empty and your basic kit does not exist, prioritise that first; it is all in the basic 72-hour kit.

Setting it up in 30 minutes: commissioning

Home installation is simple, and the time to test it is NOW, on a good day, not with the power off:

  1. Choose a location with a clear view of the sky. Mount the terminal on a roof, high balcony or large window facing a wide angle of the sky. The right mounting bracket prevents the first gust of wind from bringing it down.
  2. Connect it and let it calibrate. The terminal orients itself and searches for satellites; the app tells you whether the position is good. If the app reports poor signal at the first location, raise or move the terminal before accepting it.
  3. Power it from your backup system. Check that it starts with the power station and note how many Wh it uses in one real hour of use. That figure, measured by you, is worth more than any internet table for planning your days of autonomy.
  4. Test the use cases that matter to you: family video call, checking the warnings map, messages. Check whether your home router also starts from the battery — if not, you will have WiFi with nothing behind it.
  5. Leave EVERYTHING labelled and accessible: cables, adapters and manual in a waterproof bag with the terminal. In a night-time blackout, no one improvises well.

A safety detail: if there is a thunderstorm or a severe weather warning, disconnect the outdoor terminal. You can check the official AEMET warnings… using Starlink itself while there is power, of course.

Redundancy: Starlink should not stand alone

No single system saves an emergency, and satellite is no exception: a tree fallen on the antenna, a sandstorm or a failure in the constellation leave you without a route. Sensible preparedness stacks independent routes, in this order of increasing cost:

  1. Emergency radio powered by batteries, hand crank or solar — official information without internet, at almost zero cost. Base of the Communication Kit.
  2. Phone with coverage and data SIM — if the local tower holds up. The analysis of which data SIM survives a blackout best and of emergency 4G routers cover this layer.
  3. Lightweight satellite messaging — devices such as a satellite messenger that send position and short messages without mobile coverage, always with a clear view of the sky: the most reliable way to say 'I'm okay' when nothing else works.
  4. Starlink — full bandwidth, the last step and the most power-hungry.

The complete philosophy — when to combine each route and in what order — is developed in the companion guide Emergency connectivity: Starlink, radio and satellite and in how to communicate without a mobile network. This article focuses on making sure that, if you decide to include Starlink, it actually works.

Coverage and legality in Spain

Two clarifications that save trouble:

  • Coverage. Residential service availability in Spain is not uniform: there are areas with quotas or waiting lists and others where portable service has restrictions on use while moving. Check coverage with your exact address BEFORE buying the terminal; official verification is done on the operator's website and saves you from paying for equipment you cannot activate.
  • Installation. Mounting an antenna on the roof or façade of a community building subjects the work to the community's rules and, in heritage areas or on accessible rooftops, to additional procedures. On isolated roofs and detached houses it is much more straightforward, but check the municipal ordinance again if you have doubts.
  • Responsible use. Even though the terminal depends on a private network, in an emergency your consumption still counts: if there is network congestion, prioritise short messages and voice calls over streaming transmissions. The same logic as with 112: not overloading is part of being prepared.

Checklist: don't buy it until you can answer this

QuestionIf the answer is 'no'…
Do I already have water, power, first-aid kit and food for 72 h?…finish the basic kit first. Starlink is a luxury for a complete plan.
Do I have enough power for 1 kWh a day without the grid?…you need a power station or solar panel before a terminal.
Have I checked coverage with my address?…do not buy the equipment yet.
Do I have a secondary communication route (radio, SIM, messenger)?…build the basic redundancy of the communication kit.
Have I tested everything on a good day, not during the emergency?…set aside a weekend afternoon for the full test.

The four usual mistakes

  1. Buying the terminal and not the power. It is mistake number one: the blackout arrives, the terminal starts and the battery runs out in a few hours. Calculate your Wh first, then buy.
  2. Installing it on the day of the blackout. Calibration, location and cables are tested with sun and time. On the day of the emergency, you only turn on what has already been tested.
  3. Forgetting the router. Starlink gives you a connection, but if your router does not start from the battery, the home WiFi is still dead. Check that the whole chain (terminal + router + mobile phone) is powered.
  4. Getting complacent and removing the radio. Satellite connectivity is one more layer, not the base. Battery-powered radio and 112 remain the backbone of official information.

In short: Starlink in an emergency is an excellent tool for those who already have the basic layers covered and can power it without the grid. Start there — lessons from real blackouts and the first 30 minutes of a blackout show that information comes first — and decide with the complete plan in front of you: Starlink Kit if power is already sorted, or better still keep comparing alternatives in the blog guide if it is not.

panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.titulo: Portable solar panel for emergencies: 3 types and 5 mistakes (2026)
panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.resumen: Portable solar panel for emergencies: types, real watts and scenario comparison, with 5 mistakes that make it useless. Official sources.
panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.cuerpo:
When the power goes out on your street —or across half your neighbourhood—, the bottleneck is rarely food or water: it's energy. Your phone dies, the router goes down and the fridge stops keeping things cold. A portable solar panel is the cleanest way to replace that energy for as long as the blackout lasts: no petrol, no noise, no fumes and no need to wait for fuel deliveries. That said, buying “a panel” blindly is the best way to end up with something useless just when you need it. Here we explain which type you need, how much energy it really delivers and which mistakes to avoid.

What a portable solar panel is (and what it is not)

A portable solar panel is a surface of photovoltaic cells, usually foldable, that converts sunlight into direct current electricity. You cannot use that electricity directly at home: you have to store it in a battery (a power station or a battery bank with a charge controller) and from there draw the 220 V or USB ports that power your devices.

  • It is not a generator: on its own it will not run a washing machine or a tabletop fridge. It needs a battery in between.
  • It only produces during the day: the energy is generated in daylight and consumed at night, so system design is half the battle.
  • It does not depend on the grid or fuel: as long as there is sunlight, there is charge. That is its advantage over a fuel generator.

How much energy you really need

Before you look at watts, ask yourself the right question: which devices do I want to keep running, and for how long? The table below gives approximate consumption and runtime figures for a 500 Wh battery (half a kilowatt-hour of usable capacity), a common size for home power stations:

DeviceApproximate consumptionRuntime with 500 Wh
Phone (full charge)10–15 Wh per chargeDozens of charges
Laptop50–70 Wh per chargeAbout 6–8 charges
Router or 4G modem10–15 W continuousSeveral days in cycles
10 W LED bulb10 W continuousDozens of hours
12 V portable fridge40–70 W in cyclesHalf a day without recharging
Hand-crank radio charger0 W (generated by hand)Permanent backup

Notice the pattern: lighting and connectivity are cheap to maintain; the fridge is expensive. If your priority is staying informed and reachable, a small panel is enough. If you want to keep food fresh, you need a considerably bigger system. For the full calculation by scenario, take a look at how many watts a portable solar panel really needs.

The three types of panel (and which one is right for you)

  • Rigid monocrystalline: more watts per euro and more efficient, but it takes up space and does not fold. Worth it if you are going to install it permanently on a balcony or in a van.
  • Folding travel panel (PET or ETFE): folds like a wallet, weighs only a few kilos and fits in a car boot or a cupboard. It is the star format for an emergency kit, because what matters is not having a panel, it is having it where you are when the power goes out.
  • All-in-one (panel + built-in battery): total simplicity and a good companion for the sofa or a camping table, although the battery tends to be smaller.

When comparing, look beyond the watts: cell type (monocrystalline versus polycrystalline), water resistance (IP rating), the connectors it comes with (MC4, XT60 or a universal DC cable) and, above all, whether it is compatible with the battery you already have. A great panel that will not connect to your battery is worthless.

Comparison by scenario: what power rating to go for

ScenarioRecommended panelRecommended batteryOn the site
Phone, radio and lights only20–60 W folding200–300 WhBlackout kit
Light remote work for 72 h (phone + laptop + router)100–200 W folding500–1000 WhElectricity kit
Home with a fridge and proper light bulbs300–600 W (two panels)2000 Wh or moreProfessional kit
Balcony or fixed caravan100–200 W rigidDepends on useHome kit

How much a panel produces per day (the figure nobody advertises)

The watts in the catalogue are instantaneous power under laboratory conditions, not daily energy. In practice, in Spain a well-oriented 100 W panel usually delivers around 300–500 Wh per day in summer, and considerably less in winter, under overcast skies or with partial shade. The useful rule: assume real output well below the figure on the box and design with a margin. A cloudy day is not a panel blackout, but it does cut output a lot.

How to get the most out of it on the day of the blackout

  • If there is advance warning, charge the battery beforehand: starting with the battery at 100 % buys you half a day of leeway.
  • Orientation and angle: facing the sun, at an angle of about 30–45°. A panel in shade produces close to zero, not “a little less”.
  • Time of day: it produces mainly from 10:00 to 17:00; that is the window to use for charging.
  • Order of priority: first information and communication (phone, router, radio), then lighting and, if there is any left over, the fridge.
  • Switch off and disconnect: devices on standby also draw power; switching off what you do not need can extend runtime by several hours.

The five mistakes that make your panel useless

  • Buying a panel without a battery and discovering that it will not run anything at 220 V.
  • Looking only at the watts and forgetting the battery's Wh: the system is panel plus battery.
  • Leaving the panel behind a window pane: glass cuts a large part of the output.
  • Storing the battery discharged for months; the cells will suffer when you need them most.
  • Not checking connectors and compatibility until the day of the blackout.

What to buy: three entry points

  • Budget entry point: a small 20–40 W folding panel, designed to keep phones, flashlights and the radio charged. It is the one recommended by the blackout kit and sits in the 40–80 € range: view portable solar panel on Amazon.
  • Recommended option for 72 h: a 100–200 W folding panel with high-efficiency cells, which can already run a laptop and a portable fridge without drama: search for 200 W folding solar panels.
  • Complete solution: a solar generator with the panel included (300–500 Wh battery), all in one backpack. In the 250–450 € range and ready to connect: search for portable solar generators.

If you already have the battery and just want to expand, search directly for 100 W folding solar panels. And if the foreseeable emergency is a long outage lasting several days, the panel is only one piece: review it as part of the solar generator for emergencies and the guide to power banks for the emergency kit.

Where it fits into your preparedness

A portable panel does not live on its own: it lives inside a kit. In the basic 72-hour kit, electrical power is one of the essential categories alongside water, light and communication. In the electricity kit you will find the complete combination of panel, battery and accessories, and if the blackout coincides with a DANA or a weather warning, it is worth reviewing the first 30 minutes of a DANA blackout before you even connect anything. For when it is time to preserve food, here is what keeps without a fridge and what to throw away, and if the night drags on, the best stove for getting through the night without power.

Official sources

  • IDAE (Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving) — official information on self-consumption and energy efficiency.
  • European Commission — Preparedness Union Strategy — the European recommendation to have 72 hours of self-sufficiency.
  • Red Eléctrica de España — official data on supply and grid operation.

With a panel, a battery and a little discipline, three days without power stop being an energy problem and become an organisational problem. And that is always something you can prepare for.

nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.titulo: Portable cooler for emergencies: how long it lasts without power (2026)
nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.resumen: Portable cooler for emergencies: types, actual power consumption, off-grid power, and AESAN's 4-hour rule to avoid throwing away food.
nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
Three days without power at home and the first thing that spoils is the fridge: meat, fish, milk, leftovers. Keeping food under control is one of the most reassuring things when a long blackout hits, a DANA leaves a neighborhood without supply, or a storm brings down the line. An emergency portable fridge does not replace your refrigerator, but it buys you time: it keeps food below the recommended temperature while the grid comes back.

In this article we explain which type suits you depending on the scenario, how much energy it really uses, how to power it when there is no outlet, and what AESAN says about when food must be thrown out. At the end you have a checklist to get everything ready before the power goes out, because once the current is gone you can no longer freeze anything.

What is a portable fridge and what is it not?

A portable fridge is an insulated box with a compressor, heating element or absorption pump that lowers the temperature inside. It runs on 220 V (the household outlet), 12 V (the car cigarette lighter) or, with the right adapter, a portable battery or a solar panel. It is used in the car, in the garage, in the country house or on the balcony of the emergency kit.

What it is not: a substitute for the domestic freezer. Nor is it a quiet-compressor camper van fridge that cools to −20 °C all week without power: every model has a limit, and that limit depends on the outside temperature, how many times you open the lid and the power it receives.

The three types, in a table

TypeHow it coolsBestWorst
CompressorSame principle as your home fridge, with gas and motorIt actually cools, withstands outside heat and lowers the temperature considerablyThe most expensive and the heaviest
ThermoelectricPeltier effect: a plate that cools one side and heats the otherCheap, light, no moving parts, almost no maintenanceCools little: about 15–20 °C below ambient, not suitable for freezing
AbsorptionHeat applied to an ammonia solutionAlmost silent and runs on gas or the car's heating elementVery sensitive to tilting, consumes quite a lot and is uncommon

The practical rule: if what you need is to keep food cold for several days with little energy, choose compressor. If it is a weekend extra with ice and cold packs, a thermoelectric may be enough. And if what you carry is medication that cannot exceed a certain temperature, the criteria change: reliability rules there, not price.

How much energy it uses and how long it lasts off-grid

Consumption depends on size, insulation and climate, but as a rough guide, a medium-sized compressor fridge does not consume continuously: the compressor cycles, with peaks of tens of watts and rest periods. Thermoelectric models do tend to consume more steadily while switched on. Before buying, check the model's energy label and multiply it by the hours you want to cover; that tells you what battery you need.

In portable battery terms: a portable solar panel with a power station of medium capacity can keep a compressor fridge running for much of the day if it gets sun, while a normal powerbank is only good for short bursts or very efficient models. Something similar happens with the car: the 12 V socket is convenient, but do not drain the starter battery, because that is what will start the vehicle when you need to leave.

The four-hour rule (what AESAN says)

The Spanish Agency for Food Safety and Nutrition makes it clear in its recommendation after blackouts: as long as the home fridge stays below 5 °C for less than four hours without opening the door, in principle no food needs to be discarded; after those four hours, perishables must be thrown away (meat, fish, chicken, eggs, milk, fresh cheese and leftovers). The freezer maintains freezing temperature for at least 24–48 hours without being opened, and food that still has ice crystals can be refrozen.

That is where the portable fridge comes in: it serves as a bridge for the most delicate foods right when the fridge stops being reliable. And a detail that AESAN repeats and that is hard to believe: never taste food to see if it is still good; neither appearance nor smell is a guarantee. To learn how to keep eating without cold, see our guide to keeping food without a fridge or cold and the menu for three days without power.

What to put inside (and what not to)

  • Goes in: milk and dairy products you will consume soon, eggs, meat and fish already portioned, leftovers from the previous meal, fresh cheese, cut fruit and refrigerated medication if there is any.
  • Stays out: canned goods, soft drinks, alcoholic beverages, chocolate and condiments: AESAN reminds us that many foods we keep in the fridge do not need it and keep perfectly well at room temperature.
  • Useful at the bottom: cold packs or ice packs frozen in advance. They give the initial boost and extend runtime when energy is scarce.
  • For measuring: a fridge thermometer with min/max recording. Without it you are guessing, and if you have medication or baby food, guessing is not good enough.

If a long outage is forecast, the sensible thing is to prioritize: first what spoils soonest, then the rest. That priority order is the same one we use in expiry control and rotation.

How to use it well during the emergency

Performance comes down to the details. Pre-cool the inside with ice or frozen bottles before loading it, so you do not spend the first hour of battery bringing the empty space down to temperature. Close the lid immediately and resist the temptation to peek every few minutes: every opening lets heat in. If it is in the car, keep it away from direct sunlight and the dashboard; the outside temperature sets its ceiling. And if you are going to power it with a portable battery, leave some margin: that same battery also lights, charges the phone and powers the radio in the communication kit.

Five common mistakes

  • Buying a thermoelectric expecting compressor performance: if you really need to lower the temperature, the Peltier plate falls short when the ambient temperature rises.
  • Relying on opening it to check: opening the fridge or portable fridge to “take a look” shortens runtime and raises the temperature of all the contents.
  • Leaving the 12 V socket on all night with the car parked: you can end up without enough battery to start just when you need it most.
  • Storing food that is already expired or half-eaten: nothing gets fixed inside the fridge; it only gets cold.
  • Not having a thermometer: without a temperature reading, there is no possible decision about what to keep and what to throw away.

Checklist to get it ready before the blackout

  • Freeze cold packs or water bottles in advance; if a storm is forecast, that is the moment.
  • Set the fridge to the minimum necessary setting and do not open it while the outage lasts: you gain hours of margin.
  • Check that the portable fridge and its cables are accessible, not buried in the storage room.
  • Keep the portable battery charged and locate the 12 V cable.
  • Place the fridge thermometer and note the starting temperature.
  • Decide in advance what to consume first: perishables first, always.
  • Review the rest of the inventory with the blackout kit and the home kit.

Official sources

  • AESAN — What to do with food in the fridge and freezer after a power outage.
  • General Directorate of Civil Protection and Emergencies (MITECO) — information and self-protection plans.
  • AEMET — weather warnings to know in advance when an outage may arrive.

Where it fits into your preparation

The portable fridge is one more piece of the setup, not the heart of the kit. It fits into the basic 72-hour kit and complements the flashlights and emergency solar power. If the scenario is a DANA-type storm, also review the sequence for the first 30 minutes; and if you are going to buy one, compare models with honest searches: 12 V / 220 V compressor portable fridge, reusable cold packs, min/max fridge thermometer and small portable fridge with cold packs.

mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.titulo: Best emergency data SIM (2026): which provider saves you
mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.resumen: Emergency data SIM: how to choose a provider, set up two different networks and check coverage before a power outage in Spain.
mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.cuerpo:
When the power goes out, the first thing many people check is not the fridge: it's whether they have a signal. A long blackout, a DANA or a strong storm can leave mobile phone towers without power, and then each network shows its true colors. This article does not aim to declare a universal “best operator” — no such thing exists — but to give you criteria for choosing the best data SIM for emergencies in Spain and, above all, for not depending on a single network.

What is the first thing to fail when the power goes out?

Mobile base stations do not work by magic: they need electricity. When the outage hits, each tower stays alive as long as its battery or generator lasts — in practice, a few hours — and then it goes down. Towers physically damaged by wind, trees or flooding take much longer to come back, because they need repair, not just recharging. That is why in a wide blackout coverage degrades in waves: first 4G disappears in outlying neighborhoods, then only some areas are left with signal.

There are two additional effects worth anticipating. The first: the network becomes congested. Everyone wants to notify their loved ones at the same time, and calls take up a lot of bandwidth; messaging and SMS use much less and often get through first. The second: the rest of the services also depend on the power grid. Red Eléctrica de España (REE), the system operator, publishes the status and incident notices, and 112 emergency centers run on their own backup power: 112 is called only in a real emergency, never just to “find out what's going on”.

What “best SIM” really means

The honest answer depends on three things: where you live, where you work and where you travel. An operator that wins on your street can be the worst in your family's village. That is why this article is not going to sell you a winner: it is going to give you the method.

Type of SIMHow it worksWhen it fits
Operator with its own networkDeploys and maintains its own tower infrastructure.You want priority and proven coverage without relying on third parties.
Virtual operator (MVNO)Rents a large operator's network; they tend to invest less in their own rural coverage.You are looking for price and only need data where coverage is already good.
Secondary backup SIMCheap, ready and active only for the bad day.The golden rule: two SIMs from different networks, not different brands.

Pay attention to a nuance that is always ignored: if two different brands share a network, that means both go down at the same time. Before buying, check the virtual operator's terms: during congestion, the host's own network may be prioritized, and that difference shows up exactly on the day you need it most.

The golden rule: two different networks, always

Redundancy is the cheapest lever in all of preparedness. With a dual-SIM phone — or with two phones, one on each network — you protect yourself against the most common scenario: one network saturates or goes down and the other keeps working. The second SIM does not have to be expensive or have a lot of data: its job is to get a short message through and allow a call when the main one fails.

  • If you live with more people, ideally you have SIMs from different networks at home, not all from the same operator.
  • Test the secondary one from time to time: a SIM forgotten in a drawer often ends up disconnected for inactivity.
  • If the network goes down completely, use other routes: communicating without a mobile network covers the alternatives (WiFi messaging, radio, paper) and the backup 4G router keeps the whole house connected with a single SIM.

Coverage: check it, don't assume it

Mobile phone bars measure signal strength, not real service quality, and even less so under stress. The reliable reference is the coverage maps published by the operators themselves and the regulator's information: the Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) is the body that oversees the telecommunications sector in Spain and publishes reports on coverage and service quality.

Check three points before deciding: your home (including the bedroom and the landing), your workplace or business, and your usual route — including secondary roads. If you live or travel in mountain areas, consider an external mobile antenna: with a weak signal, a couple of decibels of gain make the difference between sending a message and not sending it.

How much data do you really need in an emergency?

Much less than you think. In a blackout scenario, the essentials are messaging, the occasional call, offline maps and checking official notices: with a small monthly data bundle you have more than enough, as long as you are not streaming. Three habits help more than any unlimited plan:

  1. Download the maps of your area for offline use before the network is unavailable.
  2. Prioritize SMS and lightweight messaging while the network is congested; calls only if essential.
  3. Turn off syncing and background data: in a blackout every percentage point of battery counts.

If you are going to prepare the SIM calmly, a well-chosen prepaid data SIM and a periodic top-up prevent you from finding yourself without credit on the very day of the outage. Never commit exact prices to memory: compare the current offers yourself, because they change every campaign.

Checklist: what to check before the next warning

  • Activate and test the SIM — test call, mobile data and an SMS, on the phone where you are going to use it.
  • The account, up to date — without credit or with an unpaid bill, the line can be cut off just when you need it.
  • PIN and PUK written down — on paper, outside the phone: if you ask for the PIN, the device asks for the PUK and without it the card is blocked.
  • Coverage checked — home, work and route, with the operator's map in front of you.
  • Second network ready — activated, tested and at hand (not in a drawer untested for years).
  • Power for the phone — charged power bank and, if you can, solar support: without battery, the best SIM in the world is useless. See the blackout kit and the guide to the best emergency power bank.
  • Phone numbers on paper — those of your closest people and 112, written down: if the phone dies, memory helps too.

The rest of the communication kit

The SIM is the main piece, but it does not work alone. With one or two well-chosen SIMs you can build a redundancy chain that goes from the simplest to the most powerful:

  • Portable router or mifi — shares the connection with several devices: portable mifi with battery or the full comparison in best emergency 4G router.
  • External antenna — for weak areas: outdoor 4G antenna.
  • Satellite backup — when not a single tower is left standing, Starlink in emergencies is the Plan B that saves the day, with its page at Starlink kit.
  • Radio and short messages — PMR446 radios do not need any tower.

All of this fits into the central communications page: communication kit, with the essentials ordered by priority.

Five mistakes that repeat in every emergency

  1. Trusting only the bars: they measure strength, not whether the network will accept your call at nine at night on a chaotic day.
  2. Two SIMs on the same network (even if they are different brands): they go down together and the “redundancy” was an illusion.
  3. Forgetting the secondary SIM: a prepaid SIM without top-ups may be disconnected for inactivity under each operator's terms.
  4. Using up the data the day before: streaming and downloads the previous day leave the bundle empty just when it is time to check in.
  5. Confusing home WiFi with coverage: the home router does not work without power; the SIM and the phone are what you have left.

Official sources so you don't improvise

Before believing any campaign, consult the sources directly: the telecommunications regulator (CNMC) for coverage and quality data, Red Eléctrica de España (REE) for the status of the power grid, and the official channels of Protección Civil and 112 for recommendations during incidents. In a blackout, updated official information is worth more than any rumor in a messaging group.

Where it fits into your preparedness

A well-chosen data SIM is cheap insurance against isolation: it costs little, takes up no space and only requires you to test it from time to time. It fits any scenario, from a DANA or blackout in the first 30 minutes to a long-lasting outage. Build your preparedness in layers: basic 72-hour kit for the essentials, communication kit to connect, and if you live in an isolated area, mountain kit. The best SIM is not the cheapest or the most advertised: it is the one you still have active, tested and with a second network waiting alongside it.

mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.titulo: Best emergency 4G router: internet when everything else fails (2026)
mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.resumen: Emergency 4G or 5G router: types, how to choose one, where to place it and what to check before the next blackout or DANA in Spain.
mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.cuerpo:
When a DANA cuts the fibre, a blackout takes out the neighbourhood exchange or the mobile network gets saturated because everyone wants to call at the same time, the internet stops being a luxury and becomes a safety tool: knowing what is happening in your area, receiving the AEMET or Protección Civil alert, letting your people know and, if needed, asking for help via WhatsApp instead of waiting for the line to come back.

The temptation is to use your phone as an emergency router. It works for a few hours and then nothing works: a phone battery doesn't last long when sharing a connection, the screen turns off and the thing gets hot. The real alternative is a 4G or 5G router with a battery, designed to stay on for days, share WiFi with several people and leave your phone free for calls.

Why a router and not your phone?

The differences aren't about convenience, they're about endurance:

What you measurePhone sharing a connection4G/5G router with battery
Real battery lifeBetween two and four hours of active useEight to twelve hours depending on model and load
Connected devicesOne or two before it strugglesTen or more without breaking a sweat
SignalInside your pocket or backpackPlace it by a window or with an external antenna
The device's own batteryYou drain it and are left without a phoneIndependent: your phone stays available
Continuous useIt heats up and slows downDesigned to stay on

And there's a detail that matters a lot in an emergency: if the router is by the window and the phone is in your pocket, the network is received by whoever has the better antenna, not whoever is in more of a hurry.

What you need for it to work on the bad day

A router alone doesn't perform miracles. To be ready when you need it, you need three things, and all three are bought or prepared weeks in advance:

  • A SIM with active data. If you haven't topped it up for months, there's a good chance the line has been cut for lack of credit. Check your card's validity today, not on the day of the alert. The comparison of emergency data SIMs explains what to look for (validity, coverage and enough gigabytes).
  • Power to recharge it. One of these routers uses little power, but if the blackout drags on you need to charge it: a power bank with enough capacity or a portable solar panel will keep you from being left in the dark. In the blackout kit and the electricity kit, backup power is already covered.
  • Coverage where you will be. The network goes down sooner on an industrial estate with no neighbours than in a city centre. Check your operator's coverage map before buying, and if you live or take shelter in a weak-signal area, consider external LTE antennas: in the mountains or at a country house they change the conversation.

The three types of emergency router

There is no single “best router”: there are three formats and each one solves a different scenario.

FormatWho it's forBest bitWhat to watch
4G mobile router with battery (MiFi)Evacuation backpack, car, people on the moveSmall, charges from a power bank, fits in a pocketLower antenna power and fewer devices at once
Home 4G/5G router with backup powerHouse, flat, fixed shelterCoverage throughout the home and genuinely stableNeeds mains power: think about a UPS or generator
Router with external antennasWeak-signal area, countryside, mountains, garagePlug-in RP-SMA antennas and much better receptionMore setup and more cables to carry

If your priority is the backpack, go for the small format. If your priority is keeping the whole house connected during a multi-day blackout, go for the home router with backup power. Take your time looking at portable 4G routers with battery, 4G routers for home or portable MiFi devices.

How to choose it: six points that really matter

  • Battery, not “portable”. It should clearly state how many hours it lasts when powered on and whether it can run while charging. Eight hours or more is a good baseline to get through the night.
  • 4G bands and, if you can, 5G. In congested areas 5G relieves pressure; in rural areas 4G with good low-band support rules, as it reaches farther.
  • No-contract SIM. An unlocked router lets you change operator when yours gets congested. Before buying, confirm it isn't carrier-locked.
  • External antenna connector. Even if you won't use it today, having RP-SMA antennas available saves you from changing router later.
  • WiFi for several devices. Child's tablet, work laptop, TV and family phones: if the router supports few clients, it drops as soon as half the neighbourhood shows up.
  • Simple administration. It should be configurable from a phone and let you restart it with one button: at three in the morning nobody wants to touch IPs.

Signal is won or lost by where you put it

The golden rule is incredibly boring and it works: near the window, high up and with no metal around it. A router hidden behind the TV or in the hallway cupboard loses decibels you need. Put it on a balcony, a shelf or the highest table; if you have an external antenna, point it towards the window with the best view of the horizon.

Before trusting coverage, check it where you will be: operators publish their maps and CNMC, as the telecommunications regulator, maintains information on coverage and service quality. We explain it in detail in how to check coverage before buying the SIM.

Security: a router is a door into your home

A router with the factory password and outdated firmware is the fastest way for someone to slip into your network when you're distracted. Three actions, five minutes:

  • Change the admin and WiFi passwords to ones that aren't the label on the bottom.
  • Update the firmware from the app or panel; if your device no longer receives updates, consider replacing it.
  • Keep guest devices separate from important equipment (the work laptop and the home tablet don't have to be on the same network).

INCIBE, the National Cybersecurity Institute, reminds the public in its guides that the home network is the first line of defence: its home security recommendations are the natural complement to any emergency router.

The day of the alert: five-minute checklist

  1. Charge the router to 100% and place it by the window or at the highest point in the house.
  2. Check that the SIM has credit and that you're getting some signal (the bar in the router app is enough).
  3. Connect only the essentials: phones, radio and laptop. Leave the console and TV on 4G separately if data is tight.
  4. Share the network with your people straight away so nobody keeps asking for the password.
  5. Follow official alerts: AEMET publishes forecasts and weather warnings (aemet.es) and Protección Civil coordinates self-protection recommendations (proteccioncivil.es). If there is immediate risk, 112 always comes first.

The mistakes that leave the router useless

  • Buying the router but not the SIM. The device works, the line doesn't: it happens more often than you'd think.
  • Leaving it uncharged for months. Batteries drain; a quarterly check (and a full charge) prevents the surprise.
  • Thinking there's coverage because your phone has bars. Your phone and the router don't see things the same way; check the map and do a real test at the point where you'll use it.
  • Using up data on downloads. In an emergency gigabytes run out fast: prioritise messaging and alerts, leave streaming for later.
  • Thinking it's the complete plan. If the network goes down completely, a router doesn't conjure a signal out of nothing. That's the next layer.

When there is no coverage: plan B

A 4G router depends on the mobile network. If you live in an area where that network is weak, you need redundancy, and there are three paths we already cover on the blog: real connectivity redundancy (satellite, radio and mobile), Starlink as an emergency connection for those who can afford it, and PMR446 radios to talk short-range without depending on anyone. Communication without a mobile network covers the whole scheme.

The idea isn't to have everything: it's to decide in advance what your first route is, what your second is, and who you'll meet if both fail. That simple agreement is worth more than any gadget.

Where it fits into your preparedness

The emergency router is the communications piece of the kit. If you're building yours from scratch, the communication kit brings together the essentials and the DANA and flood kit covers the scenario that most often leaves entire neighbourhoods without a line. And if you prefer to start with the basics, the 72-hour kit guide gives you the foundation on which everything else rests.

Official sources

  • INCIBE — National Cybersecurity Institute: security guides for home networks and the public.
  • AEMET — State Meteorological Agency: official forecasts and storm warnings.
  • Protección Civil — General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies: self-protection recommendations for emergencies.

AEMET — Spanish State Meteorological Agency
Civil Protection — SGPCyE (Ministry of the Interior)

generador-solar-emergencia-72h.titulo: Emergency solar generator: how much runtime it gives and 5 mistakes (2026)
generador-solar-emergencia-72h.resumen: How much battery do you actually need? Real capacity in watt-hours, what it can and can't charge, how many panels you need, and 5 mistakes when choosing (2026).
generador-solar-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
Three days without power is not an exotic scenario in Spain: it is what happens when a storm leaves an entire neighborhood without supply, when the grid goes out of kilter in the middle of a cold snap, or when roadworks cut a cable. Protección Civil kept the alert for showers and storms on the peninsular Mediterranean coast and the Balearic Islands in place on 16 October 2026, and autumn storms are, year after year, the most frequent cause of local electricity cuts. What decides whether that night is uncomfortable or unpleasant is not the blackout: it is whether you had somewhere to plug in the hallway light, the mobile phone and the fridge.

An emergency solar generator solves exactly that: it turns sunlight into electricity stored in a battery, with no noise, no fumes and no fuel to store. Below is the full calculation —how much energy you really need, how much battery and how many panels are required— and the mistakes that leave many people with a device that cannot even run the fridge.

1. What a solar generator is (and what it is not)

It is worth getting the names right, because shops use them as if they were synonyms and they are not:

  • Folding solar panel: it only generates electricity while the sun is shining on it. Without a battery it stores nothing.
  • External battery or portable power station: it stores energy and delivers it through an AC outlet, USB or 12 V. It does not charge itself: it needs someone to charge it.
  • Solar generator: the two together —panel + battery— in a kit that works from the first minute. This is what we are talking about here.
  • Petrol or diesel generator: it burns fuel to produce power. It works at night and under clouds, but it makes noise and smoke and needs refueling.

The practical difference is simple: solar does not depend on an external supply that runs out; as long as there is sun it keeps charging, and it can stay set up on the balcony for weeks. In exchange, its output depends on the sky. If you want to see solar versus fuel head to head, the comparison between a generator and a portable power station breaks down scenarios, noise and running costs; and if the solar route already suits you, the post on portable solar panels covers the three types and the buying mistakes.

2. The calculation that matters: watt-hours

The whole decision comes down to a single figure: the watt-hours (Wh) each device consumes each time you use it, and how many Wh fit in the battery. Nothing more. Power (W) tells you how much it uses while running; capacity (Wh) tells you how long it lasts.

DeviceTypical useApproximate consumption
Mobile phoneOne full chargeAround 10–15 Wh
LaptopWorking for 4 hoursBetween 40 and 60 Wh per charge
4G/Wi-Fi routerOne hour switched onAround 10 Wh
LED bulbOne night of useBetween 5 and 10 Wh
Emergency radioSeveral hoursA few Wh per hour
Portable car fridgeOne hour of cyclingAround 30–50 Wh
Battery charger4 AA batteriesLess than 20 Wh

These are rule-of-thumb estimates, not laboratory measurements: your laptop may use considerably more if it has a graphics card. The idea to hold on to is the order of magnitude —charging a mobile phone costs a tiny fraction of what heating water costs—, because that is where the battery size comes from.

3. How much battery you need by scenario

With the table above, setting yourself up for the night is arithmetic. Three real scenarios, with no extra gear:

72-hour scenarioWhat it supportsRecommended capacity
Basic survivalMobile phones, flashlights, radio, router for short periodsBetween 300 and 600 Wh
Home in remote modeThe above plus laptop, LED lighting and portable fridgeBetween 1,000 and 1,500 Wh
High autonomyThe above plus tools, a small pump and continuous chargingAbove 2,000 Wh

The temptation is to buy the biggest battery “just in case” and end up with no panels, which is the mistake in point 5. Remember that the battery produces nothing: it only stores. A 12 Wh mobile phone charged four times a day is about 50 Wh per day; a portable fridge that runs in cycles can consume in one day what three mobile phones use in a week. If your priority is the fridge —for medicines or for food from the home fridge—, prioritize capacity over extras.

If you are after the minimum, low-cost version, the highest-capacity power bank handles level 1 without installing anything; and the plan for the first 30 minutes of a DANA or a blackout tells you what order to act in when the power goes out just as you are having dinner.

4. How many panels and how long they take to charge

Panels are sized with a rough but reliable rule: in good conditions, a 100 W panel delivers around 300–400 Wh on a full day of sun (direct light from morning to afternoon, at a reasonable angle). In other words, three effective hours of sun is the usual reference point for the calculation. From there:

PanelApproximate daily outputWhat it is for
20–40 WAbout 60–140 WhMobile phone, flashlights, radio. Small, steady charging
100 WBetween 300 and 400 WhHome in remote mode: mobile phones, LED lights, router, some fridge use
200 WBetween 600 and 800 WhDaily laptop use and fridge with margin
400 W (or two 200 W panels)More than 1,000 WhLarge batteries and quick recharges between storms

The sky is in charge, and in autumn and winter it is even more so: with drizzle or overcast sky, output falls to a fraction of the nominal figure —often to half or less— and the days are shorter. AEMET is the official source for knowing what sky to expect this week; Red Eléctrica de España (REE) publishes how the electricity system is behaving. The practical rule: size for the worst day of the year, not for the best day in August. If you live in the north or in a foggy area, add 50% more panel to whatever the calculation gave you.

5. What it powers and what it does not, without any misleading claims

This is the part that many product sheets keep quiet about. The short list:

  • Yes, with room to spare: mobile phones, tablets, laptops, flashlights and LED bulbs, radio, router, security cameras, battery chargers, hand tools, fans.
  • Yes, with a tight margin: portable fridge (in cycles), capsule coffee machine, iron, small microwave —anything that heats water uses a lot, a very great deal.
  • No, forget it: ceramic hob and oven, electric water heater, air conditioning, resistive heating, heat pump, hairdryer. An electric water heater can use in half an hour what the entire battery stores for three days.
  • With a separate calculation: well water pump, soldering iron, workshop compressor. They can be started with large batteries, but you have to calculate it device by device and check the start-up surges.

If your priority is heating in winter, electricity is not the way: see the post on heaters that work without power and the blackout kit, which organizes priorities, light and heat in the same place. To keep the home safe while the grid comes back, the electricity kit brings together everything that plugs in.

6. The five most common mistakes

  1. Buying only a battery, without panels. A portable power station without a panel is an expensive brick: you charge it at home and when the power goes out you use it once. If you cannot pay for both, start with the panel.
  2. Counting on August sun to get through a November blackout. Sizing is done for the worst day, not the best.
  3. Measuring in watts instead of watt-hours. “It has 1,000 W” does not say how long it lasts; “it has 1,000 Wh” does.
  4. Leaving the battery discharged in the storage room. Lithium batteries lose charge on their own: recharge it every three months and leave it at half charge if you are not going to touch it for a long time.
  5. Buying by the number of outlets rather than by power. Eight sockets that only accept light loads are no use for anything that heats.

And a sixth that is pure foresight: not buying anything. The difference between an afternoon blackout and a three-day one is almost never money; it is having looked at it in advance.

7. Setting it up in five steps

  1. Place the panel in the sun, facing south and at the angle specified by the manufacturer; on a window or balcony it works, but it performs less well.
  2. Connect the panel to the battery with the appropriate cable (panels have MC4 connectors; the battery comes with its own or you buy it separately).
  3. Wait for the battery to accept charge: with good light it starts filling within minutes.
  4. Connect your devices to the battery —AC outlets for 220 V items, USB for small devices— and switch off what you are not using.
  5. Complete the cycle every day: take the panel out into the sun in the morning, leave the battery in place and note down how much you consumed. With three nights of records you know whether you have spare capacity or not enough.

So that the night has light without burning through the battery, switch off what you do not need and turn on only two or three LEDs: a hallway LED bulb uses in an hour what a mobile phone uses in minutes.

8. Safety: what you need to know before plugging anything in

The good thing about the solar route is that it burns nothing inside the home: there is no carbon monoxide, no smoke and no fire risk from combustion. Fuel generators, by contrast, must never run in an enclosed space or near ventilation grilles —which is why the carbon monoxide detector is part of the same conversation.

The points you do need to watch with solar equipment:

  • Water and exposed connections: bring the panel in when it really rains and protect the sockets. Wet connectors corrode and stop charging properly.
  • Heat and ventilation: the battery copes better at a cool room temperature with airflow; do not put it under the bed or in a closed cupboard while charging.
  • Supervised charging while people are at home, as with any device that contains lithium.
  • Zero noise, zero red tape: because it makes no noise, you do not impose noise on the community. If you end up using a fuel generator as backup, check the noise rules of the residents' association before starting it.

9. What to check before paying anything

Buying checklist, in order of importance:

  • Real capacity in Wh, not mAh (mAh at 5 V is not the same as at 12 V, and shops play with that).
  • Output power in W —enough for what you want to plug in—, and if the manufacturer lists start-up surges, check them.
  • Battery type: lithium with LFP chemistry lasts many more cycles than others; for occasional emergency use, whichever you have at hand and well looked after.
  • Solar charging input on the same connectors as your panels, without improvised adapters.
  • Warranty and spare parts availability in Spain, not just an online shop.
  • Real weight: if it weighs more than you want to carry up to the balcony, you will not use it.

If you prefer to buy separate parts, here are direct searches for the most common items: portable power stations, folding solar panels and a 20–40 W folding solar panel that is already verified in our catalog for charging small devices. Affiliate links: if you buy through them, kit72h receives a commission at no extra cost to you.

10. How this fits into a 72-hour plan

Light is only one piece. The recommendation set out in official guides —three days of self-sufficiency without basic services— is the axis around which the whole site is built, and there electricity sits alongside water, food, documents and communication. Secretaría General de Protección Civil y Emergencias publishes preventive recommendations by scenario, and the European Commission's Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO) sets out the European approach to citizen preparedness; on the official sources page you will find them all linked in detail.

The sensible order, if you are starting from zero: cover communication and information first (mobile phone with battery and radio), then light, then cold and food. With the plan in the basic 72-hour kit and the list in the blackout kit you have the base; the solar generator is what gives that plan electrical autonomy. If you also want to stay connected when fiber goes down, communication without a mobile network explains what works and what does not when the network goes down.

Summary in three lines

The calculation: aim for 500 Wh if you only want mobile phones and light, and 1,500 Wh if you want a fridge and a laptop. Recharging: 100 W of panel gives around 300–400 Wh per day in good sun, and half or less on a cloudy day. Discipline: battery charged and panel tested before it is needed, not during. With that, a three-day blackout becomes a day of working in the shade of the balcony.

conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.titulo: Emergency connectivity: Starlink, radio and satellite (2026)
conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.resumen: Emergency connectivity: what to do when all networks go down. Starlink, amateur radio, PMR446 walkie-talkies and satellite messenger, with a plan B.
conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.cuerpo:
When the power grid goes down, the internet is the first thing to go. Then mobile coverage. In a DANA, a prolonged blackout or an earthquake, the three most widely used systems —WiFi, mobile and fibre— can fail at the same time. And without communication, there is no coordination, no information and no help.

This is where serious preparedness separates itself from improvisation. It is not about buying the most expensive gear: it is about having three independent systems that work autonomously. If one fails, the other two remain operational. If two fail, the third holds up.

This guide covers the three layers of emergency connectivity, from the easiest (Starlink) to the most robust (HF radio), with products, costs and when to use each one.

Layer 1: Satellite internet — Starlink

Starlink is the closest thing to terrestrial broadband internet that exists. It works from anywhere on the planet with a clear view of the sky, without fibre infrastructure or cell towers.

How does it work?

A flat terminal (the 'Dishy') is placed on a roof, balcony or garden and points to SpaceX's satellite constellation orbiting at an altitude of 550 km. The terminal draws between 50 and 100W in normal operation (5-10W in standby), so a lithium battery or a 200W solar panel keeps it running indefinitely.

Emergency specifications

  • Speed: 50-200 Mbps download, 10-20 Mbps upload (Gen 3)
  • Latency: 30-80 ms (identical to fibre in practical use)
  • Coverage: Global in areas with a clear view of the sky — Spain is covered across most of its territory
  • Installation: 5 minutes, no tools required
  • Power consumption: 50-100W (running) · 5-10W (standby)
  • Weather resistance: Resistant to winds of up to 120 km/h, rain, snow and hail

Costs

Plan Terminal price Monthly price Use
Residential ~500-600 EUR ~50 EUR/month Fixed, same location
Mobile in transit ~1200 EUR ~45 EUR/month Mobile (car, boat, camping)
Temporary ~500-600 EUR ~100 EUR/month One-off emergency, cancellable

When should you use Starlink in an emergency?

Starlink is ideal when you need real internet — video calls, downloading documents, access to emergency systems — and no terrestrial infrastructure is available. It is especially useful for:

  • Emergency shelters or coordination points that need connectivity
  • Command centres that need to transmit information
  • Households in rural areas without fibre or 4G coverage
  • Evacuation to an area where the network has gone down

Limitation: The terminal is large (57 x 57 x 3 cm, 4.5 kg). It is not portable in an emergency backpack. It requires a fixed location with a clear view of the sky.

View Starlink on Amazon ↗

Layer 2: Cellular connectivity — redundancy

Mobile is the most widely used communication system. And that is why it is also the most vulnerable: a single operator going down leaves everyone disconnected. The key is to have two different operators and a router that manages them.

Industrial 4G/5G router with dual SIM

An industrial router such as the Peplink MAX BR, Gargoyle or similar accepts two SIMs from different operators (e.g. Movistar + Orange). If one tower goes down, the router switches to the other automatically. They also offer:

  • WAN/LAN: Ethernet ports to connect WiFi routers or a switch
  • VPN: you can connect your home router to a remote point
  • PoE: powered over network cable, ideal for roof installation
  • External antennas: SMA connectors for high-gain antennas
  • Web monitoring: dashboard to view network status, battery and signal

High-gain panel antenna

In rural areas, 4G signal can be weak but usable if the antenna is correctly aimed at the nearest tower. An 18-23 dBi panel antenna improves signal by 10 to 20 dB.

Procedure:

  1. Install the antenna on a 3-5 metre mast on the roof or facade
  2. Aim it at the nearest tower (apps such as CellMapper show towers on a map)
  3. Connect the coaxial cable (LMR-400, low loss) to the 4G/5G router
  4. Configure the router with the two SIMs

Search 4G/5G panel antennas ↗ · Search industrial routers ↗

Layer 3: Satellite messaging — the last resort

When everything goes down — Starlink off due to lack of power, router without signal, and no radio at all — the satellite messenger is the last system still working. It does not require terrestrial infrastructure or a clear view of the sky to send text messages.

Garmin inReach Mini 2

The best-known satellite communication device for emergencies. It works on the Iridium network (global coverage, including the poles). It offers:

  • Two-way messages by SMS or to predefined contacts
  • Global SOS (connects to rescue coordination centres)
  • Integrated GPS with real-time location
  • Battery life of 2-3 days in normal mode (weeks in power-saving mode)
  • Water-resistant (IPX7), drop-resistant
  • Smartphone app: send messages from your phone without the device

Cost: ~350-450 EUR device + 30-50 EUR/month data plan

Zoleo

Alternative with a web dashboard: you can see your family's location in real time from any browser. It works on Iridium and Globalstar networks (dual network for a higher chance of connection).

Cost: ~300-400 EUR device + 30-50 EUR/month plan

When should you use the satellite messenger?

It is the device that should never be the only one, but it should always be in your evacuation backpack. It is used to:

  • Send an SOS signal when there is no other means
  • Communicate your location to family when you are lost
  • Confirm to family that you are OK when connectivity is restored
  • Receive emergency alerts (on some models)

View Garmin inReach Mini 2 ↗

Layer 4: Radio — the system that does not fail

Radio is the oldest, cheapest and most reliable communication system. It does not depend on satellites, it does not need infrastructure, and it does not become congested with traffic. When everything else fails, radio keeps working.

Professional PMR446 walkie-talkies

PMR446 walkie-talkies are the most basic and accessible communication system. They do not require a licence, work on 16 predefined channels and have a range of 2 to 5 km in open terrain (less in the city).

A set of 4 professional walkie-talkies (Motorola Talkabout or similar) costs ~100-200 EUR and is shared among family members. They are useful for:

  • Coordinating family evacuation (who goes where, when)
  • Communication at home during an emergency (between floors)
  • Coordination with neighbours or nearby rescue teams
  • Communication in areas with no mobile signal (even if only 2 km)

Specifications: 16 channels, 0.5 W power (the legal maximum for PMR446 without a licence), IP67 (water-resistant), LCD, VOX (hands-free), LED lights.

Search PMR446 walkie-talkies ↗

Amateur HF radio (CETIC licence)

Amateur radio is the deepest layer of emergency connectivity. With a shortwave antenna and an HF radio, you can communicate with any point on the planet via ionospheric propagation. It does not need any infrastructure at all.

To get started:

  • Licence: free exam at CETIC (Telecommunications Industry Testing Centre). You can prepare with free online material.
  • Radio: Icom IC-7100 or Yaesu FT-710 as a starting point (~600-1200 EUR)
  • Antenna: shortwave or dipole antenna (100-300 EUR)
  • Range: local (VHF) → regional (HF daytime) → international (HF night)

Amateur radio operators actively collaborate with Protección Civil in Spain through REDVOL (Volunteer Emergency Telecommunications Network). If you have a licence and want to help, there are local groups in every region.

Search HF radios ↗

Triple redundancy strategy

Professional preparedness is not based on a single system, but on triple redundancy: three independent systems that work autonomously. If one fails, the other two remain operational. If two fail, the third holds up.

Layer System Total cost Independence When it fails
1 Starlink (satellite) ~500 EUR + 50 EUR/month No terrestrial infrastructure No power / no clear view of the sky
2 Industrial 4G/5G router (2 SIMs) ~400-800 EUR + 80 EUR/month Alternative operator Towers down + no power
3 Satellite messenger ~350 EUR + 30 EUR/month Independent satellite network No battery
4 PMR446 walkie-talkies ~100-200 EUR Zero infrastructure No battery / limited range
5 Amateur HF radio ~600-1200 EUR No infrastructure at all Requires a licence + skill

The minimum functional budget

The essentials for decent connectivity when networks go down:

  • PMR446 walkie-talkies (4 units): ~150 EUR
  • Industrial 4G/5G router + 1 panel antenna: ~600 EUR
  • Satellite messenger (Garmin inReach): ~350 EUR
  • Minimum total: ~1.100 EUR (without subscriptions)

With Starlink it rises to ~1.600 EUR initially + ~80 EUR/month in subscriptions, but you get real broadband internet.

What you do not need to buy (yet)

Amateur HF radio is the most powerful layer but requires training and a licence. It is not essential for most households. If you are interested, start with PMR446 walkie-talkies and the satellite messenger; HF radio is a learning path you can begin studying once you have the basic systems covered.

Summary: what to buy, when and why

The three-layer rule

Each layer is an independent system. If one fails, the other two keep working.

antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.titulo: External mobile antenna: real coverage in mountains and valleys (2026)
antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.resumen: A practical guide to external mobile antennas: how to diagnose signal, which type is worth it in each case, how to install it and which mistakes to avoid in the mountains.
antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.cuerpo:
If you live or spend time in a mountain area, a deep valley or the countryside, you already know the symptom: one signal bar, dropped calls and data that won't start just when you need it most. An external mobile antenna is not a tech toy: it is the cheapest way to turn patchy coverage into a stable connection at home, in the cabin or in a second home. This guide explains what is failing, how to diagnose it in ten minutes, what type of solution suits you and how to install it without making the mistakes that leave the improvement at nothing.

Why the signal fails right there

Mobile coverage is not uniform across the map: operators' towers are designed to serve population centers and communication routes, and the terrain does the rest. A hill between you and the tower, a narrow valley or a building with thick walls reduce the strength of the signal reaching your device. As a result, two houses a hundred meters apart can live in different realities.

Official data confirms this. The Ministry of Economic Affairs, Trade and Business reports national fifth-generation mobile network coverage (5G NSA+SA) of 99.27% as of 30 June 2025, with 98.10% in standalone mode. That percentage is a national average: it does not tell you what happens in your back yard or on the north slope. That is why the first step is not to buy, but to check the official map and then measure at your own location.

And an important nuance: an external antenna does not create signal where there is none. What it does is capture the signal that already exists, however weak, and bring it indoors with fewer losses. If no operator reaches your location even with an antenna on the roof, the answer is not an antenna but another technology: satellite or radio. That is why it is worth reading first what works when the mobile network goes down and Starlink in an emergency so you don't spend money on the wrong solution.

A 10-minute diagnosis before spending money

  • Check the official CNMC and Ministry coverage maps for your exact address: you will see 4G and 5G coverage by block and by operator, and that is where you start ruling things out.
  • Try several spots and several windows: go up to a high floor, step out into the garden, move to the opposite side of the building. Note where the mobile phone performs best; that spot tells you where the cable should enter.
  • Change operator before blaming the device: with a second prepaid SIM (or a neighbor's phone) you can check whether the problem is your network or the location.
  • Try another device: an old phone with a damaged antenna or a blocking case can mimic poor coverage. If two devices behave the same in the same place, the problem is the network.
  • Measure before and after: note the bars or, better, the signal level shown by the phone itself in service mode. Without a baseline measurement, you won't know whether the antenna has done anything.
  • Check whether the failure is in data or voice: sometimes calls work and browsing does not (or the other way round). The solution and the right equipment are not the same.

What type of solution you need

There is no universal antenna: it depends on the distance to the tower, the number of users and whether the problem is outside or inside the house. Here is the quick decision map.

SolutionWhen it fitsWhere it is installedApproximate cost
Omnidirectional external antennaSeveral towers around or tower not visible; simple domestic useMast or wall, as high as possibleFrom about 30 to 80 €
Directional antenna (Yagi / panel)Specific, known tower at some distance; high gainPointed at the tower, on the roof or balconyFrom about 40 to 120 €
Repeater / signal amplifierWeak but existing signal outside and dead inside the buildingExternal antenna + indoor unit + cableFrom about 100 to 300 €
4G/5G router with external antennasYou want internet at home, not just calls: several devices at onceOn the router, antennas outsideFrom about 60 to 200 €
Indoor WiFi extenderThe signal arrives well but dies between floors or wallsIn the hallway, between the router and the dead spotFrom about 25 to 70 €

Omnidirectional antenna: the simple option

It captures signal from any direction, so there is no need to point it at anything. It is the best option if you do not know where the nearest tower is or if your area changes operator often. It usually comes with a window mast and pre-terminated coaxial cable. Look for a high-gain external 4G/5G antenna.

Directional antenna: the best performer in remote areas

It points at a specific tower and concentrates all the gain in that direction. It performs much better than an omnidirectional antenna when the tower is far away, but it requires aiming: a few degrees of error can eat up the improvement. It is worth it if you can see the tower from home or locate it on the official map.

Repeater or amplifier: when the problem is the building

If there is signal outside and none inside (concrete walls, metal-cavity windows, basements), an antenna alone is not enough: you need a unit that receives outside, amplifies and re-transmits inside. It is the typical solution for stone houses and old buildings. Use CE-marked equipment designed for domestic use: a badly adjusted repeater saturates the tower cell and can make the network worse for all your neighbors.

Router with external antennas: if what you want is internet

If your goal is to bring stable WiFi to several rooms, the shed or the workshop, the way to go is a 4G/5G router that accepts external antennas (with standard connectors) and, if you travel or change location, with a dual SIM slot so you can switch operator. There are industrial 4G/5G routers with dual SIM and external antennas on the market designed for exactly this; if the problem is only WiFi inside the house, a long-range WiFi extender with directional antenna is usually enough. Also compare emergency 4G routers and check which data SIM saves you before signing anything.

How to install it: six steps

  1. Choose the outdoor point: as high and clear as possible, ideally with line of sight to the tower and no metal nearby (gutters, metal blinds, awnings).
  2. Aim it (if directional): locate the tower on the official map, align the antenna and secure the mast loosely so you can correct it.
  3. Run the cable at the shortest possible length: every meter of thin coaxial cable reduces gain; if you need a long run, use lower-loss coaxial cable and avoid unnecessary bends.
  4. Seal the penetration: the hole in the wall must be sealed against water and damp — in the mountains, a costly leak ends up costing more than the antenna itself.
  5. Connect to the indoor unit and power it (if it is a repeater or router): keep the indoor antenna away from the outdoor one to avoid feedback and a noise loop.
  6. Measure again and compare with your diagnosis notes. If the improvement is marginal, check the aiming, connections and cable length before considering the installation good.

Four mistakes that cancel out the improvement

  • Antenna behind metal-cavity glass or a metal roller shutter: the shielding cuts the signal almost completely. If you cannot take it outside, do not expect miracles.
  • Cheap cable that is too long: it is the number one cause of installations 'that don't work'. Buy suitable coaxial cable and cut off the excess.
  • Amplifying noise instead of signal: if there is nothing outside to amplify, the repeater multiplies interference. Diagnosis first, gain second.
  • Not measuring before and after: without measurement, subjective impression rules and you end up discarding a solution that perhaps only needed two degrees of aiming.

What to check before a warning or a blackout

The antenna is part of the same circuit as the rest of your connectivity, and in an emergency several links fail at once. Before a storm, a DANA or a planned outage arrives, go over the first 30 minutes checklist: check that the router and repeater are protected by a surge protector, keep a charged power bank for your phone and a crank radio with solar panel to hand as a way to get warnings when the data network goes down completely. And if the scenario is spending days without service, set up the rest of the circuit: communication kit, Starlink kit and mountain kit.

Also remember that the antenna needs electricity: in a prolonged blackout, the mobile network goes down sooner than people think because the towers' backup batteries are not infinite. That is why coverage should not be your only channel — PMR446 radio and connectivity redundancy exist for that.

Verdict

A well-chosen external antenna is one of the best value-for-money improvements you can make in a country or mountain house: no building work, no monthly fee and an immediate effect on calls and data. The rule is always the same — measure first, choose the type according to where the problem lies (outside, inside or in the equipment itself), install with a short cable and correct aiming, and measure again. And if the budget is tight, start with what is free: the official map, trying a different window and a second SIM to find out whether you lack an antenna or lack coverage.
