terremoto-espana-que-hacer.titulo: Earthquake in Spain: what to do before, during and after (2026)
terremoto-espana-que-hacer.resumen: What to do before, during and after an earthquake in Spain: official recommendations, IGN data and the lessons of the Granada sequence.
terremoto-espana-que-hacer.cuerpo:
On Tuesday 18 August 2026, at 10:37, a magnitude 4.8 earthquake 5 kilometres deep struck the province of Granada, with the epicentre north-west of Gójar. That same day there were four tremors of magnitude 4 or above, with aftershocks of 4.3 and 4.2 in Alhendín, and the Junta de Andalucía ordered the preventive evacuation of six blocks in Las Gabias: 371 homes and around 600 people out of their houses while engineers checked pillars and cracks. Three people were slightly injured.

The important thing isn't the magnitude: it's that hundreds of families were left not knowing when they could go back. Earthquakes don't announce themselves, so the only part of the script you control is you — and only if you work on it before the shaking starts. This is the sequence recommended by Civil Protection, with data from the Instituto Geográfico Nacional (IGN).

Spain shakes more than you think

The IGN's National Seismic Network located 5,729 earthquakes on the Spanish mainland during 2025, of which 182 were felt by the population. The total varies a lot from one year to the next — when a seismic series like the Granada one starts, it shoots up — but the pattern is always the same: thousands of tiny movements, a handful you can feel and, now and then, one that really registers.

Year (mainland Spain)Earthquakes locatedFelt by the populationMagnitude above 4
202111,32980625
20228,84330823
20235,0991986
20244,9162033
20255,7291827

In 2025 there were 7 earthquakes above magnitude 4 and none reached 6: almost all of them go unnoticed. The problem is the one that doesn't.

Why it shakes and why nobody can predict it

Spain sits on the edge of the Eurasian plate where it collides with the African plate, along the Azores-Gibraltar-Tunisia fracture zone; that's how Civil Protection's seismic risk guide puts it, and it is just as blunt about what we can't do: "There is currently no method capable of predicting the time, place and magnitude of an earthquake". There is no app and no advance notice. The only thing that works is being ready when it arrives without warning.

What has been worked out is the building. Spain's seismic-resistant construction standard, NCSE-02 (Real Decreto 997/2002), sets out as its purpose preventing the loss of human life and reducing economic damage. Not all buildings are in the same situation: that's why, in Las Gabias, engineers inspected each block before authorising the return, and why the Patronato de la Alhambra closed the Nasrid Palaces preventively that afternoon. No house is "safe" or "dangerous" in the abstract: it gets inspected and decided with the report in front of you.

Before: five things for this week (they cost 0 €)

  • Secure the bookcase, the TV and the tall wardrobes to the wall. In an earthquake, what injures you is almost never the floor: it's what falls off it.
  • Find the gas shut-off valve and check that it turns. After the shaking you'll have seconds and your hands will be trembling. If you smell gas, don't switch anything on: no light switches, no matches.
  • Closed shoes and a torch next to the bed, tied on or under the mattress: broken glass isn't visible in the dark.
  • A written family agreement: a meeting point and a contact outside the province, because local lines get overloaded first. You'll find it in the family emergency plan.
  • Documents, first-aid kit and backpack near the door: the emergency folder with ID, deeds and insurance policy, the medication in the first-aid kit and the backpack already packed.

During: you have between five and thirty seconds

The official recommendation fits into three verbs: drop, cover and hold on. Get on all fours, get under a sturdy table and hold on to it: it will move with you and protect you from whatever falls. Three don'ts prevent the rest of the injuries:

  • Don't run out to the stairwell and don't use the lift: stay where you are until the shaking stops.
  • Don't run down into the street from upper floors. Stay away from windows, mirrors, shelves and façades. If you're already outside, head for an open space away from cornices and cables.
  • If you're in a car, stop in an open spot: not under bridges, not next to streetlights, not under cables.

After: the part almost everyone forgets

  • Shoes on before you set foot on the floor. Just awake and in the dark, the glass is on the floor and you can't see it.
  • Don't go back inside until it's been checked. In Granada the evacuations were preventive, because of cracks that grew between one inspection and the next; if you see new cracks or a door that no longer closes, don't go in and report it.
  • Expect aftershocks in the hours that follow: nobody can tell you which ones or when, so the rule is the same as at the start.
  • Reliable information, not rumours. ES-Alert is the "reverse 112" that Civil Protection sends via Cell Broadcast and its Civil Protection Alert level can't be switched off on your phone; a battery radio does the rest, as covered in communicating without a mobile network and official resources on your phone.
  • Document before you move anything: photos of cracks and fallen objects for your insurer and the council: no evidence, no claim.

Three myths that come back with every seismic series

"It doesn't really happen here." On 11 May 2011 Lorca shook at magnitude 5.1 and intensity VII: nine dead and more than 300 injured. On 25 December 1884 the Arenas del Rey earthquake (Granada) destroyed some 4,400 houses and damaged another 13,000, with around 800 fatalities according to the geophysics institute of the University of Granada. What kills isn't the magnitude: it's distance, the ground and the state of the building.

"You can know when the next one will come." No: that's the literal wording from Civil Protection. Be wary of anyone announcing dates.

"Magnitude explains everything." Magnitude measures the energy released and doesn't change as you move away from the epicentre; intensity — the European EMS scale, from I to XII — measures how it was felt at a specific place and drops with distance. A 4.8 five kilometres under the outskirts of a provincial capital is felt across the whole metropolitan area; the same 4.8 far away is barely noticed.

Your list for this week

  1. Screws and a driver: TV and bookcase strapped to the wall.
  2. Find the gas shut-off valve and test it.
  3. Closed shoes and a torch next to the bed.
  4. Write down the family agreement: meeting point and a contact outside the province.
  5. Update the document folder, the medication and the date on the backpack.
  6. Keep the battery radio charged and find the official warning channels.

The item-by-item detail is in the earthquake kit and in the evacuation backpack; if you're only going to put one together, make it the basic 72-hour kit, the one that keeps you going when the building holds but there's no power, water or gas.

kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.titulo: Emergency kit at work: what to keep and what to do (2026)
kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.resumen: A kit for the nine hours away from home: what to keep in your office drawer and how to get out of a building in a real evacuation. INSST regulations cited.
kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.cuerpo:
It's 9:12 on a Tuesday. You're on the third floor of a building with forty people, your backpack on the back of your chair, your car in the basement and your phone at 30%. If the fire alarm went off right now: do you know which door you exit through from your desk, where the assembly point is, and what you have in your drawer to get through the next two hours without depending on anyone?

Almost all the emergency kits we prepare are for home. And that's fine, because home is where you sleep. But add the rest of the day: nine hours at work, two commuting and only eight of sleep. Your backpack in the cupboard covers exactly the part of the day when almost nothing ever happens. This guide is for the other part: the kit that goes with you, the one kept in a drawer, and the two questions you can ask at your office today to find out whether you'd get out of the building in three minutes or fifteen.

1. Work is where you're most likely to be caught off guard (and it's not your fault)

At home you know the noises, you know which door creaks and you go out in the dark without thinking. In an office building you decide almost nothing: you depend on someone else's alarm, someone else's stairwell, whether the stairwell door is locked, whether the work downstairs has left boxes in the corridor. And you depend, above all, on habit: almost every evacuation alert you've experienced in your life was a drill, so your brain decides, without being asked, that “it'll be another test alert.” People who leave a building late almost never leave late for lack of information: they leave late because they believed it wasn't serious.

That bias has a cheap antidote called knowing your route. And your company has a legal obligation to have everything else sorted out. Article 20 of Law 31/1995 on Occupational Risk Prevention obliges the employer to analyse possible emergency situations and adopt the necessary measures for first aid, firefighting and evacuating workers, designating the staff responsible for putting them into practice. And when the building's activity falls within its scope, the Basic Self-Protection Standard (Royal Decree 393/2007) also requires a self-protection plan with a regulated structure and content, including drills, maintenance and periodic reviews.

Translated into real life: that document exists, it's in a management or prevention drawer, and you haven't read it. It isn't a company secret: it's information you can ask for. The INSST (Instituto Nacional de Seguridad y Salud en el Trabajo) has published the reference guide on emergency plans and self-protection plans, and there you find the detail that fails most in practice: the plan is written once and forgotten, when what keeps it alive is drills and reviews.

2. The kit that goes with you: nine things that fit in a drawer

You don't need to turn your desk into a bunker. The idea is to cover the two hours after an incident without depending on anyone: water, light, battery, your medicines and footwear for walking if you have to get home on foot. All of this fits in a 40 cm drawer or in a cloth bag hanging from the seat.

What to keepWhat it's really forApprox. price
1 L water bottle and food that won't melt (bars, nuts, a can and a can opener)If you have to wait at the assembly point or walk back, the first thing you notice isn't hunger: it's thirst and a foggy head. Replace it every six months.3-8 €
10,000-20,000 mAh powerbank with a short USB-C or Lightning cableWith no signal and no light, your phone is your map, your flashlight and your contact with home. A phone at 30% is two hours of anxiety; with a powerbank, two days. Charge it on the first Monday of every month.20-40 €
Your personal medication for 24-48 h and a photo of the prescriptionNobody builds a work kit thinking about their own pill. If you take something for a chronic condition (thyroid, blood pressure, asthma, anti-anxiety medication), carry an extra dose; ask your doctor or pharmacist how to store it and whether it tolerates office temperature.as prescribed
Small flashlight or headlamp and a whistleIn a blackout, emergency stairs have their own lighting until the building's battery runs out. A whistle uses no power and can be heard farther than your voice.10-20 €
Two or three FFP2 masksSmoke, construction dust, mud or simply a corridor full of people coughing. They also help on your commute if there is ash or poor air quality.5-10 €
Paper and USB copies of key documents, and five important phone numbers written by handYour phone is your address book and also the first battery to run out. Five numbers on paper (family, doctor, insurance) weigh nothing and work without a battery.0-10 €
20-30 € in small notes in two different placesWithout power, card terminals don't take payments: no coffee, no bus, no taxi. With 5 and 10 € notes you don't depend on someone having change.20-30 €
Closed shoes and socks in the drawerIf the evacuation happens on a day of heels or flip-flops —or with wet feet— walking two kilometres goes from being a nuisance to being an injury.20-40 €
Thin fleece or scarf and a packable raincoatDrills and real evacuations always end the same way: people standing in the street unable to go back for their jacket. In January that means 40 minutes at 4 °C.15-30 €

The criterion for choosing each item is the same one we use in the basic 72-hour kit: things that solve what will really happen, not what looks good in a photo. If you work on a computer all day and want the home version, the reasonable starting point is to know how to build your 72h kit without overspending.

3. The self-protection plan: it exists, it's mandatory and nobody has read it

Here's the biggest shortcut in this guide. You don't have to design anything: someone in your building has already done it, and all you need is four questions and a three-minute walk.

  • Where is the plan and when was the last drill? The INSST reminds us that evacuation drills must be carried out at least once a year and that taking part in them is how errors are detected before they become serious. If your company hasn't held one since before the pandemic, you already know something useful.
  • Who is the emergency coordinator for my floor and who is my evacuation warden? When the alarm goes off, someone has to do a headcount. If you don't know who that is, you're one of the people nobody is going to count.
  • Where exactly is the assembly point? Ask for the address, not “across the street.” And check that it isn't somewhere where the wind leaves you breathing the building's smoke.
  • Which two evacuation routes apply to me from my desk? Always two: if the main one fills with smoke, the second has to be in your head, not just on the green sign.
  • How do you alert a deaf colleague or someone with reduced mobility? A deaf person cannot hear the alarm (you need visual alerts or someone to tell them), and a stopped lift leaves wheelchair users with no way out. There is a solution —refuge points, visual alarms, designated assistance— but it only works if someone knows their name in advance. In many buildings that person is a visitor or a colleague who is just passing through.

The walk is the rest: today, leave your desk and go down to the street following the evacuation route, counting doors and looking at where the exits you never use are. It takes three minutes. The same route, with smoke, in a hurry and with forty people going down, is not the same. And while you're at it, check something you can actually fix: that your backpack, your boxes or your scooter aren't blocking an evacuation route, because routes must always be signed and clear.

At home the logic is the same and you prepare it the same way: if you haven't done it yet, start with the family emergency plan and not with buying things. And if someone in your household depends on medical equipment, the finer detail is in monitoring and chronic conditions without power.

4. The alarm goes off: how to get out of a building without leaving anyone behind

Self-protection plans and INSST guides agree on the essentials, and almost all the mistakes seen in a real evacuation are on this list:

  • Never the lift. In an emergency it stops exactly where you don't want it to. If you're already inside and it stops, press the alarm or door-open button, call 112 from inside the lift and say which floor you're on: 112 answers even if you have no signal from your operator and even if your phone has no credit.
  • Leave the work, but take your key and phone. Not the laptop: it's heavy, gets in the way and is useless at the assembly point.
  • Go down on the correct side and don't cut across against the flow: a good share of the jams on an emergency stair are people going up to look for someone.
  • If there's smoke, stay low. Hot smoke collects above. A damp handkerchief over your mouth doesn't protect you from carbon monoxide, but it traps some particles and gives you seconds of visibility.
  • Close doors as you leave. A closed door delays the fire by minutes that matter a lot; leaving them open gives the corridor to the smoke.
  • At the assembly point, count your people. And here's the advice that prevents the most problems and almost nobody practises: agree in advance who is responsible for whom. You, with the new colleague, the intern or the visitor who doesn't know the building; someone else, with whoever moves more slowly. If nobody is responsible for anybody, everyone assumes.
  • Don't go back in. Not for your backpack, not for your phone, not for your car, not “just a second.” It's the classic mistake in every real evacuation, and in fires with casualties there is almost always someone who went back.

If you can't get out: make yourself visible and make sure you're counted

There is a case almost nobody practises and that happens more often than it seems: the exit is worse than your spot. The corridor full of smoke, the stair unusable, an emergency door that hasn't been opened in two years. Then the right decision is to stop trying to get out.

  • Close the door and seal the gap with a wet towel or a piece of clothing. You buy time and keep smoke out of the room.
  • Call 112 and say three things: street and number, floor, and which façade you're on (“fourth floor, window facing the square”). That phrase is what gets them to find you sooner.
  • Make yourself seen: a light-coloured garment showing from the window, your phone flashlight if it's dark, and the whistle if you have it. And shout to let people at the assembly point know: from outside they can tell the fire service which floors are occupied.
  • Don't jump from the window as a general rule. On upper floors it's an almost certain injury, and smoke moves faster than it seems.

That same pattern —close, seal, alert and make yourself visible— is the one used when the danger is outside rather than inside: smoke from a nearby fire, chemical smoke from an industrial estate, a leak. The difference is that then the order comes from Protección Civil, via ES-Alert or radio: if they tell you not to go out, you don't go out, even if your car is in the basement and you have a meeting at ten.

5. When the emergency is outside the building: blackout, red warning and basements

Not everything that happens to you at work starts inside. A long power cut, a DANA with a red warning or a Protección Civil alert on your phone arrives with the building intact and the problem outside: no train, no bus, no lift and the car park turned into a trap.

  • The ES-Alert notification is the Protección Civil National Alert Network: it sounds on your phone even if it's on silent, it targets phones in a specific area and it can't be switched off. That loud, flat tone is not a hoax or a test: it's the official instruction. Read it in full before you move and do what it says (stay put, don't go out, don't drive).
  • Never go down to the basement to get your car with an orange or red warning, or when water is already running down the ramp. Garage ramps are among the first places to flood and where the most people are rescued. If water rises up the ramp, you go up to the highest floor.
  • Blackout in the office: phone or drawer flashlight, never candles or lighters (and no combustion appliance in an enclosed space). If the building has no generator, the lifts stop: don't use them for even a second after a cut. And if there is a SAI or UPS, what really deserves continuity is the router and the phone: shut down sensitive equipment so it doesn't suffer the surge when power returns, just as you do at home.
  • Communicating when the network is saturated: send a text with the essentials instead of calling. On a congested network a short message usually gets through before a call, and it lets you say where you are and that you're okay. The details are in communicating without a mobile network.
  • Walking back? It can be the best decision and also the worst. With a red warning, don't move: fifteen centimetres of moving water can sweep a person away, and underpasses and dry riverbeds fill in minutes. Once the warning is over, go through places you know, in closed shoes, and tell someone your route and expected arrival time.
  • The commute is part of the kit too. If you drive, don't depend on the office: water, a blanket, a flashlight and a powerbank live in the car all year. The detail is in the car kit, and the lessons of 28A —network down, card terminals dead, people trapped in tunnels— in what we learned from the 28 April blackout.

And if it drags on and you have to get home without transport, the reference is the evacuation kit: what to take if you have to leave on foot and spend the night away. If you live alone, add one more layer: the plan for living alone starts with deciding who will call you if something happens.

6. What you can do today, in fifteen minutes

  1. Put five things in the drawer: water, bars, a headlamp, a powerbank with a cable and your medication. With that you're no longer helpless in a four-hour outage.
  2. Ask about the plan and the assembly point. An email to occupational risk prevention is enough: it's information your company has and that you can request.
  3. Walk the route from your desk to the street and count doors. Notice where the second exit is.
  4. Write down five phone numbers on paper and keep them in your wallet; and turn on AEMET alerts on your phone if you haven't already.
  5. Set a calendar reminder every six months to check expiry dates and recharge the powerbank. A kit that isn't checked is a box of old things.

And the mistakes that repeat, so they don't happen to you:

  • Confusing “I've thought about it” with “I've done it.” Thinking about where you'd get out is not the same as having walked it once.
  • The powerbank always flat. It's no use if it had gone six months without charging on the very day the power goes out.
  • Deciding on the spot who helps whom. You decide beforehand, without rushing, and in writing if necessary.
  • Going out with a red warning “to get home sooner.” That is exactly the moment to stay still and on high ground.
  • Going down to the basement to get the car. We repeat the advice because it's the mistake that puts the most people in hospital in every DANA.

A work kit isn't bought all at once and you don't need to spend 200 euros: it's nine objects, four questions and three minutes of walking slowly and looking at doors. Today, on your coffee break, you can do the five things on the list. Tomorrow, if the alarm goes off, you'll know it isn't just another alarm.

salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.titulo: Mental health and sleep in an emergency: how to keep going (2026)
salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.resumen: Sleeping, eating and staying calm are not the soft part of the plan: they are the decisions you make after two nights without sleep. WHO framework, shifts and rest.
salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.cuerpo:
It's 21:40 and the power goes out. In twenty minutes you've sorted the fridge: you know what to throw out and what not to. What no one has taught you to sort out is the other part. The child asking whether the lights will come back before bed, your mother calling you frightened at two in the morning because she can't see anything, or your own brain at three still running through the list of things that could still go wrong. Emergencies aren't won with flashlights and water bottles alone: they're won by sleeping, eating and keeping your head on straight. This is the part of the kit that doesn't go in a box.

And it's not a soft or secondary issue. Sustained stress takes away your appetite and your sleep, and when you've gone two nights with almost no sleep you make worse decisions: you leave the door open, you drive at night to “get there sooner”, you don't see the puddle across the road. The WHO has studied this for years in its emergency guidelines and the conclusion is very practical: what helps in the first 72 hours isn't a speech, it's four concrete things — safety, information, human contact and rest — and all of them can be prepared today.

1. What official manuals say: look, listen, connect

The reference guide in Spanish is “Psychological first aid: guide for field workers”, by the WHO with War Trauma Foundation and World Vision International. It's designed for people helping others in a disaster, but the framework is so simple that it works just as well for a neighbour, for your father or for yourself. It boils down to three actions.

  • Look: check that you're in a safe place, who needs help first and what basics are missing: water, warmth, a dry spot, real information. Before talking about feelings, deal with thirst, cold and noise.
  • Listen: approach, introduce yourself, ask what they need right now and don't force them to tell their story. The guide itself recalls a conclusion from the WHO's mhGAP working group: someone who is very distressed should be offered psychological first aid, not forced to go over what happened. Let those who want to talk talk, yes; interrogate those who don't, no.
  • Connect: help them reach family, services that are working and practical information. A good piece of information delivered in time (when the power will come back, where there's drinking water, which road is closed) calms more than any nice phrase.

What you can do in the next 10 minutes: drink a glass of water and eat something even if you're not hungry. Sit down and do two minutes of slow breathing (four seconds in, six seconds out). Use the 5-4-3-2-1 technique — name quietly five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch, two you can smell, one you can taste — when you notice your head going round in circles. And tidy one single room to turn it into your “command room”: a table with the radio or a charged phone, the flashlight, water, paper and pen. Visible order translates into calm.

What seems like a good idea but isn't: using alcohol to sleep (it gets you through the first part of the night asleep and the second part awake and more anxious), having the TV or radio on rolling news at all hours (it feeds the sense of catastrophe and doesn't give you a single useful fact), borrowing a sleeping pill from a neighbour (if you use something to sleep, do it through your doctor or pharmacist) and saying “we'll sleep when this is over”, because sleep debt also gets paid in the next day's decisions.

2. Sleeping when there's no light, no silence and no calm

The second or third night of an emergency is the most critical moment: you've used up the first day's adrenaline and you arrive exhausted, but your head won't switch off. Four measures solve a good part of the problem, and none of them costs money if you already have the kit put together.

  • Fixed schedules. Go to bed and get up at the same time, even if you're not working and you sleep in fits and starts. Your internal clock doesn't understand blackouts: it understands routine.
  • The bed is only for sleeping. If you haven't fallen asleep after 20-30 minutes, get out of bed and do something calm in dim light — read, write, tidy — until sleep comes back. It's the classic sleep-guide recommendation and, against rebound insomnia, it works better than tossing and turning.
  • Less caffeine in the afternoon and no stimulants in the early hours. Coffee, tea and cola drinks have an effect for hours; if you're on watch, ration them.
  • Cover screens and use a battery-powered clock. Your phone keeps you informed and steals your sleep: set two times a day to check the news — in the morning and late afternoon — and leave the phone charging in another room at night. An 8-12 euro battery-powered alarm clock saves you from checking the time at 3:40 in the morning.

For the environment, three common-sense things that almost nobody prepares: darkness (an eye mask, or an improvised curtain, because a streetlight or an LED can leave your face lit up all night), silence (foam earplugs; if the noise is outside, a station talking quietly or a constant radio sound masks it better than nothing) and coolness or warmth depending on the season — if the problem is cold or heat, you have the full rules in how to maintain body temperature without electricity. And a golden rule: never sleep on bare floor; a mat, cardboard and a blanket in layers, as explained in dressing in layers.

If something at home needs watching — a sick person, the water level, the neighbour downstairs — don't let the same person always do it. Divide the night into blocks and write it on paper, not from memory:

BlockWho watchesWho sleeps
22:00 - 01:00Person APerson B
01:00 - 04:00Person BPerson A
04:00 - 07:00Person APerson B (or a 30-min nap)

The watch shift is short on purpose: three hours can be sustained, six cannot. And one last tool that almost always works: the notebook next to the bed. Before you go to bed, write down the three or four worries that are going to wake you and what you can do about each one tomorrow. Getting them out of the mental loop and leaving them on paper is the cheapest way to get your brain to let them go.

3. Children: routine calms more than any explanation

A child doesn't need to know the full truth of a disaster: they need to know what is going to happen in their day. The presence of an adult who doesn't shout and routine — water, teeth, story, light — do more than any conversation. Three rules for tonight:

  • Tell them the truth, but short and with a plan. “There's no power because there's a very big outage. We're at home, there's water and food, and Mum and Dad are here. Tomorrow we'll look at it with the flashlight.” No impressive details and no promises you can't keep (“the power will definitely come back tomorrow” is a promise; “I'll tell you as soon as they know” is not).
  • Give them a job. What lowers childhood fear most is having a role: carrying the flashlight, noting the times, checking the water bottles, handing out the blankets. It's their way of feeling they control something.
  • Sleep next to them if they ask. This is not the night to teach them to sleep alone. The attachment object (blanket, soft toy, pacifier, story) comes out of the cupboard and goes into the evacuation backpack right now.

Also: no rolling news in front of them, and a dim light in the hallway all night so they don't wake up in total darkness they don't recognise. If after several days the child isn't eating, isn't sleeping or is very irritable, talk to your paediatrician. You have the age-by-age details in babies and children in an emergency and the materials in the baby and breastfeeding kit.

4. Older people, people with chronic illness and those who live alone

Here preparation happens before the disaster, not during it. Darkness disorients an older person faster than hunger: they lose their sense of the hallway, get up at night and fall. Concrete solutions:

  • Beacon lights in the hallway and bathroom. Four LED lights that switch on by themselves cost less than 15 euros and prevent the most common fall during a blackout. Everything the older person's kit needs is detailed on its page.
  • A towel at the edge of the bed and a clear path. No chairs or boxes between the bed and the door: at night and without light, they become an obstacle.
  • A call at the same time, every day. It's not a chat: it's a status check. And always with a designated backup person, because the person who calls also gets sick. It's the basis of what I covered in living alone and being prepared.
  • Give notice in person, not by WhatsApp. If there's hearing loss, a message is no use: you have to knock on the door, and do it speaking loudly and facing them. The same goes for mobile alerts, which should be explained beforehand.

With chronic medication, the order of the day is to keep to the schedule and not improvise doses: a pill organiser and a written list, with the days marked. If there are insulins or medicines that need cold, check how to secure 2-4 weeks without a pharmacy and always consult your doctor or pharmacist for any decision about doses or storage. And if the person has cognitive impairment, don't argue with their reality: redirect — water, blanket, hand, song, photo —.

5. The one who holds everything together also collapses

In every home there's someone who acts as the switchboard: they call, organise, don't sleep and after three days they burn out. If you're that person, this is for you.

  • Nobody watches two nights in a row. Write it on the fridge door in big letters, because it's the first thing everyone skips.
  • Eat and drink even if you're not hungry. Five minutes of salty food and a glass of water every three hours do more than a coffee on the run.
  • Name a backup out loud. “If I can't, you call Marta and she knows where everything is.” Above all, leave the important phone numbers written on paper: the full list is in the official resources you should have saved.
  • Go outside for five minutes a day. Air, street, walking. The WHO has documented it: physical activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression and improves sleep, and that counts double when everything is upside down.

And put an honest limit on your role: you don't have to fix anyone. Accompanying, sorting out the practical things and handing over the baton is already all that can be done on the first day. If you or someone in your home have gone several days without sleeping or eating, if sadness sets in or ideas of not going on living appear, that isn't managed with willpower: call 024, the suicide prevention helpline of the Ministry of Health, free and available 24 hours a day, or 112 if the emergency is immediate. For any clinical doubt, consult your doctor or pharmacist.

6. Your rest and head kit: ten items and a seven-day plan

None of these items is expensive and all of them get used at home on any bad night, not only in a disaster. Put the small things in a cloth bag inside the basic 72-hour kit and leave the big things in the bedroom.

ItemWhat it's really forGuide price
Foam earplugs (5 pairs)Sleeping with a radio station, a generator or a street on alert3-6 €
Cloth eye maskReal darkness when there are streetlights, candles or an LED on5-8 €
Headlamp with red modeMoving around at night without waking anyone and without ruining your sleep10-15 €
Battery-powered alarm clockKnowing the time without turning on the phone at 4 in the morning8-12 €
Battery or hand-crank radioOfficial information without network or battery, and constant sound to sleep15-25 €
Small notebook and penEmptying the worry loop before bed and writing down phone numbers2-4 €
Deck of cards or pocket bookTwo hours of quiet activity without screens, children included5-10 €
Extra light blanketSleeping warm without sweating: layers, not a heavy blanket10-15 €
1.5-litre water bottleHaving water next to you stops you getting up in the dark and drinking less1 €
Minimal toiletry bag and wipesWashing your face and teeth brings back a sense of normality4-6 €

And this is the seven-day plan to have all this sorted before you need it, at fifteen minutes a day:

  • Day 1. Write the key phone numbers on a sheet of paper (112, 024, doctor, school, two neighbours, two relatives) and the family meeting point. One paper copy in your wallet and another stuck inside the hall cupboard.
  • Day 2. Set up the command table: radio, flashlight, charger, water, paper, pen. One table only, always the same one.
  • Day 3. Buy earplugs, an eye mask and a battery-powered clock. They go in the bedside drawer, not in the storage room.
  • Day 4. Prepare the “dinner without power”: cans, nuts, fruit and water within reach, and a tray with what you need (can opener, spoon, napkins) so you don't open cupboards in the dark.
  • Day 5. Try a two-hour night without mains electricity at home: flashlights, properly safe candles, no screens. You'll discover what's missing before you need it.
  • Day 6. Explain the plan to the children and give them a specific task (flashlight, water list). Ten minutes is enough.
  • Day 7. Call the family member who lives alone and agree the time of the daily call. And tell a neighbour who to alert if they don't see you.

With this you have covered what no flashlight can fix: sleeping, eating, not losing your head and knowing who to call. If you want to divide the work by scenario, start with putting together your 72-hour kit and with the first decisions in a blackout; and if tonight you're already in the middle of the mess, the urgent stuff is in home or lockdown kit.

conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.titulo: Keeping food without a fridge: what lasts and what to throw out (2026)
conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.resumen: What to throw out and what to save when the power goes: AESAN's official times and temperatures for fridge, freezer and pantry, and reliable home methods.
conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.cuerpo:
The power goes out at 21:40. By 21:55 you've already opened the fridge “to see what's there,” by 22:10 the freezer, and the next day you're staring at a warm fridge with meat, fresh cheese and leftovers you don't know whether to throw away. That moment—deciding what can be saved and what goes in the bin—is exactly what this guide solves: hours and temperatures measured by the Spanish Agency for Food Safety and Nutrition (AESAN) during the blackout of 28 April 2025, plus a pantry you can set up today so you don't depend on refrigeration.

And it's not a whim: the EU Preparedness Union Strategy (March 2025) asks households to have enough supplies for 72 hours. Almost every kit list includes water, a flashlight and a radio, but very few say which foods really keep without refrigeration or cooking. That's what you'll find here, plus what you can do in 20 minutes after you finish reading.

1. The hours that decide everything: your fridge without power

The first thing to understand is that the enemy isn't “the blackout”; it's the temperature each food has reached. A fridge doesn't warm up instantly when the circuit breaker trips: it holds the cold like a cool box, which is why what matters most isn't how long the outage lasts, but how many times you've opened the door. With the door closed, a well-stocked fridge keeps food below 5 °C for about 4 hours; a full or half-full freezer keeps food frozen for 24 to 48 hours. With the door opened every few minutes, those figures fall apart on their own.

The official AESAN rules, published after the 28A blackout and included by the Ministry of Social Rights, Consumer Affairs and Agenda 2030, are as follows:

  • Outages of less than 4 hours (without opening the door): you don't need to throw anything away because of the blackout.
  • Outages of more than 4 hours: temperatures have probably exceeded 5 °C, so throw out perishables: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, fresh cheese and leftovers. Throw them out even if you cook them well: the risk isn't eliminated by the heat of the frying pan, and those foods can also contaminate others through contact.
  • Whole fruit and vegetables: they keep without refrigeration if they still look good. Cut up or already in a prepared salad: into the bin.
  • Freezer: if the food still has ice crystals, is hard and cold, it can be refrozen. If it has completely thawed but is still cold, eat it that day. If you're not sure how long it has been thawed, throw it out.
  • Canned goods, soft drinks, chocolate and drinks that you kept in the fridge out of habit: they don't need refrigeration and are perfectly fine.

And the rule that sums them all up: never taste a food to decide whether it's safe, and don't trust smell or appearance. If in doubt, throw it out. Throwing away 12 euros of food is infinitely cheaper than food poisoning in the middle of an emergency, with emergency departments overwhelmed and no way to get there by car.

SituationWhat to do
Outage < 4 h, door closedEverything is still fine. Don't throw anything away.
Outage > 4 hThrow out perishables: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, fresh cheese, leftovers.
Whole fruit/vegetablesThey keep. Cut up or prepared, throw them out.
Freezer, 24–48 h without openingIf ice crystals remain: it can be refrozen. Thawed and cold: eat that day. In doubt: throw it out.
Canned goods and closed packaged foodsPerfect outside refrigeration. Once opened, refrigerate and eat within 2–3 days.

2. What really keeps without refrigeration

Here's the heart of the matter: a prepared home isn't one with a full fridge; it's one with a pantry that doesn't depend on the fridge. These shelf lives are approximate—they depend on temperature, humidity and how you store things—but they're useful for deciding what to buy extra the next time you go to the supermarket:

FoodWithout refrigeration, closedKey to keeping it
Canned goods (tuna, sardines, cooked pulses, tomato)2–5 yearsDry place, no knocks or dented cans. Once opened: refrigerate and eat within 2–3 days.
Dried pulses, rice, pastaYearsAirtight container in the dark. Moisture is the only thing that ruins them.
UHT / powdered / condensed milkMonths unopenedOnce opened, refrigerate and use within 2–3 days. Powdered milk is the most heat-resistant.
Olive oil12–18 monthsDark and cool. Light and heat make it go rancid before the date.
Honey, salt, sugarPractically indefiniteClosed container. If honey crystallizes, it hasn't gone bad: that's normal.
Nuts and dried fruit6–12 monthsAirtight container; in heat they go rancid even if they don't look bad.
Whole cured sausage (chorizo, salchichón, ham)WeeksWhole, hung in a dry, ventilated place. Sliced and packaged, it does need refrigeration.
Potato, onion, garlic, sweet potato, whole squashWeeksDark, dry and ventilated, kept separate from each other. Potatoes and onions never together.
Unwashed eggsWeeks in a cool placeIf it's hot, move them to the coolest spot in the house and eat them soon.

Notice the pattern: everything that keeps without refrigeration has three things in common—it's dry, it's acidic or it's factory vacuum-packed. And everything that spoils quickly is moist and only mildly acidic: fresh meat, fish, fresh dairy, leftovers. With that criterion you can already set up half your pantry without memorizing any table.

3. What you should never do (and some popular advice that's bad)

There are habits that circulate in every emergency and are downright dangerous. These four in particular:

  • Tasting food to see if it's still good. It's the first thing AESAN says not to do. Pathogens that grow in heat don't reliably change taste or smell.
  • Trusting the appearance of home-canned food. The botulism toxin doesn't change colour, smell, taste or texture: a contaminated jar can taste perfectly fine. And botulism is mainly associated with home-canned low-acid vegetables—chillies in oil, asparagus, green beans, beetroot, corn—according to AESAN documents. If a home-made jar has a bulging lid, releases gas when opened or smells odd: into the bin, without tasting it.
  • Freezing “so as not to waste it” food that has already been out of refrigeration for hours. The freezer slows things down; it doesn't fix them. An opened container, a lifted lid or a lunchbox that has been on the counter all afternoon doesn't become safe just because you put it in the freezer: what has already multiplied is still there. Freeze what was cold; throw out what was lukewarm.
  • Leaving cooked food at room temperature “for a while.” AESAN is clear: cooked food should be eaten straight away, or kept above 60 °C, or below 5 °C. The lukewarm range is exactly where germs thrive.

And one that does work, even if it sounds like Grandma's advice: heating home-canned food thoroughly before eating it. Public health documents recommend boiling or heating food for at least 10 minutes at 80 °C or above: botulinum toxin is destroyed by heat, so a well-boiled stew is much safer than that same jar eaten cold on toast. Even so, the best measure is not to make low-acid vegetable preserves without a tested recipe and without acidifying with citric acid.

4. How to set up a pantry that doesn't depend on the fridge

Buying isn't the same as storing. I've seen 200-euro pantries ruined by a damp corner. What matters:

  • Where: cool (ideally below 20 °C), dry, dark and ventilated. The three worst places in a Spanish home: on top of the fridge or next to the oven, a sun-facing balcony, and a damp garage or storage room. Check AEMET warnings and, if weeks above 35 °C are coming, move delicate foods to the coolest part of the house.
  • In what: an airtight glass jar with a seal or a plastic container with a rubber lid. Open plastic bags and cardboard boxes are an invitation to moths and weevils.
  • The trick almost nobody uses against bugs: if you have freezer space, leave the packet of pulses, rice or flour inside for 48–72 hours before transferring it to the jar. It kills the eggs and larvae that were already in the packaging and stops an infestation appearing three months later.
  • Cans: don't stack them in unstable towers, don't let them get wet (a rusted can eventually perforates), and don't use dented ones. Always put the fatter cans at the bottom. And a bulging can is not opened: it goes in the bin.
  • Humidity: use the silica gel packets that come in shoeboxes and mix them into jars of pasta and biscuits.
  • Date and order: write the month of purchase on the lid with a marker and follow the FIFO rule: new at the back, old at the front. A 10-minute review twice a year stops you discovering the problem just when you need it.

How much should you buy? Start with what's realistic: 72 hours of food that needs neither refrigeration nor cooking (the basic 72-hour kit gives you the list), then one week and, only when that rotates well, the jump to a 30-day kit. If you're unsure where to start, I explain it in detail here: 72-hour kit or 30-day kit.

5. Preserving food without refrigeration when the fridge isn't coming back

If the outage stretches beyond a day or two, you have three resources and quite a few traps. The real resources, in order of reliability:

  • Vinegar and acid: vinegar lowers the pH below 4.6, where Clostridium botulinum cannot grow. Vinegar-pickled vegetables are the safest and fastest home method: cut, blanch, cover with vinegar and brine, close and store in the dark. Pickled garlic and onion keep for months.
  • Salt: salting and strong brines draw moisture out of food by osmosis and slow bacteria. It works with fish, pork belly and vegetables. It's not suitable for everything: salted meat has to be cooked afterwards.
  • Drying: sun and air for tomatoes, peppers, figs, grapes or mushrooms, or the oven at minimum temperature if you have gas. It requires dry air; in humid northern areas it ends up mouldy before it dries.
  • Fermentation: sauerkraut, kimchi or pickles fermented with 2% salt acidify on their own and keep for months. They need a clean jar, vegetables kept under their own liquid and a cool place.
  • Sugar: jams and preserves with plenty of fruit and plenty of sugar keep without refrigeration once opened if you cover them well and don't put dirty spoons in.

And the traps, which are worth being clear about because they cause most home poisonings: covering vegetables in oil (chillies, garlic, dried tomatoes) creates exactly the oxygen-free environment botulism needs, if you haven't acidified it first; home vacuum-sealing leftovers without sterilizing isn't preserving, it's culturing; smoking by eye at home isn't a safe long-term preservation method. And if you make preserves in a water bath, bear in mind that boiling at 100 °C doesn't destroy spores: it's only reliable with acidic foods (tomato, sweetened fruit, pickles) or with a pressure cooker and tested recipes. For everything else, it's better to freeze, dry or not do it. And if in doubt, ask your doctor or pharmacist: they can advise you on citric acid, doses and preserves.

If you're in the middle of an emergency and the food is already warm or thawed, the important thing is to eat it in order: first the perishables that were in the freezer and have thawed, then the fridge and, finally, the pantry. You'll find complete menus without cooking or refrigeration in what to eat if the power goes out: three-day menus and the details of how to store everything in storing water and food at home.

6. What you can do today in 20 minutes

None of this is any use if it stays theoretical. You can do these six things this afternoon, with what you already have or with a small shop:

  • Put a thermometer in the fridge (a few euros) and check that it's at 4 °C or below. If it isn't, you've been paying for electricity for nothing.
  • Set aside the last shelf for what survives without refrigeration: cans, nuts, chocolate, oil. That way, when the power goes out, you know what not to touch.
  • Freeze half-filled water bottles or jugs in the free spaces in the freezer: they act as cold accumulators and, when they thaw, they're drinking water. And tell everyone at home: the fridge does not get opened.
  • Write the time of the last outage on the fridge door and a note with the 4-hour rule. In an emergency, nobody remembers the figures.
  • Put an airtight jar of pulses and another of rice in the pantry, and add them to the shopping list when you use them.
  • Review your actual kit: blackout kit, home kit and, if you cook with gas or want to eat hot food, a gas stove with cartridges and ventilation. With that and a well-stocked pantry, a three-day outage stops being a food problem.

What happened on 28 April 2025 left a very specific lesson in Spanish households: the fridge held out, water came out of the tap as soon as pressure returned, and what failed was not knowing what to do with the food. It's solved in one afternoon, and that afternoon is today. You'll find the full review of the day after the blackout in lessons from 28A and water—the other pillar—in water: how much you need and how to purify it.

panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.titulo: Portable solar panel: how many watts you really need (2026)
panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.resumen: Most emergency kit panels sell you fantasies: how many real watts to expect, what wattage to buy and how to pair it with a power bank.
panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.cuerpo:
The blackout of 28 April 2025 left half the country without power and with a phone at 2%. Most people solved it with the power bank they already had charged. But if the power goes out for several days and there is no sun (or it rains for weeks), the power bank drops to zero and does not recharge. This is where the portable solar panel comes in, and why almost everything sold on Amazon does not do what it promises.

I am not going to sell you a 300-watt panel for your balcony. I am going to tell you what a real panel can do — or cannot do — when the power goes out, and which panel + battery combo makes sense for getting through a week without the grid.

The trap of advertised watts

An advertised 100-watt portable solar panel rarely delivers 100 real watts. The reason is not a scam — it is physics: panels are measured under standard test conditions (STC), which are 1000 W/m² irradiance, a cell temperature of 25 °C and an AM 1.5 spectrum. In real life:

  • Irradiance in Spain never reaches 1000 W/m² on a sustained basis (even in summer, the ceiling is usually between 800 and 950 W/m²; official data from AEMET and IAE confirm this).
  • Cell temperature easily rises to 45-65 °C under direct sun: each degree above 25 °C reduces power by 0.3% to 0.5%. At 55 °C, a panel loses between 9% and 15% of its power.
  • The angle of incidence of the sun changes constantly; if the panel is not perpendicular to the sun, you lose 20-40% of performance.

A 100 W panel correctly oriented on a clear June day in Spain delivers between 60 and 80 real watts, and only for about 5-6 hours of the day. A 50 W panel correctly oriented delivers between 30 and 40 real watts. That is the figure you need to use for your calculations.

How much energy do you need in an emergency?

Before buying, you need to know what you are going to charge. Here is the minimum that most people need to keep running:

  • Phone (full charge): between 10 and 15 Wh (a modern 4000 mAh phone at 3.7 V is ~15 Wh; with charger efficiency and losses, you need ~12-15 Wh net).
  • Battery-powered FM radio: 0-2 Wh (if it uses AA batteries, the panel will not charge them; if it has a USB port, between 1 and 2 W).
  • LED headlamp: between 2 and 5 Wh per charge.
  • Power bank you recharge: a 20,000 mAh power bank at 3.7 V is 74 Wh; with boost losses, you need to put about 90 Wh net into it to recharge it.

This gives an idea of how much a panel generates on a real sunny day:

Advertised panelReal watts (good day)Equivalent sun hoursWh/dayPhone charges
30 W18-22 W5 h90-110 Wh6-8
50 W30-40 W5 h150-200 Wh10-15
100 W60-80 W5 h300-400 Wh20-30

Do not be fooled: with a 30 W panel you can already recharge a 20,000 mAh power bank every two or three days in summer. In winter, multiply the time by two or three (fewer sun hours, low angle). On a cloudy day: multiply by three or four.

The combo that really works: panel + power bank

A solar panel on its own is not much use in an emergency: it generates energy when the sun shines, not when you need it. What you need is generate + store. The minimum useful combo is a 30-50 W panel plus a power bank of at least 20,000 mAh. Here is how it works:

  • You generate with the panel when there is sun (between 10:00 and 16:00, preferably with the panel facing south and perpendicular to the sun).
  • You store it in the power bank, which is already part of your basic 72h kit.
  • You consume it when you want: at night, in the rain, with your phone in your pocket.

The key is that the power bank has a USB input that supports the voltage and amperage coming from the panel. A 50 W panel generates between 5 and 6 V at 8-10 A: you need a power bank that accepts that input (most modern ones do). If not, you will have to use a solar charge controller (PWM or MPPT), which adds cost and complexity.

What panel size is enough?

For household use in a crisis:

  • 30-50 W (the minimum): charges a phone between 6 and 10 times a day in summer. Recharges a 20,000 mAh power bank every 2-3 days. It fits in a backpack. This is what I recommend for most households if you are only going to charge a phone and a radio.
  • 50-100 W (the reasonable option): recharges the power bank every day in summer, every two days in winter. Enough to keep a phone, radio and headlamp running without worry. It takes up a little more space but fits in a car trunk or on a terrace.
  • 100-200 W (the portable maximum): you recharge the power bank several times a day. It is useful if you need to power something else (a room LED light, a USB fan), but you start to need structure and a fixed surface. It is not a backpack item: it is a terrace item.

What to look for (and what not to) when buying a panel

The current market has everything. The important thing is to distinguish what works from what is decoration:

  • Monocrystalline panels are more efficient (higher conversion percentage) than polycrystalline ones: a 100 W monocrystalline panel weighs less and takes up less space than a polycrystalline panel of the same wattage. The price difference is minimal.
  • Folding or rigid panel: folding ones are practical to carry in a backpack; rigid ones are more durable and are installed permanently on a terrace or balcony. There is no major difference in performance if both are monocrystalline.
  • Built-in controller: many panels already include a PWM regulator or a direct USB connector. If they do not, you need a separate controller (from 5 to 20 €). Always check that it is compatible with your power bank.
  • Avoid panels with a built-in battery: the battery heats up in the sun, degrades and is also much heavier. The right approach is a separate panel + power bank.
  • Water resistance matters: look for panels rated IP65 at minimum if you are going to use them outdoors. During a DANA it rains, and you are not going to keep the panel under a roof.

Typical mistakes

  • Buying a large panel without thinking about where to install it: a 100 W panel needs about 6-7 m² of surface area to deploy (double-panel folding models measure ~1.5 x 1 m; four-panel models, ~2 x 1 m). If you do not have a terrace or balcony facing south, it ends up in the shade of a tree and is useless.
  • Not having a power bank charged in advance: the panel generates energy when the sun shines; if you do not store it, you lose the hours without sun. The power bank is the bridge between generation and consumption.
  • Pointing the panel at the sky: the sun is not always overhead. In winter, at 10 a.m. or 4 p.m., the angle is very low and performance drops by 30-50%. Adjust the panel angle according to the time of day.
  • Covering the panel without realizing: a leaf, a coaster, a patch of thick fog. If the panel gets dirty, output drops by 10-30%. Clean it from time to time.
  • Confusing watts (W) with watt-hours (Wh): the panel says 100 W: that is 100 watts when the sun is perfect at that instant. Wh are what you generate in a day (W × h). To know how many phone charges you can expect, multiply the real watts by the equivalent sun hours.

What if there is no sun for weeks?

That is the real limitation of the portable solar panel: it does not generate when there is no sun. And in Spain, the months with the highest risk of crisis (autumn and winter) are precisely the ones with the least sun. That is why the panel is a complement, not the base of the kit. The base is the charged power bank (which you already discuss in the blackout kit) and the battery-powered radio. The solar panel is what ensures that, when the sun returns, you do not have to depend on anyone to recharge.

The EU recommends 72 hours of self-sufficiency; a solar panel helps you go beyond those three days if the crisis drags on and the sky clears. But if the only thing you have is a panel and not a power bank, you have nothing.

Practical summary

  • Reasonable minimum: a 30-50 W monocrystalline panel + a 20,000 mAh power bank.
  • Ideal: a 50-100 W panel + a large power bank (20,000-30,000 mAh) with a flexible USB input.
  • Fixed installation: if you have a south-facing terrace, a fixed 100 W rigid panel is best: you do not have to orient it, it does not move, it generates all day.
  • Remember: the panel is not the base of the kit. The charged power bank, the battery-powered radio and non-perishable food are. The solar panel takes you from 3 days to a week if the sky clears.

The blackout kit includes a power bank and solar panel as recommended items; the guide to eating without power details the order of consumption; the basic kit is the base to which you add any other item.

seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.titulo: Passive home safety: saves lives without you doing anything (2026)
seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.resumen: Smoke alarms, fire extinguishers and electrical standards are not decoration: they are your home's first line of defence: what to fit, where, and how to maintain it.
seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.cuerpo:
A home fire is the most likely emergency and the one that gives you the least time to react: a fire can sweep through an entire apartment in less than five minutes, and toxic smoke kills more people than flames. Home passive safety is all the elements that work without you doing anything: detectors, fire-resistant materials, extinguishers and electrical installation standards that act before you have to run. They are not unnecessary expenses: they are your family's first line of defense.

What passive safety is

In safety engineering, a distinction is made between active protection (extinguishers you press, sprinklers you trigger, calls to 112) and passive protection (detectors that sound on their own, fire doors that block the spread of smoke, cables that do not catch fire, materials that do not spread flame). Passive protection is what warns you or protects you while you sleep, without you having to decide anything. And it is also the most undervalued in Spanish homes.

The Technical Building Code (CTE), Basic Document DB-SI, already requires fire-resistance levels for construction elements and the installation of detection systems in new buildings. But in a private home, responsibility for detectors and extinguishers is yours. And it should not cost you more than 60 euros a year.

1. Smoke detectors: the first warning

Smoke detectors are the single element that saves the most lives in a home fire. They warn you in the first minutes, when you can still get out or call for help, and they do so at night, when you are not conscious. The Community of Madrid has standardized this in all its guides:

  • Optical: recommended for bedrooms, living rooms and rest areas — they detect slow-combustion and smoldering smoke, the most dangerous because it is invisible at first but already kills.
  • Heat: for kitchens or storage rooms, where normal cooking smoke would not trigger false alarms. They activate at a fixed temperature (usually 57 °C).
  • Location: on the ceiling, at least 3 meters from bedrooms. Each floor of the home needs at least one. In single-story homes under 60 m², one may be enough, although two are recommended: living room and hallway.
  • Monthly test: press the test button every month. Change the batteries when clocks change, just like clock batteries.
  • Every 10 years: replace the entire detector. It does not last forever: the sensor gets dirty and degrades.

Price: 8-15 € per new optical detector. A pack of 4 detectors with batteries included costs around 30-50 €. It is not a luxury: it is what separates a scare from a tragedy. And in many buildings they are already installed under new-build regulations, but check that they work.

2. Electrical safety: preventing short circuits and overloads

Faulty electrical installations are the leading cause of home fires. Not because of a mysterious wiring failure, but because of overloads you can control:

  • Do not daisy-chain power strips: plugging one power strip into another multiplies the risk of a short circuit. A power strip has limited capacity, and a heater or hairdryer can overload it.
  • Power strip with switch and thermal protection: buy power strips with an internal fuse that cuts out if there is an overload. They cost 3-5 € more than a normal one and are the difference between a blackout and a fire.
  • Residual current device and circuit breaker in the electrical panel: they are required by regulations and must react in milliseconds if they detect a leakage current or a short circuit. If your panel does not have them or you are unsure, an electrician can check them in an hour.
  • Old wiring: if your home is more than 25-30 years old and an electrician has never checked it, do it. Aluminum cables or installations with deteriorated insulation are a latent risk.

Price: a safe power strip, 10-20 €. A professional electrical inspection, 60-120 €.

3. Kitchen: the highest-risk area

The kitchen is the room where most home fires start: ignited grease, oil on fire, gas left on without a flame. The recommendations are simple, but you do not apply them until it happens to you:

  • Never leave the kitchen unattended when there is an open flame. If you have to leave, turn it off. Fire spreads in seconds.
  • Extinguisher near the kitchen: class F (flammable liquids and fats), specific for kitchen fires. A water extinguisher on a pan of burning oil can be counterproductive — class F is the right one.
  • Lids or a kitchen fire spray: if a pan catches fire, put the lid on and cut off the fire. The oxygen goes away and the flame goes out on its own. Never throw water on burning grease.
  • Keep flammable items away from flames: towels, kitchen cloths, plastic bags and scouring pads away from the burner.

Price: class F extinguisher, 15-25 €. The pan lid, free if you already have one.

4. Extinguishers and how to choose them

One extinguisher does not work for everything. In a Spanish home, what you need is:

  • ABC powder (6 kg): the most versatile for the home. It works on wood, gas, flammable liquids and electricity up to 1000 V. It is what Protección Civil recommends for homes.
  • CO₂ (2 kg): ideal for sensitive electrical equipment (computer, TV, electrical panel). It leaves no residue, but it does not work on wood fires or grease.
  • Water with additive (6 L): good for wood and textiles, not for electricity or grease. Less versatile than ABC powder but cleaner.

Location: in a central hallway, accessible, not in the kitchen (where heat could render it ineffective) or in a closed cupboard. On the wall, at eye level, with a strap or bracket costing 8-12 €.

Maintenance: an extinguisher lasts 5-10 years and needs servicing every 5 years by an authorized company. Check the pressure gauge monthly: the needle in the green means it is fine; in the red, it has no pressure.

Price: ABC powder extinguisher 6 kg, 15-25 €; 5-year service, 20-30 €.

5. Fire doors and fire-resistant materials

Bedroom doors are the first barrier that delays fire if it comes from outside. A solid wood door or one with a fire-resistant core can delay the spread of fire by 30 to 60 minutes more than a hollow door. This is not an exaggeration: it is what allows you to call 112 and for the fire department to arrive in time.

Fire-resistant materials are already included in the construction of new buildings (the CTE's DB-SI requires it). But in homes built before 2006 they are not always present: a window without curtains or with thick curtains without fire-retardant treatment, a hollow front door, exposed cables — these are the weak points you can fix.

6. Evacuation plan

Passive safety is useless if no one knows what to do when the detector sounds. A three-step evacuation plan:

  1. Get out immediately: do not try to save belongings or check every room. Every second counts.
  2. Meet outside: at a pre-agreed point — the sidewalk in front, the streetlight on the corner — and count everyone. If someone is missing, tell 112 before going back in.
  3. Never go back inside: houses burn from the inside and the ceiling collapses in minutes. The fire department will go in to look for you.

Write this plan down and stick it near the exits. Practice with the family: have the children run out when the detector alarm sounds, without thinking, like a game. Firefighters recommend it.

Quick investment summary

ItemPriceService lifeProtects against
Smoke detectors (pack of 4)30-50 €10 yearsFire while sleeping, toxic smoke at night
ABC extinguisher 6 kg15-25 €5-10 yearsFirst minutes of a real fire
Power strip with fuse10-20 €IndefiniteElectrical overload
Class F kitchen extinguisher15-25 €5-10 yearsGrease and oil fire
Electrical inspection60-120 €Recheck every 10 yearsFaulty installation

Total investment: 130-235 € for real protection for 10 years. Less than 20 € a year to protect your home and family from the most likely home emergency.

Common mistakes

  • Silencing the detector because of false alarms: if the kitchen sets it off, switch to a heat detector in that location. Do not remove it or cover it with plastic film: that is what most families who suffered fatal fires did in data from Protección Civil.
  • Putting the extinguisher in the cupboard under the sink: if the kitchen catches fire, you are not going to open a cupboard full of cleaning products to look for the extinguisher. Put it on the hallway wall.
  • Forgetting the meeting point: an extinguisher without an evacuation plan is like a parachute without knowing at what height to open it.
  • Not checking the extinguisher: a pressure gauge in the red is an ornamental extinguisher. Check it once a month, like changing the detector batteries.

Passive safety items are not an extra: they are the foundation of any prepared home. If you do not yet have smoke detectors or an extinguisher, the home kit and the basic 72h kit include these items in their lists. For a complete evacuation plan, read the family emergency plan.

vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.titulo: Dressing in layers: the technique that prevents deadly cold (2026)
vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.resumen: It's not fashion or hiking: it is the recommendation from Health and Civil Protection against hypothermia: the three layers, which fabrics, and why cotton fails.
vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.cuerpo:
The Ministry of Health's Cold Weather Plan for the 2025-2026 season records that every winter low temperatures cause hundreds of avoidable deaths in Spain. They are not mountain accidents: they are older people in flats without sufficient heating, workers walking home in wet clothes, outings that run long when the temperature drops. The most repeated recommendation in official guides is always the same: dress in layers. Not for fashion — for physics.

Why layers and not one thick garment?

The human body loses heat mainly through the skin. Clothing does not generate heat: it traps it. And the best thermal insulator there is is still air. Three layers of thin fabric trap three air pockets; a single thick garment traps one. That is why Civil Protection and the Ministry of Health repeat word for word: “Bear in mind that several layers of thin clothing protect more than a single thick one, because they form insulating air pockets between them”.

Layers also let you adjust temperature. If you are walking and feel hot, take off a layer and do not sweat. If you sweat in a single thick garment and then stop, that wet clothing becomes a body cooler. Cotton cannot handle it: moisture takes you to hypothermia faster than dry cold.

The three layers: function and material

Layer 1: the base (next to the skin)

Its only job is to move sweat away from the skin. If the base gets wet, nothing you wear over it will save you. Valid options:

  • Merino wool: natural, absorbs moisture without losing heat, smells less than synthetic. Ideal for all-day wear. A 150-200 g merino base T-shirt costs between €25 and €50.
  • Polypropylene or technical polyester: synthetics move moisture away quickly and dry in hours. They are cheaper (€5-15) but can smell sooner and do not regulate temperature as well as wool.

Cotton is never used as a base layer. It absorbs sweat, holds it and stays stuck to the skin. When it gets wet — and it will get wet — it conducts cold like a sheet of water. In mountaineering slang, cotton “kills you”: it is literally the most dangerous material for cold emergencies. The Ministry of Health and the WHO agree: synthetic fibres and wool are the recommended options.

Layer 2: insulation (the most important)

This is where real heat is generated. The mid layer traps the air your body heats. Options:

  • Fleece: the king of value for money. Light, warm, dries fast. A mid-weight fleece costs €15-30 and works for everything: from a night without power to a Sunday walk.
  • Plika (PrimaLoft, Thinsulate, etc.): synthetic insulations that imitate down but work when damp. Ideal if there is a risk of rain. In rain jackets or insulated vests. Price: €20-60.
  • Down: the best insulator by weight, but if it gets wet it loses 90% of its capacity. Good for the kit at home, not for wearing if it rains or you sweat.

For the emergency kit, a fleece is the most versatile option: it works when damp, takes up little space, costs little and covers the widest temperature range.

Layer 3: the barrier (wind and rain)

Protects from the outside. Without this layer, wind strips the heat from the inner layers in minutes. It is called a “shell” in technical jargon.

  • Rain jacket or waterproof: with a waterproof membrane (IP ≥ 1500 mm) and sealed seams. A lightweight rain jacket (50-150 g) is so small it fits in any backpack. Price: €15-40 for basic functional models.
  • Rigid (hardshell): if prolonged heavy rain is expected (a DANA in winter, for example). More expensive (€40-80) but lasts for years.

The key is that the outer layer is breathable: if it is not, sweat inside condenses on the inside and you end up wet. Look for “breathable” or “breathable membrane”.

What does not get dressed properly: head, hands and feet

Ten percent of official sources forget it, but this is where frostbite and mild hypothermia begin:

  • Hat or scarf: heat is lost through the head. A wool or fleece hat costing €5-12 makes the difference between a mild night and constant shivering. A scarf protects the neck and stops wind getting under the coat.
  • Gloves: mittens are warmer than gloves (fingers share heat). A pair of wool or fleece gloves, €8-20.
  • Socks: two thin pairs work better than one thick pair (another air pocket). Merino wool or synthetic, never cotton. A pair of wool socks for emergencies costs €8-15.
  • Waterproof footwear: wet soles are the fastest entry point for cold. Waterproof boots or, at least, slip-resistant overshoes (€5-12) if you walk on snow or ice.

The system in practice: what to wear for each scenario

There is no single recipe for every temperature, but these combinations cover you from a Madrid winter to a snowfall in the Sistema Central:

Approximate temperatureCombinationTotal weight (clothing)
+5 °C to 10 °CBase + rain jacket~300 g
0 °C to +5 °CBase + fleece + rain jacket~700 g
-10 °C to 0 °CBase + fleece + Plika + rain jacket~1,000 g
Below -10 °CDouble base (merino + synthetic) + thick Plika + waterproof parka + gloves + hat + double socks~1,800 g

For an emergency kit in a backpack, the base + fleece + rain jacket combination covers most winter scenarios in Spain and weighs under 1 kg in total.

Signs that something is wrong

The Ministry of Health and the Cold Weather Plan identify clear signs of hypothermia. If you detect them in yourself or another person, adding warm layers is the first step:

  • Uncontrollable shivering: the body tries to generate heat by fighting back. It is no longer uncomfortable; it is an emergency response.
  • Confusion or drowsiness: the brain loses function. The person may deny being cold.
  • Difficulty speaking: words become confused or impossible.
  • Clumsy hands: you cannot do up buttons or light a lighter.

If frostbite appears (skin white, yellowish, numb and firm) — do not rub the area and put it in warm (not hot) water. If you cannot walk on your feet, do not try to walk: you will make the injury worse.

Common mistakes

  • “A jacket is enough for me”: if it rains, if you sweat, if it is windy — it is not enough. A rain jacket on top is the difference between a night at home and a night in the emergency department.
  • Cotton as “I always wear it”: the denim shirt, the thick cotton sweater… they are normal daytime clothes. In an emergency, cotton is your enemy. Wool and synthetics keep you dry.
  • Not covering head and hands: you can have your torso covered and lose 40% of your heat through your head and extremities. A hat and gloves are not optional in extreme cold.
  • Storing warm clothing in the storage room: if the power goes out in January, you need warm clothing where you can grab it in 30 seconds, not where “you keep the winter stuff”.

What to include in the kit

For each family member, a bag with the basics to layer up:

  • Merino wool or synthetic base T-shirt
  • Mid-weight fleece
  • Lightweight rain jacket
  • Wool or fleece hat
  • Pair of gloves (wool or fleece)
  • Two pairs of wool socks
  • Scarf or thick neckerchief

This weighs less than 2 kg per person, takes up the space of a medium bag, and covers you from a January power cut to an isolated snowfall. If you live in northern or mountain areas, add a Plika (PrimaLoft) layer or a thermal vest.

A fact that is not scary: temperatures are rising

Winter 2025-2026 was, according to AEMET, the sixth warmest winter since 1961. Average temperatures were 1 °C above normal. That is not nothing: the last eight winters have been warmer than normal. But extreme cold waves do not disappear because of the average: when they come, they come suddenly (like the Arctic air episode that Civil Protection warned about in December 2026) and temperatures can drop 15-20 °C in hours. The layering system works for that sharp drop — the one almost nobody is prepared for.

This post does not replace advice from a healthcare professional. If you have questions about how to dress in cold weather due to specific medical conditions (diabetes, vascular problems, medication), consult your doctor. The full list of recommended materials for winter emergencies is in the warmth and shelter section of the basic 72h kit.
