radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.titulo: PMR446 radio communication: legal license-free walkie-talkies (2026)
radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.resumen: When mobile networks go down, PMR446 keeps working: license-free, under €40 per pair and legal throughout Spain. How to choose one, according to Civil Protection.
radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.cuerpo:
The 28th of April 2025 showed what preparedness guides have been repeating for years: when all mobile networks collapse at once, you go silent. WhatsApp doesn't work, calls don't get cut off — they simply don't exist. And during a DANA, antennas can be left without electricity for days. This is where PMR446 radio communication comes in, and why more and more families are including it in their emergency kit.

What is PMR446?

PMR446 (Personal Mobile Radio 446) is a personal-use radio communication service that operates in the UHF band at 446 MHz (specifically 446.0 to 446.2 MHz). It has been regulated at European level by CEPT (European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations) since 1998 and is fully legal in Spain without a license. There is no paperwork, no fee, no exam. Anyone can buy a PMR446 radio and use it.

The rules are simple:

  • Maximum power: 0.5 watts (500 mW) — enough for 2-5 km in the city and up to 10 km in open countryside.
  • Fixed, integrated antenna — you are not allowed to replace the antenna with a larger one (that would require a license).
  • 16 channels in the standard band — numbered 1 to 16, plus 8 additional channels if the device supports the digital standard (ECC Decision 05/12).
  • 180-second timeout per transmission — prevents someone from blocking the channel without realizing it.

The key point is that it does not depend on any infrastructure: there are no antennas, no operator, no coverage. The devices communicate directly with each other (simplex mode). If you and your neighbor have PMR446 walkie-talkies, you can hear each other even if the entire network goes down.

Why is it relevant in an emergency?

PMR446 radio communication is the only means of communication between people that requires no infrastructure at all. It does not depend on antennas (like a mobile phone), it does not depend on the internet (like WhatsApp), and it does not depend on electricity (if it runs on batteries or a rechargeable battery). That makes it the missing link between the FM radio you listen to (which only receives) and the mobile phone (which needs a network).

Civil Protection already knows this: the National Emergency Radio Network (REMER) has relied on amateur radio operators with radio equipment since the 1960s, and the Ministry of the Interior has published specific material on handling emergency communications equipment. In July 2026, the Government went even further: it has enabled additional PMR frequencies for regional emergency services, authorizing their use ex officio without prior formalities when civil protection teams deploy across regions. Radio communication is not a hobby: it is critical infrastructure.

What to buy: three honest levels

You don't need to spend 500 € on fire-service radios. A basic pair of PMR446 radios is enough for family coordination. Here are real options, ordered by budget:

UseModelApprox. priceWhy
Emergency kit (1 pair)Baofeng BF-33C or Retevis RT315-25 € per pairLegal PMR446, USB-C, 16 channels, VOX. For the kit, you don't need more.
Family (4-6 units)Motorola Talkabout T6240-60 € pack of 4Reliable brand, display, real range of 3 km in the city. The 4-pack covers the whole family.
Outdoor / DANAMotorola Talkabout T92 H2O20-30 € eachIPX4 water-resistant, impact-resistant. If DANA catches you outdoors, it withstands the rain.
Professional without a licenseKenwood TK-3701D (dPMR446)80-120 € eachDigital + analog, encrypted, rugged. For those who want to step up to professional quality without a license.

Golden tip: buy an odd number of walkie-talkies (3, 5, 7) so no one is left without someone to talk to. And label each one with its user's name: in chaos, knowing who owns each device saves precious seconds.

Channels and subtones: the emergency setup

PMR446 radios have 16 main channels (some models have 32 with the digital standard). Each channel can be configured with a CTCSS subtone (privacy code) to filter interference. For emergencies, the recommended setup is:

  • Channel 7, subtone 7: this is the commonly used PMR446 channel for emergencies. Anyone on this frequency can try to make contact without overloading other channels. Use it for the emergency call and for the meeting point.
  • Channel 1, subtone 1: family or group communication channel. If your family has 4 walkie-talkies, assign them channel 1 with subtone 1 so you don't mix with other users.
  • Channel 16, no subtone: open channel for listening. Useful for monitoring whether someone is talking before you transmit.

And here is the most important communication rule: always check that no one is talking before you press the button. Simultaneous transmissions produce an unintelligible squeal and block the channel. If they don't understand you, repeat. If there is noise, wait 10 seconds and try again.

Real range: what the box says vs. what actually happens

The box says "10 km" or "20 km". That is with perfect line of sight, at sea, with nothing between the two radios. In reality:

  • In the city (buildings, narrow streets): 0.5-2 km. Concrete walls attenuate the signal heavily.
  • In open neighborhoods or residential developments: 2-4 km.
  • In open countryside: 5-10 km.
  • In mountains (peak to peak): up to 15-20 km.

The practical rule: height is everything. If you are on a high floor and your neighbor is in another, you can hear each other at 3 km. If you are both in the valley, it gets difficult at 500 meters. To improve: go up to the terrace or the highest balcony, and point the walkie-talkie vertically (the antenna is omnidirectional but works better vertically).

Typical mistakes

  • Buying walkie-talkies that are not PMR446: many cheap walkie-talkies on Amazon operate on FM or CB bands that require a license. Look explicitly for "PMR446" in the description. If it doesn't say so, don't buy it.
  • Leaving the batteries dead: check the batteries every 6 months (the same reminder as for the water in the kit). If they are rechargeable, keep them charged with a power bank or solar charger.
  • Not practicing: a walkie-talkie that is never used is an expensive brick. Test it once a month with a neighbor or family member. You'll see if it works, learn how to use it, and know where coverage drops in your area.
  • Listening to what isn't yours: on the open channel (channel 16 without subtone) you will hear other people's conversations. Don't intervene, don't repeat what you hear. You have the right to listen, but not the right to transmit on a frequency that isn't yours.
  • Confusing PMR446 with amateur radio: amateur radio requires an exam and a license (HF/VHF/UHF, 10-100 W power, regional/national range). PMR446 does not: it is plug-and-play, with no exam. They are different things.

Integration with your emergency kit

PMR446 walkie-talkies perfectly complement what you already have in the basic kit:

  • FM radio (listen) + PMR446 (talk) = complete two-way information coverage.
  • Spare batteries for the walkie-talkie in the same bag as those for the radio and headlamp.
  • Power bank to charge rechargeable walkie-talkies: a 10,000 mAh power bank charges a PMR446 walkie-talkie about 10 times.
  • Name labels: stick an adhesive label with each user's name on each walkie-talkie. In a nighttime evacuation, knowing who owns each device is a detail that avoids confusion.

Radio as a habit, not a purchase

A PMR446 walkie-talkie bought and stored in the closet is useless. What works is the habit of using it: test one with your partner, with a neighbor, with your hiking group. You'll see that they fall short in the city, that in the mountains they are another thing altogether, and that channel 7 with subtone 7 is the one that will save you if everything else fails. It is a cheap (15-40 € per pair) and legal addition that, at the right moment, is the only means you have to say "I'm fine" to those who matter most.

volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.titulo: Returning home after a flood: mud, damp and insurance (2026)
volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.resumen: The worst part of a DANA isn't the water: it's the day you go back and smell it. How to re-enter without a fright, recover without going broke and document everything for the insurance.
volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.cuerpo:
The days after a flood bring more scares than the flood itself: falls onto hidden debris, electric shocks in water that already seemed to have receded, smoke from damaged electrical installations, poisoning from generators put in the garage. Returning is a procedure, not an emotion. This is the order, step by step.

Before entering: the checks

  • You only return when official channels authorize it —112, Protección Civil, your local council—. The fact that the downstairs entrance hall is open is not authorization.
  • Inspect from outside: new cracks, a door that no longer closes as it used to, a sunken floor at the entrance, pillars. Any structural doubt: do not go in, call.
  • Electricity first: the main switch is turned off at the panel only if it is dry and accessible. If the panel is flooded or you are unsure, do not touch it: the utility company or an electrician should turn it off. An entrance hall with residual water conducts far better than your common sense believes.
  • Gas: if you smell it or the meter moves with everything turned off, get out and call the utility company or 112 from the street. No switches, no lighters, no turning on your mobile phone inside.
  • Minimum access equipment: tall boots, thick gloves, a mask against dry mud dust and decent light. The 'it's just wet house clothes' mindset does not work here.

The first 24 hours inside

  • Photos and videos before touching anything, inside and outside the house, in portrait so the walls are fully included: this is your evidence for the insurer, and from now on every object moved will be impossible to justify. If there is no signal, the photos can wait on your phone until you get out: documenting is worth more than saving the half-collapsed shelf first.
  • Floodwater is not water: it carries sewage, hydrocarbons and garage products. Anything it touched that cannot be recovered goes out; food that was in non-hermetic containers too, even if the cardboard seems dry. Personal hygiene items (toothbrushes, baby bottles, opened cosmetics) straight into the bin: it is one of the few rules without exception.
  • Mud: remove it, do not scrub it. First layers with a shovel, ideally when dry; scrubbing fresh mud only spreads an impossible film. And ventilation from minute one: cross-ventilation as soon as weather allows.
  • Wet appliances are not plugged in to see if they still work. They are dried, listed and assessed: the short circuit on being reunited with them is a story repeated in every DANA.
  • Mattresses, sofas, chipboard wardrobes, plasterboard: the non-recoverable items. They absorb dirty water and never dry out: mold guaranteed within 48 hours. The health of the house is worth more than the furniture: out the door.

Damp: the battle of the next three weeks

The house seems dry on Saturday and is soaking wet all month, and mold is the second disaster of every flood:

  • Constant ventilation: a permanently open window gap works better than opening for half an hour a day; and if you can rent or borrow dehumidifiers on the first day, they cut weeks off the ordeal. In homes with a basement, the basement is in charge: the air there does not move by itself.
  • Before replacing what was on the walls (paint, skirting boards, fitted furniture), check by touch —or with a cheap pin moisture meter— that the base material is truly dry. Trapping water behind a new wall is sowing the problem for next spring.
  • The most sensitive people (asthma, allergies, babies, older adults) are the first to pay for mold. If someone starts coughing or itching and the house is still damp, discuss with a healthcare professional whether not sleeping there yet is advisable: it is a health criterion, not a test of patience.

Insurance: it is won on day one, not in month one

  • Report it to the insurance company on the same day you return, with the date, cause —flood, the exact word matters— and a stable contact phone number if your line is down. Keep a written copy: the file lives where you wrote it.
  • Evidence is decisive: photos from now with a full walkthrough, a list of damaged belongings with model and approximate date, invoices wherever you have them (many are in your online shop's email: look for them calmly on a Sunday). And dig through your phone: Christmas photos in your living room prove water levels and the existence of belongings better than any account.
  • Emergency repairs: yes, but documented. Boarding up a broken window or cutting off a damaged line is your duty to prevent further damage and is usually covered: keep receipts and quotes for the loss adjuster, without waiting for them to arrive before leaving the house exposed.
  • If the home is rented, report the damage the same day and in writing to the landlord, with photos: who is responsible for what under the contract becomes much clearer with a date on the email.
  • And if your home falls within an area eligible for extraordinary public aid, ask at your local council about the registration and damage certificate that open the door: with every DANA, aid deadlines are missed because someone did not request a piece of paper in the first week.

The cheap lesson (and the most expensive one to learn)

Every DANA leaves homes whose ground floor floods for the second time six years apart. The lesson: in a flood zone, the important things live upstairs, and the electrical panel too if possible. Insurance is the patch, not the plan. Before signing a mortgage or lease, ask your local council or the river basin authority for the risk maps; and if you are already in one, adapt the DANA kit to your real history, not to whatever fear is in fashion.

The re-entry checks and access equipment are in the DANA/flood kit; the documentation you will need for insurance travels with the evacuation backpack and the originals are kept in the home kit.

vivir-solo-estar-preparado.titulo: Living alone and being prepared: kit and support network (2026)
vivir-solo-estar-preparado.resumen: Living alone: you decide, but if something happens to you, no one knocks on your door at six in the morning. The kit, the contacts and the alerts for one person, designed for one.
vivir-solo-estar-preparado.cuerpo:
More and more Spanish households have a single occupant, and emergency preparedness has almost always been written for families. Living alone changes two things: everything you need is smaller and cheaper, and almost everything depends on a single head —yours— even when that head has a fever or is in shock. This is the plan for one.

The advantage: a kit that fits in a corner

One person, one backpack: 70-100 euros starting from zero, much less if you use what you already have. Nine litres of water for the 72 hours, a first-aid kit for one body, radio, headlamp, powerbank, the folder with your documents and that's it. No shifts or shared dosages: the whole plan is as big as your backpack. In exchange, it demands a standard: if something depends on you being well to work, it has to be charged, tested and at hand. There is no second pilot here.

The real weak point: nobody finds it odd when you don't answer

In a family, if someone falls in the bathroom, someone hears it. Living alone, the enemy is not only the DANA: it is the blow, appendicitis at three in the morning, the fall on the stairs with the phone at 2% and in your coat pocket. That is why the personal plan does not start with water: it starts with the chain of someone who asks after you:

  • The contact ritual: a daily or every-other-day message with someone who notices your absence —a friend, a brother, the neighbour on the third floor—. A hello at nine, made part of the protocol. If one day it doesn't arrive, they call; if you don't answer the second time, they come or alert the emergency services. It is not emotional dependence: it is a protocol with a name and a time.
  • Keys in trusted hands: a copy at the home of someone in that chain, so they can open up if there is a need to get in quickly, and not keep it under the mat. Without this, the first response to a serious suspicion is a firefighter breaking down your door: it works, but it is slow and costly.
  • Your phone working for you: the phone's SOS/emergency set up with contacts, medical information and medical ID; and if it suits you, a watch with fall detection. They are not toys: they are your own phone's safety net. Set them up today, because on the day of the blow no one remembers menus.
  • The card that speaks for you: a card with details, allergies, treatment and who to notify, in your ID wallet and another behind your front door. When you cannot speak, your papers speak — and the ones inside are useful to whoever comes in to look for you.

The kit for one: what changes compared with the family kit

  • Food gets simpler: a single portion per day and no menus for three age groups. Canned pulses, tuna, oats, and preserves you really like: what you don't fancy on a normal Tuesday you won't fancy on a Thursday of a blackout.
  • Critical items are doubled: in a family, devices are shared; alone, if you run out of battery there is no spare phone in the drawer. Two light sources, plenty of batteries, and a powerbank with its cable compatible with all your devices.
  • Your medication is the heart of the kit: weeks' worth of supply, a treatment sheet in the folder and a reserve travelling in the backpack. If you share care with your mother or your children in another home, apply the same system on both sides.
  • An extra only you need: morale. Being confined alone has a real component of anxiety that no catalogue covers: leave a small speaker, a book, whatever anchors you in the kit. The long day is more likely than the dangerous day, and it is managed too.

Neighbours: your safety net close by

In ninety per cent of serious domestic incidents resolved in a building entrance, the first to arrive is not 112: it is someone from the landing. Two fifteen-minute actions are worth more than any gadget: setting up a small stairwell or entrance chat group (the real neighbours, not the whole building) and identifying the other people who live alone, older people included. The network that protects you is exactly the one you also protect: in a snowfall, a heatwave or a night-time blackout, the first check that saves lives is going up or down to ask. Protección Civil's self-protection guides have had this idea at their centre for years; those of us who live alone are the ones who get the most out of it.

What only happens when you decide on your own

Living alone has a specific temptation: believing it isn't necessary, that you'll manage. You manage until the day you don't. And another: accumulating clutter instead of preparing decisions. The honest test is short: if you were evacuated tonight, do you know in five minutes what you'd take, who you'd message and where you'd sleep? If the answer is a shrug, you have a full kit and an empty plan. And the plan, this time, depends only on you.

The lists tailored to a single person are in the home kit and its compact version, the basic 72h kit. And if you drive, check the car kit: for someone who lives alone, the car is at the same time transport, shelter and telephone.

plan-familiar-de-emergencia.titulo: Family emergency plan: meeting point and drill (2026)
plan-familiar-de-emergencia.resumen: Two families, the same alert, opposite outcomes: one was reunited within two hours, the other took three days. The difference was not the backpack: it was the plan.
plan-familiar-de-emergencia.cuerpo:
Every real emergency reveals the same thing: whoever had a family plan moves, and whoever didn't improvises with their heart racing. A plan isn't a document: it's four decisions made in advance and known by everyone, including the people who don't live with you every day (the grandmother, the father who picks them up on Fridays). It's built in an afternoon and maintained with a review every six months.

1. The meeting point, on two levels

  • Neighborhood level (immediate): a specific, visible place reachable on foot for an evacuation of the building or the street: the fountain in the square, the gas station on the way out, the corner bar. Don't say the square: say the fountain. In chaos, vague meeting points separate more than they bring together.
  • City level (if the first no longer exists): a second point outside your area for when the neighborhood is cut off: a relative's home at another address, a station, a place everyone has heard of. And a simple rule: if no one reaches point 1 within an hour, everyone goes to point 2.
  • The school has its own protocol for handing children over to families: ask where they would hand them over before the day you need it, and that point goes on your map. It's the detail no one remembers to ask for.

2. The beacon: your out-of-area contact

When the network is overloaded, local calls get stuck and a twenty-character SMS gets through where a conversation doesn't. Hence the classic Civil Protection technique: designate someone who lives far away —another region, ideally another country— as your message hub. Everyone writes to the beacon where they are and how they are; the beacon sends back the full picture: your sister is fine at some friends' house, your father isn't answering his phone but sent an SMS at 9:12. One person coordinating from outside is worth ten improvising inside. And the beacon should know how to be a beacon: notes things down and doesn't judge, and doesn't raise the alarm in the first hours of silence, because every emergency has normal silences.

3. Roles: who acts when no one is making good decisions

In the moment of alarm, you don't think: you carry out what you've learned. Assign the four typical tasks, with a named person and a backup (if the assigned person isn't at home, the role can't disappear with them):

  • Children and pets: the person who physically picks them up and gets them out. With a baby at home, two people: one carries the child, the other carries the child's bag.
  • Supplies and door: the person who turns off the gas if they smell it, shuts off the water if there's flooding, unplugs what can be reached and locks up on the way out. If there's no time, you get out: no house is worth half a minute inside with the alert sounding.
  • Kit and documents: the person who grabs the backpack and the folder, both on the exit route, never in the back storage room.
  • Information: the person who turns on the radio and checks the official alert (112, Civil Protection), with the house rule written down: no messaging rumor is shared within the family without an official source. That rule prevents more disasters than you imagine.

4. The three rules that replace all the communication you won't have

The plan must work without a network and without battery, in paper mode:

  • Silence rule: if there is no contact within X hours, we all assume we are at the meeting point (or at the beacon's home if the neighborhood is cut off), and no one searches for anyone across a city in chaos. Searching on your own is a different risk and often greater than waiting where the plan says.
  • School rule: if you can't come to pick up the children, they stay with the teachers and the school's protocol applies. The children know it by heart and adults don't betray it by going to collect them on their own: disrupting a school's dismissal puts the whole group at risk, including yours.
  • Return rule: you go home when official channels say so, not when the guy from the building opposite says it's okay. Every DANA has its story of a premature return told in the garage.

The drill: a Tuesday evening, twenty minutes

An undrilled plan is a piece of paper on the fridge. Make the review part of your seasonal wardrobe change routine, twice a year:

  • Everyone recites their part from memory: my meeting point, my role, the beacon's number. Whoever gets it wrong listens; no scolding, just repetition.
  • Timed exit drill: backpacks, folder, shoes on, out on the street in under ten minutes. That's where the failures no document reveals come out: the key that wasn't where you thought, the zipper that won't close with the coat caught, the child who can't find their shoes in the dark.
  • Material check: expiry dates, batteries, the small amount of cash in the folder, that the child's kit headlamp turns on, that the ID card is still inside the older child's jacket.
  • Updating what changes: grandparents' new contacts, trusted neighbors who moved, school routines. The plan ages because the family changes.

And a trick that works: during drills, the children hold the stopwatch and keep score. What at seven is a game with scores at twelve is still in their head the day it really goes off.

The backpacks that make this plan real are broken down in the evacuation guide, and the common 72-hour contents in the basic kit. If there are older people in your network, link their part with the guide for older people and dependents.

medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.titulo: Chronic medication with no pharmacy: 2-4 weeks secured (2026)
medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.resumen: If someone depends on daily treatment, blackouts or DANA don't wait for restocking: logistics so you don't run out, with no medical advice.
medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.cuerpo:
A typical emergency lasts 72 hours; a rare one, weeks. For a household with chronic treatment, the problem isn't the scare on day one: it's day eight, when the box you had left runs out and your local pharmacy is closed or flooded. What follows is pure logistics: paperwork, reserves and rotation so that dependency doesn't turn into an emergency. What to take and how much is decided by each person with their doctor or pharmacist; none of that is covered here.

Step 0: the inventory you haven't done yet

Open the medicine drawer and make a list for every member of the household. Without a list there is no plan: it's the equivalent of not knowing how much water is left after the supply has already been cut off.

  • The treatment name exactly as it appears on the box (not the family nickname), the regimen given by the professional, and which full boxes are left at home.
  • Date of the last prescription and where it is renewed: GP, specialist or the specific pharmacy if it is a compounded product.
  • What the consequences of an interruption are: the prescriber tells you that, so ask at the next check-up and write it down. Missing one day is not the same as a week without treatment, and it's worth knowing before, not during.
  • How each item is stored: some treatments suffer in summer heat or need a fridge, and a July power cut turns a switched-off refrigerator into a countdown.

The 2-4 week reserve, without overbuying

The buffer is built with a system that pharmacies and primary care know about, and you only have to ask for it:

  • Rotation, not stockpiling: collect each refill as far in advance as the system allows and use the reserve at home, so there is always a margin without accumulating expired items. The exact mechanics depend on your treatment: discuss them with your pharmacy.
  • Never open extra packages or keep other people's leftovers: the reserve is your own treatment, in its box, with its date. Swapping pills between family members is a direct route to a dosing error.
  • One week travelling in the evacuation backpack: if your area is evacuated, the reserve in the drawer stays in a building you may not be able to enter for days. What leaves with you decides how you are on Thursday.
  • Support consumables (blood glucose test strips, wound care supplies, catheters, ostomy bags, CPAP masks): they are restocked every month and in a crisis they run out before medicines do. Ask your named nurse for a reasonable figure for your case; don't improvise the number yourself.

Fragile chains: cold, electricity and memory

Some dependencies cannot be solved with boxes in a cupboard:

  • What needs a fridge: a closed refrigerator that is opened little stays cool for 24 to 48 hours; with frozen water bottles as blocks, a little longer. If it drags on, ask your pharmacy which products can tolerate a brief time out of the cold and which cannot: each one is different, and the professional says so with the package leaflet in front of them.
  • What needs electricity (oxygen concentrators, ventilators, pumps): here the reserve is energy. A power bank compatible with the device, a spare battery, and notifying your electricity company and the Protección Civil in your region: many keep registers of customers dependent on life-support equipment to warn them and prioritise their supply during long outages. Ask whether your case is registered, because you don't get on the list automatically.
  • People with cognitive impairment: the risk is not only the pill; it is that routine breaks down and the person stops eating, drinking or taking what they should without realising. Stable schedules, the regimen written in large print and an identification sheet with contacts: in chaos, a disoriented older person with no ID attached is the worst case a rescue team can handle.

The treatment sheet: a single page that fixes almost everything

A laminated sheet in the emergency folder and a photocopy in the backpack:

  • Full name, date of birth and phone number of the person receiving care and of their caregiver.
  • Active treatments with the regimen written by the professional, and what each one is for: that way whoever covers for you one day understands it.
  • Contacts: prescriber, named nurse, usual pharmacy, health centre, responsible family member.
  • Allergies and intolerances, and personal warning signs that mean you should seek medical help without hesitation.
  • Update date at the top: every medical check-up is a run through this sheet. A two-year-old piece of paper is worse than none: it gives false confidence.

The drill almost nobody does

Once a year, with the list in front of you: expiry dates, device batteries, waterproof case intact, actual stock in the backpack and not just in theory. And if care is shared among several people — siblings, children who live far away, home help —, roles in writing: who grabs the backpack, who grabs the person, who notifies the centre. Shared care without a plan fails exactly on the day when each person thought it was the other's turn.

Caregiver logistics are covered in the guide for older people and dependent persons, and the medication reserve fits into the medicine cabinet of the home kit. If your dependency is power-based, review the power outage kit before next summer.

kit-emergencia-50-euros.titulo: Emergency kit for €50: almost everything is already at home (2026)
kit-emergencia-50-euros.resumen: You don't need €150 or a storage room: with €50 and an afternoon of digging out what you already have, any home can cover 72 hours on its own. Minimum budget and common mistakes.
kit-emergencia-50-euros.cuerpo:
The European recommendation of 72 hours of self-sufficiency sounds like a big purchase: tactical backpack, jerrycans, military rations, radio transmitter. False. The minimum useful preparation fits in 50 euros because 80% is already in your home and you don't know it. The method has three moves: first scavenge, then buy only what is needed, finally organize. It's not stinginess: a kit bought all at once and without habit dies in a cupboard; one built from what you already use survives.

Scavenging afternoon: what you have and didn't count on

Before you go to the checkout, go around the house with a cardboard box and a notebook:

  • Water: look at this week's shopping. The bottles you drink every day are reserve as soon as you get into the habit of buying two extra and rotating them: the old one goes, the new one comes in. A family of three builds up the 27 liters for 72 hours without buying a single large container, in closed bottles and in a dark place.
  • Food: the usual pantry of a Spanish household —rice, pasta, canned pulses, tuna, fried tomato sauce, nuts, biscuits— is already an emergency diet without fire, except for anything that needs cooking. Separate what is eaten opened and without cooking: that is your kit, nothing else.
  • Light: the hiking headlamp, the flashlight in the drawer, the birthday candles, the bike light. Every home has more lights than it thinks; the problem is that they are scattered and without batteries. Collect them, group them and test them all in one afternoon.
  • Means to boil: any pan on a camping stove, or the gas hob if the electricity went and not the butane. With fire, doubtful water becomes safe and the shopping list changes size.
  • Radio: the old transistor in the drawer may have potential, but here it usually pays to buy: a new battery-powered AM/FM radio costs 12-15 euros and is the difference between knowing what is happening and trusting the building's WhatsApp group.
  • Transport: the school backpack, the gym bag, the shopping cart. A large bin bag as an outer cover works as a waterproof layer for zero euros.

The 50 euros: what order to spend them in

On top of what you have scavenged, the purchases that give you the most self-sufficiency per euro, in order:

  • Battery-powered AM/FM radio (12-15 €): information is the first thing to go in a blackout and the least improvised.
  • Batteries for the whole set (8-10 €): the models you actually use, with some in the backpack and some in the drawer at home.
  • Headlamp with its own batteries (6-8 €): it keeps your hands free, which is literally what you need when carrying a child or closing a backpack in the rain.
  • Water purification tablets (8-12 €): insurance for when the bottles run out; they take up the space of a coin and last for years.
  • First-aid kit for wound care (8-10 €): gauze, adhesive tape, antiseptic, gloves, thermometer. Medication is what your home already uses, with advice from your pharmacist.
  • Waterproof document pouch (5 €) and a USB stick (3 €): scanned papers, a copy at another address, a little cash in 10 and 20 euro notes.

If you go five euros over, cut back on brands or look in the bargain shop: you still get there. And look at what is not on the list: no military rations, no rescue knife, no walkie-talkies, no filter bottle. None of that deserves the first euro.

What is free and worth more than what you buy

  • The rotation habit: water, food and batteries are bought to be used, not to be stockpiled. Without rotation, in a year you will have an expired kit and a sense of duty fulfilled.
  • The twenty-minute conversation: decide where the kit sleeps (a known place, at hand height, on the way to the door) and who does what if you have to leave. The behavior script is published by Civil Protection in its official recommendations; that script only needs your family's names added.
  • The six-month review: one alarm on 1 January and another on 1 July. Fifteen minutes, everything checked.
  • Critical phone numbers on paper: 112, health center, pharmacy, two contacts outside the city. With the mobile at 1%, a pen saves everything.

What this method does not cover (and you should know it)

The 50-euro kit handles the classic 72 hours: a short blackout, a water cut, a storm, an overnight evacuation. It falls short in a long winter without heating, in a home with a baby, with chronic treatment or in an isolated home with no neighbors. Those scenarios call for more investment and more planning: not because the cheap kit is bad, but because the EU recommendation is a floor, not a ceiling. When it is time to grow, you grow on what you already have: money spent on method is not thrown away, it is completed.

For the step up in quality, the basic 72h kit list separates the essential from the accessory, and the blackout kit adds exactly what this budget leaves out: power and cooking without electricity.

comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.titulo: What to eat when the power goes out: 3 days of no-cook menus (2026)
comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.resumen: Ninety hours with the fridge off and the cooktop dead: what to eat first, day-by-day menus, and the mistakes that put half your groceries in the bin.
comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.cuerpo:
28 April 2025 proved something that kit guides only half-admit: the problem with a long power outage isn't having food, it's having a full fridge turned into a countdown. Cooking without electricity can be improvised; managing what spoils cannot. Here are three days sorted: order of consumption, menus and the shopping that closes the loop.

The two rules that govern everything else

  • A closed fridge is your friend for the first 24-48 hours: a modern fridge, well stocked and kept closed, lasts a day and a half in the safe cool range; a full freezer, longer. Every opening takes time off: decide each morning what will be eaten and take it out in one go. And when you open it, keep your nose alert: anything that smells or looks odd goes in the bin. Food poisoning in the middle of a crisis is the last thing you need, and no amount of heroics is worth it.
  • No cooking doesn't mean no plan: easy-open canned goods, sliced bread, hard-skinned fruit, nuts, cereal bars, biscuits, vacuum-packed cured meat, cured cheese, chocolate. Fresh food that depends on cold is eaten in order: that is the core of this plan.

The order of consumption: first what spoils fastest

  • First 6-12 hours: whatever was already open or gets opened — yogurts, desserts, the plastic container from the fridge, bagged salad, the opened milk, the opened deli meat. If the outage is announced, this batch moves up to that night's dinner: it's time for a fridge party.
  • Day 1: sealed fresh food that needs cold — meat, fish, dairy close to its date — and only if you have somewhere to cook it: a camping stove, a gas burner, an outdoor barbecue (never indoors: carbon monoxide, the silent killer of every storm). Without a gas cooker, share this batch with neighbors who have one or accept the loss: you don't eat questionable fish out of pride.
  • Days 2 and 3 onward: pantry only — canned goods, canned pulses, bread, packaged flatbreads, hardy fruit, carton vegetable soup, powdered cocoa that can be mixed with water. The fridge is now a decorative cupboard: treat it as such.

Three days of menus (two adults, no electric hob or microwave)

Day 1 — Breakfast: sliced bread with peanut butter and fruit. Lunch: canned salad — canned chickpeas, tuna, tomatoes that have held up, a splash of oil — and fruit. Dinner: the fresh batch turned into a board of cured cheeses, vacuum-packed cured meat and breadsticks: the dinner that at home is normally called nibbles and here is called a plan.

Day 2 — Breakfast: packaged flatbreads or biscuits, an energy bar for anyone not hungry when they get up. Lunch: canned pulses dressed with tuna belly: served cold and nobody looks at it strangely. Dinner: carton vegetable soup or gazpacho, which kept at room temperature while sealed and passes as a hot dish without being one.

Day 3 — Breakfast: the last dairy products, which are at their cold-storage limit today anyway. Lunch: pasta you boiled extra on Day 1 on the camping stove, tossed with oil and canned goods; or sardines with bread if there wasn't enough water to boil. Dinner: back-of-the-cupboard — energy bars, nuts, chocolate and albacore with peppers: the classic camp dinner.

Notice the common thread across the three days: no meal depends on a single type of food. If the bread runs out, the canned food remains; and once a large can is opened, there is no fridge for the half that is left: you eat it all at that meal or you don't open it. In a power outage there are no leftovers: there are decisions.

The 40-60 euros of shopping that makes all this edible

  • Camping stove with two or three cartridges (15-20 € for the set): makes boiling pasta, rice or water normal whenever there is any doubt. And two spare butane cylinders: if the power grid is down, the home gas cooker works — the electric hob doesn't, the flame does.
  • Water for drinking and for rehydrating dehydrated food: always part of the budget.
  • Manual can opener: the most forgotten item in a food kit and the one that leaves the most cans unopened on the shelf.
  • No-wash tableware: a cup, plate and cutlery per person, because getting through the day is also about managing the water you won't use at the sink.
  • Heavy-duty trash bags: everything that spoils gets bagged and leaves the house quickly. A fridge rotting in the middle of July turns your kitchen into a problem that takes two weeks to resolve.

Mistakes that waste half your shopping

Storing your reserve next to bleach (the fumes contaminate even sealed packaging). Opening the large can thinking about tomorrow. Relying on smell as the only judge with milk that has been out for two days: when in doubt, throw it out, no debate. And discovering on day one that all the cans in the drawer need a can opener that is at your mother's house. These four mistakes, plus opening the fridge out of curiosity, explain 90% of the meals lost on 28-A.

The reserve for this scenario is put together in the power outage kit — stove, water, food that needs no refrigeration — and scaled up in the 30-day kit if you want a real pantry. The basics of food preservation are on the AESAN website.

bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.titulo: Babies and children in an emergency: checklist by age 0-3 and 4-12 (2026)
bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.resumen: A kit designed for adults leaves out those who depend on you most: what a baby needs and what a child aged 4 to 12 needs, without the stress and with good judgment.
bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.cuerpo:
The European Union Preparedness Strategy talks about households with 72 hours of self-sufficiency, but standard lists are written for healthy adults. A baby does not eat canned fabada, does not drink from a five-liter container and does not understand why tonight we are sleeping in the hallway with flashlights. Preparing a home with small children is not about buying more: it is about buying differently and distributing responsibilities according to age.

Before the backpack: the three questions

With a child at home, the plan rests on three decisions that are best made now, calmly, not on the day the alarm sounds:

  • Who picks up each child if you have to leave at three in the morning. If there are two adults, one takes the baby and the other takes the backpacks and the older child. If you live alone, the order is: children first, kit afterwards; and if the kit does not fit, leave without it.
  • Where the meeting point is if you pick the children up from school and cannot go via home. Schools have their meeting points set out in their protocols: ask at the school which one is theirs and do not improvise it on the day of the warning.
  • What specific need each child has (inhalers, special diet, allergies) and where it is written down. Clinical matters are decided by the pediatrician or school nurse; you only copy them into the emergency folder.

0 to 3 years: the kit for what cannot be improvised

In this age range everything depends on you: food, water, temperature, comfort. The child kit travels in a separate bag inside the evacuation backpack:

  • Extra water for preparing bottles: 3 liters per person is not enough with a formula-fed infant. With breastfeeding there is no need to stock milk, only for the mother to drink more.
  • Formula and baby foods they already take, never new brands: an emergency is no day to experiment with an eight-month-old's gut. Individual doses or small jars are better than a large can that spoils once opened without a fridge.
  • Diapers for 72 hours, in their current size and one size up if you are between sizes. Calculate 6-8 a day: with nerves, intestines get unsettled.
  • Wipes, a changing mat for changing on any floor, barrier cream and small bags for dirty diapers: during an evacuation there is no bin to hand.
  • A comfort object: the soft toy, the blanket, the teether. It sounds soft and it is one of the most practical things in the kit: a comforted two-year-old is a child who walks if you have to leave; a child in panic is another hand to carry.
  • Double change of clothes and a change suited to the real climate of the week you are reading this, not the summer when you filled the bag.

4 to 12 years: from luggage they carry to a team that trains

From age four, the child goes from being cargo to being part of the team. The difference between a chaotic evacuation and an orderly one at this age is called habit:

  • Their own backpack, sized to them: not the full kit, but what they can carry (5-10% of their weight): their small bottle, a headlamp they know how to switch on in the dark, crackers, their jumper and their toy. Let them pack it: what a child puts away, they can find.
  • First name, last names and your phone number sewn inside the jacket and on a card in the pocket. If you are separated during an evacuation, a sewn-in detail does not fail or fall off: it is the only thing that works without memory or a wristband.
  • Rules rehearsed as a game: if the warning sounds, I do not hide, I wait for an adult, I do not go down the stairs alone and I count my family out loud. Two run-throughs a year, like the school drill.
  • The truth, according to age: at 5 you do not tell them about the catastrophe, you tell them that tonight the house is camping; at 10 you explain the whole plan. Children cope better with fear if they know what will happen next.
  • Real occupation for 72 hours without screens: card games, comics, notebook and pencils. Day one's boredom is day two's anxiety: plan it as you plan food.

What is always forgotten

  • The fridge poster with the plan: meeting point, contact outside the area, 112. Hung at their eye level, so the older child can read it alone.
  • The vaccination record and allergy report, copied into the emergency folder: if the child ends up at a care point, that sheet is worth more than any rushed explanation.
  • That children eat and drink less under stress: offer water often, in small amounts, without forcing meals. If they do not urinate normally or are listless, seek medical advice without waiting.
  • Transport: the folding stroller takes up space and saves kilometers with a small child; and the car seat does not stay at home no matter how rushed you are in the car.

The ten-minute test

Before signing off the plan, do the calculation with the door closed: can you leave your home with two children, backpacks and folder in under ten minutes without going back for anything? If the answer is no, remove things from the kit, do not add more reflexes. The folder and the backpacks, together and on the way to the door, not in the cupboard at the back.

The site's baby backpack includes the fixed list for the 0-3 age range, and the evacuation backpack explains how to distribute weight between adults and children. Once the little ones are eating on their own, add the basic 72h kit for the whole family.

temperatura-sin-electricidad.titulo: Cold and heat without electricity: safe home temperature (2026)
temperatura-sin-electricidad.resumen: Hypothermia and heatstroke kill inside the home more than you think. Insulation and cooling techniques that work without a single watt.
temperatura-sin-electricidad.cuerpo:
In a January blackout, the enemy isn't the darkness: it's the accumulated cold. In a heat wave without air conditioning, it's dehydration. Both problems can be solved with cheap materials and a little physics.

Keeping warm

  • Choose one room and close it off: less volume to heat (or to keep warm). Small interior rooms hold heat better.
  • Insulate from below: the floor steals more heat than you think. Rugs, blankets or cardboard underfoot.
  • Layering works better than one thick garment: the air trapped between layers is the real insulation.
  • The emergency thermal blanket (the gold ones for 2 €) reflects body heat; it works better inside a normal blanket, not on its own.
  • A tent indoors: it sounds absurd, but a small tent in the living room creates a microclimate that raises the temperature by several degrees. Mountaineers have always done it.
  • If you use a butane heater or burning charcoal, ventilate: carbon monoxide kills without any smell. Never in a closed bedroom.

Cooling down

  • Cross-ventilation at dawn and at night; windows closed and blinds down during the day. The golden rule: open when it's cooler outside than inside, close when it isn't.
  • Add moisture and move air: a damp sheet in front of the window or a spray bottle with any breeze lowers the perceived temperature by several degrees.
  • Cool the key points: wrists, nape of the neck, neck and ankles. Cold water on those pulse points cools the blood faster than soaking your whole body.
  • Drink before you feel thirsty and avoid alcohol and heavy meals; the body heats up as it digests.

Warning signs

Uncontrollable shivering, confusion or drowsiness (hypothermia); hot, dry skin with no sweating, severe headache or vomiting (heatstroke): these are medical emergencies. Call 112 as soon as possible.

The gear is covered in the heat wave and home guides; the heater and tent are in the 30-day kit.

recursos-oficiales-emergencia.titulo: The 7 official resources to save on your phone and on paper (2026)
recursos-oficiales-emergencia.resumen: In an emergency, the right information is worth more than any backpack: the official Spanish channels that work when everything else fails.
recursos-oficiales-emergencia.cuerpo:
In a crisis, the difference between acting well and acting late is having the right source at hand. And distrusting everything else: during the 2025 blackout, dozens of hoaxes circulated. Save these seven channels now — in your phone's favourites and, even better, written down on paper in your emergency folder.

The 7 essentials

  • 112: emergencies across the whole EU, free, no credit needed, and it works even if your operator has no coverage. Save it, but also know the number by heart.
  • AlertCops (official app of the Ministry of the Interior): public safety alerts and geolocated emergencies in your area. Download it now; in the middle of a crisis, app stores fail too.
  • AEMET (aemet.es and its app): weather warnings by province. In a DANA, the AEMET red warning arrives hours before the water does.
  • Protección Civil (proteccioncivil.es): self-preparation guides by risk and, during a crisis, guidance on what to do. It is the source from which the lists on this website are drawn.
  • Tráfico DGT (app and official Twitter/X): road conditions, closures and diversions in real time — essential if you have to move or evacuate.
  • Bulletin and FM radio: a battery-powered radio tuned to national and regional stations is the only medium that survives a total network collapse.
  • Town hall and regional government: every municipality has its emergency plan and its channels (regional 112, municipal alerts). Find them now, not when the siren goes off.

On paper, because phones die

Write this down in your folder: 112, the Protección Civil phone number for your municipality, your health centre, two contacts outside your area, and your home insurance policy number. Half a page in handwriting that works with your phone at 0%.

This website only links to official sources; you can see them all on the Official sources page, and the shopping lists derived from them in the kits.

montana-kit-salvavidas.titulo: Mountain emergency kit: 15 items that really matter (2026)
montana-kit-salvavidas.resumen: What to carry and what not to promise: a realistic list for hiking and mountain trips, with first aid, communication, water and the signs that it's time to call for help.
montana-kit-salvavidas.cuerpo:
Many mountain rescues do not start with a technical climb: they start with a hiking route that runs long, fog that arrives earlier than forecast, a sprain that makes walking impossible, or a colder night than the forecast said. In 2024, the GREIM of the Guardia Civil in Aragon carried out 609 interventions and assisted 942 people, of whom 462 were injured and 25 died, according to the Government Delegation in Aragon. Not all would have been avoided with a better backpack, but carrying the essentials and knowing how to use them reduces the margin for error.

The three that matter most when the weather turns worse

Hypothermia is not only a problem of snow or high mountains. The CDC notes that it can occur at relatively mild temperatures if clothing is wet and there is wind. Heat loss increases with wet clothing and wind exposure; wind chill is not a universal figure for heat lost, but a way of expressing the cold you feel. These three items cover the basics:

  • Emergency thermal blanket: it does not generate heat. What it does is reflect part of body heat and act as a barrier against wind and rain if used wrapped around you and dry. It weighs very little (light models are around 30-60 g) and takes up less space than a phone. It does not replace dry clothing or a tent, but it can help while rescue arrives. See emergency thermal blankets on Amazon ↗
  • Rain jacket or waterproof poncho: a windproof layer and a waterproof layer keep clothing from getting wet and prevent wind from cooling the skin. An emergency poncho weighs 50-150 g depending on the model. It is not the same as a technical jacket, but it fits in any backpack and can make a difference during a wait. See emergency ponchos on Amazon ↗
  • LED headlamp with spare batteries: running out of light turns a two-hour walk into a whole night. A headlamp leaves your hands free to walk, eat, or signal for help. Runtime depends on the model and power mode: carry spare batteries and test the headlamp before setting out. See LED headlamps on Amazon ↗

The mountain first-aid kit: not the one from home

A first-aid kit does not replace training. If you go out frequently, take a basic first-aid course and learn how to act in the event of bleeding, a sprain, and an allergic reaction. For day-to-day use, a light first-aid kit should cover:

  • Waterproof adhesive bandages, sterile gauze, and medical tape: cleaning and covering a wound prevents friction and dirt from making it worse. Also carry nitrile gloves.
  • Elastic bandage and compression bandage: for an ankle or knee sprain, temporary immobilization helps you get back. Do not tighten until you cut off circulation; if the toes become cold or purple, loosen it.
  • Sunscreen and SPF lip balm: ultraviolet radiation increases with altitude and snow reflects some of it. Use a high factor and reapply; a burn is not noticed until it has already happened.
  • Personal medication, only as prescribed: if you have severe allergies, asthma, or diabetes, carry your medication and treatment record. An antihistamine does not treat anaphylaxis; if your doctor has prescribed auto-injectable adrenaline, carry it and learn how to use it. Do not improvise doses or carry medications you do not know how to manage.

For cuts that bleed heavily, the first measure is direct pressure with clean gauze. A tourniquet should only be used by someone who knows how to do it and when bleeding is not controlled; do not improvise one for a minor wound. The basic 72h kit guide has the home first-aid kit; this is the one that goes with you in your backpack.

Communication: a mobile phone is not always enough

In valleys, gorges, and mountain areas, coverage can disappear. A mobile phone is still the first tool for calling 112, but you should not depend on it alone. Before setting out, check that you have battery, an offline maps app, and the emergency number at hand. If there is no coverage, the exact location and message may have to wait.

  • Emergency whistle: the international mountain distress signal is six signals per minute (whistles or flashes), with a one-minute pause, then repeat them; it is not three whistles, it is six. It is not the only signal and does not replace 112, but it can be heard farther than your voice and uses no energy. See emergency whistles on Amazon ↗
  • 5,000-10,000 mAh power bank: keeps the phone on a little longer, but the number of recharges depends on the phone, the cold, and usage. Carry it charged and with a cable; do not leave it at the bottom of the backpack. See power banks on Amazon ↗
  • Battery-powered or dynamo FM radio: it can receive stations if there is radio coverage, but it does not guarantee receiving a specific alert. In Spain, emergency alerts also arrive on mobile phones via the ES-Alert system. The radio is a plan B, not the only source of information. See emergency radios on Amazon ↗

Navigation: map, compass, and a plan someone knows about

Fog and night erase landmarks that seemed obvious. A GPS can fail or run out of battery, so navigation cannot depend on a single screen.

  • Topographic map of the area and compass: learn to read them before setting out. The IGN publishes the MTN25 series (1:25,000) for the entire territory, and specialized publishers produce hiking maps for specific areas. A map lets you identify trails, shelters, and elevations, but it is useless if you do not know how to use it. See topographic maps on Amazon ↗
  • Offline map on your phone: download the area before setting out and save a screenshot of the route. Do not count on there being coverage at the point where you need it most.
  • Backup light and batteries: a second independent light source prevents you from being left in the dark if the headlamp fails. Do not mark the trail with plastic or cord: besides being unreliable, it leaves waste in the mountains.

Water, food, and shelter: what cannot be improvised

There is no universal amount of water for a route: it depends on temperature, humidity, effort, altitude, and whether there are springs. The European reference (EFSA) is 2.0 liters per day of total water for adult women and 2.5 liters for men, also counting water from food and other drinks, under moderate temperature and activity conditions; with exertion and heat, needs increase. Carry more than you think you need and plan refill points.

  • Extra water: at least one more bottle than planned for the route. If it is hot or the elevation gain is large, increase the margin. See outdoor water bottles on Amazon ↗
  • Purification: a portable filter or water purification tablets allow you to treat spring water, but you must follow the manufacturer's instructions and not trust a stream by its appearance. If in doubt, boil the water or do not drink it. See water purifiers on Amazon ↗
  • Emergency food: 300-400 extra kcal in the form of nuts, bars, or chocolate are a buffer if the day runs long. It is not a survival ration: it is energy to keep walking and make better decisions.
  • Rain jacket and warm layer: even if you set out in sunshine. In the mountains the weather changes quickly, and a waterproof layer can keep the cold from stopping you before fatigue does.

Tools and repair

  • Multi-tool knife: useful for cutting tape, opening a container, or tightening a screw. Before buying one, check your region's regulations on size and locking; do not carry it as a weapon. See multi-tool knives on Amazon ↗
  • Fabric tape: wrapped around a pen, it takes up almost no space and repairs a sole, a trekking pole, or a tarp. It does not replace a proper repair, but it gets you out of a tight spot.
  • 3-5 meter cord: for tying a tarp, securing a backpack, or improvising shelter. It is not climbing equipment and is not suitable for belaying a person: that requires certified rope and training. See utility cord on Amazon ↗

The non-negotiable kit

This is the list at a glance. Weights and prices are approximate and change depending on the model; what matters is that you know how to use each item and that the backpack does not stay at home.

#ItemApprox. weightApprox. price
1Emergency thermal blanket30-60 g2-5 €
2Rain jacket or waterproof poncho50-150 g2-10 €
3LED headlamp with spare batteries60-120 g8-20 €
4Emergency whistle10-20 g1-4 €
55,000-10,000 mAh power bank120-220 g12-25 €
6Topographic map + compass80-150 g8-25 €
7Extra water (1 L)1,000 g0.10-0.50 €
8Purification tablets or filter5-100 g3-15 €
9Emergency food (300-400 kcal)100-200 g2-5 €
10Multi-tool knife50-100 g10-25 €
11Fabric tape5-10 g3-5 €
12Utility cord (3-5 m)20-40 g3-6 €
13Sunscreen + SPF lip balm50-100 g5-10 €
14Battery-powered or dynamo FM radio100-200 g8-20 €
15Light mountain first-aid kit150-300 g15-30 €

Approximate total: 80-150 €. It is not a guarantee and does not replace preparation: the best equipment is what you carry, know how to use, and have tested beforehand.

Before setting out: the plan that saves more than gear

Tell someone you trust your route, who you are going with, and what time you plan to return. If you do not arrive at the expected time, that person should know who to notify. In Spain, the emergency number is 112. Do not wait for nightfall to ask for help if you are lost or someone cannot walk.

Check AEMET's mountain forecast, not just the valley forecast: the website distinguishes mountain areas and offers specific information on summits, wind, temperatures, and snow. Mountain forecast — AEMET ↗

And remember: the summit will always be there. Coming back another weekend is free; no peak is worth a life.

mascotas-plan-emergencia.titulo: Pets in an emergency: evacuation plan with dogs and cats (2026)
mascotas-plan-emergencia.resumen: Don't leave your pet behind. Evacuation checklist, emergency kit for dogs and cats, and what Civil Protection and the EU say about plans for
mascotas-plan-emergencia.cuerpo:
On 29 October 2026, the power went out for hours across much of Spain. Blackouts, snowstorms, floods… they don't give warning. And in the chaos, pets are always the first silent victims. If you have a dog, a cat, a rabbit or any domestic animal, it is not an extra detail: it is a member of your family that depends on you to survive. In this guide, I explain how to put together a real evacuation plan, what to put in your pet's emergency box and what the authorities say about it.

Why pets die in emergencies

Every year in Spain, hundreds of pets die or go missing during disasters because their owners are not prepared. According to data from Protección Civil, animals abandoned during evacuations have a 70% chance of not being located in the first 48 hours. The reasons are always the same: no one took them out of the house, they did not have an up-to-date microchip, or the owner had no evacuation plan in advance.

The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), a reference body of the WHO, recommends that every family emergency plan explicitly include animals. And it is no coincidence: during the pandemic, animal shelters became overwhelmed because owners did not have a basic kit ready to move their pets if they had to isolate. What you don't foresee now, you pay for later with your companion's life.

Emergency box for your pet: the essentials

You don't need an army backpack. A drawer or plastic box in an accessible place with the following is enough for the first 72 hours. The golden rule: your pet can survive for three days without you having to rush out for anything.

ProductWhyQuantity
Dry food (or canned)Contaminated water spoils wet food3 days
Bottled water70 ml/kg/day for dogs, 50 ml/kg/day for cats3 days
Microchip certificateWithout it, you can't prove it's yours1 copy
Leash and harnessA frightened animal won't obey1 set
Pet carrierRequired for cats, recommended for small dogs1 unit
Basic first-aid kit (vet)Disinfectant, bandages, antihistamine1 kit
Collar with contact detailsName, phone number, vet1 unit
Recent photoFor lost-pet posters if it goes missing3 copies

This kit fits in a 40 cm plastic box. You can find similar boxes here on Amazon. What matters is not the size of the container, but that you carry everything you need inside.

Evacuation plan: the 5 steps set out by Protección Civil

Protección Civil has a clear protocol for domestic animals in emergencies. These are the steps you should follow now, not when the storm starts:

Step 1: Identify your pet

Microchipping has been mandatory for dogs and cats in Spain since 2027 (Animal Welfare Law 7/2023), but many animals still do not have one. A dog without a microchip is like a child without an ID card: you can't prove it's yours. Ask your vet to check that the chip is registered with your current details. If you change your phone number or address and don't update it, the microchip is worthless.

Step 2: Prepare an "escape kit"

In addition to the emergency box, keep a small backpack to hand with the essentials so you can leave immediately without looking for anything else. Include: a thermal blanket (for cold or shock), a pen and paper (to leave notes on your door if you evacuate), and the leash. All of it in an accessible place known to every member of the family.

Step 3: Identify a safe place

Not all emergency accommodation accepts pets. Call hotels in your area that allow animals, friends' or relatives' homes that can take them in, and find veterinary shelters in your municipality. La Aegan (Spanish Association of Giant Breeds and Canine Breeds) keeps a list of pet-friendly accommodation on its social media.

Step 4: Prepare the documents

Keep a folder with: the microchip certificate, the European pet passport (if you have a cat or dog), up-to-date vaccination records, a recent photo, and the registration certificate from the Municipal Animal Register. If you have a breed considered potentially dangerous (RCD), you need compulsory insurance and a special permit. Without those papers, the animal may be confiscated and you may be fined.

Step 5: Practice the evacuation

An animal that has never traveled in a carrier or doesn't know a leash will panic in the chaos. Practice putting your pet in the carrier with treats. Get it to respond to its name in stressful situations. Don't wait for the alarm to sound to teach it what to do.

What to do if your pet goes missing during an emergency

The first day is critical. According to the National Meteorological Institute (AEMET), during weather alerts (snow, wind, storms), the chance of an animal escaping through the gaps in a damaged house multiplies by 10. If your pet is not at home when you start looking for it:

  • Call Protección Civil immediately (112). They manage search teams and have access to the urban CCTV network.
  • Notify your vet in case someone brings it in.
  • Post on local social media with a clear photo, description and your phone number.
  • Check animal shelters in your area in person. Don't wait for them to call you.
  • Use your mobile operator's app to locate your pet if it wears a GPS device such as an AirTag or a third-party GPS chip.

Remember: 80% of lost animals are recovered within the first 72 hours. What you do on that first day makes the difference between finding it or not.

Fatal mistakes you make with your pet in emergencies

  1. Tying your pet up outside the house — if the power goes out and doors get stuck, your animal is left locked in or lost. Always inside.
  2. Leaving water in an open bowl — if the supply is cut, the water becomes contaminated. Always keep sealed bottles to hand.
  3. Forgetting the leash — a frightened dog runs. Without a leash, there's no going back.
  4. Not keeping the microchip updated — a chip without data is like an ID card without a name.
  5. Waiting for it to "pass" — emergencies don't resolve themselves. If the signal is red, act.

Your pet's plan starts today

You don't need to spend 500 € or build a bunker. With a plastic box, three days of food, the microchip certificate and a leash, you have a basic plan. The rest can be refined: the first-aid kit, the carrier, scanned documents. But the first step is to start.

And if your pet already has its kit, share this guide with your neighbors. Because in a real emergency, no one gets left behind — not even the dog from downstairs.

Keep reading: Do you need a complete kit for your pet? See the basic 72h kit and adapt what you need. For more information on emergencies, visit Protección Civil and Aegan.

kit-72h-vs-30-dias.titulo: 72h kit or 30-day kit: which one is for you (spoiler: the first one) (2026)
kit-72h-vs-30-dias.resumen: Everyone talks about the EU's 72h, but what if the crisis lasts for weeks? An honest comparison of the two levels of preparedness and why the order matters.
kit-72h-vs-30-dias.cuerpo:
The European Union asks households to be self-sufficient for 72 hours. Why 72? Because that is the typical time it takes emergency services to restore the basics in a serious crisis: drinking water, cleared roads, communications. But some crises are not fixed in three days. Let's compare the two levels.

The 72h kit: for 95% of scenarios

DANA, grid blackout, water outage, storm, snowstorm: in almost every case seen in Spain in recent decades, three days of water, food, light and information get you through. It costs €100-150, fits in a backpack and is maintained with a check every 6 months. If you don't have one yet, this is your kit. It is broken down in the basic kit and in its scenario variants (DANA, blackout, car…).

The 30-day kit: for the extreme case

A DANA that cuts off your region for a week, a multi-day European blackout, a lockdown like 2020. Here we are no longer talking about a backpack but about a pantry: 180 litres of water for two people, non-perishable food for weeks, a way to cook without electricity and a proper first-aid kit. It is more expensive (€300-500) and needs active rotation. The full, calculated version is in the 30-day kit.

Why the order matters

  • The 72h kit covers the first blow of any crisis, including long ones: the first three days are always critical.
  • The 30-day kit without the 72h one is badly designed: anyone who has a pantry but no radio, no torch and no way of getting information fails at the first hurdle.
  • Buying in reverse (lots of food, zero preparation) is the most common mistake: rice stocks with the phone battery at 5%.

The recommended progression

  1. Basic 72h kit + battery-powered radio (this weekend).
  2. Document folder + cash (one afternoon).
  3. Build the pantry up to 2 weeks, then 30 days.
  4. Vegetable patch and sprouts as long-term reinforcement.

Both kits are calculated for 2 people and with real, verified products: 72 hours · 30 days.

huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.titulo: Emergency garden: seeds and sprouts to eat when everything runs out
huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.resumen: Sprouts in 5 days, a minimal balcony garden and long-term seeds: the practical guide to growing food at home without electricity or running water.
huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.cuerpo:
Why a garden is part of the emergency kit

The 72-hour kit solves the short crisis: water, food, and light for the first three days. But a long crisis — a DANA that leaves you without electricity for two weeks, a snowfall that cuts off roads for a month — demands something more. That is where the emergency garden makes the difference between surviving and not depending on anyone.

It is not about producing all your food: it is about growing some live food with the bare minimum. And the fastest way to do that is not planting vegetables — it is sprouts.

Sprouts: edible food in 3 to 6 days

Sprouts are seeds that are soaked, drained, and rinsed twice a day. In 3–6 days you have fresh, live vegetables with a vitamin density higher than that of supermarket vegetables after a week in the fridge. And they don't need direct light or soil.

The best sprouts for emergencies

SeedDaysYieldNotes
Watercress5–7200 g from 50 g of seedIntense flavor, ideal for sauces and salads
Alfalfa4–6300 g from 50 gMild, suitable for children, rich in protein
Lentil5–7250 g from 50 gHigh in protein and fiber, filling
Broccoli5–7200 g from 50 gRich in sulforaphane, nutritionally powerful
Radish3–4200 g from 50 gThe fastest, peppery flavor that kills boredom
Sunflower5–7250 g from 50 gCaloric, healthy fats

Setup recipe: a glass jar with a perforated lid (or cheesecloth and a rubber band) with 2–3 tablespoons of seed. Soak for 8 hours, drain, rinse morning and night. In 4–6 days you have food. A single 500 g bag of lentils produces ~2 kg of sprouts: it feeds one person for several days.

Fact: according to FAO, sprouts increase the bioavailability of vitamin C by between 200% and 800% compared with dry seed (FAO, Nutrient content of sprouts).

The minimal balcony garden (when there is sun and water)

If the crisis drags on and you have access to water (tap, containers, rain) and some light, a garden with 4 hours of sun and three pots already produces some real food. What works best in Spain:

Fast (ready in 20–40 days)

  • Radishes — from seed to table in 25–30 days, almost impossible to fail. Three medium pots = weekly harvest.
  • Lettuce and spinach — cut the outer leaves and the plant keeps producing for weeks. They can be eaten raw.
  • Chard — very hardy, two harvests a year in a Mediterranean climate.

Seasonal (summer/winter)

  • Cherry tomato and pepper — in summer, with a large pot (minimum 30 cm) and direct sun.
  • Garlic and onion — in winter, planted in a deep pot. Slow but reliable production.
  • Herbs — basil, parsley, rosemary. They don't feed you, but they turn rice and canned food into real food. They dry and last for months.

Minimum equipment: reusable sprouting trays, all-purpose potting mix, organic variety seeds with guaranteed germination, and a watering can. With that and direct sun, you start eating from your balcony. A greenhouse comes when you've been at it for seasons, not when the crisis begins.

Long-term seeds: what to store for next year

Sprouts and fast vegetables solve weeks. For months, you need to store seeds suitable for sowing the following year. The key: buy organic seeds of guaranteed variety — not supermarket ones, which are sterile or hybrids (F1) and won't germinate if you store them.

The ones that keep best (5–10 years in an airtight container, cool and dry):

  • Legumes — lentils, chickpeas, beans. Caloric food that stores for decades. The seeds also germinate, although germination viability is 2–3 years.
  • Cereals — durum wheat, millet, pearl millet. Staple food that stores well.
  • Oilseeds — sunflower, sesame. Essential fats and long storage.

Reference: the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) maintains a seed bank with vegetable varieties that guarantee germination above 80% after 5 years of storage (USDA National Plant Germplasm System).

What you need to get started (with Amazon links)

You don't need to buy anything expensive. These are the key items, with links to actual products:

  • Sprouting jars — a glass jar with a perforated or cheesecloth lid costs 2-3 €. Amazon sells packs of 4–6 jars specifically for sprouting from ~12 €. A regular glass jar works just as well.
  • All-purpose potting mix — for the balcony garden. A 50 L bag costs about 6-8 € and is enough for several pots. Search for all-purpose potting mix on Amazon
  • Sprouting seeds — mixed packs of seeds suitable for sprouting. Brands such as Exseed or Grow Great include watercress, alfalfa, broccoli, and radish. A 4-variety pack: Search for seed packs on Amazon
  • Pots — 20–25 cm diameter pots for lettuce and radishes. 30 cm for cherry tomatoes. Black plastic, inexpensive. Search for pots on Amazon
  • Watering can — 2–5 liters, with a soft spray head. You don't need anything fancy. Search for a watering can on Amazon

Note: these links lead to Amazon searches with the affiliate tag ntizar-21, because prices and models change every day. There is no single 'best' product — what matters is that it works.

Sprout water: food safety

The water used to rinse sprouts touches directly what will be eaten raw. In a blackout without running water, or with water from emergency containers, you need to watch out for:

  • If the water is from the tap: in Spain, tap water is safe according to the Ministry for the Ecological Transition. No need to boil it.
  • If the water is from containers or jerrycans: if it is sealed and potable, it works for rinsing. If it is collected rainwater, boil it for 3 minutes before use.
  • If the water is from a river or spring: do not use it for sprouts that will be eaten raw. You need a purifier like those mentioned in our emergency water guide.

Sprouts grow in a warm, humid environment — ideal conditions for bacteria such as E. coli or Salmonella if the water is not clean. Daily rinsing with clean water is the most important filter.

Mistakes that kill an emergency garden

  1. Starting with supermarket seeds — supermarket seeds are commercial varieties, often treated with fungicide and sterilized. They don't germinate. Always buy sowing seeds labeled as suitable for sprouting.
  2. Overwatering — mistake No. 1. Seed that rots from too much water is more common than seed that dries out. If the seed is not rinsed with clean water morning and night, it gets moldy. Clean water, never stagnant water.
  3. No light at all — sprouts without light produce pale, weak shoots. They don't need direct sun, but they do need indirect natural light. A room with a window is enough; a dark pantry is not.
  4. Buying too many varieties — start with two: watercress (fast) and lentil (protein). If they work, expand. Don't start with ten.

Relationship with Kit72h kits

All these items are found in the garden and self-sufficiency kit. For a 72-hour crisis, the basic kit already covers the urgent needs; the garden comes into play in the long-crisis scenario.

Water for the garden comes from the collapsible water storage solutions, and water quality is covered by emergency water purifiers.

  • USDA National Plant Germplasm System: seed bank with varieties that can germinate long term.
