el-conocimiento-dartnell.titulo: Dartnell's “The Knowledge”: what to read to rebuild everything after collapse
el-conocimiento-dartnell.resumen: Lewis Dartnell explains step by step how to rebuild civilization from scratch: agriculture, soap, medicine, energy. The manual your 72h kit cannot do without
el-conocimiento-dartnell.cuerpo:
There is a question that an emergency kit only half answers: what if things don't get fixed in 72 hours? What if you had to start from scratch? Because kits buy time, but knowledge is what turns that time into a new life.

What is «El Conocimiento»?

El Conocimiento: Cómo reconstruir nuestra civilización desde cero (The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World After an Apocalypse, 2015), by Lewis Dartnell — an astrobiology researcher at the University of Westminster — is a practical manual, not a doomsday essay. The premise is simple but powerful: you don't need to reinvent anything, just remember where the wheel is written down.

Dartnell starts from a realistic assumption: that society collapses tomorrow due to a pandemic, a prolonged power outage, a DANA like the one in Valencia in 2024, or a solar event (a G5-level CME like the Carrington Event of 1859). There are no elite survivors or underground bunkers: ordinary people, with limited access to tools, have to start over. The good news is that 99% of the necessary knowledge already exists in library books or old manuals.

And the best part: all the knowledge needed for the first 6 months (the most critical) is condensed into ~300 pages that you can read in a weekend.

The 7 blocks of essential knowledge

Dartnell organizes the manual into blocks that build on one another. They are not theory: they are practical recipes with local ingredients. These are the blocks that matter most in a Spanish prolonged emergency scenario:

1. Food — what you can't do without

The first problem after the collapse is not the lack of food, it is the lack of knowledge to produce it. Dartnell explains why growing wheat and legumes is the basis of all survival: wheat gives flour (bread), legumes give protein and fix nitrogen in the soil. The wheat-legume-crop rotation was the basis of Mediterranean agriculture for millennia, and still is.

The book details how to preserve seeds (select the best ears and store them in a dry place), how to make quick compost (organic waste + ash + water), and why composting at 60 °C eliminates pathogens and weed seeds. It also covers preservation methods without electricity: sun drying, salting, and preservation in fat (confit) that Spaniards already practiced in the Middle Ages.

If you are interested in starting today with practical products, the self-sufficient garden guide brings together the essential tools for growing in any space, and the 30-day kit expands your pantry beyond 72 hours.

2. Water — purifying without electricity

Water is the most critical resource: without it, the first week is already deadly. Dartnell describes three purification methods without electricity: boiling (5 min at a rolling boil, enough for 99.9% of pathogens), sand and charcoal filtration (a homemade filter with gravel, fine sand and charcoal reduces bacteria and improves taste), and chlorination with bleach (two drops of unscented bleach per liter, wait 30 min). The combination of filter + boiling gives reliable drinking water in any condition.

The European Union Preparedness Strategy (March 2025) recommends storing 3 liters per person per day just for drinking. For 72 hours, a family of 4 needs 36 liters. Water is renewed every 6 months and stored in opaque containers, away from sunlight.

3. Energy — from water to fire

Humanity's first technological leap was fire, but the first one that multiplies your work capacity is the water wheel. A basic water mill grinds grain, drives a bellows for the forge and pumps water. Dartnell details how to build it with local materials: wood, stone and ropes. A 2 m diameter wheel with a flow rate of 50 l/s produces enough energy for a rural house.

For the Spanish case: a stream with minimum flow during the rainy season (November-April in much of Spain) is enough to keep a mill running. In summer, battery backup power and solar generation take over. For those who need total autonomy in a blackout, the professional energy kit covers everything from 800 W of solar panels to SAI and Starlink.

4. Chemistry — soap, alcohol and acid

Soap is probably the most important chemical invention in history: hygiene is what has most reduced mortality since 1800. Dartnell explains the process of saponification: mixing fats (tallow, used oil) with caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) and water. The soda is obtained from wood ashes washed with water (leaching) and concentrated by boiling with ashes. With a homemade thermometer (boiling water = 100 °C) the reaction is controlled.

Ethyl alcohol is produced by fermenting sugars (the same process as beer or wine) and distillation. It serves as a disinfectant, fuel and preservative. Sulfuric acid is obtained by heating gypsum (calcium sulfate) to 900 °C, condensing the vapor, and diluting — with due precautions. From sulfuric acid, other essential compounds can be made: potassium nitrate for gunpowder, copper sulfate as a fungicide, and chlorine to purify water.

5. Medicine — prevent rather than cure

Without modern antibiotics, collapse medicine reduces to prevention and basic treatments. Dartnell emphasizes that most post-collapse deaths would be from infections, dehydration and hunger, not from wounds. The keys:

  • Hygiene: wash hands with soap, treat water, dispose of waste away from homes.
  • Natural antiseptics: honey (antibacterial), alcohol (disinfectant), chamomile tea (anti-inflammatory).
  • Basic anesthesia: DMT from coca leaves was historically studied, but in Spain the use of chamomile and rosemary as painkillers is tradition.
  • Fractures: immobilization with splints and bandages, elevation, ice (winter snow).

A well-assembled evacuation kit includes a tourniquet, gauze, bandages and antiseptic — things that cannot be made at home in 24 hours.

6. Materials — from clay to glass

Ceramics (clay + fire) are the basis of craftsmanship: pottery, bricks, tiles. Dartnell explains how to identify clay in the field (it feels greasy to the touch, can be shaped when wet) and fire pieces at 1000 °C (a field kiln with a chimney reaches the necessary temperatures). Glass is made from sand (silica), ash (sodium carbonate) and lime (calcium carbonate), melted at 1200 °C. In practice, glass is the hardest to produce — but ceramics are enough for most domestic needs.

7. Society and organization

Dartnell's last chapter is about the most forgotten topic: social organization. In a collapse, the individual does not survive: the community survives. The book proposes an organizational model based on «knowledge circles» — groups of 20-30 people where each member contributes a specialty (farmer, healer, blacksmith, builder). A community of 300-500 people (the size of a traditional Spanish village) is the minimum viable to maintain agriculture, crafts, defense and education.

Why this book now

Spain has had three years of extreme weather events: the DANA in Valencia (2024) left 200 dead and thousands affected; the 2023 heatwave was the most intense in 500 years; the fires in Galicia and Lisbon showed the vulnerability of rural areas. The Spanish Protección Civil has updated its emergency plans incorporating scenarios of «prolonged supply collapse» — the same scenario that Dartnell explores.

The difference between being prepared and being ready is knowledge. An emergency kit gives you water and food for 72 hours, but knowledge gives you the tools so that, when it runs out, you are not left in the dark.

Where to get it?

Currently there is no Spanish edition of «El Conocimiento» on Amazon Spain. The original English edition (The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World After an Apocalypse, ISBN 0099575833, paperback) is available:

View «The Knowledge» on Amazon

Even with an intermediate level of English (B1), the book is fully accessible: Dartnell writes for the general public, not for academics. The recipes and processes are illustrated with clear diagrams that can be understood regardless of language.

If you read it, combine it with practice: a seed sprouter on the windowsill teaches more about survival agriculture than a hundred pages. Start small, start now. And always — knowledge is what no one can take away from you.

dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.titulo: DANA or blackout: the first 30 minutes, minute by minute (2026)
dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.resumen: The first 30 minutes decide almost everything: Civil Protection sequence minute by minute (0-10 information, 10-20 home, 20-30 plan) for a DANA or blackout.
dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.cuerpo:
In an emergency, the first thirty minutes decide almost everything: what information you have, where you are and what resources you have left. Civil Protection reduces it to three actions — get informed, secure your home and decide — and the European Commission has insisted since its Preparedness Union Strategy that every household should be able to sustain itself for at least 72 hours on its own while help arrives. This is that sequence, stage by stage, with the mistakes that recur in every DANA warning and every power cut.

If you take away only one idea: the first ten minutes are for information, not action. Almost all avoidable damage in the first half hour — a car swept away in a garage, a television burned out just as the power comes back, a call to 112 to ask something the radio is answering — comes from skipping that order.

Minute 0–10: get informed and communicate without overwhelming the network

When the power goes out or the warning arrives, the reflex is to call and post. Both make the situation worse:

  • 112 is for emergencies involving people at risk: injured people, people trapped, fire, water rising inside an occupied home. To find out whether the warning affects you or why the power is out, there are much faster channels.
  • Messages before calls: WhatsApp or SMS use far less of the network and can be sent even when voice lines are overloaded. An “I’m OK” by message is almost always enough.
  • Battery-powered or hand-crank radio: FM is the only source that stays alive when the mobile network goes down, and it is where the authorities give instructions by voice. A hand-crank and solar emergency radio costs little and depends on neither the network nor the power.
  • Look at the scope, not just the alert: a warning is not the same across the whole territory. Cross-check what you hear with AEMET's weather warnings and with information from your town council or local Civil Protection.

If you receive an emergency message with an alarm on your mobile — the ES-Alert system that Spanish Civil Protection uses to alert the population by phone — it is not a hoax or a mistake: it is the same warning given by radio and public address systems. And if the power cut affects only your building entrance or your street, report it to the building; if there is no power across the whole neighbourhood and you see people in the street, it is a distribution cut and you should wait, without inventing diagnoses. In the 28 April 2025 blackout, confusion about the scope was exactly what fed the wave of hoaxes: the lessons from that day still apply to either scenario.

Everything you need to have located before it is needed — numbers, stations, contacts and where your documents are — is organised in official emergency resources and in the household emergency folder.

Minute 10–20: secure the home (DANA script, blackout script)

Here the path splits.

If water is coming (DANA or flooding)

  • Get out of the basement, garage and ground floors and take upstairs anything that can get wet: documents, footwear, pictures, keys, chargers and medication.
  • Do not go down to get the car. Thirty centimetres of water is enough to sweep a vehicle away, and the garage is the most dangerous place in the building when water comes in.
  • If water enters the home and you can do so without getting wet, turn off the power at the electrical panel and do not use the elevator or any connected appliance.
  • Do not cross streams, fords, tunnels or flooded streets, on foot or by car: the current is much stronger than it looks and you cannot see the bottom.
  • Close shutters and windows, and keep papers you cannot replace in a waterproof bag.

The scenario kit is in DANA kit; the exit plan, in evacuation kit; and what to do when the water recedes and you return home — mud, damp, insurance — in returning home after a flood.

If the power goes out (blackout)

  • Disconnect sensitive equipment — television, computer, audio equipment: the surge that comes when the supply is restored is what burns out electronics. Leave one switch on with a small lamp: it will let you know when the power is back.
  • Do not open the fridge. With the door closed, the cold lasts quite a while; every time you open it, you shorten that.
  • Use a flashlight, not a candle if there are children or pets or if you are going to sleep. And if you use a gas heater, a brazier or a camping stove to get through the cold, ventilate or do not use it while sleeping: carbon monoxide has no smell and is the classic cause of domestic poisoning. A carbon monoxide detector is the genuinely cheap safeguard.
  • Prioritise what you power: mobile and router first, fridge afterwards. A SAI for home keeps the router and equipment running without you noticing, and a solar generator gives hours of power with no noise or fumes; the comparison between the two is in generator vs power station. The whole scenario laid out in blackout kit.

If you want to go beyond the flashlight in the drawer, the search for rechargeable emergency flashlights ↗ and the power banks with good capacity ↗ show each option with its current price; the criteria for choosing are in best emergency power bank.

Minute 20–30: decide whether to stay or go

By default, stay at home if there is no structural risk, no water coming in and no one has ordered you to evacuate: it is the safest place and the one with your resources. Leaving makes sense only if there is an evacuation order, if the building is unsafe or if the water keeps rising.

If you stay:

  • Ration your mobile battery: airplane mode, minimum brightness and data only when you need it. A charged power bank is several full charges; without one, your mobile will die just when you need it most.
  • Take stock of what you have: water, ready-to-eat food, flashlight, batteries, first-aid kit and medication. If something is missing, the basic 72-hour kit and the guide to how much water you need and how to store it give you the exact calculation.
  • Have the family plan decided: meeting points, a contact outside the city and which number to call. That is prepared calmly, not in the 30 minutes: family emergency plan.

If you go, take only what fits in a backpack and can be carried on foot: layers for warmth, water, some food, documents in a waterproof bag, charger and power bank, basic first-aid kit, regular medication, flashlight, whistle and some cash. The full list is in how to assemble your 72-hour kit.

The 30 minutes in a table

StageObjectiveTypical mistake
0-10 minKnow what is happening and whom to listen toCalling 112 to ask questions or sharing the first thing that appears on social media
10-20 minSecure the home according to the scenarioGoing down to the garage for the car or leaving equipment plugged in when the power comes back
20-30 minDecide: stay or leave, and with whatImprovising the exit without documents, water or a meeting plan

Five mistakes that recur in the first half hour

  1. Using 112 as an information line. Questions are resolved with the radio, the mobile and official channels; 112 is reserved for those in danger.
  2. Going down to the garage to save the car. It is the mistake that causes the most personal injury in flash floods.
  3. Heating with a brazier or gas heater without ventilating, or sleeping with it on. Carbon monoxide slips in without warning; the carbon monoxide detector guide explains it.
  4. Turning everything on at once when the power comes back and opening the fridge every two minutes. Sensitive equipment should be unplugged beforehand and plugged back in gradually.
  5. Believing and sharing any figure or hoax that circulates. In the 2025 blackout, dozens of hoaxes caused real harm; always verify before forwarding.

After the 30 minutes

The first half hour passes and the long part begins: follow only instructions from official sources (112, Civil Protection, local authorities and FM radio), do not touch fallen cables or attempt repairs yourself, and wait for the utility company to restore the supply. If water has come in, check before using anything again; if the outage drags on, food and cold are managed with the guides to eating without power for three days and rotating emergency food.

And when everything returns to normal, restock what you have used: a backpack that is used on the first day and not restocked stops being useful for the next emergency. That is, literally, the last step of the 72-hour plan.

Official sources

  • Civil Protection — General recommendations by hazard (Government of Spain).
  • Civil Protection — Public alert system (ES-Alert).
  • European Commission — Preparedness Union Strategy.
  • AEMET — Weather warnings.

Summary in three lines

First information, then home, decision last: those are the three stages of the first half hour, in that order. In a DANA, do not go down to the garage; in a blackout, do not turn everything on at once and the flashlight comes before the candle. Stay at home unless there is an evacuation order or real risk, and if you leave, leave prepared and with an agreed meeting plan.

comunicar-sin-red-movil.titulo: Communicating without a network: what works when mobile service goes down (2026)
comunicar-sin-red-movil.resumen: In every major emergency, mobile networks collapse within minutes: ways to communicate that don't rely on masts, some free and others for less than €40.
comunicar-sin-red-movil.cuerpo:
On 28 April 2025 it became clear: when everyone tries to call at once, the network goes down. And during a DANA, antennas can be left without power or fibre for days. If your family plan depends on WhatsApp, you don't have a plan. Real alternatives, from free to cheap:

1. SMS and short messages

SMS uses a minimal signal that works when calls and data don't. Agree with your family: if the network is struggling, don't call — send a short SMS with your status and location.

2. The out-of-area contact

Classic Civil Protection technique: designate a person who lives far away (another region, another country) as your contact point. Local calls get overloaded; a long-distance or out-of-region call sometimes gets through. Everyone calls that person, and they coordinate.

3. Battery-powered FM/AM radio

It's not for talking, it's for finding out: when telecommunications collapse, broadcasting (large transmitters, their own antennas) is the last information channel still standing. The battery-powered or hand-crank radio is the most underrated item in the kit.

4. PMR446 walkie-talkies

For €30–40 a pair, no licence required in Spain, 2–5 km in the city (further in the countryside). Perfect for coordinating between homes in the same residential complex or on a campsite. Store them with fresh batteries and don't use them as toys.

5. Off-grid messaging

Mesh apps (antenna-free bridges, such as Bluetooth radio links between nearby phones) exist, but they all require both people to have them installed beforehand. Install them now on your family's phones — in the middle of a crisis you can't download anything.

The family plan in one sentence

If there's no network: everyone sends an SMS to the out-of-area contact with “I'm OK / where I am / what I need”, and we meet at the agreed point if 24 hours pass with no contact. Write that point down on paper: under the bell tower, the motorway service station, auntie's house.

The radio and power banks that keep this communication going are in the basic 72h kit and in the power outage kit.

como-montar-tu-kit-72h.titulo: How to build your 72-hour emergency kit: the complete guide (2026)
como-montar-tu-kit-72h.resumen: Since March 2025, the EU recommends 72 hours of self-sufficiency: water, food, light and a first-aid kit in one backpack for €100-150, step by step and without overspending.
como-montar-tu-kit-72h.cuerpo:
How to build your 72-hour emergency kit: the complete guide (2026)

Since March 2025, the EU Preparedness Strategy has recommended that every household keep supplies to be self-sufficient for 72 hours. And it is not just a desk document: with the 2024 DANA storms, prolonged power outages and heatwaves that leave millions without power, assembling a 72h kit is the cheapest and most effective self-protection measure you can take today.

You don't need to be a survivalist or spend thousands of euros. A decent basic emergency kit costs between 60 and 120 € and fits in a medium-sized backpack. In this guide I explain exactly how to put it together, step by step, without hassle.

Step 1: choose the scenario that worries you

Before buying anything, ask yourself what type of emergency is most likely in your area. In Spain the most frequent are:

  • DANA storm or flooding: torrential rains that cut off supplies, leave areas without power and isolate entire neighbourhoods. The Mediterranean coast is especially vulnerable.
  • Prolonged blackout: cold spells that drive up electricity demand and cause outages lasting hours or days.
  • Heatwave: extreme heat leaves many communities without water and hospitals become overwhelmed.
  • Wildfires: especially in summer, they can cut off access to your area and leave it without electricity.

The basic 72h kit covers all four scenarios. If your main risk is a specific one, you can add a specialised kit such as the blackout, DANA or wildfire kit.

Step 2: water — what you can't improvise

Water is the most critical resource and the hardest to replenish after an emergency. The rule set by the EU and Civil Protection is clear: 3 litres per person per day for drinking alone. For 72 hours, that is 9 litres per person.

For a family of four you need to store at least 36 litres of drinking water. The right strategy combines three elements:

  1. Bottled water or water in jerrycans: buy 6 litres per person to start with. Store it in a cool place away from direct sunlight.
  2. Purification tablets or a filter: as a plan B, if the supply is cut you can purify tap or river water. Micropur tablets or filters such as LifeStraw are cheap and weigh next to nothing.
  3. A hydration kit: oral rehydration sachets. During heatwaves or floods, dehydration is a real risk.

Replace the water every 6 months — set a reminder on your phone when you assemble the kit. If you don't want to think about it, the 7-day Swiss reserve includes 9 litres per person with an expiry date and automatic rotation.

Step 3: food you can eat without cooking

In an emergency, there may be no gas or electricity for cooking. The food in your 72h kit must be non-perishable, ready to eat and require no refrigeration.

The essentials include:

  • Canned goods: pulses, fish in oil, vegetables. Include a manual can opener (don't forget it).
  • Energy bars and nuts: calorie-dense, lightweight and with no problematic expiry.
  • Freeze-dried meals: military-style rations that only need hot water. Ideal if weight matters to you.
  • Eat what you like: if you force yourself to eat something you can't stand, you'll reject it when you need it most. The test is simple: would you eat it on a normal Sunday?

For 72 hours, allow between 2,000 and 2,500 kcal per person per day. A basic 72h kit already brings together the most practical options, but if you want extra margin, the 30-day kit expands the pantry using the same logic.

Step 4: light and power — don't underestimate the dark

When the power goes out, it's not just the darkness. It's not being able to call on your mobile, not having heating, not being able to see whether there is water, not being able to open the car door with the electric key. Light and power are critical.

The minimum viable setup:

  • A headlamp per person: it keeps your hands free and is the most useful thing after an earthquake or flood when you have to move with your hands occupied.
  • A power bank of at least 20,000 mAh: charges your mobile 4–6 full times. A 10,000 mAh power bank falls short over 72 hours.
  • A battery or dynamo radio: during a general blackout, the internet may be slow or unavailable. A radio is your link to the authorities. A dynamo one also works if the batteries run out.
  • Spare batteries: buy a pack of AA and AAA batteries and store them with the kit.

If a blackout is your main fear, add the electricity kit (60-200 €) or go straight for the professional power kit with SAI, solar panels and LFP battery.

Step 5: basic first-aid kit — what you need to know

You don't need a combat first-aid kit. With the basics you cover 90% of situations:

  • Dressings: sterile gauze, bandages, medical tape, tweezers and nitrile gloves.
  • Antiseptic: chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine for cleaning wounds.
  • Painkillers and fever reducers: paracetamol and ibuprofen (two different active ingredients, in case one doesn't work for you).
  • Regular medication: if someone in the household takes chronic treatment, keep at least 7 days' supply. In an emergency, the pharmacy may be closed for days.
  • Anti-diarrhoeals: diarrhoea in an emergency without access to clean water can be serious. Loperamide + oral rehydration solution.

A kit for older people includes these same items with adapted doses, but the basic first-aid kit works for any adult.

Step 6: documents and money — paper before the paper runs out

In a real emergency, offices close, ATMs don't work and card payments may be impossible if power and network go down. Prepare:

  • Stamped photocopies of DNI, NIE and passport of every family member. If you can, get them certified at your town hall.
  • Deeds and policies: insurance, mortgage, rental contract. A digital copy on a sealed USB drive.
  • Contact list: GP, pharmacy, car insurance, electricity and gas company. Written on paper: don't rely on your phone's contacts.
  • Cash: small notes (5, 10 and 20 €). Without ATMs or online commerce, cash is the only way to pay.

The advice from Spanish Civil Protection is to create an emergency folder with all of this together. If you don't want to put it together yourself, the evacuation kit includes a dedicated document organiser.

Step 7: the backpack — not just any backpack

The container is as important as the contents. Look for a backpack with these features:

  • Minimum capacity: 30 litres. Less is not enough for 72 hours and more than one person.
  • Waterproof or with a rain cover included: if it rains, the water shouldn't soak the contents.
  • Padded straps and a waist belt: if you have to walk with it, the belt distributes the weight and saves your back.
  • Reflective: if you have to move at night along a road, make sure you can be seen.
  • Discreet colour: it doesn't have to be black, but avoid bright colours that identify it as an emergency backpack.

You can reuse a backpack you already have. If not, a second-hand hiking backpack is enough: you don't need expensive gear.

Mistakes everyone makes

After analysing hundreds of user questions, these are the most common mistakes when assembling a 72h kit:

Buying food you won't eat

The most common mistake. If nobody in your household eats canned tuna, don't buy it just in case. In an emergency you'll be eating what you have for three days straight. Stress doesn't improve your palate.

Forgetting the can opener

It sounds like a joke, but it isn't. Thousands of cans without a can opener are food that goes to waste. Put it in the top layer of the backpack, visible.

Storing it in the storage room

The kit has to be where everyone in the household knows about it. If only you know where it is and you end up in hospital, the kit is useless.

Setting an expiry date and not checking it

Set a reminder every 6 months. Replace the water, check the batteries and the food. An expired kit is worse than having no kit.

Not preparing the children

Children need extra warmth (a sleeping bag or thermal blankets), their favourite food (so they eat something) and a comfort object (a soft toy, a book). Don't underestimate the emotional factor in an emergency.

How much does it cost to assemble the kit?

A basic 72h kit can be assembled for between 60 and 120 €, depending on whether you reuse a backpack and whether you choose generic or specialist brands. Here is an indicative breakdown:

  • Water and purification: 10-15 €
  • Non-perishable food: 20-30 €
  • Flashlight + radio + power bank: 25-40 €
  • Basic first-aid kit: 15-20 €
  • Backpack: 0-30 € (free if you reuse one)
  • Documents and cash: 0 €

The basic 72h kit from Kit72h brings together all the essentials in a verified list with direct links to each product. If you prefer a more complete approach, the 30-day kit includes expanded supplies for a full month.

Keep reading

  • Basic 72h kit — the EU's 16 items
  • Evacuation kit — escaping safely
  • Family emergency plan: the steps nobody tells you about
  • How much water to store at home: Switzerland's official reserve
  • Best emergency power bank: 2026 comparison
  • Official sources — EU, Civil Protection and more

The best time to assemble your 72h kit was a year ago. The second best time is today. Start with the basic kit list and build it up little by little. You don't need to buy everything on the same day.

coche-kit-emergencia-2026.titulo: Car and emergencies: what is mandatory in 2026 and what is advisable
coche-kit-emergencia-2026.resumen: The connected V-16 beacon is now the only legal warning device: what else should the glove compartment carry for a DANA, a snowfall or a breakdown at night.
coche-kit-emergencia-2026.cuerpo:
The car kit is the only one you carry with you every day, and also the most regulated. Since 1 January 2026 the main rule changed —the connected V-16 beacon replaced triangles as the only legal means of signalling—, but the rule only covers part of the problem: signalling that you are stopped. It doesn't cover running out of water on a road cut off by a DANA, spending the night in the car at minus fourteen degrees after a snowfall, or a headlight failing in the middle of a six-hour traffic jam. This article reviews both halves: what the law requires and what you should add on your own account.

We've ordered it the way you would actually use it: first the mandatory items, then the prioritised emergency equipment, then the three most common scenarios in Spain (flooding, snow and breakdown) and finally the six-monthly check that keeps everything working. The full list, with links and one-click basket, is in the car kit.

What is mandatory in Spain in 2026

The DGT is clear: since 1 January 2026 the approved connected V-16 beacon is the only legal means of signalling a vehicle immobilised on the roadway. You can check that your model is certified in the DGT's official list of V-16 devices: any orange light from a DIY store won't do; it must have the type approval and the connectivity (geolocation) required by the rule.

Triangles are no longer a valid means of signalling a stop: they can stay in the trunk, but they no longer fulfil the legal function. The offence for driving without a beacon is minor and carries an 80 € fine, but the real reason for the rule is flesh and blood: the DGT estimates that around 25 people die each year after being hit by vehicles on the road after getting out of their car, many while placing triangles. With the V-16 you don't get out of the car: it is switched on from inside and, in addition to the light, sends the vehicle's position to other drivers. The details of the rule, the fine and how to choose one are in the V-16 beacon guide.

Complete the mandatory on-board items with this short list:

  • Reflective vest inside the passenger compartment, within reach before you get out (and put it on before you touch the trunk).
  • Documentation: vehicle registration, ITV card and insurance receipt.
  • Connected V-16 beacon with the battery in date (many have a non-replaceable battery: if it is expired, it is useless).
ItemMandatory?Why it matters in an emergency
Approved connected V-16 beaconYes (since 1/1/2026)Signals without getting out of the car and alerts by position, not just by light
Reflective vestYes, inside the passenger compartmentThe first thing that saves you when opening the door on a road with traffic
Vehicle documentationYesAvoids problems if the car has to be moved or secured
TrianglesNo (they no longer signal)Useful as visual reinforcement, but they do not replace the V-16
First-aid kit, thermal blanket, water, flashlightNoWhat turns the car into a shelter when the emergency lasts for hours

What is worth adding (by priority)

The mandatory items get you out of legal trouble; these get you out of real trouble. Ordered from most to least useful, thinking about a typical Spanish scenario: a breakdown on a motorway, a road cut off by torrential rain or a winter traffic jam.

  • Emergency thermal blanket (3-8 € approx.): a snow traffic jam or a breakdown in February becomes endless without one; it takes up less space than a notebook. Thermal blanket.
  • LED flashlight with magnet (10-25 € approx.): change a wheel at night without anyone holding anything; the magnet attaches it to the bumper. Magnet flashlight.
  • Compact first-aid kit (15-30 € approx.): gauze, bandages, antiseptic and gloves; the list of what it includes and what is unnecessary is in the emergency first-aid kit. Car first-aid kit.
  • Water and something to eat (2-5 € and 10-15 € approx.): two bottles per person and energy bars; renewed every six months. Bottled water.
  • Power bank or 12 V jump starter (25-50 € approx.): your phone is your radio, your map and your way to alert 112; a dead phone cuts off all those options. 12 V car power bank.
  • Chains or textile snow socks (30-80 € approx.) if you cross the north or the mountains in winter: first check that your car accepts the model in your size. Snow chains.
  • Tow chain or tow strap (15-30 € approx.): gets a car out of a muddy shoulder without waiting for a tow truck.

With that, the car stops being just transport and becomes the 72-hour kit you already carry with you: several of these items are exactly the same ones we recommend for home.

Scenario 1: water — never cross a ford

It is the mistake that costs the most lives in DANA events. Moving water hides the road surface: a branch, worn asphalt or an open drain are enough. And it doesn't take that much water: 20 cm already makes the vehicle hard to control and 30 cm of moving water sweeps away a passenger car.

The recommendations of Civil Protection, collected by the Ministry for the Ecological Transition, are blunt: do not cross flooded sections on foot or by car, do not park in dry ramblas or on riverbanks, and if there is a warning of intense rain do not go down into garages or basements. If water catches you while driving:

  • Do not enter: find another route, even if it is a long detour. Turning back is always cheaper than the alternative.
  • If the water rises and the car stops, get out through the windows (not the doors, which will have the water on their side) and move to higher ground. The Red Cross sums it up like this in its flood guide: if you find yourself trapped, get out of the vehicle as soon as possible.
  • Call 112 and give the exact location: road, PK, municipality and direction. In an emergency 112 is the only number, and it works throughout Spain.

If you live in an exposed area, the car can also help you evacuate in time. The full protocol, with ES-Alert warnings and document bags, is in the DANA / flood kit.

Scenario 2: cold — the snowfall that cuts off the road

In the north of the peninsula, a storm can leave a motorway cut off for hours. Spending that night in the car with the heating on is possible, but with two safety conditions: never with the engine running in a garage or enclosed space (carbon monoxide has no smell and kills in minutes) and with the exhaust pipe clear of snow so it does not become blocked. Outdoors, with the window open a finger's width, it is safe.

The thermal blanket, a hat and hot water in a thermos make those hours bearable. And before setting out in winter, check the AEMET forecast (aemet.es → Warnings): an orange or red snow warning is not decoration; it is a sign that that route may have no way out.

Scenario 3: breakdown — the five minutes that matter most

A puncture on the M-40 at six in the evening is annoying; what is dangerous is what comes next. The protocol, in order:

  1. Pull onto the hard shoulder as far as you can and turn on the V-16 from inside, before getting out.
  2. Put on the vest before opening the door.
  3. Get out on the side away from traffic, with passengers off the road (behind the barrier, not in front of it).
  4. Keep things visible: the magnet flashlight on the bumper helps others brake earlier.
  5. If you have to wait, the blanket and water in the trunk decide whether the wait is twenty minutes or four hours.

In summer the script is the same but in reverse: ventilation, water and never leave anyone (not even a dog) inside a car parked in the sun.

How to maintain the kit: two checks a year

The car kit doesn't fail for lack of things; it fails because of expired items. The most convenient check is at the clock change, twice a year:

  • Water renewed (it should be changed every six months; if it has spent the summer in the trunk, you know what it's like).
  • Batteries and the V-16 battery in date.
  • First-aid kit: remove expired items and restock.
  • Flashlight and power bank charged.
  • Chains checked and in their bag, not buried under everything in the trunk.

Ten minutes, twice a year. It is the cheapest maintenance there is for something that can matter to you for an entire afternoon. The full shopping list, prioritised and with one-click basket, is put together in the car kit, and if the car is only one piece of a bigger plan, how to build your 72-hour kit shows you how to fit everything together.

carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.titulo: Home emergency folder: documents, cash and copies ready to evacuate (2026)
carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.resumen: What goes in the emergency folder, how to back it up on paper and in the cloud, how much cash you need and what to review every six months.
carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.cuerpo:
After every DANA, major fire or prolonged blackout in Spain, the same scene repeats: families leaving home with only the clothes on their backs and, weeks later, unable to prove where they lived, what was insured or what medication they needed. The emergency folder is the part of the 72-hour kit with the best return: a folder, a waterproof pouch, a USB drive and an afternoon of work that save weeks of paperwork. It does not replace the evacuation backpack; it complements it: if the backpack gets you through the first day, the folder gets you through the following month.

What goes inside: seven sections and nothing else

The typical mistake is stuffing in piles of “papers” and then being unable to find anything when you need to sign something. Organize it by sections, with dividers or labeled sleeves:

  • Identity: a photocopy of the DNI or NIE for each household member, including minors, plus the family record book. The copy lets you process paperwork even if you lose the original; in an evacuation, the original travels in the backpack, not in the house.
  • Housing: the deed or a land registry extract if you own your home, the lease if you rent, and the cadastral reference (it appears on the IBI receipt and in the Catastro online office). If you rent, add the landlord's or agency's contact details: without that phone number, any procedure stalls.
  • Insurance: home, car and any health or life policies, with the policy number and claims phone number handwritten on the first page. In a claim, a phone number at hand is worth more than a perfect policy.
  • Health: each person's health card, a report of regular medication, known allergies and the children's vaccination records. If someone is on chronic treatment, keep a recent prescription in the health sleeve.
  • Money and utilities: the IBAN of your accounts, the mortgage or loan contract, and the latest electricity, water, gas and community fee bill with the customer or contract reference for each service: this is what lets you claim or reconnect after an outage without searching through email.
  • Vehicle: vehicle registration certificate, roadworthiness test card (ITV) and insurer details. Useful if you need to move, if the car is damaged or if you are asked for them at a checkpoint during the emergency.
  • Contacts outside the area: two or three trusted phone numbers outside your city or region. If your area loses network coverage, someone outside can coordinate calls and alerts.

The three levels: home, backpack and cloud

One format is not enough. Paper survives a phone with no battery and a blackout; the digital copy survives a flooded or smoking house. The emergency folder works by being copied in three places at once:

LevelWhere it livesWhat it contains
PaperWaterproof pouch at home, always in the same placeCopies, policies, contracts and essential contacts
PortableEvacuation backpack or grab-and-go document bagOriginal ID documents, some cash and the health card
DigitalEncrypted cloud + USB drive stored outside the homeAll documents scanned, named and password-protected

Cash and cards when the power goes out

During the power outage of 28 April 2025, large areas of the country were left without card terminals and with many ATMs out of service for hours. The lesson is not “withdraw a lot of money” but “keep just enough available for two or three days, in small notes”:

  • Discreet cash: enough for food, fuel and pharmacy for a few days, in small notes, stored away from original documents. Do not announce it or photograph it.
  • Cards under control: write down each card number and each bank's customer service phone number in the finance section, or keep them in an encrypted password manager. If you lose your wallet, calling the bank is the first thing to do; having the details at hand cuts the call in half.
  • Two places for cash: some in your wallet and some in the backpack or car. If the emergency catches you away, the cash at home does not exist.
  • Sensitive files, never in the gallery: photos of documents and cards go inside a password-protected compressed file or the phone's encrypted notes app, not loose in the gallery.

Digital copy: do it right, once

  • Scan each document as a legible PDF, with good light and the full page: if the margin is cut off, it is useless.
  • Name the files meaningfully (dni-maria.pdf, home-policy.pdf), not img_4471.jpg. When you need them, you need them now.
  • Store the set in the cloud and on a USB drive that is not at home: work, a relative's house or the car glovebox.
  • Encrypt the package with a password that is not the same as your phone's, and write that password on paper, somewhere different from the folder. If you lose both together, the folder protects nothing.

Keep it alive: two reviews a year

An out-of-date folder is a false folder: it gives you the feeling of being prepared and fails just when you open it. It takes ten minutes and there are two easy dates not to forget:

  • Clock change (March and October): review policies, contracts, phone numbers and make sure the minors' documents are still valid.
  • Start of the school year: update vaccination records, medication and school or work contacts.
  • After any life change: moving house, changing banks, changing utility provider or car, update the folder the same day. It is the procedure everyone puts off and the one you are most grateful for later.

Four mistakes that cancel out the effort

  • Everything in a drawer with clothes: if the clothes get wet, everything gets wet. A waterproof pouch costs little and solves the whole problem.
  • Originals with no copy elsewhere: a sole deed or vehicle registration certificate is useless if it is lost with the house.
  • No digital copies: arriving at a registry office or an insurer with nothing on your phone stretches any procedure by several days.
  • Never reviewed: a six-year-old folder with old phone numbers and policies is more misleading than having nothing.

Checklist for this week

  • Seven labeled sleeves or a binder with dividers.
  • ID photocopies for everyone, including minors.
  • Housing: deed, lease or cadastral reference.
  • Insurance with policy number and claims phone at hand.
  • Health: health card, medication and vaccination records.
  • Finances: IBAN, mortgage and latest bill for each utility.
  • Two contacts outside your region and cash in small notes.
  • Everything scanned into an encrypted PDF and copied to the USB drive kept elsewhere.

The folder is only one piece: the family emergency plan decides who does what, the 72-hour kit guide assembles the rest and the first 30 minutes guide organizes what you do that same day. If you have to leave home, the evacuation backpack already includes a waterproof pouch and USB drive, and the home kit leaves room to store originals where they won't get wet. And if you live alone, the living alone checklist gives you the same framework without depending on anyone.

botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.titulo: Emergency first-aid kit: what to actually pack (and what is unnecessary) (2026)
botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.resumen: The list of what your family really needs in a health emergency, without unnecessary items. How much of each item, expiry dates and where to buy everything with
botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.cuerpo:
The emergency first-aid kit is not the one with the most items

A useful first-aid kit is not the one packed with 200 pharmacy items: it is the one that has what your family actually uses, in sufficient quantity, in date and at hand when an emergency strikes. Most generic supermarket pharmacy kits contain the basics and fall short in real emergencies — from a deep cut to an allergic reaction or a fever that will not go down.

In Spain, according to data from the Spanish Ministry of Health, more than 60% of calls to 112 are for non-urgent problems that could be resolved with a well-stocked first-aid kit. In real emergencies — blackouts, floods, snowstorms — the first-aid kit is the first thing people look for.

The essentials: the basics

This is what must NOT be missing, with enough for 72 hours:

What to includeMinimum quantityPurpose
Elastic bandages4 unitsImmobilize sprains, hold dressings in place
Adhesive dressings (various sizes)20 unitsSmall cuts, blisters, superficial wounds
Adhesive plasters20 unitsMinor wounds for children and adults
Sterile gauze swabs (10×10)10 unitsCover medium and large wounds
Hypoallergenic paper tape1 rollHold bandages and gauze without irritation
Nitrile gloves2 pairsProtect yourself when treating wounds (avoid cross-infection)
Antiseptic (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)2 bottlesClean wounds before covering them
Medical adhesive tape (Micropore)2 rollsHold dressings without sticking to the skin

Medication: what makes the difference

Plasters alone are not enough. An emergency without painkillers is unnecessary suffering. According to the Spanish Society of Community Pharmacy, self-medication is the first line of action in 78% of minor cases. The essentials:

  • Paracetamol (tablets or children's syrup): fever, pain. Dose by weight, never above 4 g/day in adults.
  • Ibuprofen (400 mg): inflammation + pain (sprains, wound inflammation). Do not take on an empty stomach.
  • Loratadine or cetirizine (tablets): allergic reactions, hives, bites and stings. One tablet a day.
  • Oral rehydration salts (sachets): diarrhoea, vomiting, dehydration. Essential in DANA or floods where tap water may be contaminated.
  • Antacids (compound): stress gastritis, poor diet during an emergency.
  • Antibiotic ointment (Fresomicina): prevent infection in small wounds.

⚠️ Important: if anyone in the family takes chronic medication (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid), include at least 7 days of extra stock. Ask your doctor about the right amount.

What is unnecessary (and takes up space)

The ideal first-aid kit stays light. Avoid these unnecessary items:

  • Digital thermometer (it is expensive and fragile — carry an analogue mercury one; it costs 5 € and does not break)
  • Instant ice packs (they take up space and expire after 2 years — carry a small towel for cold compresses)
  • Over-the-counter antibiotics (in Spain they have NOT been sold without a prescription since 2021: it is illegal and dangerous)
  • Generic 'multi-purpose' products without a clear active ingredient
  • Pre-packaged complete supermarket first-aid kits: they usually contain the basics in insufficient quantities (2 plasters, 1 small bandage) and charge you 60% more for the pretty box

Expiry dates: check every 6 months

The Spanish Agency of Medicines (AEMPS) recommends checking expiry dates every 6 months. Expired medicines not only lose effectiveness: in some cases (such as tetracyclines) they can produce toxins. Use a mnemonic rule: when the clocks change (March and October), check the first-aid kit. Write the review date on an adhesive label inside the box.

ProductUsual expiryAlternative if it expires
Paracetamol3-5 yearsAlways keep 2 extra sachets in another box
Deworming medicines2-3 yearsReplace if the emergency coincides with parasite outbreaks
Antibiotic ointments2-3 yearsPovidone-iodine liquid (expires less quickly)
Oral rehydration salts2-3 yearsHomemade salt and sugar (9 g salt + 50 g sugar in 1 L drinking water)

Kit by family profile

The first-aid kit varies depending on who lives with you. Civil Protection gives these recommendations by profile:

Family with babies (0-2 years)

  • Physiological saline solution (nasal spray): 3 extra bottles for congestion and cleaning
  • Children's paracetamol (syrup) with a dosing syringe
  • Emergency diapers (5 units) in case there is no water for changing
  • Hydrogel burn dressing for minor burns

Older people

  • Copy of regular medication (at least 7 days of extra stock)
  • Fibrin thrombin powder for wounds that do not close (pressure ulcers)
  • Glucose meter with test strips (if they are diabetic)
  • Moisturizing lip balm (older skin cracks easily)

People with allergies

  • Specific antihistamine (if already prescribed)
  • Anti-dust mite products for covers (prevention)
  • High-protection sunscreen (some medicines increase photosensitivity)

Pets

  • Antiseptic for minor wounds (2% chlorhexidine)
  • Non-adherent gauze to cover wounds without sticking
  • Collar to restrain an injured animal and prevent bites

Where to buy the whole kit in one go

You do not need to go to three different pharmacies. Here are search links for all the essentials:

Complete basic first-aid kit (dressings, bandages, gauze, antiseptics): Search on Amazon →

Emergency medication (paracetamol, ibuprofen, loratadine): Search on Amazon →

Gloves and protective equipment: Search on Amazon →

Oral rehydration salts and electrolytes: Search on Amazon →

The first-aid kit inside the 72h kit

The first-aid kit is not independent: it is part of the Basic 72-Hour Kit and fits perfectly into the emergency backpack. If your priority is to build the whole kit from scratch, the step-by-step guide walks you through each category.

Remember: the most important thing is not what you carry in the first-aid kit, but knowing how to use it. Practice opening the bandages, applying the antiseptic and putting on a dressing at least once a year. An emergency leaves no room for clumsiness.

How much does it cost to put together an emergency first-aid kit?

A well-stocked first-aid kit costs between 25 € and 45 € if you buy the components separately at a pharmacy or online. A pre-packaged supermarket first-aid kit can cost the same and include fewer products.

Where should the first-aid kit be stored?

In a dry place at room temperature (between 15 and 25 °C), accessible but out of reach of children. Not in the bathroom: humidity speeds up expiry. In the evacuation kit, it goes in the backpack in a waterproof compartment.

How many times a year should it be checked?

Twice a year: in March and October, along with the clock change. It is the ideal time to replace expired items and restock what has been used.

If you found this article useful, share it with anyone who has children or older people at home. Preparedness is a way of caring for those you love most.

apagon-lecciones-28a.titulo: Blackout: lessons from 28 April 2025 in Spain (2026)
apagon-lecciones-28a.resumen: Spain's biggest blackout in history left images of endless queues and dead mobile phones. What we learned, in a practical list.
apagon-lecciones-28a.cuerpo:
On Monday, 28 April 2025, at 12:33, the power went out across the entire peninsula. Within minutes, metro systems, traffic lights, ATMs and card terminals stopped working; mobile networks collapsed within hours. For many, it was the first time they saw first-hand why an emergency kit is recommended. These are the lessons.

1. Information is the first thing to go missing

With no mobile phone or television, the only reliable source was a battery-powered or hand-crank radio. Those who had one knew what was happening; those who didn't relied on rumors. If you only buy one thing after reading this, make it the radio.

2. Cash became king again

Without card terminals, only shops with a manual till and cash could operate. Those who carried small bills could buy; those who didn't had to wait. Keep €10–20 bills at home for 2–3 days.

3. Your phone's flashlight isn't enough

Leaving your phone's flashlight on for hours drains the battery you need in an emergency. Use a dedicated flashlight or headlamp, with spare batteries. Candles only with extreme care — they are a common cause of fires during blackouts.

4. The elevator is not a game

People were trapped for hours. If you live on a high floor, assume that during a blackout the stairs are your route; if you have reduced mobility, have a plan agreed with your neighbors.

5. Traffic lights don't work: the road belongs to the worst driver

Cities turned into a chaos of unmarked intersections. If you drive during a blackout, treat it as an intersection where traffic from the right has priority and be extra vigilant.

6. The wait was long

In many areas the power came back within hours, but in others it took all night. A kit designed for 72 hours comfortably covers a national blackout; the 30-day kit covers the extreme case of something like this dragging on.

The complete list for this scenario is in the blackout kit: radio, light, power, cooking without electricity and cash, in five sections.

almacenar-agua-comida-casa.titulo: How to store water and food at home so it doesn't spoil (2026)
almacenar-agua-comida-casa.resumen: A poorly stored emergency pantry is money down the drain: where, how, and in what order to rotate each food so it lasts until the day you need it.
almacenar-agua-comida-casa.cuerpo:
Buying the kit is the easy part. Storing it properly so it still works the day you need it (sometimes years later) is the part almost everyone gets wrong. Rules that apply just as much to a bag of rice as to a radio:

The three enemies: heat, light and moisture

The ideal place is cool, dark and dry: an interior hallway cupboard is usually better than the typical storage room next to the boiler or on the terrace. Never directly on the floor (moisture, pests) or next to cleaning products (fumes contaminate even sealed containers).

Water: the calendar rules

  • Sealed commercial containers: replace every 6-12 months. It is not that the water expires: the container degrades and residual chlorine evaporates.
  • Store it away from sunlight and strong odors; plastic absorbs petrol, bleach or detergents.
  • If there is advance warning (storm, water outage), fill the bathtub, buckets and pots: this is non-drinking water, perfect for the toilet tank and hygiene.
  • To store your own water long term, use only new food-grade containers with airtight lids.

Food: first in, first out

  • Write the purchase date on each pack with a marker. Without a date, in six months you will no longer know what is old.
  • Real rotation: use the emergency pantry in your day-to-day cooking and restock when you shop. A reserve that is never eaten gets thrown away; one that is rotated never expires.
  • Approximate shelf life when stored well: cans and jars 3-5 years (or more), rice and pasta 2-3 years, dehydrated/military food 2-5 years, powdered milk 2-3 years sealed. Bars and nuts: much less, about a year.
  • Discard bulging cans, cans rusted at the seams or with deep dents: botulism is non-negotiable.

Inventory every 6 months

The same reminder as for water: check expiry dates, container condition, radio and flashlight batteries, and that the document folder is still complete. Half an hour twice a year keeps your kit alive; without it, in two years you have a storage room full of expired stuff.

The quantities per person and period are calculated in the 72-hour kit and in the 30-day kit, with real Amazon prices for each pack.

agua-cuanta-y-como.titulo: Emergency water: how much to store, how to keep it and how to make it drinkable
agua-cuanta-y-como.resumen: 3 litres per person per day: 9 L for 72 h and 36 L for a family of 4. Bottles, water containers, tablets or filter: how much, where and how often to replace it.
agua-cuanta-y-como.cuerpo:
Why water is the first thing to run out

A human can go weeks without food, but only 3-5 days without water — and in summer, or if you have to exert yourself (evacuate, salvage belongings), the margin drops to 24-36 hours. In Spain, according to data from Civil Protection, 80% of emergencies affecting households are not natural disasters but supply cuts: DANAs that contaminate water, blackouts that stop pumps, burst pipes. Water reaches the tap, but when it is cut off, it is cut off.

The European Union Preparedness Strategy (EU Strategy for Risk and Disaster Prevention, updated 2025) recommends that every household keep supplies for at least 72 hours. Water is the heaviest item and the one people underestimate most.

The 3-litre rule: broken down

3 litres per person per day just for drinking. That is the baseline figure set by the WHO and Civil Protection. But if you want to be realistic:

  • Summer / heat (>30 °C): increase to 4-5 L/person/day. Sweat, thirst and the need to wash your hands (basic hygiene in an emergency without running water) drive consumption up.
  • Winter / temperate climate: 3 L is enough if you only account for drinking.
  • Basic hygiene (handwashing, cleaning wounds, rinsing your mouth): add 1-2 L/person/day if tap water is still available for non-drinking use.
  • Cisterns and sinks: if you have advance warning (storm, DANA), fill the bathtub and sinks. That is 100-200 L of reserve for non-food use to flush the toilet and clean.
Situation1 person (72h)2 people (72h)Family of 4 (72h)
Drinking only (winter)9 L18 L36 L
Drinking + hygiene (temperate)15 L30 L60 L
Summer / heat21 L42 L84 L

A family of 4 needs a minimum of 36-60 litres for 72 hours. That is 8-12 five-litre containers. It is more than most people plan for, and that is why in practice they run out of water on the first day.

How to store it without mistakes

Having water is not enough: you have to store it properly. Water does not expire, but the container does, and a degraded container can contaminate what is inside.

Food-grade containers (the recommended option)

5-8 L polyethylene containers are the standard. The advantages:

  • They fit well in a cupboard or under the bed (they are not round bottles that fall over).
  • They are reusable — when you change the water every 6 months, empty, rinse and refill.
  • Price: 3-5 € per new 5 L container. 20-30 € for 5 units (which covers a family's basic need).
  • Container shelf life: food-grade plastic lasts between 2 and 5 years. If the container is cloudy, yellowish or cracked, replace it.

Commercial water bottles

Useful for a quick start: a pack of 6x1.5 L or 12x0.5 L can be bought at any supermarket and fits in the kitchen. But they are not the long-term solution: they take up more volume per litre, generate more waste, and PET plastic is less resistant over time.

Water bags or watertight bags

Water bags (also called "flexible pallets" or 10-20 L "bag-in-box") are the ideal option for large reserves. They take up less space than containers (they stack), are cheap (2-4 € each for 10 L), and you can leave them half full without the material deforming. Ideal for the garage or storage room.

What you should NEVER do

  • Reuse soft drink or juice bottles to store water: the plastic in those bottles is not designed to hold drinking water long term, and sugar or lactic acid residues feed bacteria.
  • Store containers in the garage in direct sunlight: UV radiation degrades plastic and transfers flavours to the water. Always a cool, dark place.
  • Leave containers next to cleaning products: solvent vapours can pass through the plastic and contaminate the water.

Renewal: when and how

Stored water should be renewed every 6 months. Set a reminder on your phone or stick a label on the cupboard with the date of the last renewal. The mnemonic rule: when the clocks change (March and October), check the containers. Use the old water to water plants or clean, and refill with fresh tap water.

If you use water purification tablets (see below), you can extend that window to 12 months, because the chlorine in the tablets keeps the water sterile for longer.

Making water safe to drink: three methods that work

If tap water is available but not safe to drink (a DANA contaminates the supply, for example), you have three options:

1. Boiling (the most reliable)

1 minute of boiling eliminates 99.9% of pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa). The WHO recommends it as a universal method. Disadvantage: you need fuel (gas, electricity) and the water has to cool before you can drink it. Ideal as a one-off emergency method, not for maintaining long-term reserves.

2. Purification tablets (the kit option)

Chlorine (such as ACCUQUICK) or colloidal silver. The process is simple: one tablet per litre, wait 30 minutes, and the water is safe to drink. They take up minimal space (a tub of 50 tablets fits in your pocket), last for years, and are the preferred option of Civil Protection as a supplement to the emergency kit.

Buying tablets: Search for water purification tablets on Amazon →

3. Water filter (for prolonged emergencies)

Ceramic or membrane filters (such as Berkey or pump filters) remove bacteria and protozoa (but not viruses without additional chlorine). Useful if the emergency lasts more than 72 hours and you have no fuel to boil. Price: 30-80 €. Disadvantage: they require maintenance (change the filter every 1000-2000 L) and do not remove heavy metals or chemicals.

Quick comparison

MethodCostTimeAdvantageLimitation
BoilingAlmost 0 €5-10 min/litreRemoves everythingNeeds fuel
Tablets (ACCUQUICK)~2 €/100 units30 min/litreLightweight, long termDoes not filter sediment
Ceramic filter30-80 €ImmediateNo power, directMaintenance, no viruses

How much water do you need depending on your household?

Not all households consume the same. If you live with:

  • Babies: add 2 L/person/day (infant formula, bottles, cleaning). A 6-month-old baby needs ~200 mL for drinking + 500 mL for formula.
  • Pets: a medium-sized dog drinks 1-2 L/day; a cat, 0.3-0.5 L/day. See the pet kit.
  • Older adults: older people feel less thirsty and can become dehydrated without realising it. Make sure they always have water within reach.

Mistakes everyone makes

1. Not having enough. "There is always tap water" — not when the supply is cut off by a burst pipe. A family of 4's 36 L runs out in a day if they are only meant for drinking.

2. Storing water badly. Containers in the sun, next to bleach, or in recycled soft drink bottles for 3 years. The result is water that tastes of plastic and cannot be drunk.

3. Forgetting hygiene. In an emergency without running water, washing your hands with soap and water is the number one way to prevent disease. An extra 1-2 L for hygiene is never too much.

4. Not knowing how to purify water. Having 36 litres stored is excellent. But if they become contaminated and you do not know how to purify them, the damage is done. Always keep a tub of ACCUQUICK tablets or a filter in the kit.

How much does it all cost?

The full water setup for 72h (family of 4) costs between 25 € and 50 €:

  • 8 x 5 L containers (new): ~24 €
  • Tub of 50 ACCUQUICK tablets: ~12 €
  • 1 portable water filter (optional): ~15-30 €

Buying containers: Search for food-grade water containers on Amazon →

Buying tablets: Search for water purification tablets on Amazon →

Water in the 72h kit

Water is the backbone of any emergency kit. It is part of the Basic 72-Hour Kit, which brings together the 21 verified essentials. If your priority is to have everything ready in one go, the DANA kit includes water containers and tablets as part of the setup.

Remember: storing water is not a one-off act — it is a habit. Every 6 months, check. Every clock change, verify. And do not wait for the tap to run dry to realise you have nothing.

Can you drink tap water after a DANA?

It depends. DANAs (isolated high-level depressions) usually contaminate rivers and aquifers with sediment and bacteria, but rarely affect the water treatment plant. However, authorities may issue a "do not drink tap water" notice if local pipes become contaminated. Always follow Civil Protection instructions and, if in doubt, boil the water or use water purification tablets.

How long does unopened bottled water last?

If it is in a closed commercial container (factory PET bottle), the water theoretically lasts indefinitely. What degrades is the container: PET becomes brittle over time and with UV radiation. Practical recommendation: change the water every 2 years if it is in an unopened commercial bottle.

Can you purify puddle or river water?

Technically yes, but it is not recommended unless strictly necessary. Purification with tablets or boiling removes pathogens, but does not remove heavy metals, pesticides or chemical contaminants. If you have no other option, boil the water (10 min) and then use tablets. As a previous step, filter it through a clean cloth to remove visible particles.
